item.title: 一个模型同时控多个角色：LiveAct 把「谁在动」绑到各自的动作流上，512×448 跑到 17.7 FPS ｜ LiveAct: Towards Real-Time Multi-Agent World Models with Heterogeneous Action Interfaces
item.description:
一句话：多智能体视频世界模型用语言描述的异构动作接口，把每条动作流绑到它在画面里对应的实体，512×448 达 17.7 FPS。

要点：

  • Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation 用语言驱动的空间门控加按智能体分组的注意力，把每条动作流绑到目标视觉实体
  • Schema-Guided Action Adaptation 给每个控制维度写一段语言说明，再把同步数值调制成语义 token，同一位维可以是攻击、转向或机械臂指令
  • 把整套接口搬到分块因果生成器（教师强制 + 考虑 rollout 的分布匹配），六套游戏与多机操作数据上智能体归属准确率 0.898 / 0.942

为什么值得看：多人对战、联机玩法的动作流从来不是一路，单玩家聚合控制撑不住；这套「动作流→实体」的绑定方式可以直接借到引擎侧的动作重映射与回滚预测。

中文摘要：现有的交互式视频世界模型几乎都假设「一个受控主体、一套任务专用动作接口」，而真实的多智能体场景里，多个实体各自被独立控制、共同决定下一帧的样子。LiveAct 的做法是把这件事拆成两半：空间上用语言驱动的门控加按智能体分组的注意力，保证每条动作流只作用于它该控制的那个实体；语义上用「给每个控制位写一句语言说明」的办法，让同一个张量维度在不同任务里可以是攻击键、转向指令或机械臂命令。整套接口再用教师强制与考虑 rollout 的分布匹配搬到分块因果生成器上，实现流式生成。在六个跨越游戏与多机操作的数据源上，无需输入智能体位置或身份裁剪，归属准确率达 0.898 与 0.942，因果生成器在 512×448 下跑到 17.70 FPS。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-25

LiveAct: Towards Real-Time Multi-Agent World Models
with Heterogeneous Action Interfaces

Abstract

Interactive video world models predict how an environment evolves under user actions, but most existing systems assume one controlled agent and one task-specific action interface. We study multi-agent video world modeling, where one model generates a joint visual future for multiple controlled agents while interpreting heterogeneous controls ranging from binary game buttons to continuous robot commands. This task presents two complementary challenges. First, every agent-indexed action stream must control its intended visual entity independently. Second, the model must adapt the meaning of each control variable across different tasks, where the same tensor dimension may denote an attack, steering command, or robot command. We introduce LiveAct, centered on a Heterogeneous Action Interface (HAI) whose two components mirror this decomposition. To support independent control, Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation uses language-driven spatial gates and agent-specific attention to bind each action stream to its intended visual agent. To accommodate heterogeneous controls, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation describes each control variable in language and modulates its semantic token with the synchronized numerical value. We further transfer the complete interface to a blockwise causal generator through teacher forcing and rollout-aware distribution matching, enabling efficient streaming generation while retaining agent-specific control and action semantics. We instantiate the formulation on six multi-agent sources spanning games and multi-robot manipulation, and evaluate visual quality, action following, agent attribution, and latency. Across games and robot manipulation, LiveAct reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy without agent locations or identity crops, and the causal generator attains 17.70 FPS at 512×448.

1 Introduction

Video world models [41, 60, 11, 23, 2, 17, 56, 58, 12, 20, 16] turn interaction into conditional generation [22, 9, 8, 59, 57]: given visual history and actions, they synthesize the observations that follow. Such models can provide scalable experience for game simulation, robot learning, planning, and interactive content creation [7, 53]. Existing systems increasingly support persistent and low-latency rollout, but most still expose a single aggregate player or camera-control stream [44, 6]. Such a generation paradigm is insufficient for inherently multi-agent environments, where independently controlled entities act concurrently and jointly determine the visual future. We therefore study multi-agent video world modeling: given an initial frame, a scene description, and a set of frame-level action streams for multiple agents, the model generates a shared visual future in which each stream controls its intended agent while all agents remain consistent with one another and the environment.

Existing interactive world models cover this setting only in part, and the shortfall lies in the action interface rather than the video backbone. Multi-agent control has relied on numerical action vectors, which keep exact values but typically reach the right entity through spatial priors supplied at inference time and leave control semantics implicit in task-specific dimensions [50, 30, 13]. Language-based actions transfer semantics across entities and tasks but give up the synchronized numerical values that continuous control requires [63]. Tab. 1 summarizes the landscape: no current interface is at once multi-agent, real-time, semantically grounded, and numerically exact. We ask whether one interface can satisfy all four requirements without inference-time masks, boxes, poses, or reference images.

However, a unified action interface must still address two challenges: who each action stream should control in a shared visual scene, and what each control dimension means across heterogeneous tasks. These requirements lead to two key challenges.

  • (1)

    maintaining independent control over multiple interacting agents. A model must keep each agent responsive to its own action stream while capturing interactions. The action tensors of each agent are injected sequentially at input, but do not ensure that their effects remain correctly attributed in the shared visual feature space. Commands may be assigned to the wrong agent or inadvertently drive multiple entities (Fig. 2a), especially when agents overlap, look similar, or jointly manipulate an object. Achieving independent control therefore requires agent-specific conditioning that separates command attribution.

  • (2)

    unifying action conditioning across heterogeneous control spaces. Action vectors do not share a universal semantic coordinate system: their dimensions, ordering, and meanings are defined by task-specific action spaces. As a result, the same action dimension or pattern may encode different behaviors (Fig. 2b). Directly conditioning on raw vectors therefore leads to action semantics being tied to task-specific dimensions and ordering. Language can expose what each control dimension means, but does not preserve the exact frame-synchronized binary or continuous values needed for execution. Unified action conditioning thus requires separating what a control means from what value it takes, and representing both in a shared action interface.

    • LiveAct addresses these challenges with a Heterogeneous Action Interface (HAI), which factorizes action conditioning into semantic adaptation and agent-specific visual injection. For independent control, Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation derives an agent-specific spatial gate from the agent description, so that each branch selectively updates the visual tokens associated with its intended entity while attending only to the corresponding action stream. For heterogeneous action conditioning, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation converts each control dimension into a semantic token defined by its schema and injects the synchronized numerical value through affine modulation, decoupling control meaning from task-specific vector layouts. This provides a shared semantic interface for heterogeneous control spaces. Together, these two designs provide a common action representation while preserving agent-specific effects in the shared visual space. The resulting residuals are injected through zero-initialized projections, preserving the pretrained visual prior at initialization.

    Beyond accurate control, interaction requires efficient incremental rollout without repeatedly regenerating the visual history. We therefore retain the complete HAI when transferring a bidirectional video teacher to a blockwise causal generator through Teacher Forcing for autoregressive (AR) Tuning and Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) for Streaming Video [54, 15, 48, 49]. Causal temporal alignment maps raw actions to compressed video latents, while a global latent offset advances action windows together with the cached rollout. Causal generation thus accelerates a fixed control interface rather than redefining who acts or what each action means.

    We evaluate LiveAct across six multi-agent environments spanning interactive games and robot manipulation, covering both discrete and continuous control spaces. Experiments assess visual fidelity, action adherence, agent attribution, and real-time efficiency. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We formulate real-time multi-agent video world modeling under heterogeneous action spaces and identify two coupled challenges overlooked by existing action interfaces: binding each indexed action stream to its intended visual agent and jointly representing task-specific control semantics and synchronized numerical values in a shared interface.

  • •

    We propose LiveAct, a real-time multi-agent video world model built around a Heterogeneous Action Interface. HAI combines Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation for language-driven stream-to-agent binding with Schema-Guided Action Adaptation for value-preserving semantic control, and is retained during teacher-forced causal adaptation and rollout-aware distribution matching for real-time streaming generation.

  • •

    We build a dataset of 17,951 multi-agent trajectories, totaling 119.54 hours of raw video, and a 108-clip benchmark spanning four games and two robot-manipulation sources. LiveAct reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy on games and robots without locations, masks, or identity crops, and generates at 17.70 FPS at 512×448.

    • 2 Related Work

    Multi-agent video world models. Multi-agent video world models jointly predict an environment under multiple agents’ observations or controls, and must coordinate shared dynamics while preserving the identity of each condition stream. Solaris jointly models synchronized observations from multiple Minecraft agents [36]; MultiWorld combines a multi-agent condition module with a global state encoder across game and robot manipulation [50]; and Gamma-World uses permutation-equivalent agent encoding and sparse hub attention [20]. Complementary systems focus on binding independent controls to visual entities: ActionParty jointly predicts persistent subject-state tokens initialized from subject locations [30], WanToFight grounds locally causal keyboard streams with first-frame character references [13], and Incantation binds language actions to individual entities [63]. Across these designs, the central control problem is to preserve per-agent condition provenance and ensure that each action affects its intended entity. The Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation component of our HAI addresses this problem by conditioning the visual queries on each agent’s language description. without masks, boxes, coordinates, or reference images at inference time.

    Action-controllable world models across domains. World models learn environment dynamics for imagined interaction [7]. Genie learns latent actions from unlabeled videos [3], DIAMOND uses diffusion for Atari and Counter-Strike dynamics [1], and GameNGen predicts DOOM frames from past observations and actions [44]. LingBot-World 2.0 couples camera poses and time-varying semantic prompts for open-ended interaction [6]. Real-world simulators extend action-conditioned prediction to diverse interactions [53] and continuous robot trajectories [61], while Incantation expresses per-entity actions in natural language to support semantic transfer [63]. Most interfaces choose between numerically precise but task-specific vectors and language interfaces that make control semantics explicit. Within our HAI, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation combines the two: language identifies the task-dependent meaning of each control variable, while synchronized binary or continuous values retain frame-level control.

    3 Method

    Given an initial frame I₀, a scene description c, and ordered action streams A={A⁽ⁱ⁾}ᵢ₌₁^N_ag for N_ag agents, where A⁽ⁱ⁾=[a_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾]∈ℝ^T×C gives the value of control dimension j at raw frame τ∈{1,…,T} (raw frame 0 is I₀), paired with agent descriptions G={gᵢ} and a control schema S={sⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^C, multi-agent world modeling aims to synthesize the shared visual future in which each stream drives its own agent while all agents remain consistent with one another and with the scene. We write ℂ=(c,A,S,G) for the full condition. In this section, we first discuss the motivation and two failure modes of existing action interfaces in Sec. 3.1. We then introduce Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation in Sec. 3.2, which decides who responds to each stream, and Schema-Guided Action Adaptation in Sec. 3.3, what each control dimension means and what value it takes; Sec. 3.4 assembles them into the Heterogeneous Action Interface. Finally, Sec. 3.5 carries the same action-conditioning mechanism into causal streaming rollout. Fig. 3 summarizes this three-stage design.

    3.1 Motivation

    Although the indexed action tensor preserves the numerical trajectory of each stream, it does not establish the correspondences required to condition a shared visual representation. The stream index i separates A⁽ⁱ⁾ from the other streams but provides no visual evidence associating it with the tokens of its intended agent. Likewise, the control index j identifies a coordinate only within a task-specific action space and therefore lacks a consistent interpretation across tasks.

    Cross-Agent Misattribution. Keeping the action streams separate preserves their provenance in action space, but does not establish their recipients in visual space. An agent-index embedding can distinguish A⁽ⁱ⁾ from A^(i^′), yet contains no visual evidence linking index i to the appearance of agent i. Consequently, the command from one stream may be attributed to the wrong visual agent or inadvertently affect multiple agents. The missing correspondence must therefore be established on the query side of action conditioning: the visual features that read A⁽ⁱ⁾ should be grounded in the description gᵢ of its corresponding agent.

    Control-Semantics Collapse. An action vector contains C control dimensions, where the j-th coordinate provides the numerical value of one control at a given time step. However, the index j itself carries no explicit semantic meaning beyond the definition of its task-specific action space. Compressing all C dimensions into a single action embedding further obscures the identity of individual controls, making it difficult for the model to distinguish which control produces a particular effect. The action representation should therefore keep each control dimension distinct while jointly encoding its schema-defined semantics and frame-level numerical value.

    These two requirements are complementary: expressive action tokens cannot resolve agent binding, while agent-aware queries cannot recover missing control semantics. HAI therefore separates the two, using Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation for query-side binding and Schema-Guided Action Adaptation for key–value-side control representation, coupled through cross-attention.

    3.2 Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation

    To prevent cross-agent misattribution, we condition the visual queries on each agent’s description gᵢ, encouraging each action stream to affect its corresponding visual agent without requiring explicit spatial supervision or inference-time spatial inputs.

    Agent semantic representations.

    By construction, each action sequence A⁽ⁱ⁾ is paired with an agent description gᵢ. We encode this description with the frozen umT5 [35] text encoder and project it to an agent embedding:

    eᵢ^G=Pool(T5(gᵢ))∈ℝ⁴⁰⁹⁶, qᵢ=Proj_G(eᵢ^G)∈ℝ^D.

    		(1)

    Here Pool denotes a pooling layer and D is the backbone width. The resulting qᵢ provides the semantic identity associated with action stream A⁽ⁱ⁾.

    Spatial query modulation.

    A global identity vector does not by itself indicate where the corresponding agent appears. For latent frame k, let Xₖ=[x_k,1,…,x_k,N]^⊤∈ℝ^N×D contain the N patchified visual tokens. We compute a token-dependent gate from the visual feature, the agent representation, and their element-wise interaction:

    λ_k,n⁽ⁱ⁾=sigmoid (AgentGate([x_k,n,qᵢ,x_k,n⊙qᵢ])),(2)
    x_k,n⁽ⁱ⁾=x_k,n+λ_k,n⁽ⁱ⁾AgentDelta(qᵢ).

    Here, AgentDelta(qᵢ)∈ℝ^D supplies an identity-dependent feature direction, while the scalar λ_k,n⁽ⁱ⁾ controls its strength at each spatial token. Because x_k,n varies across space and time, the same agent description can induce different modulation strengths throughout the video. The gate is a soft, learned modulation rather than a segmentation mask or an explicitly supervised object assignment.

    Stacking the modulated tokens gives Xₖ⁽ⁱ⁾=[x_k,1⁽ⁱ⁾,…,x_k,N⁽ⁱ⁾]^⊤. Each Xₖ⁽ⁱ⁾ is computed from the same unmodified state Xₖ and only preconditions the queries for agent i; it is not written into the backbone as a separate residual. The agent-conditioned states remain separate until cross-attention forms the action residuals.

    3.3 Schema-Guided Action Adaptation

    To prevent control-semantics collapse, we construct a separate action token for each control dimension j at each time step τ. Each token combines the schema description sⱼ, which specifies what the control means, with its synchronized numerical value a_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾, which specifies its current state. The resulting tokens are used as keys and values in cross-attention.

    Semantic control representations.

    Raw dimension indices cannot express task-specific control semantics. We therefore encode description sⱼ of every control variable with the same text encoder:

    eⱼ^S=Pool(T5(sⱼ))∈ℝ⁴⁰⁹⁶, uⱼ=Proj_S(eⱼ^S)∈ℝ^D.

    		(3)

    The resulting token turns coordinate j into a named control such as an attack, steering command, or robot command. The schema description and numerical value are paired by control dimension, allowing a shared representation to accommodate heterogeneous control layouts within a single model.

    Value-modulated control tokens.

    Language alone expresses action meaning but does not preserve the synchronized binary or continuous trajectory. For agent i, raw-frame index τ, and control dimension j, a value encoder shared across control dimensions maps the scalar a_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾ to affine vectors:

    (γ_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾,β_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾)=MLP_mod(a_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾),(4)
    h_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾=uⱼ⊙(1+γ_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾)+β_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾.

    Thus, uⱼ specifies what a control variable represents, while the synchronized value determines its current modulation. Unlike early aggregation, this construction retains C tokens per time step, allowing visual queries to select individual controls. We add learned time and agent embeddings,

    h̃_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾=h_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾+e_τᵗⁱᵐᵉ+eᵢⁱᵈˣ,

    		(5)

    and collect these tokens into H̃⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝ^T×C×D, retaining a separate token for every control dimension at every time step before temporal windowing.

    3.4 Assembling the Heterogeneous Action Interface

    After constructing the agent-conditioned visual queries and schema-guided action tokens, we assemble the HAI through per-agent cross-attention. For latent frame k and agent i, Xₖ⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝ^N×D queries the aligned action window Hₖ⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝ^M×D (Eq. 8), where r is the temporal compression ratio of the video VAE and M=rC in the one-latent window used by our main model:

    ΔXₖ⁽ⁱ⁾=CrossAttn(Xₖ⁽ⁱ⁾,Hₖ⁽ⁱ⁾).

    		(6)

    The visual tokens serve as queries and the action tokens as keys and values, producing one control residual per agent. We insert this layer after text cross-attention and before the feed-forward sublayer in each transformer block. The shared visual state Xₖ of latent frame k is then updated as

    X̂ₖ=Xₖ+∑ᵢ₌₁^N_agΔXₖ⁽ⁱ⁾.

    		(7)

    All agents read from the same shared visual state Xₖ, while their control residuals are computed independently before aggregation. We zero-initialize each cross-attention output projection, so that the augmented model initially preserves the pretrained backbone behavior.

    3.5 Efficient Causal Rollout

    To enable streaming rollouts, we convert the bidirectional diffusion teacher into a causal generator while addressing action alignment and exposure to self-generated history. Teacher Forcing for AR Tuning first adapts the model to causal attention, followed by DMD on autoregressive rollouts.

    Causally aligned action conditioning.

    Each video latent should read only the controls of its own physical interval. Since the VAE encodes I₀ separately and compresses every r raw frames into one latent, future latent k≥1 covers raw frames Iₖ={r(k-1)+1,…,rk}, and the action memory of agent i stacks the control tokens in this interval:

    Hₖ⁽ⁱ⁾=[h̃_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾]_τ∈Iₖ, 1≤j≤C∈ℝ^rC×D.

    		(8)

    In the causal generator, k is the global latent index rather than the position within the current chunk, so every latent keeps its physical controls as the KV cache advances.

    Teacher Forcing for AR Tuning.

    After obtaining a bidirectional model, this stage then transfers its parameters to a blockwise causal generator [62]. Each target chunk is denoised using only clean preceding chunks, with a causal mask. The HAI remains at the same transformer locations and receives the same aligned conditions, so this stage isolates the change in temporal information flow from errors caused by self-generated history. At inference, preceding chunks are retained in the KV cache and reused when generating the next one.

    DMD for Streaming Video.

    Teacher forcing still trains on clean history, leaving an exposure gap at deployment. DMD addresses this gap by optimizing autoregressive rollouts [54, 15]. Starting from the initial latent z₀, the VAE encoding of I₀, the generator produces ẑ=G_θ(z₀,ℂ) while reusing its self-generated KV cache. The frozen bidirectional teacher serves as the real score, while a trainable bidirectional fake score initialized from the same teacher tracks the generator distribution. At diffusion timestep t, their denoised predictions from the same noised sample ẑₜ and condition ℂ define the unnormalized distribution-matching gradient δ_DMD=μ_fake,φ(ẑₜ,t,ℂ)-μᵣₑₐₗ(ẑₜ,t,ℂ). Backpropagating the normalized gradient through G_θ exposes the causal model to its own rollout history while retaining few-step chunk-wise generation.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Data Collection

    As shown in Fig. 4, we assemble a six-source dataset of 17,951 independent multi-agent trajectories from four competitive multiplayer games and collaborative multi-robotic sources, totaling 119.54 hours of raw video. Each sample contains an initial frame, a scene description, synchronized per-agent action streams, agent descriptions, and a task-specific control schema, with binary controls for games and continuous controls for robots. For evaluation, we build a benchmark of 108 clips drawn from trajectories held out from training, with one 81-frame clip per trajectory; all comparisons and ablations in this section are conducted on this benchmark. Details are provided in Appendix.

    4.2 Implementation details

    We build LiveAct on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [45], which contains 30 transformer blocks with a hidden width of D=3072 and 24 attention heads; its VAE compresses every r=4 raw frames into one latent. We insert the HAI after text cross-attention and before the feed-forward sublayer in every block and fine-tune the full DiT together with the HAI, while the umT5 encoder, which encodes agent and schema descriptions, and the VAE remain frozen. Each agent is represented by C=12 schema-aligned control dimensions. Stage 1 trains the bidirectional teacher for 10k steps with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴ and a global batch size of 16. Stage 2 then trains the causal generator for 6k steps with a learning rate of 2×10⁻⁶, and Stage 3 runs 700 iterations with learning rates of 2×10⁻⁶ for the generator and 4×10⁻⁷ for the fake score; both causal stages use a global batch size of 24 with FSDP. At inference, the teacher uses 50 denoising steps, and the causal generator predicts four latent frames per chunk with four denoising evaluations at timesteps [1000,750,500,250].

    4.3 Comparison with Baselines

    Baselines. We evaluate LiveAct on two complementary tracks—Multi-Agent Video Games and Multi-Robot Manipulation—under the same protocol for visual quality, action following, and agent attribution. We compare against representative interactive and multi-agent video world models covering three control paradigms: language-serialized actions (LingBot-World 2.0 [6], Incantation [63]), per-agent numerical controls (MultiWorld [50], ActionParty [30]), and reference-guided method (WanToFight-style [13]).

    Metrics. Following MultiWorld, we report FVD, LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM for reconstruction quality. Because frame-paired metrics can favor static or averaged predictions, we complement them with Motion Magnitude Error (MME) and an Aesthetic score using the LAION [37] improved predictor. For a more comprehensive control evaluation, we trained inverse dynamics models only on real clips: they recover the executed controls from a generated video, yielding Act-F1 over discrete game events and a normalized error (NRMSE) on continuous robot commands. To evaluate agent attribution, Attr-Acc measures whether the recovered per-agent controls match the commanded streams better under the intended agent assignment than under pairwise agent swaps; higher is better, with a chance level of 0.5. See appendix for more details.

    Quantitative Results. Shown in Tab. 2, among the four non-reference-conditioned methods, LingBot-World 2.0 gives the best game FVD and Aesthetic score but follows actions weakly; MultiWorld retains competitive robot PSNR and SSIM but has low agent attribution; Incantation reaches comparable game Act-F1 yet suffers severe visual drift on robots; and ActionParty provides the best robot reconstruction but the weakest action following. WanToFight-style is the strongest baseline overall, combining strong reconstruction with 0.886 robot Attr-Acc using identity crops, although its game Attr-Acc remains 0.552. LiveAct obtains the best results among the evaluated methods on both tracks, with FVDs of 338.5 and 270.2, game Act-F1 of 0.594, robot NRMSE of 0.558, and Attr-Acc of 0.898 and 0.942. It also achieves the best MME and obtains the highest Aesthetic score.

    Qualitative Results. As shown in Fig. 5, the language-serialized models lose the robot scene (LingBot-World 2.0, Incantation). On the game track, they keep the stage but not the commanded attacks. MultiWorld and ActionParty keep the coarse layout but blur the agents: the fighters and arms blur into faint, duplicated silhouettes. WanToFight-style preserves both scenes and agents and executes the kick, but misses the second agent’s command. LiveAct reproduces the kick and the opponent’s response at the same frames as the ground truth and carries the arm along the ground-truth path, showing that each stream is both executed and bound to the intended agent.

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    Effectiveness of Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation (AASM). Removing it keeps the action tokens intact but makes the queries identical for both agents, and control collapses in both domains (Tab. 3): game Act-F1 drops from 0.594 to 0.172 and Attr-Acc from 0.898 to 0.592, while robot NRMSE rises from 0.558 to 0.931. In Fig. 6, the two streams no longer stay on their own agents, which is the cross-agent misattribution of Sec. 3.1: binding cannot be recovered from the action side alone.

    Effectiveness of Schema-Guided Action Adaptation (SGAA). Replacing it with a conventional flat action encoder, an MLP that maps each frame’s full action vector to a single token, keeps agent modulation but reintroduces control-semantics collapse in visual, and performance again drops in both domains: game Act-F1 falls to 0.225 and Attr-Acc to 0.603, while robot NRMSE rises to 1.120 and Attr-Acc falls to 0.484. Attribution degrades even though agent modulation is retained, indicating that the queries can only route controls they can interpret; the two components are therefore complementary. Finer-grained SGAA ablations are provided in the Appendix.

    Effectiveness of real-time distillation. Stage 1 denoises the full sequence and cannot stream. Stage 2 enables blockwise causal generation but remains slow at 1.66 FPS. Stage 3 reduces each chunk to four denoising steps and reaches 17.70 FPS, 10.7× faster than Stage 2. On games, Act-F1 rises from 0.539 to 0.594 and Attr-Acc from 0.844 to 0.898. Autoregressive generation is better suited to these discrete actions: each frame is conditioned only on past context and the controls aligned to that frame, rather than denoising the full sequence jointly. On robots, NRMSE rises from 0.430 to 0.558 and Attr-Acc falls from 0.969 to 0.942. Per-stage settings and results are in the Appendix.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented LiveAct, a multi-agent video world model for heterogeneous control across games and robot manipulation. Its Heterogeneous Action Interface combines Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation, which binds each indexed action stream to its visual agent through language-conditioned queries, with Schema-Guided Action Adaptation, which couples each control’s language-defined semantics with its synchronized numerical value. Per-agent cross-attention integrates the two within a shared visual representation. Teacher Forcing for AR Tuning and DMD for Streaming Video transfer the interface unchanged to few-step causal rollout. Across six sources, LiveAct achieves best reconstruction and control and reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy without location, mask, or identity input, while its causal generator runs at 17.70 FPS at 512×448.


    Supplementary Material

    Appendix

    Supplementary video. Please see the accompanying demo.mp4 for additional video results.

    Appendix A Additional Related Work

    Structured conditioning in video diffusion. Video diffusion models provide temporally coherent generative priors [10], while diffusion transformers and open video foundation models offer scalable token backbones [28, 24, 46, 49, 25, 21, 47, 5, 32, 34, 33, 59, 57, 51, 52, 39, 38, 45, 19, 18, 14]. Control signals are commonly injected through concatenation, adaptive modulation, or cross-attention. Our distinction is representational rather than merely architectural: a padded action vector is decomposed into per-dimension control tokens, each token carries a task-specific semantic description, and its time-varying scalar modulates rather than replaces that semantic representation. Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation then keeps each stream’s provenance intact until cross-attention.

    Causal video generation and diffusion distillation. Streaming video generation restricts attention to past chunks and caches their keys and values. Self Forcing reduces exposure bias by training on autoregressive model rollouts [15, 64, 40]; Causal Forcing motivates causal teacher initialization before few-step distillation [62]; and distribution matching distillation expresses the generator update through real- and fake-distribution scores [54]. Recent multi-agent systems also combine bidirectional teachers, causal students, and rollout-aware distillation [36, 20, 13]. We adopt this training paradigm to carry the complete HAI into efficient rollout while keeping physical action intervals aligned.

    Appendix B Method Details

    B.1 Problem Formulation

    We follow the notation of Sec. 3: N_ag agents with ordered action streams A={A⁽ⁱ⁾}ᵢ₌₁^N_ag, A⁽ⁱ⁾=[a_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾]∈ℝ^T×C, a control schema S={sⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^C, and agent descriptions G={gᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N_ag. The interface enforces

    \begingathereda_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾\longleftrightarrow(gᵢ,sⱼ), i∈{1,…,N_ag}, j∈{1,…,C},\endgathered

    		(9)

    so each numerical control dimension is paired with an agent identity and a task-specific semantic description; the controls of every source are padded to a common width of C=12, while S preserves source-specific control semantics.

    Let z₀ be the VAE encoding of I₀ and z^1:F-1 the future video latents over F latent frames in total. The DiT backbone patchifies these latents into visual tokens X∈ℝ^FN×D, where each latent frame contributes N spatial tokens of hidden dimension D. The desired conditional distribution is

一句话：多智能体视频世界模型用语言描述的异构动作接口，把每条动作流绑到它在画面里对应的实体，512×448 达 17.7 FPS。

要点：

  • Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation 用语言驱动的空间门控加按智能体分组的注意力，把每条动作流绑到目标视觉实体
  • Schema-Guided Action Adaptation 给每个控制维度写一段语言说明，再把同步数值调制成语义 token，同一位维可以是攻击、转向或机械臂指令
  • 把整套接口搬到分块因果生成器（教师强制 + 考虑 rollout 的分布匹配），六套游戏与多机操作数据上智能体归属准确率 0.898 / 0.942

为什么值得看：多人对战、联机玩法的动作流从来不是一路，单玩家聚合控制撑不住；这套「动作流→实体」的绑定方式可以直接借到引擎侧的动作重映射与回滚预测。

中文摘要：现有的交互式视频世界模型几乎都假设「一个受控主体、一套任务专用动作接口」，而真实的多智能体场景里，多个实体各自被独立控制、共同决定下一帧的样子。LiveAct 的做法是把这件事拆成两半：空间上用语言驱动的门控加按智能体分组的注意力，保证每条动作流只作用于它该控制的那个实体；语义上用「给每个控制位写一句语言说明」的办法，让同一个张量维度在不同任务里可以是攻击键、转向指令或机械臂命令。整套接口再用教师强制与考虑 rollout 的分布匹配搬到分块因果生成器上，实现流式生成。在六个跨越游戏与多机操作的数据源上，无需输入智能体位置或身份裁剪，归属准确率达 0.898 与 0.942，因果生成器在 512×448 下跑到 17.70 FPS。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-25

LiveAct: Towards Real-Time Multi-Agent World Models
with Heterogeneous Action Interfaces

Abstract

Interactive video world models predict how an environment evolves under user actions, but most existing systems assume one controlled agent and one task-specific action interface. We study multi-agent video world modeling, where one model generates a joint visual future for multiple controlled agents while interpreting heterogeneous controls ranging from binary game buttons to continuous robot commands. This task presents two complementary challenges. First, every agent-indexed action stream must control its intended visual entity independently. Second, the model must adapt the meaning of each control variable across different tasks, where the same tensor dimension may denote an attack, steering command, or robot command. We introduce LiveAct, centered on a Heterogeneous Action Interface (HAI) whose two components mirror this decomposition. To support independent control, Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation uses language-driven spatial gates and agent-specific attention to bind each action stream to its intended visual agent. To accommodate heterogeneous controls, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation describes each control variable in language and modulates its semantic token with the synchronized numerical value. We further transfer the complete interface to a blockwise causal generator through teacher forcing and rollout-aware distribution matching, enabling efficient streaming generation while retaining agent-specific control and action semantics. We instantiate the formulation on six multi-agent sources spanning games and multi-robot manipulation, and evaluate visual quality, action following, agent attribution, and latency. Across games and robot manipulation, LiveAct reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy without agent locations or identity crops, and the causal generator attains 17.70 FPS at 512×448.

1 Introduction

Video world models [41, 60, 11, 23, 2, 17, 56, 58, 12, 20, 16] turn interaction into conditional generation [22, 9, 8, 59, 57]: given visual history and actions, they synthesize the observations that follow. Such models can provide scalable experience for game simulation, robot learning, planning, and interactive content creation [7, 53]. Existing systems increasingly support persistent and low-latency rollout, but most still expose a single aggregate player or camera-control stream [44, 6]. Such a generation paradigm is insufficient for inherently multi-agent environments, where independently controlled entities act concurrently and jointly determine the visual future. We therefore study multi-agent video world modeling: given an initial frame, a scene description, and a set of frame-level action streams for multiple agents, the model generates a shared visual future in which each stream controls its intended agent while all agents remain consistent with one another and the environment.

Existing interactive world models cover this setting only in part, and the shortfall lies in the action interface rather than the video backbone. Multi-agent control has relied on numerical action vectors, which keep exact values but typically reach the right entity through spatial priors supplied at inference time and leave control semantics implicit in task-specific dimensions [50, 30, 13]. Language-based actions transfer semantics across entities and tasks but give up the synchronized numerical values that continuous control requires [63]. Tab. 1 summarizes the landscape: no current interface is at once multi-agent, real-time, semantically grounded, and numerically exact. We ask whether one interface can satisfy all four requirements without inference-time masks, boxes, poses, or reference images.

However, a unified action interface must still address two challenges: who each action stream should control in a shared visual scene, and what each control dimension means across heterogeneous tasks. These requirements lead to two key challenges.

  • (1)

    maintaining independent control over multiple interacting agents. A model must keep each agent responsive to its own action stream while capturing interactions. The action tensors of each agent are injected sequentially at input, but do not ensure that their effects remain correctly attributed in the shared visual feature space. Commands may be assigned to the wrong agent or inadvertently drive multiple entities (Fig. 2a), especially when agents overlap, look similar, or jointly manipulate an object. Achieving independent control therefore requires agent-specific conditioning that separates command attribution.

  • (2)

    unifying action conditioning across heterogeneous control spaces. Action vectors do not share a universal semantic coordinate system: their dimensions, ordering, and meanings are defined by task-specific action spaces. As a result, the same action dimension or pattern may encode different behaviors (Fig. 2b). Directly conditioning on raw vectors therefore leads to action semantics being tied to task-specific dimensions and ordering. Language can expose what each control dimension means, but does not preserve the exact frame-synchronized binary or continuous values needed for execution. Unified action conditioning thus requires separating what a control means from what value it takes, and representing both in a shared action interface.

    • LiveAct addresses these challenges with a Heterogeneous Action Interface (HAI), which factorizes action conditioning into semantic adaptation and agent-specific visual injection. For independent control, Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation derives an agent-specific spatial gate from the agent description, so that each branch selectively updates the visual tokens associated with its intended entity while attending only to the corresponding action stream. For heterogeneous action conditioning, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation converts each control dimension into a semantic token defined by its schema and injects the synchronized numerical value through affine modulation, decoupling control meaning from task-specific vector layouts. This provides a shared semantic interface for heterogeneous control spaces. Together, these two designs provide a common action representation while preserving agent-specific effects in the shared visual space. The resulting residuals are injected through zero-initialized projections, preserving the pretrained visual prior at initialization.

    Beyond accurate control, interaction requires efficient incremental rollout without repeatedly regenerating the visual history. We therefore retain the complete HAI when transferring a bidirectional video teacher to a blockwise causal generator through Teacher Forcing for autoregressive (AR) Tuning and Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) for Streaming Video [54, 15, 48, 49]. Causal temporal alignment maps raw actions to compressed video latents, while a global latent offset advances action windows together with the cached rollout. Causal generation thus accelerates a fixed control interface rather than redefining who acts or what each action means.

    We evaluate LiveAct across six multi-agent environments spanning interactive games and robot manipulation, covering both discrete and continuous control spaces. Experiments assess visual fidelity, action adherence, agent attribution, and real-time efficiency. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We formulate real-time multi-agent video world modeling under heterogeneous action spaces and identify two coupled challenges overlooked by existing action interfaces: binding each indexed action stream to its intended visual agent and jointly representing task-specific control semantics and synchronized numerical values in a shared interface.

  • •

    We propose LiveAct, a real-time multi-agent video world model built around a Heterogeneous Action Interface. HAI combines Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation for language-driven stream-to-agent binding with Schema-Guided Action Adaptation for value-preserving semantic control, and is retained during teacher-forced causal adaptation and rollout-aware distribution matching for real-time streaming generation.

  • •

    We build a dataset of 17,951 multi-agent trajectories, totaling 119.54 hours of raw video, and a 108-clip benchmark spanning four games and two robot-manipulation sources. LiveAct reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy on games and robots without locations, masks, or identity crops, and generates at 17.70 FPS at 512×448.

    • 2 Related Work

    Multi-agent video world models. Multi-agent video world models jointly predict an environment under multiple agents’ observations or controls, and must coordinate shared dynamics while preserving the identity of each condition stream. Solaris jointly models synchronized observations from multiple Minecraft agents [36]; MultiWorld combines a multi-agent condition module with a global state encoder across game and robot manipulation [50]; and Gamma-World uses permutation-equivalent agent encoding and sparse hub attention [20]. Complementary systems focus on binding independent controls to visual entities: ActionParty jointly predicts persistent subject-state tokens initialized from subject locations [30], WanToFight grounds locally causal keyboard streams with first-frame character references [13], and Incantation binds language actions to individual entities [63]. Across these designs, the central control problem is to preserve per-agent condition provenance and ensure that each action affects its intended entity. The Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation component of our HAI addresses this problem by conditioning the visual queries on each agent’s language description. without masks, boxes, coordinates, or reference images at inference time.

    Action-controllable world models across domains. World models learn environment dynamics for imagined interaction [7]. Genie learns latent actions from unlabeled videos [3], DIAMOND uses diffusion for Atari and Counter-Strike dynamics [1], and GameNGen predicts DOOM frames from past observations and actions [44]. LingBot-World 2.0 couples camera poses and time-varying semantic prompts for open-ended interaction [6]. Real-world simulators extend action-conditioned prediction to diverse interactions [53] and continuous robot trajectories [61], while Incantation expresses per-entity actions in natural language to support semantic transfer [63]. Most interfaces choose between numerically precise but task-specific vectors and language interfaces that make control semantics explicit. Within our HAI, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation combines the two: language identifies the task-dependent meaning of each control variable, while synchronized binary or continuous values retain frame-level control.

    3 Method

    Given an initial frame I₀, a scene description c, and ordered action streams A={A⁽ⁱ⁾}ᵢ₌₁^N_ag for N_ag agents, where A⁽ⁱ⁾=[a_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾]∈ℝ^T×C gives the value of control dimension j at raw frame τ∈{1,…,T} (raw frame 0 is I₀), paired with agent descriptions G={gᵢ} and a control schema S={sⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^C, multi-agent world modeling aims to synthesize the shared visual future in which each stream drives its own agent while all agents remain consistent with one another and with the scene. We write ℂ=(c,A,S,G) for the full condition. In this section, we first discuss the motivation and two failure modes of existing action interfaces in Sec. 3.1. We then introduce Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation in Sec. 3.2, which decides who responds to each stream, and Schema-Guided Action Adaptation in Sec. 3.3, what each control dimension means and what value it takes; Sec. 3.4 assembles them into the Heterogeneous Action Interface. Finally, Sec. 3.5 carries the same action-conditioning mechanism into causal streaming rollout. Fig. 3 summarizes this three-stage design.

    3.1 Motivation

    Although the indexed action tensor preserves the numerical trajectory of each stream, it does not establish the correspondences required to condition a shared visual representation. The stream index i separates A⁽ⁱ⁾ from the other streams but provides no visual evidence associating it with the tokens of its intended agent. Likewise, the control index j identifies a coordinate only within a task-specific action space and therefore lacks a consistent interpretation across tasks.

    Cross-Agent Misattribution. Keeping the action streams separate preserves their provenance in action space, but does not establish their recipients in visual space. An agent-index embedding can distinguish A⁽ⁱ⁾ from A^(i^′), yet contains no visual evidence linking index i to the appearance of agent i. Consequently, the command from one stream may be attributed to the wrong visual agent or inadvertently affect multiple agents. The missing correspondence must therefore be established on the query side of action conditioning: the visual features that read A⁽ⁱ⁾ should be grounded in the description gᵢ of its corresponding agent.

    Control-Semantics Collapse. An action vector contains C control dimensions, where the j-th coordinate provides the numerical value of one control at a given time step. However, the index j itself carries no explicit semantic meaning beyond the definition of its task-specific action space. Compressing all C dimensions into a single action embedding further obscures the identity of individual controls, making it difficult for the model to distinguish which control produces a particular effect. The action representation should therefore keep each control dimension distinct while jointly encoding its schema-defined semantics and frame-level numerical value.

    These two requirements are complementary: expressive action tokens cannot resolve agent binding, while agent-aware queries cannot recover missing control semantics. HAI therefore separates the two, using Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation for query-side binding and Schema-Guided Action Adaptation for key–value-side control representation, coupled through cross-attention.

    3.2 Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation

    To prevent cross-agent misattribution, we condition the visual queries on each agent’s description gᵢ, encouraging each action stream to affect its corresponding visual agent without requiring explicit spatial supervision or inference-time spatial inputs.

    Agent semantic representations.

    By construction, each action sequence A⁽ⁱ⁾ is paired with an agent description gᵢ. We encode this description with the frozen umT5 [35] text encoder and project it to an agent embedding:

    eᵢ^G=Pool(T5(gᵢ))∈ℝ⁴⁰⁹⁶, qᵢ=Proj_G(eᵢ^G)∈ℝ^D.

    		(1)

    Here Pool denotes a pooling layer and D is the backbone width. The resulting qᵢ provides the semantic identity associated with action stream A⁽ⁱ⁾.

    Spatial query modulation.

    A global identity vector does not by itself indicate where the corresponding agent appears. For latent frame k, let Xₖ=[x_k,1,…,x_k,N]^⊤∈ℝ^N×D contain the N patchified visual tokens. We compute a token-dependent gate from the visual feature, the agent representation, and their element-wise interaction:

    λ_k,n⁽ⁱ⁾=sigmoid (AgentGate([x_k,n,qᵢ,x_k,n⊙qᵢ])),(2)
    x_k,n⁽ⁱ⁾=x_k,n+λ_k,n⁽ⁱ⁾AgentDelta(qᵢ).

    Here, AgentDelta(qᵢ)∈ℝ^D supplies an identity-dependent feature direction, while the scalar λ_k,n⁽ⁱ⁾ controls its strength at each spatial token. Because x_k,n varies across space and time, the same agent description can induce different modulation strengths throughout the video. The gate is a soft, learned modulation rather than a segmentation mask or an explicitly supervised object assignment.

    Stacking the modulated tokens gives Xₖ⁽ⁱ⁾=[x_k,1⁽ⁱ⁾,…,x_k,N⁽ⁱ⁾]^⊤. Each Xₖ⁽ⁱ⁾ is computed from the same unmodified state Xₖ and only preconditions the queries for agent i; it is not written into the backbone as a separate residual. The agent-conditioned states remain separate until cross-attention forms the action residuals.

    3.3 Schema-Guided Action Adaptation

    To prevent control-semantics collapse, we construct a separate action token for each control dimension j at each time step τ. Each token combines the schema description sⱼ, which specifies what the control means, with its synchronized numerical value a_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾, which specifies its current state. The resulting tokens are used as keys and values in cross-attention.

    Semantic control representations.

    Raw dimension indices cannot express task-specific control semantics. We therefore encode description sⱼ of every control variable with the same text encoder:

    eⱼ^S=Pool(T5(sⱼ))∈ℝ⁴⁰⁹⁶, uⱼ=Proj_S(eⱼ^S)∈ℝ^D.

    		(3)

    The resulting token turns coordinate j into a named control such as an attack, steering command, or robot command. The schema description and numerical value are paired by control dimension, allowing a shared representation to accommodate heterogeneous control layouts within a single model.

    Value-modulated control tokens.

    Language alone expresses action meaning but does not preserve the synchronized binary or continuous trajectory. For agent i, raw-frame index τ, and control dimension j, a value encoder shared across control dimensions maps the scalar a_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾ to affine vectors:

    (γ_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾,β_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾)=MLP_mod(a_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾),(4)
    h_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾=uⱼ⊙(1+γ_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾)+β_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾.

    Thus, uⱼ specifies what a control variable represents, while the synchronized value determines its current modulation. Unlike early aggregation, this construction retains C tokens per time step, allowing visual queries to select individual controls. We add learned time and agent embeddings,

    h̃_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾=h_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾+e_τᵗⁱᵐᵉ+eᵢⁱᵈˣ,

    		(5)

    and collect these tokens into H̃⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝ^T×C×D, retaining a separate token for every control dimension at every time step before temporal windowing.

    3.4 Assembling the Heterogeneous Action Interface

    After constructing the agent-conditioned visual queries and schema-guided action tokens, we assemble the HAI through per-agent cross-attention. For latent frame k and agent i, Xₖ⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝ^N×D queries the aligned action window Hₖ⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝ^M×D (Eq. 8), where r is the temporal compression ratio of the video VAE and M=rC in the one-latent window used by our main model:

    ΔXₖ⁽ⁱ⁾=CrossAttn(Xₖ⁽ⁱ⁾,Hₖ⁽ⁱ⁾).

    		(6)

    The visual tokens serve as queries and the action tokens as keys and values, producing one control residual per agent. We insert this layer after text cross-attention and before the feed-forward sublayer in each transformer block. The shared visual state Xₖ of latent frame k is then updated as

    X̂ₖ=Xₖ+∑ᵢ₌₁^N_agΔXₖ⁽ⁱ⁾.

    		(7)

    All agents read from the same shared visual state Xₖ, while their control residuals are computed independently before aggregation. We zero-initialize each cross-attention output projection, so that the augmented model initially preserves the pretrained backbone behavior.

    3.5 Efficient Causal Rollout

    To enable streaming rollouts, we convert the bidirectional diffusion teacher into a causal generator while addressing action alignment and exposure to self-generated history. Teacher Forcing for AR Tuning first adapts the model to causal attention, followed by DMD on autoregressive rollouts.

    Causally aligned action conditioning.

    Each video latent should read only the controls of its own physical interval. Since the VAE encodes I₀ separately and compresses every r raw frames into one latent, future latent k≥1 covers raw frames Iₖ={r(k-1)+1,…,rk}, and the action memory of agent i stacks the control tokens in this interval:

    Hₖ⁽ⁱ⁾=[h̃_τ,j⁽ⁱ⁾]_τ∈Iₖ, 1≤j≤C∈ℝ^rC×D.

    		(8)

    In the causal generator, k is the global latent index rather than the position within the current chunk, so every latent keeps its physical controls as the KV cache advances.

    Teacher Forcing for AR Tuning.

    After obtaining a bidirectional model, this stage then transfers its parameters to a blockwise causal generator [62]. Each target chunk is denoised using only clean preceding chunks, with a causal mask. The HAI remains at the same transformer locations and receives the same aligned conditions, so this stage isolates the change in temporal information flow from errors caused by self-generated history. At inference, preceding chunks are retained in the KV cache and reused when generating the next one.

    DMD for Streaming Video.

    Teacher forcing still trains on clean history, leaving an exposure gap at deployment. DMD addresses this gap by optimizing autoregressive rollouts [54, 15]. Starting from the initial latent z₀, the VAE encoding of I₀, the generator produces ẑ=G_θ(z₀,ℂ) while reusing its self-generated KV cache. The frozen bidirectional teacher serves as the real score, while a trainable bidirectional fake score initialized from the same teacher tracks the generator distribution. At diffusion timestep t, their denoised predictions from the same noised sample ẑₜ and condition ℂ define the unnormalized distribution-matching gradient δ_DMD=μ_fake,φ(ẑₜ,t,ℂ)-μᵣₑₐₗ(ẑₜ,t,ℂ). Backpropagating the normalized gradient through G_θ exposes the causal model to its own rollout history while retaining few-step chunk-wise generation.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Data Collection

    As shown in Fig. 4, we assemble a six-source dataset of 17,951 independent multi-agent trajectories from four competitive multiplayer games and collaborative multi-robotic sources, totaling 119.54 hours of raw video. Each sample contains an initial frame, a scene description, synchronized per-agent action streams, agent descriptions, and a task-specific control schema, with binary controls for games and continuous controls for robots. For evaluation, we build a benchmark of 108 clips drawn from trajectories held out from training, with one 81-frame clip per trajectory; all comparisons and ablations in this section are conducted on this benchmark. Details are provided in Appendix.

    4.2 Implementation details

    We build LiveAct on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [45], which contains 30 transformer blocks with a hidden width of D=3072 and 24 attention heads; its VAE compresses every r=4 raw frames into one latent. We insert the HAI after text cross-attention and before the feed-forward sublayer in every block and fine-tune the full DiT together with the HAI, while the umT5 encoder, which encodes agent and schema descriptions, and the VAE remain frozen. Each agent is represented by C=12 schema-aligned control dimensions. Stage 1 trains the bidirectional teacher for 10k steps with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴ and a global batch size of 16. Stage 2 then trains the causal generator for 6k steps with a learning rate of 2×10⁻⁶, and Stage 3 runs 700 iterations with learning rates of 2×10⁻⁶ for the generator and 4×10⁻⁷ for the fake score; both causal stages use a global batch size of 24 with FSDP. At inference, the teacher uses 50 denoising steps, and the causal generator predicts four latent frames per chunk with four denoising evaluations at timesteps [1000,750,500,250].

    4.3 Comparison with Baselines

    Baselines. We evaluate LiveAct on two complementary tracks—Multi-Agent Video Games and Multi-Robot Manipulation—under the same protocol for visual quality, action following, and agent attribution. We compare against representative interactive and multi-agent video world models covering three control paradigms: language-serialized actions (LingBot-World 2.0 [6], Incantation [63]), per-agent numerical controls (MultiWorld [50], ActionParty [30]), and reference-guided method (WanToFight-style [13]).

    Metrics. Following MultiWorld, we report FVD, LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM for reconstruction quality. Because frame-paired metrics can favor static or averaged predictions, we complement them with Motion Magnitude Error (MME) and an Aesthetic score using the LAION [37] improved predictor. For a more comprehensive control evaluation, we trained inverse dynamics models only on real clips: they recover the executed controls from a generated video, yielding Act-F1 over discrete game events and a normalized error (NRMSE) on continuous robot commands. To evaluate agent attribution, Attr-Acc measures whether the recovered per-agent controls match the commanded streams better under the intended agent assignment than under pairwise agent swaps; higher is better, with a chance level of 0.5. See appendix for more details.

    Quantitative Results. Shown in Tab. 2, among the four non-reference-conditioned methods, LingBot-World 2.0 gives the best game FVD and Aesthetic score but follows actions weakly; MultiWorld retains competitive robot PSNR and SSIM but has low agent attribution; Incantation reaches comparable game Act-F1 yet suffers severe visual drift on robots; and ActionParty provides the best robot reconstruction but the weakest action following. WanToFight-style is the strongest baseline overall, combining strong reconstruction with 0.886 robot Attr-Acc using identity crops, although its game Attr-Acc remains 0.552. LiveAct obtains the best results among the evaluated methods on both tracks, with FVDs of 338.5 and 270.2, game Act-F1 of 0.594, robot NRMSE of 0.558, and Attr-Acc of 0.898 and 0.942. It also achieves the best MME and obtains the highest Aesthetic score.

    Qualitative Results. As shown in Fig. 5, the language-serialized models lose the robot scene (LingBot-World 2.0, Incantation). On the game track, they keep the stage but not the commanded attacks. MultiWorld and ActionParty keep the coarse layout but blur the agents: the fighters and arms blur into faint, duplicated silhouettes. WanToFight-style preserves both scenes and agents and executes the kick, but misses the second agent’s command. LiveAct reproduces the kick and the opponent’s response at the same frames as the ground truth and carries the arm along the ground-truth path, showing that each stream is both executed and bound to the intended agent.

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    Effectiveness of Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation (AASM). Removing it keeps the action tokens intact but makes the queries identical for both agents, and control collapses in both domains (Tab. 3): game Act-F1 drops from 0.594 to 0.172 and Attr-Acc from 0.898 to 0.592, while robot NRMSE rises from 0.558 to 0.931. In Fig. 6, the two streams no longer stay on their own agents, which is the cross-agent misattribution of Sec. 3.1: binding cannot be recovered from the action side alone.

    Effectiveness of Schema-Guided Action Adaptation (SGAA). Replacing it with a conventional flat action encoder, an MLP that maps each frame’s full action vector to a single token, keeps agent modulation but reintroduces control-semantics collapse in visual, and performance again drops in both domains: game Act-F1 falls to 0.225 and Attr-Acc to 0.603, while robot NRMSE rises to 1.120 and Attr-Acc falls to 0.484. Attribution degrades even though agent modulation is retained, indicating that the queries can only route controls they can interpret; the two components are therefore complementary. Finer-grained SGAA ablations are provided in the Appendix.

    Effectiveness of real-time distillation. Stage 1 denoises the full sequence and cannot stream. Stage 2 enables blockwise causal generation but remains slow at 1.66 FPS. Stage 3 reduces each chunk to four denoising steps and reaches 17.70 FPS, 10.7× faster than Stage 2. On games, Act-F1 rises from 0.539 to 0.594 and Attr-Acc from 0.844 to 0.898. Autoregressive generation is better suited to these discrete actions: each frame is conditioned only on past context and the controls aligned to that frame, rather than denoising the full sequence jointly. On robots, NRMSE rises from 0.430 to 0.558 and Attr-Acc falls from 0.969 to 0.942. Per-stage settings and results are in the Appendix.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented LiveAct, a multi-agent video world model for heterogeneous control across games and robot manipulation. Its Heterogeneous Action Interface combines Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation, which binds each indexed action stream to its visual agent through language-conditioned queries, with Schema-Guided Action Adaptation, which couples each control’s language-defined semantics with its synchronized numerical value. Per-agent cross-attention integrates the two within a shared visual representation. Teacher Forcing for AR Tuning and DMD for Streaming Video transfer the interface unchanged to few-step causal rollout. Across six sources, LiveAct achieves best reconstruction and control and reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy without location, mask, or identity input, while its causal generator runs at 17.70 FPS at 512×448.


    Supplementary Material

    Appendix

    Supplementary video. Please see the accompanying demo.mp4 for additional video results.

    Appendix A Additional Related Work

    Structured conditioning in video diffusion. Video diffusion models provide temporally coherent generative priors [10], while diffusion transformers and open video foundation models offer scalable token backbones [28, 24, 46, 49, 25, 21, 47, 5, 32, 34, 33, 59, 57, 51, 52, 39, 38, 45, 19, 18, 14]. Control signals are commonly injected through concatenation, adaptive modulation, or cross-attention. Our distinction is representational rather than merely architectural: a padded action vector is decomposed into per-dimension control tokens, each token carries a task-specific semantic description, and its time-varying scalar modulates rather than replaces that semantic representation. Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation then keeps each stream’s provenance intact until cross-attention.

    Causal video generation and diffusion distillation. Streaming video generation restricts attention to past chunks and caches their keys and values. Self Forcing reduces exposure bias by training on autoregressive model rollouts [15, 64, 40]; Causal Forcing motivates causal teacher initialization before few-step distillation [62]; and distribution matching distillation expresses the generator update through real- and fake-distribution scores [54]. Recent multi-agent systems also combine bidirectional teachers, causal students, and rollout-aware distillation [36, 20, 13]. We adopt this training paradigm to carry the complete HAI into efficient rollout while keeping physical action intervals aligned.

    so each numerical control dimension is paired with an agent identity and a task-specific semantic description; the controls of every source are padded to a common width of C=12, while S preserves source-specific control semantics.
