Each chunk’s combined text condition is encoded independently, and the resulting context tokens are concatenated. The text attention mask routes both video and audio queries to the corresponding prompt, with padding excluded and anchor/reference queries receiving no text-attention update in the causal model. In bidirectional adaptation, the initial frame instead shares the first generated chunk’s prompt. Historical chunks use their corresponding prompts, while the target directly attends only to its current prompt. Historical context remains available through audiovisual attention, which is causal across chunks during autoregressive training and generation.

At inference, a deterministic text renderer converts the controller’s structured predictions and rule-updated state into local guidance.

A.3 Training Objectives and Distillation

Generator training optimizes the audiovisual backbone and action branches while freezing the text encoder and autoencoders. The Interaction Agent uses InternVL3-8B [(Zhu et al., 2025)] without task-specific fine-tuning, while the rule engine and prompt compiler are programmed. The loader aligns video, audio, player controls, reference images, and chunk text conditions at shared temporal boundaries.

Training hyperparameters.

We train on 16 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with a global batch size of 16 and BF16 mixed precision. Table 1 lists the generator learning rates. Consistency distillation and distribution matching use AdamW with β=(0,0.999), weight decay 0.01, and 100 warmup steps. The learned score model uses a learning rate of 10⁻⁵. Both refiner stages use 8-bit AdamW with a learning rate of 10⁻⁵, β=(0.9,0.999), weight decay 0.01, and 100 warmup steps. The domain LoRA has rank 384 and scaling parameter α=384.

Action and prompt adaptation.

Basic Dynamics data teach control-conditioned local dynamics, while the Interaction data add chunk-local behavior and outcome guidance. Arena post-training starts from the Interaction-trained bidirectional model and adapts it to sustained combat before causal training and distillation. Bidirectional adaptation uses chunk-specific text conditions and a linear-path flow-matching objective [(Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023)]. For modality m∈{v,a}, a clean latent sequence zᵐ is perturbed as zᵐ_σ=(1-σ)zᵐ+σεᵐ, with Gaussian noise εᵐ. The model predicts the flow velocity εᵐ-zᵐ and is trained by minimizing

L_bi=∑_m∈{v,a}λₘ𝔼[∥v_θᵐ(z_σ,σ;u,c)-(εᵐ-zᵐ)∥_Ωₘ²],

(8)

where c denotes the sequence of chunk text conditions and the norm averages supervised tokens, excluding the conditioning video frame and ineligible audio samples. The text attention mask restricts each generated chunk to its own text condition, while audiovisual self- and cross-attention remain bidirectional at this stage.

Sliding-window autoregressive training.

We initialize the causal model from the adapted checkpoint and train the layout in Equation 7. The anchor, reference, and available history chunks remain clean. Noise is applied only to the next chunk. For clean target latents zₖ, Gaussian noise εₖ, and noise level σ∈[0,1], the noisy input and predicted clean estimate are

z_k,σ=(1-σ)zₖ+σεₖ,(9)
ẑₖ=z_k,σ-σv_θ(z_k,σ,σ|Hₖ,uₖ,cₖ).

Here v_θ predicts flow velocity, and Hₖ, uₖ, and cₖ follow Equation 5. Superscripts v and a denote video and audio. The target-chunk reconstruction objective is

L_AR=𝔼 [w(σ)(MSE(ẑₖᵛ,zₖᵛ)+λₐMSE(ẑₖᵃ,zₖᵃ))],

(10)

where w(σ)=\exp[-2(σ-0.5)²] weights the noise level and λₐ=0.16 weights the audio loss. Squared errors are averaged over target tokens only. This stage uses ground-truth history. Bidirectional and autoregressive adaptation share the chunk-wise prompt routing used at inference, but only autoregressive adaptation enforces temporal causality through audiovisual attention.

Consistency distillation and startup coverage.

For few-step generation, the implementation follows the teacher-forcing consistency initialization in Causal-rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026a)]. This recipe builds on Consistency Models [(Song et al., 2023)], sCM [(Lu & Song, 2025)], and rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026b)]. A frozen autoregressive teacher advances a noisy sample between nearby noise levels. At the advanced point, the current student produces a clean estimate without gradients, which serves as the consistency target for its prediction at the starting point. Video and audio both contribute to this loss. Checkpoint EMA is maintained separately.

Startup and continued generation use the same sliding-window context layout. The training recipe alternates an update with four history chunks and an update with zero, one, two, or three history chunks.

The final Arena recipe further distills text classifier-free guidance [(Ho & Salimans, 2022)] into the student. The teacher combines conditional and text-unconditional predictions while retaining player actions and visual context. The student uses a single conditional forward pass per denoising step.

Self-forcing distribution matching.

After consistency distillation, we apply self-forcing distribution matching [(Huang et al., 2025)] as the second stage of the Causal-rCM [(Zheng et al., 2026a)] recipe. The objective follows DMD [(Yin et al., 2024b)] and DMD2 [(Yin et al., 2024a)], with bidirectional-teacher supervision of an autoregressive student as in CausVid [(Yin et al., 2025)]. One student starts from the initial frame, generates four startup chunks, and continues for five additional chunks using the same reference, chunk-wise prompt routing, and sliding context. No ground-truth history is inserted into this rollout. Both the startup chunks and the later chunks receive distribution-matching supervision.

A frozen bidirectional score model and a learned score model for student samples evaluate the same perturbed rollout with aligned controls and semantic conditions. These score models receive no reference-image tokens, so their text conditions describe character appearance explicitly. The final Arena recipe applies text guidance to the frozen score model, while the learned score model and student remain conditional. Their normalized difference in denoised predictions defines a stop-gradient target. The generator then replays the recorded final denoising step of each chunk to optimize a masked video–audio regression loss against that target. Rollout generation runs without gradients, avoiding storage of its full computation graph.

Video refiner training.

We construct temporally aligned training pairs from the same arena clip. Its original VAE encoding serves as the target. To construct the degraded input, we spatially downsample the RGB frames, encode them, and apply a frozen LTX-2.3 2× spatial upscaler v1.1 [(Lightricks, 2026)] to restore the target spatial size. We train a domain LoRA [(Hu et al., 2022)] on the refiner with truncated flow matching [(Lipman et al., 2023)] between the original target and a noise-perturbed upsampled latent. The refiner is first trained bidirectionally. Causal adaptation starts from this checkpoint, conditions on the first frame, character reference, and up to four clean history chunks, and applies loss only to the current chunk. Training uses ground-truth history, while deployment uses previously refined outputs. Both stages optimize only the domain LoRA, keeping the upsampler and backbone frozen. The official LTX-2.3 distilled LoRA v1.1 [(Lightricks, 2026)] is disabled for this training loss and enabled for few-step refinement at inference.

Inference settings.

The distilled Arena generator uses four denoising steps with noise levels (1,0.9375,0.8333,0.625,0). Refinement uses two denoising steps with noise levels (0.725,0.421875,0), a classifier-free guidance scale of 1, and no spatiotemporal guidance.

A.4 State Updates and Visual Verification

Prediction and state commitment.

At a chunk boundary, the controller retains the corrected state and uses predicted events to compute provisional outcomes and local guidance. Generation does not commit those predictions to the persistent ledger. After decoding, verification produces the feedback used to obtain the next retained state in Equation 2. The implementation recomputes this state from the saved pre-generation state and observed events, preventing predicted and verified damage from being counted twice. The first chunk uses the initial frame and configured state without a preceding verification step. The retained gameplay state is stored independently of the generator’s sliding visual context. When earlier frames leave that context, their recorded interaction consequences remain available to subsequent rule updates and enter generation through the current guidance.

Observation selection and shot prediction.

The online Arena implementation uses decoded RGB frames directly, without an observation refiner. Within each chunk, it selects the first frame of each uninterrupted firing interval and every fourth frame thereafter (5 Hz at 20 FPS). Before generation, the latest available frame is the preceding chunk’s last frame, or the initial image at startup. For each selected firing time, a calibrated control-to-pixel mapping estimates the image displacement from the intervening controls. We translate the latest frame accordingly, take a 320×320 crop centered on the screen, and overlay a hollow green aiming ring. The Interaction Agent receives this projected crop and a separate enemy appearance reference, and predicts whether the enemy’s body overlaps the marked aiming region.

Visual verification.

After generation, we decode the corresponding actual firing frames, the chunk’s final frame, and the frame three positions before it. Together with the pre-generation frame, these form the sampled observations Iₖ₋₁. A firing-frame audit receives the selected firing frames in temporal order, with the same ring overlay, alongside the pre-generation and two late frames. Unlike prediction, verification uses full frames rather than center crops. The ring radius is 5% of the shorter image dimension and leaves its interior unobstructed. A separate state query places the final frame first and uses the pre-generation and earlier late frame only as temporal context. It classifies the enemy as alive, dead, or not visible in the final frame. Both queries receive an appearance reference for identity only. Full frames are padded to a 2:1 canvas and the reference to a square, without cropping their contents. Aim markers appear only in the VLM inputs. The requested outcome is the condition being checked, not visual evidence, and verification uses separate calls from prediction.

The rule engine specifies intended transitions, while committed visual outcomes ground the state used for subsequent interaction. When an observed outcome contradicts a prediction, the controller revises the affected state and derives subsequent guidance from that revision. Numerical attributes remain rule-maintained rather than directly estimated from images, and occlusion alone is not treated as death.

Action constraints and opponent behavior.

Ammunition gates the executed fire commands and is consumed when a shot is permitted, independently of whether it hits. Before an enemy can attack, the Interaction Agent checks visual preconditions, including whether the enemy is visible and facing the player. When these conditions hold, attacks are sampled at a configured rate, and each attack hits with a preset probability. Successful hits subtract a fixed per-shot damage from player health. Reaching zero health disables player controls and adds the corresponding terminal outcome to guidance. For opponent behavior, the agent assesses movement feasibility from the current scene. The behavior policy combines this assessment with retained state and the configured strategy to select a movement description. Attack rules and strategy-transition conditions can be edited in the rule layer. Numerical state remains in the controller, while the generator receives observable behavior and outcome descriptions. World-side events thus combine visual assessment of the current scene with executable game rules that update player state and constrain subsequent controls.

A.5 Design Rationale

Reciprocal interaction concerns the causal effects of player actions on the world and of world events on the player. It does not require every game mechanic to be learned. Executable rules make damage, ammunition, and termination conditions explicit and configurable, while scene-conditioned behavior reasoning determines how actors act under those conditions. Their combination connects world-side decisions to persistent consequences for the player during continuous interaction.

Realizing these interactions also requires a generator that can express their consequences. Explicit state specifies intended outcomes, and text guidance communicates them, but the generator must learn to realize them as visible behavior. We therefore develop interaction data, train the conditioned generator, and connect event reasoning, executable updates, and visual feedback in an online loop. The contribution is the reciprocal generative gameplay enabled by this coordinated system, including its data and training procedure. Reconciliation supplies feedback within this loop by grounding subsequent decisions in committed observations.

Appendix B Dataset Construction

All routes share the capture and alignment pipeline below. Counts refer to accepted source recordings, excluding candidate jobs, prompt variants, and overlapping training windows.

B.1 Shared Capture and Alignment

Execution and recording.

We specify the map, assets, initial conditions, actor policies, and player controls before capture. The engine records gameplay demos together with applied inputs, frame timing, state, and interaction events. Requested controls and realized events are retained separately, with damage labels taken from realized engine events. Offline replay renders the recorded trajectory and game audio under a fixed client configuration. Presentation settings, including HUD, crosshair, and effect suppression, are versioned per route. Renderer telemetry records camera position and orientation, transforms, and projection parameters, synchronized with simulation ticks.

Time and action interface.

The capture pipelines use a 64 Hz simulation/control clock. Warm-up is removed using the recorded capture boundary before aligning model time zero. The model-facing stream uses 20 video frames per second, with four continuous movement/camera channels and fire, jump, and reload inputs under the shared action contract. Camera and movement values follow the recorded applied controls. Button resampling preserves short active runs that might otherwise disappear between sampled frames. In the long Interaction release, the action profiles explicitly remove 64 warm-up ticks and align row zero with the first video frame.

Native media differ across routes. Basic Dynamics stores 320 frames at 64 fps and 1280×720 resolution. Short and long Interaction sequences store 81 and 1,201 frames at 20 fps and 1280×720. Arena stores 1,201 frames at 20 fps and 1664×960. Representative files in all four subsets contain 48 kHz stereo game audio. The model loader resizes video and resamples audio according to the training configuration. The generator training configuration uses 832×480 video and 16 kHz stereo audio. The 81-frame layout comprises an initial frame and five 16-frame chunks. The 1,201-frame layout similarly supports 75 chunks.

Semantic labels and packaging.

We use Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite [(Google DeepMind, 2026)] (gemini-3.1-flash-lite) to separately annotate map style, weapon appearance and operation, and player and enemy appearance. Interaction releases add chunk-local motion, visibility, damage, and death descriptions derived from telemetry. Prompts distinguish no damage, nonlethal damage, a new death event, and an already-dead actor. Off-screen intervals are described using visibility records rather than invented visible motion. Player controls remain in action tensors. Enemy movement and jumping belong to semantic conditions. Where reference images are used, the manifest binds them to the appropriate actor and time interval.

B.2 Basic Dynamics

Basic Dynamics contains 50,140 five-second clips across 28 maps and nine weapons, including 39,539 without an enemy and 10,601 with a non-damaging enemy distractor. Movement, camera changes, firing, and local collision responses provide the principal supervision. The supplement emphasizes pure idle, idle-to-action, action-to-idle, interrupted action, smooth routes, and wall impacts.

Route validation and camera filtering remove unsuitable trajectories.

B.3 Interaction

Short interactions.

The short Interaction subset contains 42,000 recordings across five maps, nine weapons, and 42 model–skin–color appearances. Capture varies distance, opponent movement, direction changes, stopping, jumping, visibility transitions, and firing. Firing times are sampled deterministically from the scenario seed. Weapon-specific schedules include isolated shots, repeated taps, and bounded bursts. Opponent motion and jump programs are specified separately from player controls.

Outcome labels follow the realized engine events, yielding 6,535 no-fire examples, 16,666 misses, 14,496 nonlethal-hit examples, and 4,303 kills. The visibility allocation is 37,800 continuously visible examples, 2,100 exit-and-hold examples, and 2,100 exit-and-return examples. The annotation identifies visibility transitions within each 0.8-second chunk. The underlying timestamped records also support constructing annotations over windows of arbitrary duration within each recording. This release describes view-frustum transitions, not geometric occlusion behind arbitrary cover. Crosshair and casing effects are disabled in its capture configuration.

Each recording has one 81-frame bidirectional view and one five-chunk autoregressive view.

Long interaction sequences.

Interaction-Long contains 1,791 accepted recordings with blood-hit effects disabled during capture. Each episode contains four actor slots, arranged either as distinct actors or a controlled-return sequence, and zero, one, or two scheduled kills. The accepted collection contains 900 controlled-return and 891 distinct-actor episodes.

The maps are Bromine, Courtfun, Geoplanetary, and Stormkeep. The weapons are MachineGun, Rifle, and Shotgun. Scripted trajectories undergo collision and ground-support checks. Camera schedules use frozen calibration traces, with scan and aiming phases, rather than live feedback that tracks the current enemy.

The reference bank contains 42 appearances with five clean views each. Bindings expose the current actor reference, retain the outgoing reference through its despawn transition, and mask intervals without an actor. Each source episode provides fifteen 81-frame bidirectional windows. The autoregressive view keeps each full sequence and its 75 chunk prompts.

B.4 Arena: Sustained Combat

Arena contains 1,800 one-minute bot-versus-bot recordings in a compact arena, using MachineGun combat and a fixed opponent appearance. Independent bot controls produce ongoing movement and exchanges instead of prescribing a short outcome sequence. The capture configuration bounds locomotion and camera motion and removes crosshair and pickup clutter.

The release constructs the action stream from authoritative gameplay records. Chunk descriptions summarize opponent motion, attacks, visibility, nonlethal damage, kills, and player death from telemetry aligned with the rendered camera. Fully off-screen chunks suppress visible-motion claims. The manifest provides 75 prompts per episode and a fixed opponent reference binding. Arena trains RIGen-Arena.

B.5 Quality Control and Test Set Construction

Capture validation checks route geometry, camera behavior, and consistency between scheduled interactions and recorded events. Manifest validation checks media metadata, finite and aligned controls, complete prompt schedules, and reference bindings.

Test set construction.

We reserve 100 Interaction recordings for quantitative evaluation. Their maps and enemy appearances are excluded from all task-specific training subsets, including Basic Dynamics, Interaction, Interaction-Long, and Arena, and are not used in subsequent adaptation or distillation.

Appendix C Evaluation Details

C.1 Evaluation Protocol

The 100 Xonotic scenarios comprise 50 survival targets and 50 death targets. All RIGen variants in Table  use the same Interaction-trained generator after sliding-window autoregressive training on Interaction-Long, without Arena post-training or distillation. SCOPE and LingBot-World 2.0 receive the prescribed combat outcomes directly as text guidance.

Enemy motion is supplied by source annotations in place of online behavior selection. The interaction agent handles hit, injury, and death reasoning and correction of predicted state. All variants use their own generated video history. Online interaction variants compute guidance from that history, while RIGen (w/ Reference guidance) uses frozen reference guidance.

Fixing enemy motion gives methods common behavior requirements and focuses the comparison on motion adherence and combat-outcome realization, separating behavior selection from its execution in generated video.

We combine controlled experiments, state-dependent branching examples, and continuous closed-loop gameplay. Controlled experiments compare the realization of specified interaction outcomes. Branch comparisons show how state and strategy affect generated behavior, while RIGen-Arena demonstrates the mutual effects of player actions and world events during continued play. Together, these complementary evaluations examine outcome realization, state dependence, and reciprocal interaction in the implemented system.

The external comparisons evaluate complete systems, including their data and training recipes. Learning to realize interaction outcomes is part of the proposed method. Specifying an outcome in text alone does not ensure that a generator can express it. We therefore assess the resulting system capability against external models and use fixed-generator ablations to examine the online interaction mechanisms separately.

Evaluating generated trajectories.

Once a generated trajectory diverges from its source recording, source-engine hit and visibility labels cannot automatically serve as ground truth for the generated scene. Rule execution can be checked against configured transitions, while judging whether a generated attack hits requires independent evidence from the generated video itself. Autonomous behavior also admits multiple valid choices under the same state, calling for task-based criteria that accommodate alternative behaviors. Our benchmark uses prescribed motion and outcome targets with video-based assessment. Event-level visual correctness and autonomous decision quality require annotations or task criteria for the generated trajectories, rather than direct reuse of source-engine labels.

C.2 Metrics

Qwen3.8-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026)] judges complete generated videos offline.

Enemy Behavior.

Enemy Behavior averages satisfaction of directional motion checks within predefined time windows, first within each video and then equally across the 100 scenarios. A check receives credit only when the judge reports it as satisfied and cites visual evidence within its time window. Lateral and depth motion are checked separately, relative to the environment rather than camera-induced image motion. For death-target cases, the prescribed lethal chunk and subsequent motion requirements are excluded for all methods using the same fixed windows.

Final-state Agreement.

Final-state Agreement compares the enemy’s visible state in the final 0.8 seconds with its preassigned survival or death target. The target is withheld from the judge. Unreadable outcomes and failures remain in the denominator and receive no agreement credit. Overall FSA uses all 100 cases. Survival-target and death-target success rates each use the corresponding 50 cases, so overall FSA is their mean. FSA tests whether the prescribed final combat outcome is actually realized. Locally plausible motion and high visual quality do not establish that an opponent survives or dies as required, making outcome agreement a distinct interaction criterion. EB measures motion adherence, while qualitative sequences illustrate intermediate combat responses.

Visual quality and dynamics.

The five visual metrics use the official dimension-specific VBench pipelines on complete generated videos. Each reported score is the mean per-video normalized score multiplied by 100. Dynamic Degree is the percentage of videos meeting the official motion threshold.

The system also generates audio jointly with video.

C.3 Ablations and Reference Comparison

The ablation rows in Table  compare inference-time variants using the same video checkpoint, initial conditions, player inputs, and sampling settings.

  • 1.

    Full RIGen. Predict interaction consequences before generation, apply executable rules, and guide the current chunk. Observe the generated chunk and reconcile predicted state with its visible outcome before the next decision.

  • 2.

    Motion guidance only. Retain player inputs, scene, appearance, and source motion annotations. Remove hit, injury, and death guidance and the online interaction VLM.

  • 3.

    Semantic prompting. The VLM maintains persistent textual state and selects the next chunk’s combat outcome. Rules are supplied as text, without an executable rule engine or an independent verification-and-correction module. This variant compares agent-managed state updates with executable rules and separate visual reconciliation.

  • 4.

    Post-hoc event updates. Generate first, observe events, apply rules, and pass consequence guidance to the following chunk. There is no pre-generation prediction of current-chunk consequences.

  • 5.

    Without reconciliation. Retain pre-generation prediction and executable state updates, but do not correct the planned state from post-generation verification. The next reasoning step still sees the newly generated frames.

  • 6.

    RIGen (w/ Reference guidance). Freeze reference event guidance in advance and remove online VLM calls. Death instructions are derived from source hit annotations combined with configured health and damage rules. They specify a counterfactual task answer, not ground-truth death in the source recording. The guidance is not revised from generated observations, but autoregressive video context uses this variant’s own outputs.

    • C.4 Runtime

    Runtime is measured on a single NVIDIA GB300 GPU. In Table 2, Replay disables online VLM calls and reuses the same guidance, while Online runs the interaction loop. Both include refinement and remain below the target playback rate of 20 FPS.

item.title: 能跑不等于好玩：Recursive Game Creator 用设计师/构建者/玩家/评审四角色闭环把原型熬成产品级 ｜ Recursive Game Creator: An Agentic Product-Level Experience-Oriented Game Harness
item.description:
一句话：把「反复试玩→按体验改」做成 agent 闭环，玩家角色用代码策略批量跑轨迹，取代慢速 GUI 采集的偏差。

要点：

  • Designer 把指令与评审反馈展开成设计图（机制、剧情、反馈系统、视觉资产需求），Builder 再落成可运行的候选游戏
  • Player 是代码原生的：通过程序接口创建并执行可复用策略批量收集玩法轨迹，避开 GUI 采集带来的评估偏差
  • GameCraft-Bench 综合 77.89；GameASG-Bench 严格任务成功率 53.2%（同模型基线 +34.1%），运行时检查通过率 93.4%，用户研究里玩得更久、评分更高

为什么值得看：agent 造游戏的第一阶段只证明了「程序能跑」，第二阶段要解决的是怎么把体验变成可优化的信号；用代码化试玩代替人手点，是这套闭环能规模化的关键。

中文摘要：近期的游戏设计 agent 已经能生成可玩的游戏，但程序正确并不等于玩家觉得好玩：机制是否有趣、难度是否合适、呈现是否连贯、反馈是否及时，才是体验的来源。Recursive Game Creator 把这件事组织成一个递归回路，四个角色对应真实工作室的分工：Designer 把用户指令和 Reviewer 的反馈翻译成含机制、剧情、反馈系统与美术资产需求的计划；Builder 调用外部工具把它实现成候选游戏；Player 是「代码原生」的，直接通过程序接口创建并执行可复用策略，批量收集多样的玩法轨迹，避免 GUI 采集慢且带偏；Reviewer 用基于轨迹的指标推断玩家偏好，结合视觉证据与显式文字偏好，按游戏自身的标准打分，接受更好的版本并给出下一轮修改意见。该方法在 GameCraft-Bench 上综合分 77.89，在 GameASG-Bench 上严格成功率 53.2%、运行时检查通过率 93.4%。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

原文发布：2026-10-06

本期推送：2026-10-25

Recursive Game Creator:
An Agentic Product-Level
Experience-Oriented Game Harness

Abstract

Recent game design agents have made substantial progress in generating playable games. However, program correctness does not ensure an enjoyable experience for players. We present Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented harness to advance agentic game development from rough game prototypes into entertaining games. Recursive Game Creator organizes recursive development around four components: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user instructions and Reviewer’s feedback into detailed plans. The Builder turns these plans into candidate games. The coding-native Player creates and executes reusable policies through programmatic interfaces to efficiently collect diverse gameplay trajectories, mitigating evaluation bias caused by slow GUI-based collection. The Reviewer uses carefully designed trajectory-based metrics to induce player preferences, integrating with visual evidence and explicit textual preferences to evaluate games against game-specific criteria. Finally, the Reviewer accepts the better version and provides improvement reviews for the next round, closing the recursive loop. Our method achieves state-of-the-art overall performance of 77.89 on GameCraft-Bench. On GameASG-Bench, it achieves a strict task success rate of 53.2%, a 34.1% improvement over the same-model baseline, and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate at 93.4% among compared methods. A user study shows longer playtime and higher ratings. Project page is at: imbaldy.github.io/recursive-game-creator.

22footnotetext: Equal contribution.11footnotetext: Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Coding agents can rapidly build runnable games, but successful execution does not establish the quality of play. Engaging mechanics, appropriate difficulty, coherent presentation, and responsive feedback shape player experience. Recent agentic workflows support iterative game development [(Yan et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026)], yet translating gameplay into experience-oriented revision remains challenging. Progress toward product-level games requires a harness that connects development with repeated playtesting and adapts the game to its intended players.

We introduce Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented recursive harness to iteratively refine games. The harness mirrors a real game studio of four typical roles: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer, as shown in Fig. 2. Starting from a user instruction, the Designer expands into a comprehensive design graph that includes gameplay mechanisms, storylines, feedback systems, and visual asset requirements. The Builder calls proper external tools, implementing the game backend, organizing audiovisual assets, and managing the project. Unlike previous work [Huang et al. (2026); Hu et al. (2026)] with a GUI agent to test the game, we propose a Coding-Native Player that writes executable policies to collect gameplay trajectories efficiently and effectively. The Experience-Oriented Reviewer leverages diverse gameplay trajectories to conduct a thorough, game-specific diagnosis, including difficulty assessment, corner-bug discovery, and time-in-game recording. The Reviewer also leverages screenshots to evaluate game appearance. Finally, the Reviewer provides feedback to the Designer for next-round refinement.

Although coding agents can interact with games through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) [(Huang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a)], screenshot-driven testing may omit structured state, legal actions, events, and progress signals available through programmatic interfaces. Requiring visual interpretation and a model decision for each action adds latency and limits frequent, fine-grained rollouts. Coding agents are primarily optimized for code generation and reasoning, rather than fine-grained visual game-state interpretation. To better align gameplay with these strengths, our Coding-Native Player provides frequent, repeatable, and diverse interaction through programmatic interfaces. Player constructs reusable policies with different strategies and capabilities. We execute policies to collect trajectories. This separates fast gameplay control from policy construction and the Reviewer’s visual assessment. It also preserves directly exposed state and event information for subsequent analysis. The Coding-Native Player offers several distinct advantages, including: high-frequency control, efficient trajectory collection, diverse capability simulation, and reproducible results.

The Reviewer provides comprehensive feedback from collected trajectories. The Experience-Oriented Reviewer combines general standards such as playtime, success rate, and game-specific rubric evaluations to identify problems. Different types of games matter in different aspects. Beyond general evaluation, the Reviewer further analyzes suitable specific features of each game. For example, Responsive steering matters in racing, whereas a meaningful storyline and coherent dialogue matter in a visual novel. The Reviewer actively figures out these specific analysis criteria. The Reviewer expresses inferred preferences as structured text describing the desired experience, supporting observations, and revision priorities. Users can also supply explicit textual preferences during play. These inputs guide the next design plan, allowing refinement to address both game quality and a player’s taste.

The recursive loop connects these stages across versions. Policy execution produces trajectories. Trajectory and visual analysis produce experience and preference feedback. The Designer translates feedback into a plan. The Builder implements a new candidate for further testing. We evaluate the games on GameCraft-Bench [(Luo et al., 2026)] and GameASG-Bench [(Zhang et al., 2026c)]. In our GameCraft-Bench evaluation, three refinement rounds raise the overall score from 72.70 to 77.89 (+5.19), with improvements in every reported category. On GameASG-Bench, the harness raises the success rate from 9.47 to 25/47 tasks and achieves a highest mean runtime check pass rate of 93.4%.

We make three contributions.

  • •

    Product-level game recursive harness. We connect a multi-round closed-loop game design harness, Recursive Game Creator, that supports product-level game evolution and user-directed customization.

  • •

    Coding-native and experience-oriented game evolution. We introduce coding-native player collects diverse gameplay trajectories for comprehensive evaluation. The experience-oriented Reviewer combines general and game-specific rubrics to support preference-informed feedback.

  • •

    State-of-the-art game design capability. Recursive Game Creator achieves the highest overall score on GameCraft-Bench and GameASG-Bench among all baselines. Our user study further proves the customized game evolution ability guided by preferences inferred from human play.

    • 2 Related Work

    Applications of coding agents.

    Code generation allows agents to work beyond software development, including video creation and embodied tasks. For educational videos, Code2Video combines planning, Python code generation, and visual review to improve the rendered layout [(Chen et al., 2025b)]. VideoAgent uses generated code to create animations and combines them with slides and narration for scientific videos [(Liang et al., 2026)]. VideoCoCo uses a coding agent to write Blender programs that produce dynamic scene drafts. A video generation model then turns these drafts into realistic videos [(Li et al., 2026)]. In embodied control, Code as Policies turns language instructions into robot policy code that connects perception with control APIs [(Liang et al., 2023)]. ProgPrompt uses program-like descriptions of available actions and objects to generate robot task plans [(Singh et al., 2022)]. Voyager builds a library of reusable Minecraft skills and revises their code using environment feedback and execution errors [(Wang et al., 2023)]. Eureka extends code generation to reward design, using feedback from policy training to revise reward functions [(Ma et al., 2024)]. Across these applications, code gives agents a way to express, execute, and reuse structured behavior. These works motivate our use of executable policies for gameplay testing. Our focus is on connecting executable play, experience and preference analysis, and continued game evolution within a recursive harness aimed at product-level games.

    Game development with coding agents.

    Coding agents generate and edit game programs within an explicit runtime. General software-agent systems such as MetaGPT and ChatDev organize planning, implementation, and testing [(Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024)]. GameGPT applies role-based collaboration to game development [(Chen et al., 2025a)]. AutoUE targets Unreal Engine workflows, while OpenGame combines reusable project templates with debugging knowledge [(Yin et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026)]. Beyond initial generation, AVR-Agent iterates JavaScript content using audio-visual recordings and multimodal comparisons, and Harness-of-Harness supports persistent development with independent assessment [(Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025; Yan et al., 2026)]. Concurrent work RSIGame explores recursive self-improvement for agentic game development, using iterative evaluation feedback to refine generated games [(Wu et al., 2026)]. GameDevBench and GameCraft-Bench evaluate engine-grounded development and interactive artifacts. GameXpert-Bench extends evaluation across generation, repair, and cumulative optimization [(Chi et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026)]. However, generating runnable artifacts and repairing functional bugs do not by themselves establish an engaging player experience. We go further by connecting policy generation, trajectory collection, experience and preference analysis, and multi-round game revision, making the quality of play and continued customization explicit refinement targets.

    Feedback refinement and preference alignment.

    Self-Refine and Reflexion use feedback to revise outputs or subsequent attempts [(Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023)]. AFlow, EvoMAC, and the Darwin Gödel Machine instead optimize workflows, collaboration, or agent code [(Zhang et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b)]. A related line makes the optimization objective sensitive to human preferences. Trajectory comparisons can train reward models, while RLHF and direct preference optimization align language-model behavior with preferred outputs [(Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023)]. VideoDPO extends preference optimization to video diffusion using automatically scored pairs, which should be distinguished from direct human judgments [(Liu et al., 2025)]. In games, experience-driven procedural content generation connects player modeling to content adaptation, and experience-driven RL generates racetracks toward target affective patterns [(Yannakakis and Togelius, 2011; Barthet et al., 2024)]. These works motivate feedback tied to the intended experience, while differing in what is optimized and who supplies the feedback. Our harness uses structured preference feedback to revise the game artifact while keeping the underlying model parameters fixed. Explicit user requests and preferences inferred from play inform subsequent design and implementation rounds.

    3 Recursive Game Creator, Experience-Oriented Game Refinement

    Recursive Game Creator organizes game development as a closed loop involving the Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user requirements and evaluation feedback into a structured plan specifying intended experience, concrete changes, acceptance goals, and asset needs. The Builder implements this plan through draft and integrate stages, incorporates required assets, and performs targeted checks to produce a playable candidate.

    The Player writes and executes code policies through the game’s programmatic interface, collecting behavioral trajectories and available visual records. These trajectories capture states, actions, events, progress, elapsed time, and termination outcomes, providing inspectable evidence of play. The Reviewer combines Player reports with behavioral and visual evidence to assess the experience against shared and game-specific criteria, and compares anonymized evidence from the candidate and retained versions. These evidence-based judgments inform version retention, while the Reviewer’s findings guide the Designer’s next plan. This loop connects game construction, policy-based play, experience assessment, and iterative refinement.

    3.1 Designer & Builder

    The Designer expands the user brief into the core play loop, mechanics, progression and difficulty, visual direction, and production priorities. It combines the available game state and recent feedback with user requirements to form a plan:

    Pₜ=Design(U,Gₜ,Hₜ₋₁)=(hₜ,Δₜ,Aₜ,Xₜ),

    where U, Gₜ, and Hₜ₋₁ denote the user brief, current game, and recent feedback when available. The hypothesis hₜ states the intended experiential improvement and its basis; Δₜ specifies concrete changes and strengths to preserve; Aₜ defines acceptance goals in terms of scenes, player inputs, and observable outcomes; and Xₜ lists asset requests. This representation turns experience goals into implementation decisions and testable objectives.

    Subsequently, the Builder inherits the implementation plans from the Designer and selects implementation tools according to the game’s mechanics, interaction requirements, visual direction, and asset needs. Implementation proceeds from a playable draft to an integrated candidate:

    Zₜ=Draft(Gₜ,Δₜ), Xₜ^*=Generate(Xₜ;Zₜ), Cₜ=Integrate(Zₜ,Xₜ^*),

    where Zₜ is the draft, Xₜ denotes requested assets, Xₜ^* contains assets actually generated by the framework, and Cₜ is the integrated candidate.

    During drafting, the Builder implements the core loop and planned changes, using placeholders when needed. The framework executes asset requests and makes generated files available for integration. The Builder then checks their presentation in gameplay scenes and their interaction with collision, animation, and interaction regions. Targeted self-checks and configured project checks complement the Player’s broader play evidence. This staged workflow links asset production to its in-game integration and validation; generating an asset alone does not establish an improvement to play.

    3.2 Coding-Native Player

    The Player constructs executable gameplay policies, separating policy generation from repeated interaction. Each policy uses the game’s exposed state to choose valid actions and collect a trajectory. This enables state-based control without requiring a language-model response or visual interpretation at every action. For candidate version Cₜ at round t, policy π_t,k produces trajectory τ_t,k:

    τ_t,k=Rollout(Cₜ,π_t,k), 𝔼ₜ={(τ_t,k,V_t,k)}ₖ₌₁^K.

    Here, Cₜ is the candidate game version, π_t,k is an executable policy, τ_t,k is its trajectory, and V_t,k denotes visual records when available. The evidence set 𝔼ₜ contains records from K rollouts.

    Policy construction and execution. The Player reads the state schema, available actions, and testing objectives, then writes a policy that observes states, chooses actions, and repeats until the task ends or the rollout budget is reached. Policies run through the game’s programmatic or command-line interface. Rollout requests are dispatched as execution jobs, allowing repeated trials and separate game instances. The Player inspects outcomes and execution failures and revises policy code when needed. It does not use a conversational response as a substitute for executing the rollout.

    Diverse policies and trajectory records. Policies vary in strategy, skill, exploration, and risk tolerance. For example, one favors fast progress while another explores optional content. Their rollouts record exposed states, actions, events, progress, elapsed time, and termination outcomes. Parallel or repeated execution supplies multiple attempts and failure cases under known policy settings. These records are passed to the Reviewer. Visual capture and presentation assessment belong to the review stage. Policy and observation settings are recorded with each trajectory to support comparisons across game versions.

    Behavioral evidence and testing cost. The trajectories support estimates of completion, difficulty, explored content, and points of failure or stagnation. Direct state and event access avoids reconstructing these variables from every rendered frame. Lightweight execution and parallel sampling make repeated trials practical, while policies with different strategies can expose failures that one strategy misses. The resulting records connect gameplay behavior to the Reviewer’s diagnosis and the next design revision. Total testing cost includes policy generation, repair, execution, and review. Proxy strategies provide varied test behavior, but do not establish that they represent the full human player population. Human trajectories and explicit feedback supply additional evidence about individual preferences.

    3.3 Experience-Oriented Reviewer

    The Reviewer combines behavioral trajectories, visual observations, and user input into an experience assessment and actionable revision feedback. Its inputs are associated with the evaluated game version and policy or player session. The assessment preserves the distinction between observed behavior, inferred preference, and explicit user requests.

    Shared signals, success rate and playtime. The coding-native Player supplies many trajectories from policies with different skills and strategies. The Reviewer uses this evidence to estimate success rates and examine where play ends or gets stuck. Success that comes too easily may offer little challenge, while repeated failure may cause frustration. The goal is therefore a suitable level of difficulty for the intended players, not the highest possible success rate. Comparing outcomes across policies helps assess whether progress is achievable and whether stronger play is rewarded. For version comparisons, policy settings and observation access must remain consistent.

    The same trajectories record playtime. The Reviewer examines run times together with progress, explored content, and reasons for stopping. This helps distinguish a long run with varied activity from one spent stuck at the same point. Success rate and playtime therefore support a broader assessment of difficulty and playability. Both remain measures of the tested policies. Proxy playtime alone does not show human interest or enjoyment.

    Game-specific rubric. The Reviewer starts from shared assessment dimensions, including control responsiveness, content richness, narrative or progression pacing, visual coherence, and support for exploration or replay. It instantiates these dimensions as criteria suited to the game’s genre and intended experience. For example, a racing game may require clear track guidance, responsive steering, and visible collision feedback, while a visual novel may require coherent dialogue and choices with discernible consequences. The Reviewer checks consistency between rules, visual cues, and observed play, and explains strengths, weaknesses, and tradeoffs rather than averaging unrelated criteria.

    Visual evidence and diagnosis. The Reviewer obtains sampled screenshots and available recordings from rendered gameplay, and examines them alongside play reports without seeing source code or version order. Trajectories show where a policy succeeds, fails, or stops progressing. Rendered views show what a player could see at those moments. The Reviewer uses them to assess text readability, visual style, and action feedback. Visual review is separate from the fast control loop, so collecting a trajectory does not require interpreting an image at every step. Brief effects or missing feedback may still require a recording rather than a few frames.

    Each observation is tied to its game version, policy, and replay. The Reviewer separates what happened from why it may have happened. A failed turn could reflect poor controls, an unclear cue, or a weak policy. When the cause is uncertain, the feedback specifies what further evidence would help resolve it.

    Structured experience and preference feedback. The Reviewer translates trajectory patterns, visual findings, and explicit user input into a textual preference record. The record describes the desired experience, supporting evidence, whether a preference is inferred or user-stated, and the corresponding revision priority. A tendency to explore optional areas, for example, may suggest interest in discovery. A user’s request for less demanding combat supplies an explicit difficulty target. These observations inform design hypotheses rather than establishing preferences from playtime alone. The Designer receives this record alongside concrete changes and follow-up checks for the next revision.

    Version comparison and retention. The Reviewer compares a candidate with the retained game using the same shared signals and game-specific criteria. It checks whether the changes address the earlier revision goals and introduce new problems. The output is an A/B preference, a tie, or an unavailable judgment, with reasons and evidence paths. Feedback states the problem, its possible cause, its effect on play, and a revision goal with a follow-up check. The harness maps the Reviewer’s judgment back to the game versions and selects which artifact to retain.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate Recursive Game Creator on GameCraft-Bench and GameASG-Bench. These benchmarks test game quality and whether generated games meet their requirements. We then examine rollout coverage, representative development examples, and expert assessments of experience-oriented refinement.

    4.1 Main Results

    4.1.1 GameCraft-Bench

    GameCraft-Bench evaluates complete Godot games through replayed gameplay and game-specific rubrics covering mechanics, content depth, functional visuals, and art [(Luo et al., 2026)]. We run three refinement rounds on 45 selected tasks [(Yan et al., 2026)] from GameCraft-Bench and report category and overall scores after each round in Table 1.

    The GPT-6 Astra baseline scores 71.26 overall. Recursive Game Creator improves overall quality from 72.70 in the first round to 77.89 in the third, a gain of 5.19 points across rounds and 6.63 points over the same-model baseline. The final score exceeds the strongest reported baseline by 6.37 points, and all five categories improve across our three rounds. Action shows the largest increase, from 67.96 to 77.62 (+9.66). Its first two rounds remain below the same-model baseline Action score of 73.33, before reaching 77.62 in the third. One possible explanation is that action-game quality depends on coordinated changes to controls, collision handling, combat feedback, and progression, whose interactions can require several playtest and revision cycles. The larger late-stage gain is consistent with this interpretation, although the category scores alone do not identify its cause.

    4.1.2 GameASG-Bench

    GameASG-Bench tests whether generated browser games meet their source and behavior requirements [(Zhang et al., 2026c)]. L1 checks the source code, while L2 runs the game in a browser. P0 covers startup and the test interface, P1 covers required gameplay, and P2 covers extended features. Task success requires valid delivery, completed evaluation, and passing every L1 check and every applicable L2 P0/P1 check. We report this measure alongside check pass rates in Table 2.

    Recursive Game Creator passes 25 of 47 tasks (53.2%), with mean L1 and L2 pass rates of 98.3% and 93.4%, respectively. Its P0, P1, and P2 pass rates are 99.0%, 92.2%, and 93.9%. The mean L2 and extended-feature (P2) scores are the highest among the reported configurations.

    4.2 Qualitative Analysis of Multi-Round RSI

    Fig. 1(a) shows Twilight Front, which adds a fog-of-war display and expands its hero roster. Fig. 1(b) shows KAZE, with changing race conditions, a career garage, and car liveries. Fig. 1(c) shows See You Tomorrow, combining character dialogue, player choices, event art, and a classroom menu. These examples illustrate the range of content and interfaces supported by the recursive harness.

    We additionally ask the RSI harness to develop games with several themes and examine how they evolve through repeated revision. Fig. 3 compares an action game in panel (a), a visual novel in panel (b), and Meme Arena in panel (c). Each panel follows early, intermediate, and later versions (V1–V3), comparing corresponding mechanics, content, or presentation features. Together, these examples show how multi-round recursive self-improvement expands playable content and makes game state, available actions, and feedback easier to interpret.

    Action game, combat and progression feedback.

    The comparison in Fig. 3(a) tracks changes in character art, skill effects, encounters, boss mechanics, interface elements, and upgrade feedback. Across the displayed versions, encounter portraits and upgrade feedback accompany richer combat effects. These changes address both the available content and the way progression and combat state are communicated. The comparison shows refinement extending beyond execution and bug repair to the readability and presentation of the play loop.

    Visual novel, contextual choices and narrative presentation.

    As shown in Fig. 3(b), the visual novel evolves in dialogue, choices, scene detail, illustrated combat, emotional staging, and reading support. The game moves from prose-heavy exchanges toward separate speaking turns, illustrated events, and choices grounded in the current scene. The resulting revisions affect how readers follow the narrative and understand their available decisions, illustrating experience-oriented refinement in a genre with different demands from action games.

    Meme Arena, action cues and combat presentation.

    The Meme Arena versions shown in Fig. 3(c) retain the same three-character roster while evolving in arena detail, skill-specific effects, summon attacks, finisher emphasis, selection interfaces, and movement guidance. The scripted capture views make these feature-level changes visible across versions. Fig. 2 uses related Meme Arena views to illustrate the Reviewer’s comparison stage. Across all three games, the qualitative evidence concerns concrete revision targets, including communicating game state, presenting content, and clarifying available actions.

    4.3 Player Exploration Analysis

    As shown in Fig. 4, the coding-native Player explores an FPS scene through repeated policy rollouts. The recorded policy rollouts reach areas across the map, including building interiors. A reusable policy collects this evidence without a model call for every action. The GUI routes are illustrative, so the figure shows coverage rather than a measured speedup. A controlled comparison must match budgets and observation access, including the cost of policy construction, repair, execution, and review.

    4.4 User Study of Experience-Oriented Customization

    This assessment examines whether recursive revision moves the game toward the intended player experience, using explicit user preferences or preferences inferred by the Reviewer from gameplay as revision inputs. Table 3 reports controls, playability, depth, and art on a 1–10 scale, together with average playtime. From the first to third round, controls improve from 2 to 8, playability from 1 to 7, depth from 3 to 6, and art from 2 to 8. Average playtime rises from 1.50 to 12.41 minutes. The changes span interaction, content, and presentation, consistent with the harness’s experience-oriented revision targets.

    5 Conclusion

    Recursive Game Creator is an experience-oriented recursive harness that connects design, tool-assisted implementation, executable play, and preference-informed review. Its coding-native Player collects reusable gameplay trajectories through programmatic interfaces, while the Reviewer combines behavioral evidence, visual observations, and user input to guide version selection and subsequent revisions. This policy-to-trajectory-to-feedback loop enables continued game evolution with fixed model parameters. Across our evaluations, Recursive Game Creator achieves state-of-the-art overall performance on GameCraft-Bench and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate among compared methods on GameASG-Bench. Development examples and expert assessments characterize improvements in controls, content, and presentation. The harness provides a foundation for advancing functional prototypes toward product-level games and evaluating continued adaptation to individual players.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把「反复试玩→按体验改」做成 agent 闭环，玩家角色用代码策略批量跑轨迹，取代慢速 GUI 采集的偏差。

要点：

  • Designer 把指令与评审反馈展开成设计图（机制、剧情、反馈系统、视觉资产需求），Builder 再落成可运行的候选游戏
  • Player 是代码原生的：通过程序接口创建并执行可复用策略批量收集玩法轨迹，避开 GUI 采集带来的评估偏差
  • GameCraft-Bench 综合 77.89；GameASG-Bench 严格任务成功率 53.2%（同模型基线 +34.1%），运行时检查通过率 93.4%，用户研究里玩得更久、评分更高

为什么值得看：agent 造游戏的第一阶段只证明了「程序能跑」，第二阶段要解决的是怎么把体验变成可优化的信号；用代码化试玩代替人手点，是这套闭环能规模化的关键。

中文摘要：近期的游戏设计 agent 已经能生成可玩的游戏，但程序正确并不等于玩家觉得好玩：机制是否有趣、难度是否合适、呈现是否连贯、反馈是否及时，才是体验的来源。Recursive Game Creator 把这件事组织成一个递归回路，四个角色对应真实工作室的分工：Designer 把用户指令和 Reviewer 的反馈翻译成含机制、剧情、反馈系统与美术资产需求的计划；Builder 调用外部工具把它实现成候选游戏；Player 是「代码原生」的，直接通过程序接口创建并执行可复用策略，批量收集多样的玩法轨迹，避免 GUI 采集慢且带偏；Reviewer 用基于轨迹的指标推断玩家偏好，结合视觉证据与显式文字偏好，按游戏自身的标准打分，接受更好的版本并给出下一轮修改意见。该方法在 GameCraft-Bench 上综合分 77.89，在 GameASG-Bench 上严格成功率 53.2%、运行时检查通过率 93.4%。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

原文发布：2026-10-06

本期推送：2026-10-25

Recursive Game Creator:
An Agentic Product-Level
Experience-Oriented Game Harness

Abstract

Recent game design agents have made substantial progress in generating playable games. However, program correctness does not ensure an enjoyable experience for players. We present Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented harness to advance agentic game development from rough game prototypes into entertaining games. Recursive Game Creator organizes recursive development around four components: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user instructions and Reviewer’s feedback into detailed plans. The Builder turns these plans into candidate games. The coding-native Player creates and executes reusable policies through programmatic interfaces to efficiently collect diverse gameplay trajectories, mitigating evaluation bias caused by slow GUI-based collection. The Reviewer uses carefully designed trajectory-based metrics to induce player preferences, integrating with visual evidence and explicit textual preferences to evaluate games against game-specific criteria. Finally, the Reviewer accepts the better version and provides improvement reviews for the next round, closing the recursive loop. Our method achieves state-of-the-art overall performance of 77.89 on GameCraft-Bench. On GameASG-Bench, it achieves a strict task success rate of 53.2%, a 34.1% improvement over the same-model baseline, and the highest mean runtime-check pass rate at 93.4% among compared methods. A user study shows longer playtime and higher ratings. Project page is at: imbaldy.github.io/recursive-game-creator.

22footnotetext: Equal contribution.11footnotetext: Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Coding agents can rapidly build runnable games, but successful execution does not establish the quality of play. Engaging mechanics, appropriate difficulty, coherent presentation, and responsive feedback shape player experience. Recent agentic workflows support iterative game development [(Yan et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026)], yet translating gameplay into experience-oriented revision remains challenging. Progress toward product-level games requires a harness that connects development with repeated playtesting and adapts the game to its intended players.

We introduce Recursive Game Creator, an experience-oriented recursive harness to iteratively refine games. The harness mirrors a real game studio of four typical roles: Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer, as shown in Fig. 2. Starting from a user instruction, the Designer expands into a comprehensive design graph that includes gameplay mechanisms, storylines, feedback systems, and visual asset requirements. The Builder calls proper external tools, implementing the game backend, organizing audiovisual assets, and managing the project. Unlike previous work [Huang et al. (2026); Hu et al. (2026)] with a GUI agent to test the game, we propose a Coding-Native Player that writes executable policies to collect gameplay trajectories efficiently and effectively. The Experience-Oriented Reviewer leverages diverse gameplay trajectories to conduct a thorough, game-specific diagnosis, including difficulty assessment, corner-bug discovery, and time-in-game recording. The Reviewer also leverages screenshots to evaluate game appearance. Finally, the Reviewer provides feedback to the Designer for next-round refinement.

Although coding agents can interact with games through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) [(Huang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a)], screenshot-driven testing may omit structured state, legal actions, events, and progress signals available through programmatic interfaces. Requiring visual interpretation and a model decision for each action adds latency and limits frequent, fine-grained rollouts. Coding agents are primarily optimized for code generation and reasoning, rather than fine-grained visual game-state interpretation. To better align gameplay with these strengths, our Coding-Native Player provides frequent, repeatable, and diverse interaction through programmatic interfaces. Player constructs reusable policies with different strategies and capabilities. We execute policies to collect trajectories. This separates fast gameplay control from policy construction and the Reviewer’s visual assessment. It also preserves directly exposed state and event information for subsequent analysis. The Coding-Native Player offers several distinct advantages, including: high-frequency control, efficient trajectory collection, diverse capability simulation, and reproducible results.

The Reviewer provides comprehensive feedback from collected trajectories. The Experience-Oriented Reviewer combines general standards such as playtime, success rate, and game-specific rubric evaluations to identify problems. Different types of games matter in different aspects. Beyond general evaluation, the Reviewer further analyzes suitable specific features of each game. For example, Responsive steering matters in racing, whereas a meaningful storyline and coherent dialogue matter in a visual novel. The Reviewer actively figures out these specific analysis criteria. The Reviewer expresses inferred preferences as structured text describing the desired experience, supporting observations, and revision priorities. Users can also supply explicit textual preferences during play. These inputs guide the next design plan, allowing refinement to address both game quality and a player’s taste.

The recursive loop connects these stages across versions. Policy execution produces trajectories. Trajectory and visual analysis produce experience and preference feedback. The Designer translates feedback into a plan. The Builder implements a new candidate for further testing. We evaluate the games on GameCraft-Bench [(Luo et al., 2026)] and GameASG-Bench [(Zhang et al., 2026c)]. In our GameCraft-Bench evaluation, three refinement rounds raise the overall score from 72.70 to 77.89 (+5.19), with improvements in every reported category. On GameASG-Bench, the harness raises the success rate from 9.47 to 25/47 tasks and achieves a highest mean runtime check pass rate of 93.4%.

We make three contributions.

  • •

    Product-level game recursive harness. We connect a multi-round closed-loop game design harness, Recursive Game Creator, that supports product-level game evolution and user-directed customization.

  • •

    Coding-native and experience-oriented game evolution. We introduce coding-native player collects diverse gameplay trajectories for comprehensive evaluation. The experience-oriented Reviewer combines general and game-specific rubrics to support preference-informed feedback.

  • •

    State-of-the-art game design capability. Recursive Game Creator achieves the highest overall score on GameCraft-Bench and GameASG-Bench among all baselines. Our user study further proves the customized game evolution ability guided by preferences inferred from human play.

    • 2 Related Work

    Applications of coding agents.

    Code generation allows agents to work beyond software development, including video creation and embodied tasks. For educational videos, Code2Video combines planning, Python code generation, and visual review to improve the rendered layout [(Chen et al., 2025b)]. VideoAgent uses generated code to create animations and combines them with slides and narration for scientific videos [(Liang et al., 2026)]. VideoCoCo uses a coding agent to write Blender programs that produce dynamic scene drafts. A video generation model then turns these drafts into realistic videos [(Li et al., 2026)]. In embodied control, Code as Policies turns language instructions into robot policy code that connects perception with control APIs [(Liang et al., 2023)]. ProgPrompt uses program-like descriptions of available actions and objects to generate robot task plans [(Singh et al., 2022)]. Voyager builds a library of reusable Minecraft skills and revises their code using environment feedback and execution errors [(Wang et al., 2023)]. Eureka extends code generation to reward design, using feedback from policy training to revise reward functions [(Ma et al., 2024)]. Across these applications, code gives agents a way to express, execute, and reuse structured behavior. These works motivate our use of executable policies for gameplay testing. Our focus is on connecting executable play, experience and preference analysis, and continued game evolution within a recursive harness aimed at product-level games.

    Game development with coding agents.

    Coding agents generate and edit game programs within an explicit runtime. General software-agent systems such as MetaGPT and ChatDev organize planning, implementation, and testing [(Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024)]. GameGPT applies role-based collaboration to game development [(Chen et al., 2025a)]. AutoUE targets Unreal Engine workflows, while OpenGame combines reusable project templates with debugging knowledge [(Yin et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026)]. Beyond initial generation, AVR-Agent iterates JavaScript content using audio-visual recordings and multimodal comparisons, and Harness-of-Harness supports persistent development with independent assessment [(Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025; Yan et al., 2026)]. Concurrent work RSIGame explores recursive self-improvement for agentic game development, using iterative evaluation feedback to refine generated games [(Wu et al., 2026)]. GameDevBench and GameCraft-Bench evaluate engine-grounded development and interactive artifacts. GameXpert-Bench extends evaluation across generation, repair, and cumulative optimization [(Chi et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026)]. However, generating runnable artifacts and repairing functional bugs do not by themselves establish an engaging player experience. We go further by connecting policy generation, trajectory collection, experience and preference analysis, and multi-round game revision, making the quality of play and continued customization explicit refinement targets.

    Feedback refinement and preference alignment.

    Self-Refine and Reflexion use feedback to revise outputs or subsequent attempts [(Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023)]. AFlow, EvoMAC, and the Darwin Gödel Machine instead optimize workflows, collaboration, or agent code [(Zhang et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b)]. A related line makes the optimization objective sensitive to human preferences. Trajectory comparisons can train reward models, while RLHF and direct preference optimization align language-model behavior with preferred outputs [(Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023)]. VideoDPO extends preference optimization to video diffusion using automatically scored pairs, which should be distinguished from direct human judgments [(Liu et al., 2025)]. In games, experience-driven procedural content generation connects player modeling to content adaptation, and experience-driven RL generates racetracks toward target affective patterns [(Yannakakis and Togelius, 2011; Barthet et al., 2024)]. These works motivate feedback tied to the intended experience, while differing in what is optimized and who supplies the feedback. Our harness uses structured preference feedback to revise the game artifact while keeping the underlying model parameters fixed. Explicit user requests and preferences inferred from play inform subsequent design and implementation rounds.

    3 Recursive Game Creator, Experience-Oriented Game Refinement

    Recursive Game Creator organizes game development as a closed loop involving the Designer, Builder, Player, and Reviewer. The Designer translates user requirements and evaluation feedback into a structured plan specifying intended experience, concrete changes, acceptance goals, and asset needs. The Builder implements this plan through draft and integrate stages, incorporates required assets, and performs targeted checks to produce a playable candidate.

    The Player writes and executes code policies through the game’s programmatic interface, collecting behavioral trajectories and available visual records. These trajectories capture states, actions, events, progress, elapsed time, and termination outcomes, providing inspectable evidence of play. The Reviewer combines Player reports with behavioral and visual evidence to assess the experience against shared and game-specific criteria, and compares anonymized evidence from the candidate and retained versions. These evidence-based judgments inform version retention, while the Reviewer’s findings guide the Designer’s next plan. This loop connects game construction, policy-based play, experience assessment, and iterative refinement.

    3.1 Designer & Builder

    The Designer expands the user brief into the core play loop, mechanics, progression and difficulty, visual direction, and production priorities. It combines the available game state and recent feedback with user requirements to form a plan:

    Pₜ=Design(U,Gₜ,Hₜ₋₁)=(hₜ,Δₜ,Aₜ,Xₜ),

    where U, Gₜ, and Hₜ₋₁ denote the user brief, current game, and recent feedback when available. The hypothesis hₜ states the intended experiential improvement and its basis; Δₜ specifies concrete changes and strengths to preserve; Aₜ defines acceptance goals in terms of scenes, player inputs, and observable outcomes; and Xₜ lists asset requests. This representation turns experience goals into implementation decisions and testable objectives.

    Subsequently, the Builder inherits the implementation plans from the Designer and selects implementation tools according to the game’s mechanics, interaction requirements, visual direction, and asset needs. Implementation proceeds from a playable draft to an integrated candidate:

    Zₜ=Draft(Gₜ,Δₜ), Xₜ^*=Generate(Xₜ;Zₜ), Cₜ=Integrate(Zₜ,Xₜ^*),

    where Zₜ is the draft, Xₜ denotes requested assets, Xₜ^* contains assets actually generated by the framework, and Cₜ is the integrated candidate.

    During drafting, the Builder implements the core loop and planned changes, using placeholders when needed. The framework executes asset requests and makes generated files available for integration. The Builder then checks their presentation in gameplay scenes and their interaction with collision, animation, and interaction regions. Targeted self-checks and configured project checks complement the Player’s broader play evidence. This staged workflow links asset production to its in-game integration and validation; generating an asset alone does not establish an improvement to play.

    3.2 Coding-Native Player

    The Player constructs executable gameplay policies, separating policy generation from repeated interaction. Each policy uses the game’s exposed state to choose valid actions and collect a trajectory. This enables state-based control without requiring a language-model response or visual interpretation at every action. For candidate version Cₜ at round t, policy π_t,k produces trajectory τ_t,k:

    τ_t,k=Rollout(Cₜ,π_t,k), 𝔼ₜ={(τ_t,k,V_t,k)}ₖ₌₁^K.

    Here, Cₜ is the candidate game version, π_t,k is an executable policy, τ_t,k is its trajectory, and V_t,k denotes visual records when available. The evidence set 𝔼ₜ contains records from K rollouts.

    Policy construction and execution. The Player reads the state schema, available actions, and testing objectives, then writes a policy that observes states, chooses actions, and repeats until the task ends or the rollout budget is reached. Policies run through the game’s programmatic or command-line interface. Rollout requests are dispatched as execution jobs, allowing repeated trials and separate game instances. The Player inspects outcomes and execution failures and revises policy code when needed. It does not use a conversational response as a substitute for executing the rollout.

    Diverse policies and trajectory records. Policies vary in strategy, skill, exploration, and risk tolerance. For example, one favors fast progress while another explores optional content. Their rollouts record exposed states, actions, events, progress, elapsed time, and termination outcomes. Parallel or repeated execution supplies multiple attempts and failure cases under known policy settings. These records are passed to the Reviewer. Visual capture and presentation assessment belong to the review stage. Policy and observation settings are recorded with each trajectory to support comparisons across game versions.

    Behavioral evidence and testing cost. The trajectories support estimates of completion, difficulty, explored content, and points of failure or stagnation. Direct state and event access avoids reconstructing these variables from every rendered frame. Lightweight execution and parallel sampling make repeated trials practical, while policies with different strategies can expose failures that one strategy misses. The resulting records connect gameplay behavior to the Reviewer’s diagnosis and the next design revision. Total testing cost includes policy generation, repair, execution, and review. Proxy strategies provide varied test behavior, but do not establish that they represent the full human player population. Human trajectories and explicit feedback supply additional evidence about individual preferences.

    3.3 Experience-Oriented Reviewer

    The Reviewer combines behavioral trajectories, visual observations, and user input into an experience assessment and actionable revision feedback. Its inputs are associated with the evaluated game version and policy or player session. The assessment preserves the distinction between observed behavior, inferred preference, and explicit user requests.

    Shared signals, success rate and playtime. The coding-native Player supplies many trajectories from policies with different skills and strategies. The Reviewer uses this evidence to estimate success rates and examine where play ends or gets stuck. Success that comes too easily may offer little challenge, while repeated failure may cause frustration. The goal is therefore a suitable level of difficulty for the intended players, not the highest possible success rate. Comparing outcomes across policies helps assess whether progress is achievable and whether stronger play is rewarded. For version comparisons, policy settings and observation access must remain consistent.

    The same trajectories record playtime. The Reviewer examines run times together with progress, explored content, and reasons for stopping. This helps distinguish a long run with varied activity from one spent stuck at the same point. Success rate and playtime therefore support a broader assessment of difficulty and playability. Both remain measures of the tested policies. Proxy playtime alone does not show human interest or enjoyment.

    Game-specific rubric. The Reviewer starts from shared assessment dimensions, including control responsiveness, content richness, narrative or progression pacing, visual coherence, and support for exploration or replay. It instantiates these dimensions as criteria suited to the game’s genre and intended experience. For example, a racing game may require clear track guidance, responsive steering, and visible collision feedback, while a visual novel may require coherent dialogue and choices with discernible consequences. The Reviewer checks consistency between rules, visual cues, and observed play, and explains strengths, weaknesses, and tradeoffs rather than averaging unrelated criteria.

    Visual evidence and diagnosis. The Reviewer obtains sampled screenshots and available recordings from rendered gameplay, and examines them alongside play reports without seeing source code or version order. Trajectories show where a policy succeeds, fails, or stops progressing. Rendered views show what a player could see at those moments. The Reviewer uses them to assess text readability, visual style, and action feedback. Visual review is separate from the fast control loop, so collecting a trajectory does not require interpreting an image at every step. Brief effects or missing feedback may still require a recording rather than a few frames.

    Each observation is tied to its game version, policy, and replay. The Reviewer separates what happened from why it may have happened. A failed turn could reflect poor controls, an unclear cue, or a weak policy. When the cause is uncertain, the feedback specifies what further evidence would help resolve it.

    Structured experience and preference feedback. The Reviewer translates trajectory patterns, visual findings, and explicit user input into a textual preference record. The record describes the desired experience, supporting evidence, whether a preference is inferred or user-stated, and the corresponding revision priority. A tendency to explore optional areas, for example, may suggest interest in discovery. A user’s request for less demanding combat supplies an explicit difficulty target. These observations inform design hypotheses rather than establishing preferences from playtime alone. The Designer receives this record alongside concrete changes and follow-up checks for the next revision.

    Version comparison and retention. The Reviewer compares a candidate with the retained game using the same shared signals and game-specific criteria. It checks whether the changes address the earlier revision goals and introduce new problems. The output is an A/B preference, a tie, or an unavailable judgment, with reasons and evidence paths. Feedback states the problem, its possible cause, its effect on play, and a revision goal with a follow-up check. The harness maps the Reviewer’s judgment back to the game versions and selects which artifact to retain.
