item.title: DLSS 5 把自己当渲染管线的最后一级：一帧进一帧出，引擎渲出的帧是「不可动的底」 ｜ What’s New for Game Developers: DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, NVIDIA ACE Updates, and New RTX Kit Capabilities
item.description:
一句话：3D-Guided Neural Rendering 以引擎帧为不可改动的基础补光照与材质，严格单帧进出加运动矢量保证确定性。

要点：

  • 把引擎渲出的帧（美术几何、贴图、光照缓冲）当作不可动摇的底，模型只负责加逼真光照与材质细节，保住场景结构、角色身份与美术意图
  • 严格 one-frame-in / one-frame-out 加引擎运动矢量，输出确定、时序稳定；紧凑专用模型在单张 RTX 50 系上本地跑到 4K
  • 开发者可控项：模型选择、Structure Intensity 与 Tone Intensity、语义 AI mask 与引擎级 mask（玻璃器皿、水珠、植被等）；NBA 2K27 已上线

为什么值得看：神经渲染第一次以「后处理级、可遮罩、可调强度」的形态进商业管线：做渲染的人要开始规划 AI 阶段的插入位置、mask 通道与输入质量（RT/PT 输入会显著更好）。

中文摘要：DLSS 5 的核心是 3D-Guided Neural Rendering：它把引擎渲出的那一帧（含美术制作的几何、贴图与光照缓冲）当作不可改动的底，引擎帧决定什么必须保留，开发者决定什么可以变；模型再利用帧颜色与运动矢量补上逼真的光照与材质细节，同时守住场景结构、角色身份与美术意图。它按严格的一帧进一帧出运行，配合引擎运动矢量，因此输出确定且时序稳定，而不是像离线生成模型那样处理多帧块；紧凑的专用模型在单张 GeForce RTX 50 系上本地跑到 4K。可调项包括模型选择（可跨场景、玩法与过场混用）、Structure Intensity 与 Tone Intensity、按语义识别场景元素的 AI mask，以及用引擎级 mask 精确圈出玻璃器皿、水珠、植被等资产组。输入质量也决定上限：给到光追或路径追踪的光照，结果会明显更准。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：NVIDIA Developer（English）

原文发布：2026-09-22

本期推送：2026-10-25

Content Creation / Rendering

What’s New for Game Developers: DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, NVIDIA ACE Updates, and New RTX Kit Capabilities

Sep 22, 2026 By Phillip Singh
  • L
  • T
  • F
  • R
  • E
  • NVIDIA DLSS 5 introduces 3D-Guided Neural Rendering that uses the game engine's rendered frame as an unyielding foundation to add lifelike lighting and material detail while preserving artistic intent.
  • The technology operates on a strict one-frame-in, one-frame-out model with game-engine motion vectors for deterministic, temporally stable output running locally on GeForce RTX 50 Series GPUs at up to 4K.
  • Developers gain granular controls including model selection, Structure Intensity and Tone Intensity adjustments, semantic AI masking, and engine-level masking to direct the neural rendering effect across scenes.
  • NVIDIA ACE expands with Nemotron Speech 3.5 Streaming for low-latency speech recognition and Qwen3 TTS for high-quality text-to-speech with custom fine-tuning support.
  • The NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK adds RTX Spark support, Gemma4 integration, a Stable Diffusion plugin, and llama.cpp performance enhancements for local AI deployment alongside graphics.
  • RTX Mega Geometry 2.0 adds streaming of continuous level-of-detail clusters for high-density meshes, demonstrated with a textured glTF version of Zorah and coming soon to Gears of War: E-Day.

    • Next Steps

  • Read the DLSS 5 article for more details on 3D-Guided Neural Rendering and developer controls.
  • Access the NVIDIA In-Game Inference SDK to deploy local AI models alongside game graphics.
  • Explore the RTX Mega Geometry SDK on GitHub for high-density mesh rendering capabilities.
    • Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more

    NVIDIA DLSS 5 introduces DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering and granular controls that help game developers add lifelike lighting and material detail while preserving their artistic intent. We also look at updates to NVIDIA ACE, RTX Mega Geometry 2.0, and RTX Kit across character AI, high-density geometry, and rendering workflows.

    This post covers:

  • How DLSS 5 uses the game engine’s rendered frame as the foundation for 3D-Guided Neural Rendering and how NBA 2K27’s developer, Visual Concepts, uses DLSS 5 to enhance materials and lighting while preserving scanned facial geometry
  • New NVIDIA ACE speech and inferencing capabilities
  • RTX Kit SDK updates including RTX Mega Geometry 2.0 support for streaming continuous level-of-detail clusters

    • DLSS 5 introduces 3D-guided neural rendering with developer controls

    DLSS 5 with 3D-guided neural rendering extends the graphics pipeline as a final neural-rendering stage. It uses the game engine’s rendered frame, including its artist-authored geometry, textures, and lighting buffers as an unyielding foundation.

    The engine frame defines what must remain, while developers direct what may change. Using frame color and motion vectors, the model is designed to add lifelike lighting and material detail while preserving scene structure, character identity, and artistic intent.

    Built specifically for real-time 3D rendering, DLSS 5 delivers deterministic, temporally stable output. Operating on a strict one-frame-in, one-frame-out model with game-engine motion vectors keeps results consistent as players move. The compact, specialized model runs locally on a single GeForce RTX 50 Series GPU at up to 4K.

    Controls and integration for developers

  • Art direction:Developers can choose from among several models, mix them across scenes, gameplay, or cutscenes, and adjust Structure Intensity and Tone Intensity to tune high-frequency detail and broader lighting and color response.
  • Targeted application: Developers can use semantic AI masking to apply or hold back the effect across recognized scene elements, then use engine-level masks to isolate props or asset groups such as glassware, water droplets, and foliage.
  • Input quality: DLSS 5 noticeably elevates traditional rasterized graphics, but giving the model richer source data, like ray-traced or path-traced lighting, yields dramatically more-accurate results.

    • DLSS 5 is available now in NBA 2K27, developed by Visual Concepts and published by 2K, for all GeForce RTX 50 Series desktop and laptop GPUs. GeForce NOW Ultimate members can also experience it when streaming from NVIDIA-operated GeForce RTX 5080-powered gaming rigs in the cloud. Visual Concepts uses overall tone and style controls plus a per-pixel uplift control mask to fine-tune character detail while respecting player likenesses.

    In NBA 2K27, DLSS 5 preserves scanned facial geometry while enhancing skin subsurface scattering, light transmission through hair and ears, and contact shadows.

    For more details about DLSS 5, check out our DLSS 5 article. Sign up to be notified for DLSS updates for developers here. 

    NVIDIA ACE expands model and platform support

    NVIDIA ACE offers ready-to-integrate AI models and tools for building knowledgeable, interactive, and conversational in-game characters. The latest updates expand the speech pipeline and inference framework, making it easier for developers to run AI in their games.

    To run these models locally alongside game graphics, the NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing (NVIGI) SDK delivers a high-performance, streamlined path for deploying local AI models through in-process C++ execution.

    Key Release Highlights

  • NVIDIA Nemotron Speech 3.5 Streaming: A 600M-parameter Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model that transcribes player speech using a streaming architecture designed to minimize latency while maintaining accuracy.
  • Qwen3 TTS: A 600M-parameter Text-to-Speech model that generates high-quality audio and supports custom fine-tuning.

    • NVIDIA In-Game Inference SDK Updates

  • RTX Spark Support (Developer Preview): Adds early support for RTX Spark, NVIDIA’s new AI and graphics platform for slim laptops and ultra-efficient desktops.
  • Expanded Model Support: Integrates Gemma4 into the GPT plugin.
  • New Plugins & Samples: Adds a Stable Diffusion plugin along with sample code.
  • Performance Enhancements: Incorporates the latest 
    llama.cpp
    updates to maximize inference performance.

    • Access NVIDIA In-Game Inference SDK here.

    Updates across NVIDIA RTX Kit advance neural rendering and path tracing

    NVIDIA RTX Kit is a suite of rendering technologies for training and deploying AI in shaders, path tracing detailed scenes at game-ready performance, and rendering lifelike digital characters. The latest SDK updates expand support for high-density geometry, neural texture workflows, lighting, and texture filtering.

    RTX Kit 2026.3 updates include:

  • RTX Character Rendering 1.4 improves far-field hair BCSDF sampling and energy conservation
  • RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.1 adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction integration and some improvements to ReSTIR PT
  • RTX Neural Texture Compression 0.10 beta adds support for the Microsoft DirectX 12 Agility SDK preview with Linear Algebra, enabling RTX Tensor Core acceleration for neural texture decompression in DirectX shaders. It also adds Windows ARM64 support.
  • RTX Neural Shading 1.4 adds support for the latest DirectX Linear Algebra preview toolchain and updates its shader and sample dependencies.
  • RTX Texture Filtering 1.3 introduces Collaborative Texture Filtering, a technique designed to improve magnification quality for stochastic texture filtering. It also adds Windows ARM64 support.

    • RTX Mega Geometry 2.0 is now available

    In addition to the RTX Kit updates, RTX Mega Geometry SDK has been updated to 2.0 which adds support for streaming of continuous level-of-detail clusters for high-density meshes. The scale of detail is demonstrated in a newly released textured glTF version of Zorah.

    RTX Mega Geometry is coming soon to Gears of War: E-Day, offering GeForce games higher frame rates, higher levels of image quality, and with even more responsive controls. We sat down with the Coalition’s Studio Technical Director, Kate Rayner, and Rendering Lead, Mike Perzel to learn more about Gears of War: E-Day’s integrations of RTX Mega Geometry and DLSS.

    Video 3. RTX: Inside the Game | Gears of War: E-Day with DLSS 4.5 and RTX Mega Geometry

    Resources for game developers

    Check out the full list of game developer resources and stay up to date with the latest NVIDIA game development news:

  • Subscribe to our newsletter (select gaming as your industry)
  • Follow us on social: X, LinkedIn, Facebook, and YouTube
  • Join our Discord community

    • Tags

    Content Creation / Rendering | Gaming | DLSS | RTX Kit | Intermediate Technical | News | featured | Nsight Tools - Graphics | Unreal Engine

    About the Authors

    About Phillip Singh
    Phillip Singh is a senior developer marketing manager at NVIDIA, specializing in games and consumer AI. He is dedicated to empowering the next generation of game developers through neural rendering and AI graphics technology. Phillip earned his master's in business administration from the Santa Clara University Leavey School of Business. View all posts by Phillip Singh

    To run these models locally alongside game graphics, the NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing (NVIGI) SDK delivers a high-performance, streamlined path for deploying local AI models through in-process C++ execution.

    Key Release Highlights

  • NVIDIA Nemotron Speech 3.5 Streaming: A 600M-parameter Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model that transcribes player speech using a streaming architecture designed to minimize latency while maintaining accuracy.
  • Qwen3 TTS: A 600M-parameter Text-to-Speech model that generates high-quality audio and supports custom fine-tuning.

    • NVIDIA In-Game Inference SDK Updates

  • RTX Spark Support (Developer Preview): Adds early support for RTX Spark, NVIDIA’s new AI and graphics platform for slim laptops and ultra-efficient desktops.
  • Expanded Model Support: Integrates Gemma4 into the GPT plugin.
  • New Plugins & Samples: Adds a Stable Diffusion plugin along with sample code.
  • Performance Enhancements: Incorporates the latest 
    llama.cpp
    updates to maximize inference performance.

    • Access NVIDIA In-Game Inference SDK here.

    Updates across NVIDIA RTX Kit advance neural rendering and path tracing

    NVIDIA RTX Kit is a suite of rendering technologies for training and deploying AI in shaders, path tracing detailed scenes at game-ready performance, and rendering lifelike digital characters. The latest SDK updates expand support for high-density geometry, neural texture workflows, lighting, and texture filtering.

    RTX Kit 2026.3 updates include:

  • RTX Character Rendering 1.4 improves far-field hair BCSDF sampling and energy conservation
  • RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.1 adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction integration and some improvements to ReSTIR PT
  • RTX Neural Texture Compression 0.10 beta adds support for the Microsoft DirectX 12 Agility SDK preview with Linear Algebra, enabling RTX Tensor Core acceleration for neural texture decompression in DirectX shaders. It also adds Windows ARM64 support.
  • RTX Neural Shading 1.4 adds support for the latest DirectX Linear Algebra preview toolchain and updates its shader and sample dependencies.
  • RTX Texture Filtering 1.3 introduces Collaborative Texture Filtering, a technique designed to improve magnification quality for stochastic texture filtering. It also adds Windows ARM64 support.

    • RTX Mega Geometry 2.0 is now available

    In addition to the RTX Kit updates, RTX Mega Geometry SDK has been updated to 2.0 which adds support for streaming of continuous level-of-detail clusters for high-density meshes. The scale of detail is demonstrated in a newly released textured glTF version of Zorah.

    RTX Mega Geometry is coming soon to Gears of War: E-Day, offering GeForce games higher frame rates, higher levels of image quality, and with even more responsive controls. We sat down with the Coalition’s Studio Technical Director, Kate Rayner, and Rendering Lead, Mike Perzel to learn more about Gears of War: E-Day’s integrations of RTX Mega Geometry and DLSS.

    Video 3. RTX: Inside the Game | Gears of War: E-Day with DLSS 4.5 and RTX Mega Geometry

    Resources for game developers

    Check out the full list of game developer resources and stay up to date with the latest NVIDIA game development news:

  • Follow us on social: X, LinkedIn, Facebook, and YouTube

He is dedicated to empowering the next generation of game developers through neural rendering and AI graphics technology. item.title: 引擎给结构、模型补外观：DSolarRenderer 四步出片，768p 实时流式渲染 ｜ SolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative Reference Rendering
item.description:
一句话：把任意结构表示当参考帧塞进冻结的视频骨干，四步采样就出片，比 50 步快 12.3 倍并能流式 768p。

要点：

  • 冻结 MiniMax-H3 33B 骨干，只训两个轻量 LoRA：一个负责跟随任意结构表示，一个负责外观；结构视频走原生 reference 通路，只以纯文本描述类型
  • 结构引导的分布匹配从一个预训练四步 LoRA 出发，四步完成渲染（比 50 步快 12.3×），同时保住学到的控制能力
  • block-causal 变体把同一设计延伸到流式，768p 实时出帧；训练语料是 136K 条帧对齐片段，泛化到 11 种没见过的结构表示（姿态骨架、线稿、点云）

为什么值得看：引擎与编码 agent 能给出布局、运动与相机，却给不出真实观感；把「结构条件」抽象成与表示无关的参考帧，是不必为每个引擎写一套渲染器的现实路线。

中文摘要：游戏引擎和编码 agent 能规定场景的布局、运动与相机，但要把这种粗糙结构变成真实视频，还需要一个既能跟随结构、又能补全未定外观的渲染器。现有渲染器通常绑死某一种引擎表示，要么需要几十步去噪，要么得自己蒸馏一套代价高昂的模型，而且训练条件与目标视频并不对齐。DSolarRenderer 冻结 MiniMax-H3 33B 骨干，只训两个轻量 LoRA：结构视频以参考帧的形式进入骨干的原生参考通路，不带类型标识、只用纯文本描述表示类型，因此一个控制 LoRA 就能跟随任意结构表示；再以结构引导的分布匹配从一个预训练四步 LoRA 出发，四步完成渲染，比 50 步采样快 12.3 倍且保住控制能力。block-causal 变体把设计延伸到流式，可实时渲染 768p。作者还构建了来自引擎、仿真器与视频网站的 136K 条帧对齐语料，在 16 种结构表示上验证，并泛化到 11 种训练中未见过的表示。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-25

DSolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative
Reference RenderingSolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative Reference Rendering

Abstract

Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present DSolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that DSolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.

@

figureDSolarRenderer renders structure of any kind into realistic video. Each wedge pairs a structure (inner ring) with its rendering, and seven of the ten structure types are unseen in training. Readers can click and play the animation using Adobe Acrobat.

1 Introduction

Video generation models now produce realistic footage from a text prompt or a single image. However, visual realism alone does not ensure consistent 3D geometry, physically plausible dynamics, or temporal coherence [Huang et al., 2024; Bansal et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026a; Ying et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026c]. In game development, film previsualization, and agent-driven content creation, creators often specify the scene layout, object motion, and camera trajectory in advance. Designers block out scenes, animators key character motion, and coding agents script camera paths. These structural priors turn the task into rendering: producing realistic video that follows the specified scene and its evolution. With geometry and dynamics specified by these priors, the video model can focus on appearance synthesis, reducing the scope for structural and temporal drift. Recent systems therefore link executable world state to video generation through proxy videos [Chen et al., 2026b] or engine buffers [Zhan et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a], so that the engine determines scene evolution and a video model renders it.

Building such a renderer still faces three problems. First, control is tied to a fixed set of representations. Engine-driven renderers are built around the one representation their engine exports, such as white-box frames [Zhan et al., 2026], semantic maps [Lu et al., 2026d], proxy videos [Chen et al., 2026b], or full G-buffers [Lin et al., 2026a], and general controllable generators attach a branch per condition [Zhang et al., 2023; NVIDIA, 2025] or label the type of each input [Mao et al., 2026], so a new engine or a new kind of proxy calls for a new model. Second, rendering is slow. A large video backbone needs tens of denoising steps, and distilling a structure-conditioned model of this size from scratch is costly [Lin et al., 2026a], which keeps such renderers far from interactive use. Third, training pairs are rarely aligned frame by frame. Conditions estimated from real videos carry estimator errors and differ from engine proxies [Xu et al., 2026], and engine-paired data so far come from a single engine.

We present DSolarRenderer, which adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B Ref2VA backbone [MiniMax, 2026] and addresses the three problems in turn (fig:pipeline). For omni-structure control, structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone, each structural latent takes the RoPE [Su et al., 2021] position of the target frame it describes, and no reference carries a type identifier, as each representation is described in plain text instead, so that a single control LoRA [Hu et al., 2022] follows block-outs, semantic maps, shaded geometry, and body meshes alike. For fast rendering, we post-train a pretrained four-step LoRA of the same backbone with structure-guided distribution matching, which extends distribution matching distillation [Yin et al., 2024b] with a teacher extrapolated along the structural condition, so that the model renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant of the same design further streams 768p video in real time. For frame-aligned supervision, we collect 136K clips from eight sources whose structure is exported by game engines and simulators or fitted to YouTube videos, so that each structural frame matches its target frame in both content and timing.

We evaluate DSolarRenderer on an in-distribution test set with ground-truth videos and on a generalization benchmark that covers 16 structural representations, 11 of them unseen in training. The results show that our four-step model outperforms existing acceleration LoRAs and the official backbone, surpasses existing structure-conditioned renderers, and achieves a new state of the art in structure-conditioned video rendering. Notably, our method shows strong generalization to unseen structure. It faithfully renders pose skeletons, pencil storyboards, children’s crayon drawings, wireframes, and point clouds, none of which appears in training. Our contributions are fourfold:

  • [itemsep=3pt]

  • •

    We present a renderer that handles any structural representation with a single control LoRA through the native reference pathway, without type identifiers or added branches.

  • •

    We propose structure-guided distribution matching, which post-trains a pretrained four-step LoRA so that our model renders in four steps while preserving its structural control.

  • •

    We build a frame-aligned paired corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos, in which every structural frame is aligned with its target frame.

  • •

    Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations, including 11 unseen in training, and its causal variant renders 768p video in real time.

    • 2 Related Work

    Rendering Engine and Agent State into Video. World modeling encompasses 3D and 4D scene generation [Kong et al., 2025] and interactive proxies that provide feedback for agent learning [Yang et al., 2026b]. Recent systems let a game engine, a simulator, or a coding agent decide what happens in a scene and let a video model render it. Most of them train a renderer on one structural representation exported by their engine, such as white-box frames [Zhan et al., 2026; Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026], semantic maps [Lu et al., 2026d], depth and normal maps [Chi et al., 2026], projected 3D boxes [Huang et al., 2026b], or the proxy video of a code world model [Chen et al., 2026b; Liao and Liu, 2026], and several distill the renderer to a few streaming steps for real-time use [VAST-AI-Research, 2026; Lu et al., 2026d]. A related branch renders from full G-buffers that also carry materials and lighting [Zeng et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026c; Liang et al., 2025]. Other works avoid paired proxy data, either by learning from posed RGB-D video [Xu et al., 2026] or by showing proxy renders to a frozen model during the early denoising steps only [Liang et al., 2026]. However, each renderer is built around the representation of its own engine, so a new engine or a new kind of proxy calls for a new renderer. DSolarRenderer follows many kinds of structure with a single control LoRA, including structure it has never seen.

    Structure-Conditioned Video Generation. Controllable video generation commonly injects conditions in one of two ways. Branch-based methods attach a trainable copy or added control blocks to the backbone, from ControlNet [Zhang et al., 2023] to multi-condition variants on video backbones [Alibaba PAI, 2026; NVIDIA, 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025]. Sequence-based methods place condition tokens next to the target tokens and read them with full attention, often through a small LoRA [Tan et al., 2025; Ju et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026]. Further works steer generation through warped noise, 3D tracking videos, reference videos, predicted LoRAs, or jointly generated intrinsic channels [Burgert et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Xi et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026b], and training-free methods condition an existing model through structured first frames or a ControlNet-style world model [Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b]. However, these methods add parameters for control, label the type of each condition, or are trained on a fixed set of condition kinds. DSolarRenderer passes an untyped structural video through the native reference pathway of the backbone with one LoRA, so that the same model also follows structure unseen in training.

    Few-Step Distillation and Acceleration Adapters. Few-step video generation is usually obtained in two ways. One distills a multi-step teacher into a few-step student by distribution matching [Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Yu et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026] or consistency and flow-map distillation [Zheng et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026]. The other trains a plug-in acceleration LoRA once on a base model and attaches it to models derived from the same base [Luo et al., 2023; Lin and Yang, 2024; Yang et al., 2026a; Hao AI Lab, 2026], with recent work making such LoRAs transferable between base and distilled models [Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b]. For conditional models, several works distill the conditional model itself or re-tune its control module after distillation [Wang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026a; Sun et al., 2026], and MotionEcho [Rong et al., 2025] restores motion control at inference with guidance from the slow teacher. However, distilling a large control model from scratch is costly, and a generic few-step adapter attached unchanged lowers the visual quality and first-frame fidelity of the control model. DSolarRenderer post-trains a four-step LoRA on the frozen control model, with a distribution-matching teacher extrapolated toward its structure-conditioned prediction.

    3 DSolarRenderer: Native Reference Rendering

    DSolarRenderer turns a pretrained video backbone into a renderer by adding only lightweight adapters. In this section, we formulate the rendering task and outline the design (sec:task), describe how structural references are aligned with the target and described in text (sec:conditioning), and present the two-stage training of control and acceleration (sec:training), followed by its causal streaming extension (sec:causal).

    3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview

    Structure-Conditioned Rendering. Let V=(v₁,…,v_T) be a target video and S=(s₁,…,s_T) a structural video rendered from the same camera at the same timestamps. Depending on the source, S is a grey block-out, a semantic map, a depth map, object masks with skeletons, or a body mesh. Given S, an optional first frame I, and a text description c, DSolarRenderer models

    p_θ(V|S,I,c),

    		(1)

    where S or I may be absent while c is always provided. This yields four input combinations, namely 1structure with a first frame, 2structure alone, 3a first frame alone, and 4text alone. The structural video specifies the scene state, including the layout, geometry, character bodies, motion, and camera of every frame, but leaves materials, illumination, and tiny structures undetermined. Rendering is therefore a constrained completion problem, in which the output must agree with S wherever S is informative, while I, c, and the pretrained prior supply the remaining appearance.

    Design Overview. A large video backbone already provides a strong appearance prior, so DSolarRenderer keeps the backbone frozen and adds only lightweight adapters (fig:pipeline). Structural references enter through the native reference pathway with target-aligned positions, and fixed sentences in the prompt describe each reference. A control LoRA follows these references, and an acceleration LoRA from the same backbone enables few-step rendering.

    3.2 Frame-Aligned Reference Conditioning

    Native Reference Pathway. A renderer must match every structural frame with the target frame it describes. Instead of attaching a ControlNet branch [Zhang et al., 2023] or concatenating channels, both of which introduce parameters trained from scratch, we feed the structural video and the optional first frame through the reference pathway of the backbone [MiniMax, 2026]. This pathway packs text, reference videos, audio, and the target video into one full-attention sequence (fig:pipeline), so the control adapter can inherit the pretrained ability to read reference videos. We refer to the tokens of the supplied references as reference tokens and to those of the generated video as target tokens. Yet native reference tokens occupy a separate temporal segment before the clip and their own spatial grid, so the zero-shot backbone uses a structural video as a loose reference and copies it or changes the camera instead of following the structure.

    Frame-Aligned Positional Encoding. Since rotary position embedding [Su et al., 2021] makes attention depend on the relative offset between tokens, we supply the missing correspondence through positions. Each reference token receives the RoPE coordinates of the target token it describes. The k-th structural latent frame shares the temporal index and spatial grid of the k-th target latent frame, and the first frame is encoded as a static clip at index 0 (fig:pipeline). Tokens at the same position remain distinguishable through their timesteps, as reference tokens keep the near-clean value that the backbone assigns to reference inputs while target tokens carry the current noise level. This extends shared positions for aligned image conditions [Tan et al., 2025] to temporally aligned video and, like in-context control of video models without structural changes [Fang et al., 2025], requires no additional module.

    Untyped References with Fixed Descriptions. Structural representations from different sources constrain different aspects of the target (sec:sources). We keep reference tokens untyped in the sequence, without a type identifier or a modality embedding, so the adapter infers what a reference constrains from the structural video itself. The prompt additionally describes each representation with two fixed sentences, a definition of what it shows and a rule that names the attributes to follow and the visual properties that must not appear. For a scene block-out:

    3.3 Decoupled Two-Stage Training

    DSolarRenderer should render with few sampling steps while retaining the control learned at full steps. Training both objectives together does not achieve this, because whenever the acceleration objective can update the control adapter, it also alters how the structure is followed. Distilling a few-step student from scratch is costly at this scale and prone to instability [Lin et al., 2026a]. We therefore decouple control and acceleration into two stages on one frozen backbone, which also preserves its visual prior and keeps it compatible with adapters trained on the same weights.

    Stage 1: Control Adaptation. We train a control LoRA [Hu et al., 2022] with the flow-matching objective. Each adapted linear layer adds a low-rank update to its frozen pretrained weight W₀,

    W=W₀+ΔW_ctrl, ΔW_ctrl=α/rBA,

    		(2)

    where only the factors B and A of rank r are trained and α/r scales the update. The adapter is applied to the attention and feed-forward projections of every block. Since the backbone is a single-stream transformer, the same adapted projections process reference and target tokens, so one adapter learns both to interpret the structure and to render from it. With a clean target latent z₀, Gaussian noise ε, and noise coordinate t, the objective [Lipman et al., 2023] is

    zₜ=(1-t)z₀+tε, L_FM=𝔼_z₀,ε,t,c,S,I∥f_θ₀,φ(zₜ,t,c,R(S,I))-(ε-z₀)∥₂²,

    		(3)

    where θ₀ denotes the frozen backbone, φ the control adapter, and R(S,I) the available references. The loss is computed on the target video tokens only.

    Stage 2: Acceleration Adaptation. Because the backbone stays frozen, a pretrained four-step LoRA of the same backbone composes directly with the control adapter. We start from the rank-128 four-step LoRA of DMAD [Yu et al., 2026], which predicts a clean sample at every step and re-noises it for the next. It initializes the first 128 ranks of a rank-384 LoRA whose remaining ranks start at zero update, so training starts from DMAD’s update with room to grow, and we compose it as

    W=W₀+ΔW_ctrl+ΔW_acc.

    		(4)

    The composition already follows the structure, but the acceleration adapter was distilled for the backbone alone and has never seen the control model. The control adapter φ determines what is rendered from the structure, whereas the acceleration adapter ψ determines how four denoising steps reach the result. We therefore update only ψ from its pretrained weights and keep φ frozen, so that the control is preserved.

    Structure-Guided Distribution Matching. The teacher is the fixed Stage-1 full-step model, and a separate LoRA trained on student samples models the current student distribution. We update ψ with the distribution-matching gradient [Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a]

    ∇_ψL_DMD=𝔼 [(\tfrac∂G_φ,ψ∂ψ)^⊤w(t)(s_fake(z̃ₜ,t,ℂ)-s_teacher(z̃ₜ,t,ℂ))],

    		(5)

    where G_φ,ψ is the four-step generator, ℂ=(c,R(S,I)), and z̃ₜ is a re-noised student sample. Since full-step sampling of the backbone is blurry, the composed student is already sharper than its teacher, and plain distribution matching pulls it back toward this blur: the adapted student ends below its own starting point (sec:abl-guidance). We therefore amplify the structural signal of the teacher. With ẑ₀(ℂ) the clean prediction of the teacher and ẑ₀(ℂ_∅) its prediction after the tokens of the structural video are removed from the reference sequence, the teacher score is computed from

    ẑ₀ʷ=ẑ₀(ℂ)+(w-1)(ẑ₀(ℂ)-ẑ₀(ℂ_∅)).

    		(6)

    In ℂ_∅ the first frame and the prompt are kept unchanged. The difference isolates what the structural video contributes, such as contours, layout, and character positions, so with w>1 the student is pushed toward a target that is sharper and more decisive than the teacher itself. Setting w=1 recovers plain distribution matching. The extrapolation follows classifier-free guidance [Ho and Salimans, 2021], which distribution matching applies to the text condition of the teacher [Yin et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2026]. Here it acts on the structural condition alone. The fake-score model is a separate rank-128 LoRA initialized at the teacher, updated five times per generator update with learning rates of 2×10⁻⁶ and 10⁻⁵ for the fake-score model and the generator. We set w=1.5 and run 800 iterations, each one fake-score update, at the cost of one additional teacher forward pass per generator update (app:implementation).

    3.4 Causal Streaming Extension

    To generate video incrementally, we extend the same two-stage design to block-causal attention. The clip is split into blocks of at most five latent frames. We adapt the bidirectional control LoRA with teacher forcing so that each block attends to the prompt, the first frame, the structure of itself and the five preceding blocks, and the clean frames of the five preceding blocks, never to a later block. We then freeze this causal control LoRA and post-train a separate acceleration LoRA, initialized from the bidirectional four-step LoRA, on the student’s own block-by-block rollouts, with the bidirectional control model as the structure-guided teacher (w=1.5). Each rollout is generated without gradients and replayed as one teacher-forced sequence, so that the gradient reaches both how each block is generated and how it serves as context for later blocks. At inference, we merge the acceleration LoRA into the backbone, keep the control LoRA attached, sample each block in four steps, and update the fixed-window key–value cache before outputting the block immediately. With a streaming VAE decoder [Chen et al., 2026a] that decodes each block without future latents, the causal model renders 768p video in real time at up to 28 FPS.

    4 Engine-Aligned Paired Data

    A renderer learns to follow structure only from pairs in which the target video actually follows the structure. Conditions estimated from real videos, such as predicted depth or segmentation, carry the errors of the estimator and differ from the engine proxies that the renderer receives at test time. We therefore collect pairs whose condition is exported by an engine or fitted to the target, and use a pair as structural supervision only when its condition matches the target in time and carries enough structure. We then describe the data sources (sec:sources), the checks that decide how each source is used (sec:alignment), and the construction of prompts (sec:captions).

    4.1 Data Sources

    The training set contains 136K samples, about 243 hours of video. Every clip is a 158-frame window at 24 fps and 768p resolution. The data cover diverse sources and control types (fig:data), listed below with the condition each one supplies.

  • •

    Magpie[Zhan et al., 2026] records human-played Unreal Engine gameplay across many scenes at 60 fps, together with a synchronized grey block-out of the scene. The block-out gives the layout, the large geometry, the bodies and motion of the characters, and the camera of every frame, while materials and lighting are left to the model.

  • •

    CARLA[Dosovitskiy et al., 2017] provides urban and rural driving. Among the buffers that the simulator exports, we use semantic segmentation, which paints every class in one flat colour and thus specifies the class layout of the scene without its appearance.

  • •

    Engine recordings consist of frames together with depth, object masks, camera poses, and skeletons on shared timestamps. We render the depth as grey shading, with distant regions and the sky set to black, so that it conveys the shape of the scene near the camera.

  • •

    Blender renders of animated scenes are paired with the white-box of their scene, which describes the scene layout and the motion of the main character.

  • •

    UnrealZoo[Zhong et al., 2025] provides Unreal Engine 5 environments in first- and third-person views. Its condition combines object masks and skeletons, with one colour per object and the skeleton of each character drawn on top.

  • •

    YouTube videos [Ju et al., 2024] provide clips for body-motion conditioning. We keep videos with a clear protagonist, fit the SMPL body [Loper et al., 2015] of the protagonist with GVHMR [Shen et al., 2024] using camera and depth from VGGT [Wang et al., 2025a] and Depth Anything 3 [Lin et al., 2026b], and render it from the target camera as a grey body on a white background. This SMPL body video gives the position, pose, and motion of the protagonist, while the environment and clothing come from the first frame and text.

  • •

    WildWorld[Li et al., 2026c], a public dataset of Monster Hunter Wilds gameplay, and OmniWorld[Zhou et al., 2026], which collects footage of AAA games such as Cyberpunk 2077, contribute rich game appearance. Their structural annotations follow the frames less closely, so we use them as appearance data and supply only a first frame.

一句话：把任意结构表示当参考帧塞进冻结的视频骨干，四步采样就出片，比 50 步快 12.3 倍并能流式 768p。

要点：

  • 冻结 MiniMax-H3 33B 骨干，只训两个轻量 LoRA：一个负责跟随任意结构表示，一个负责外观；结构视频走原生 reference 通路，只以纯文本描述类型
  • 结构引导的分布匹配从一个预训练四步 LoRA 出发，四步完成渲染（比 50 步快 12.3×），同时保住学到的控制能力
  • block-causal 变体把同一设计延伸到流式，768p 实时出帧；训练语料是 136K 条帧对齐片段，泛化到 11 种没见过的结构表示（姿态骨架、线稿、点云）

为什么值得看：引擎与编码 agent 能给出布局、运动与相机，却给不出真实观感；把「结构条件」抽象成与表示无关的参考帧，是不必为每个引擎写一套渲染器的现实路线。

中文摘要：游戏引擎和编码 agent 能规定场景的布局、运动与相机，但要把这种粗糙结构变成真实视频，还需要一个既能跟随结构、又能补全未定外观的渲染器。现有渲染器通常绑死某一种引擎表示，要么需要几十步去噪，要么得自己蒸馏一套代价高昂的模型，而且训练条件与目标视频并不对齐。DSolarRenderer 冻结 MiniMax-H3 33B 骨干，只训两个轻量 LoRA：结构视频以参考帧的形式进入骨干的原生参考通路，不带类型标识、只用纯文本描述表示类型，因此一个控制 LoRA 就能跟随任意结构表示；再以结构引导的分布匹配从一个预训练四步 LoRA 出发，四步完成渲染，比 50 步采样快 12.3 倍且保住控制能力。block-causal 变体把设计延伸到流式，可实时渲染 768p。作者还构建了来自引擎、仿真器与视频网站的 136K 条帧对齐语料，在 16 种结构表示上验证，并泛化到 11 种训练中未见过的表示。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-25

DSolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative
Reference RenderingSolarRenderer: Few-Step Generative Reference Rendering

Abstract

Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present DSolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that DSolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.

@

figureDSolarRenderer renders structure of any kind into realistic video. Each wedge pairs a structure (inner ring) with its rendering, and seven of the ten structure types are unseen in training. Readers can click and play the animation using Adobe Acrobat.

1 Introduction

Video generation models now produce realistic footage from a text prompt or a single image. However, visual realism alone does not ensure consistent 3D geometry, physically plausible dynamics, or temporal coherence [Huang et al., 2024; Bansal et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026a; Ying et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026c]. In game development, film previsualization, and agent-driven content creation, creators often specify the scene layout, object motion, and camera trajectory in advance. Designers block out scenes, animators key character motion, and coding agents script camera paths. These structural priors turn the task into rendering: producing realistic video that follows the specified scene and its evolution. With geometry and dynamics specified by these priors, the video model can focus on appearance synthesis, reducing the scope for structural and temporal drift. Recent systems therefore link executable world state to video generation through proxy videos [Chen et al., 2026b] or engine buffers [Zhan et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a], so that the engine determines scene evolution and a video model renders it.

Building such a renderer still faces three problems. First, control is tied to a fixed set of representations. Engine-driven renderers are built around the one representation their engine exports, such as white-box frames [Zhan et al., 2026], semantic maps [Lu et al., 2026d], proxy videos [Chen et al., 2026b], or full G-buffers [Lin et al., 2026a], and general controllable generators attach a branch per condition [Zhang et al., 2023; NVIDIA, 2025] or label the type of each input [Mao et al., 2026], so a new engine or a new kind of proxy calls for a new model. Second, rendering is slow. A large video backbone needs tens of denoising steps, and distilling a structure-conditioned model of this size from scratch is costly [Lin et al., 2026a], which keeps such renderers far from interactive use. Third, training pairs are rarely aligned frame by frame. Conditions estimated from real videos carry estimator errors and differ from engine proxies [Xu et al., 2026], and engine-paired data so far come from a single engine.

We present DSolarRenderer, which adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B Ref2VA backbone [MiniMax, 2026] and addresses the three problems in turn (fig:pipeline). For omni-structure control, structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone, each structural latent takes the RoPE [Su et al., 2021] position of the target frame it describes, and no reference carries a type identifier, as each representation is described in plain text instead, so that a single control LoRA [Hu et al., 2022] follows block-outs, semantic maps, shaded geometry, and body meshes alike. For fast rendering, we post-train a pretrained four-step LoRA of the same backbone with structure-guided distribution matching, which extends distribution matching distillation [Yin et al., 2024b] with a teacher extrapolated along the structural condition, so that the model renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant of the same design further streams 768p video in real time. For frame-aligned supervision, we collect 136K clips from eight sources whose structure is exported by game engines and simulators or fitted to YouTube videos, so that each structural frame matches its target frame in both content and timing.

We evaluate DSolarRenderer on an in-distribution test set with ground-truth videos and on a generalization benchmark that covers 16 structural representations, 11 of them unseen in training. The results show that our four-step model outperforms existing acceleration LoRAs and the official backbone, surpasses existing structure-conditioned renderers, and achieves a new state of the art in structure-conditioned video rendering. Notably, our method shows strong generalization to unseen structure. It faithfully renders pose skeletons, pencil storyboards, children’s crayon drawings, wireframes, and point clouds, none of which appears in training. Our contributions are fourfold:

  • [itemsep=3pt]

  • •

    We present a renderer that handles any structural representation with a single control LoRA through the native reference pathway, without type identifiers or added branches.

  • •

    We propose structure-guided distribution matching, which post-trains a pretrained four-step LoRA so that our model renders in four steps while preserving its structural control.

  • •

    We build a frame-aligned paired corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos, in which every structural frame is aligned with its target frame.

  • •

    Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations, including 11 unseen in training, and its causal variant renders 768p video in real time.

    • 2 Related Work

    Rendering Engine and Agent State into Video. World modeling encompasses 3D and 4D scene generation [Kong et al., 2025] and interactive proxies that provide feedback for agent learning [Yang et al., 2026b]. Recent systems let a game engine, a simulator, or a coding agent decide what happens in a scene and let a video model render it. Most of them train a renderer on one structural representation exported by their engine, such as white-box frames [Zhan et al., 2026; Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026], semantic maps [Lu et al., 2026d], depth and normal maps [Chi et al., 2026], projected 3D boxes [Huang et al., 2026b], or the proxy video of a code world model [Chen et al., 2026b; Liao and Liu, 2026], and several distill the renderer to a few streaming steps for real-time use [VAST-AI-Research, 2026; Lu et al., 2026d]. A related branch renders from full G-buffers that also carry materials and lighting [Zeng et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026c; Liang et al., 2025]. Other works avoid paired proxy data, either by learning from posed RGB-D video [Xu et al., 2026] or by showing proxy renders to a frozen model during the early denoising steps only [Liang et al., 2026]. However, each renderer is built around the representation of its own engine, so a new engine or a new kind of proxy calls for a new renderer. DSolarRenderer follows many kinds of structure with a single control LoRA, including structure it has never seen.

    Structure-Conditioned Video Generation. Controllable video generation commonly injects conditions in one of two ways. Branch-based methods attach a trainable copy or added control blocks to the backbone, from ControlNet [Zhang et al., 2023] to multi-condition variants on video backbones [Alibaba PAI, 2026; NVIDIA, 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025]. Sequence-based methods place condition tokens next to the target tokens and read them with full attention, often through a small LoRA [Tan et al., 2025; Ju et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026]. Further works steer generation through warped noise, 3D tracking videos, reference videos, predicted LoRAs, or jointly generated intrinsic channels [Burgert et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Xi et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026b], and training-free methods condition an existing model through structured first frames or a ControlNet-style world model [Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b]. However, these methods add parameters for control, label the type of each condition, or are trained on a fixed set of condition kinds. DSolarRenderer passes an untyped structural video through the native reference pathway of the backbone with one LoRA, so that the same model also follows structure unseen in training.

    Few-Step Distillation and Acceleration Adapters. Few-step video generation is usually obtained in two ways. One distills a multi-step teacher into a few-step student by distribution matching [Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Yu et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026] or consistency and flow-map distillation [Zheng et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026]. The other trains a plug-in acceleration LoRA once on a base model and attaches it to models derived from the same base [Luo et al., 2023; Lin and Yang, 2024; Yang et al., 2026a; Hao AI Lab, 2026], with recent work making such LoRAs transferable between base and distilled models [Li et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b]. For conditional models, several works distill the conditional model itself or re-tune its control module after distillation [Wang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026a; Sun et al., 2026], and MotionEcho [Rong et al., 2025] restores motion control at inference with guidance from the slow teacher. However, distilling a large control model from scratch is costly, and a generic few-step adapter attached unchanged lowers the visual quality and first-frame fidelity of the control model. DSolarRenderer post-trains a four-step LoRA on the frozen control model, with a distribution-matching teacher extrapolated toward its structure-conditioned prediction.

    3 DSolarRenderer: Native Reference Rendering

    DSolarRenderer turns a pretrained video backbone into a renderer by adding only lightweight adapters. In this section, we formulate the rendering task and outline the design (sec:task), describe how structural references are aligned with the target and described in text (sec:conditioning), and present the two-stage training of control and acceleration (sec:training), followed by its causal streaming extension (sec:causal).

    3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview

    Structure-Conditioned Rendering. Let V=(v₁,…,v_T) be a target video and S=(s₁,…,s_T) a structural video rendered from the same camera at the same timestamps. Depending on the source, S is a grey block-out, a semantic map, a depth map, object masks with skeletons, or a body mesh. Given S, an optional first frame I, and a text description c, DSolarRenderer models

    p_θ(V|S,I,c),

    		(1)

    where S or I may be absent while c is always provided. This yields four input combinations, namely 1structure with a first frame, 2structure alone, 3a first frame alone, and 4text alone. The structural video specifies the scene state, including the layout, geometry, character bodies, motion, and camera of every frame, but leaves materials, illumination, and tiny structures undetermined. Rendering is therefore a constrained completion problem, in which the output must agree with S wherever S is informative, while I, c, and the pretrained prior supply the remaining appearance.

    Design Overview. A large video backbone already provides a strong appearance prior, so DSolarRenderer keeps the backbone frozen and adds only lightweight adapters (fig:pipeline). Structural references enter through the native reference pathway with target-aligned positions, and fixed sentences in the prompt describe each reference. A control LoRA follows these references, and an acceleration LoRA from the same backbone enables few-step rendering.

    3.2 Frame-Aligned Reference Conditioning

    Native Reference Pathway. A renderer must match every structural frame with the target frame it describes. Instead of attaching a ControlNet branch [Zhang et al., 2023] or concatenating channels, both of which introduce parameters trained from scratch, we feed the structural video and the optional first frame through the reference pathway of the backbone [MiniMax, 2026]. This pathway packs text, reference videos, audio, and the target video into one full-attention sequence (fig:pipeline), so the control adapter can inherit the pretrained ability to read reference videos. We refer to the tokens of the supplied references as reference tokens and to those of the generated video as target tokens. Yet native reference tokens occupy a separate temporal segment before the clip and their own spatial grid, so the zero-shot backbone uses a structural video as a loose reference and copies it or changes the camera instead of following the structure.

    Frame-Aligned Positional Encoding. Since rotary position embedding [Su et al., 2021] makes attention depend on the relative offset between tokens, we supply the missing correspondence through positions. Each reference token receives the RoPE coordinates of the target token it describes. The k-th structural latent frame shares the temporal index and spatial grid of the k-th target latent frame, and the first frame is encoded as a static clip at index 0 (fig:pipeline). Tokens at the same position remain distinguishable through their timesteps, as reference tokens keep the near-clean value that the backbone assigns to reference inputs while target tokens carry the current noise level. This extends shared positions for aligned image conditions [Tan et al., 2025] to temporally aligned video and, like in-context control of video models without structural changes [Fang et al., 2025], requires no additional module.

    Untyped References with Fixed Descriptions. Structural representations from different sources constrain different aspects of the target (sec:sources). We keep reference tokens untyped in the sequence, without a type identifier or a modality embedding, so the adapter infers what a reference constrains from the structural video itself. The prompt additionally describes each representation with two fixed sentences, a definition of what it shows and a rule that names the attributes to follow and the visual properties that must not appear. For a scene block-out:

    3.3 Decoupled Two-Stage Training

    DSolarRenderer should render with few sampling steps while retaining the control learned at full steps. Training both objectives together does not achieve this, because whenever the acceleration objective can update the control adapter, it also alters how the structure is followed. Distilling a few-step student from scratch is costly at this scale and prone to instability [Lin et al., 2026a]. We therefore decouple control and acceleration into two stages on one frozen backbone, which also preserves its visual prior and keeps it compatible with adapters trained on the same weights.

    Stage 1: Control Adaptation. We train a control LoRA [Hu et al., 2022] with the flow-matching objective. Each adapted linear layer adds a low-rank update to its frozen pretrained weight W₀,

    W=W₀+ΔW_ctrl, ΔW_ctrl=α/rBA,

    		(2)

    where only the factors B and A of rank r are trained and α/r scales the update. The adapter is applied to the attention and feed-forward projections of every block. Since the backbone is a single-stream transformer, the same adapted projections process reference and target tokens, so one adapter learns both to interpret the structure and to render from it. With a clean target latent z₀, Gaussian noise ε, and noise coordinate t, the objective [Lipman et al., 2023] is

    zₜ=(1-t)z₀+tε, L_FM=𝔼_z₀,ε,t,c,S,I∥f_θ₀,φ(zₜ,t,c,R(S,I))-(ε-z₀)∥₂²,

    		(3)

    where θ₀ denotes the frozen backbone, φ the control adapter, and R(S,I) the available references. The loss is computed on the target video tokens only.

    Stage 2: Acceleration Adaptation. Because the backbone stays frozen, a pretrained four-step LoRA of the same backbone composes directly with the control adapter. We start from the rank-128 four-step LoRA of DMAD [Yu et al., 2026], which predicts a clean sample at every step and re-noises it for the next. It initializes the first 128 ranks of a rank-384 LoRA whose remaining ranks start at zero update, so training starts from DMAD’s update with room to grow, and we compose it as

    W=W₀+ΔW_ctrl+ΔW_acc.

    		(4)

    The composition already follows the structure, but the acceleration adapter was distilled for the backbone alone and has never seen the control model. The control adapter φ determines what is rendered from the structure, whereas the acceleration adapter ψ determines how four denoising steps reach the result. We therefore update only ψ from its pretrained weights and keep φ frozen, so that the control is preserved.

    Structure-Guided Distribution Matching. The teacher is the fixed Stage-1 full-step model, and a separate LoRA trained on student samples models the current student distribution. We update ψ with the distribution-matching gradient [Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a]

    ∇_ψL_DMD=𝔼 [(\tfrac∂G_φ,ψ∂ψ)^⊤w(t)(s_fake(z̃ₜ,t,ℂ)-s_teacher(z̃ₜ,t,ℂ))],

    		(5)

    where G_φ,ψ is the four-step generator, ℂ=(c,R(S,I)), and z̃ₜ is a re-noised student sample. Since full-step sampling of the backbone is blurry, the composed student is already sharper than its teacher, and plain distribution matching pulls it back toward this blur: the adapted student ends below its own starting point (sec:abl-guidance). We therefore amplify the structural signal of the teacher. With ẑ₀(ℂ) the clean prediction of the teacher and ẑ₀(ℂ_∅) its prediction after the tokens of the structural video are removed from the reference sequence, the teacher score is computed from

    ẑ₀ʷ=ẑ₀(ℂ)+(w-1)(ẑ₀(ℂ)-ẑ₀(ℂ_∅)).

    		(6)

    In ℂ_∅ the first frame and the prompt are kept unchanged. The difference isolates what the structural video contributes, such as contours, layout, and character positions, so with w>1 the student is pushed toward a target that is sharper and more decisive than the teacher itself. Setting w=1 recovers plain distribution matching. The extrapolation follows classifier-free guidance [Ho and Salimans, 2021], which distribution matching applies to the text condition of the teacher [Yin et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2026]. Here it acts on the structural condition alone. The fake-score model is a separate rank-128 LoRA initialized at the teacher, updated five times per generator update with learning rates of 2×10⁻⁶ and 10⁻⁵ for the fake-score model and the generator. We set w=1.5 and run 800 iterations, each one fake-score update, at the cost of one additional teacher forward pass per generator update (app:implementation).

    3.4 Causal Streaming Extension

    To generate video incrementally, we extend the same two-stage design to block-causal attention. The clip is split into blocks of at most five latent frames. We adapt the bidirectional control LoRA with teacher forcing so that each block attends to the prompt, the first frame, the structure of itself and the five preceding blocks, and the clean frames of the five preceding blocks, never to a later block. We then freeze this causal control LoRA and post-train a separate acceleration LoRA, initialized from the bidirectional four-step LoRA, on the student’s own block-by-block rollouts, with the bidirectional control model as the structure-guided teacher (w=1.5). Each rollout is generated without gradients and replayed as one teacher-forced sequence, so that the gradient reaches both how each block is generated and how it serves as context for later blocks. At inference, we merge the acceleration LoRA into the backbone, keep the control LoRA attached, sample each block in four steps, and update the fixed-window key–value cache before outputting the block immediately. With a streaming VAE decoder [Chen et al., 2026a] that decodes each block without future latents, the causal model renders 768p video in real time at up to 28 FPS.

    4 Engine-Aligned Paired Data

    A renderer learns to follow structure only from pairs in which the target video actually follows the structure. Conditions estimated from real videos, such as predicted depth or segmentation, carry the errors of the estimator and differ from the engine proxies that the renderer receives at test time. We therefore collect pairs whose condition is exported by an engine or fitted to the target, and use a pair as structural supervision only when its condition matches the target in time and carries enough structure. We then describe the data sources (sec:sources), the checks that decide how each source is used (sec:alignment), and the construction of prompts (sec:captions).

    4.1 Data Sources

    The training set contains 136K samples, about 243 hours of video. Every clip is a 158-frame window at 24 fps and 768p resolution. The data cover diverse sources and control types (fig:data), listed below with the condition each one supplies.

  • •

    Magpie[Zhan et al., 2026] records human-played Unreal Engine gameplay across many scenes at 60 fps, together with a synchronized grey block-out of the scene. The block-out gives the layout, the large geometry, the bodies and motion of the characters, and the camera of every frame, while materials and lighting are left to the model.

  • •

    CARLA[Dosovitskiy et al., 2017] provides urban and rural driving. Among the buffers that the simulator exports, we use semantic segmentation, which paints every class in one flat colour and thus specifies the class layout of the scene without its appearance.

  • •

    Engine recordings consist of frames together with depth, object masks, camera poses, and skeletons on shared timestamps. We render the depth as grey shading, with distant regions and the sky set to black, so that it conveys the shape of the scene near the camera.

  • •

    Blender renders of animated scenes are paired with the white-box of their scene, which describes the scene layout and the motion of the main character.

  • •

    UnrealZoo[Zhong et al., 2025] provides Unreal Engine 5 environments in first- and third-person views. Its condition combines object masks and skeletons, with one colour per object and the skeleton of each character drawn on top.

  • •

    YouTube videos [Ju et al., 2024] provide clips for body-motion conditioning. We keep videos with a clear protagonist, fit the SMPL body [Loper et al., 2015] of the protagonist with GVHMR [Shen et al., 2024] using camera and depth from VGGT [Wang et al., 2025a] and Depth Anything 3 [Lin et al., 2026b], and render it from the target camera as a grey body on a white background. This SMPL body video gives the position, pose, and motion of the protagonist, while the environment and clothing come from the first frame and text.

  • •

    WildWorld[Li et al., 2026c], a public dataset of Monster Hunter Wilds gameplay, and OmniWorld[Zhou et al., 2026], which collects footage of AAA games such as Cyberpunk 2077, contribute rich game appearance. Their structural annotations follow the frames less closely, so we use them as appearance data and supply only a first frame.

item.title: 别把所有高斯都当逐帧信号：ResStreamGS 把稳定的抠出来只传一次，手机端 PSNR 涨 7.5–8.35 dB ｜ ResStreamGS: Residual-Sensitive Dual-Stream Gaussian Splatting for Mobile Volumetric Video Streaming
item.description:
一句话：按时间行为给高斯分双流：稳定高斯每 GOP 传一次，只有残差敏感的进逐帧视频流，码率降 56.5%。

要点：

  • 用轻量 probe 自适应找出残差敏感的高斯，其余在同组图像（GOP）内直接复用
  • 稳定高斯每个 GOP 只传一次，逐帧硬件可解码视频流里只留残差敏感的高斯，避免把静态区域也逐帧重压
  • 复杂全场景体视频上编码后 PSNR 提升 7.51–8.35 dB，摊薄负载最高降 56.5%，骁龙 778G 上 30.883 FPS

为什么值得看：体视频的带宽预算几乎全花在「本来没变的东西」上；按时间行为分流，比单纯调量化步长或码率控制更符合全场景内容的统计特性。

中文摘要：移动端实时体积视频要在有限带宽与算力下交付自由视点内容，很难。现有的 3DGS 流式系统（如 V3）把随时间变化的高斯属性编码进通用视频编解码器、靠硬件解码来省算力，但它们把所有高斯都当作逐帧信号处理——对全场景内容并不合适，因为其中有很大一部分在时间上几乎不动。作者的实测显示，逐帧自适应加全量视频编码会让复杂全场景内容、尤其是时间稳定区域的质量明显下降。ResStreamGS 因此按时间行为把高斯分成两条流：先用轻量 probe 自适应找出残差敏感的高斯，在同组图像内复用稳定高斯；稳定高斯每组只传一次，逐帧的硬件可解码视频流里只保留残差敏感的那部分。在复杂全场景数据上，编码后 PSNR 比 V3 式的全量基线高 7.51–8.35 dB，摊薄负载最多降 56.5%，并在骁龙 778G 平台上达到 30.883 FPS。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-15

本期推送：2026-10-25

ResStreamGS: Residual-Sensitive Dual-Stream Gaussian Splatting for
Mobile Volumetric Video Streaming

Abstract

Real-time mobile volumetric video enables immersive free-viewpoint experiences, but delivering high-quality 3D content under constrained bandwidth and computation remains challenging. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) systems, such as V3, enable efficient mobile streaming by encoding time-varying Gaussian attributes with commodity video codecs and hardware decoding. However, existing pipelines treat all Gaussians as frame-varying signals, which is poorly suited to full-scene content where large portions remain temporally stable. Our empirical study shows that frame-wise adaptation and video coding of all Gaussians cause quality degradation in complex full-scene content, particularly in temporally stable regions. To address this issue, we propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that processes Gaussians according to their temporal behavior. ResStreamGS identifies residual-sensitive primitives through lightweight probe adaptation and reuses stable Gaussians within each Group of Pictures (GOP). Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP, while only residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in the frame-wise hardware-decodable video stream. Experiments on complex full-scene volumetric videos show that ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51–8.35 dB over a controlled V3-style all-Gaussians baseline, reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5%, and achieves 30.883 FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.

Volumetric video enables users to freely explore dynamic 3D scenes from arbitrary viewpoints and supports immersive applications such as virtual reality, mixed reality, and remote telepresence. Bringing these experiences to commodity mobile devices remains challenging because a practical system must maintain high visual quality while reducing transmission, decoding, memory, and rendering costs. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides a promising representation for this setting because its explicit point-based formulation supports high-quality reconstruction and efficient rasterization [16]. To further reduce transmission and decoding costs, recent systems organize time-varying Gaussian attributes into 2D video-like representations and compress them more effectively with commodity hardware codecs such as H.264 and HEVC [41, 20, 32].

Existing Gaussian-video pipelines encode the complete Gaussian representation as a frame-varying signal. This design is effective for human-centric or foreground-dominant content, where many important primitives change together with the moving subject. Complex full-scene volumetric videos have a different temporal structure. Dynamic regions occupy only part of the scene, while large portions of the geometry and appearance remain persistent over time. Treating all Gaussians in such scenes as frame-varying signals may therefore introduce unnecessary processing and distortion.

To better understand this limitation, we conduct an empirical study by applying the same V3-style H.264 Gaussian-video pipeline to both foreground-focused and complex full-scene content. As shown in fig:v3_quality_drop, Neu3D consistently exhibits a much steeper PSNR decline across increasing QP values than Actors-HQ; under the default setting, the drops are 11.7 dB and 3.4 dB, respectively. More importantly, the qualitative results in fig:qualitative_comparison show that the errors are not limited to rapidly moving regions. Scene structures that should remain largely stable can also become visibly corrupted. These results suggest that the all-Gaussians formulation is poorly matched to the temporal structure of complex full-scene content.

These results further motivate us to examine why full-scene content suffers more degradation. Our analysis in Sec. 3 shows that the key issue lies in a mismatch between the temporal behavior of Gaussian primitives and the granularity at which they are processed. Existing pipelines repeatedly adapt and encode every primitive at the frame level, even though many primitives change little within a short frame group. As a result, stable primitives are exposed to optimization drift and codec distortion without providing benefits in temporal adaptability. This observation suggests that Gaussian primitives should not be uniformly processed at the same temporal granularity. Stable primitives can instead be reused across frames, while only primitives sensitive to temporal residuals need to remain in the frame-wise adaptation and video-coding path.

Motivated by these findings, we propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework for efficient full-scene volumetric video streaming. ResStreamGS first uses lightweight probe adaptation to identify primitives that are sensitive to temporal changes. It then selects the smallest residual-sensitive subset that preserves the reconstruction quality of the composed scene. The remaining primitives are treated as stable references and reuse their keyframe attributes within the Group of Pictures (GOP). This partition produces two synchronized streams with different temporal granularities. Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP and cached on the mobile device, while residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in a compact frame-wise Gaussian-video stream that can be decoded with commodity video hardware. In this way, ResStreamGS retains the advantages of hardware video decoding while removing persistent scene state from repeated frame-wise processing.

Experiments on full-scene volumetric videos demonstrate that this design substantially improves both reconstruction fidelity and streaming efficiency. Under the same Gaussian-video coding framework, ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51–8.35 dB over the controlled V3 all-Gaussians baseline while reducing the amortized payload by up to 56.5%. Our mobile implementation achieves 30.883 FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G mobile platform, showing that high-quality full-scene volumetric video can be played in real time on commodity mobile hardware.

Our Contributions: (1) New Perspective. We identify a temporal mismatch in Gaussian-video streaming, where primitives with different temporal behaviors are uniformly processed at the frame level. This motivates processing Gaussians according to their temporal sensitivity. (2) Novel Framework. We propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that separates stable Gaussians for GOP-level reuse from residual-sensitive Gaussians for frame-level adaptation, with quality-aware selection to preserve reconstruction quality. (3) Superior Performance. ResStreamGS substantially improves post-codec reconstruction quality while reducing the amortized streaming payload by up to 56.5%, and consistently achieves 30.883 FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G mobile platform for smooth real-time full-scene volumetric video playback in practical mobile deployment scenarios.

1 Related Work

1.1 Dynamic Scene Reconstruction via 3DGS

Dynamic novel view synthesis (NVS) reconstructs time-varying 3D scenes from videos for novel-view rendering. Early methods extend NeRF with deformation fields, scene flow, or time conditioning to model dynamic content [30, 35, 34, 26, 39, 9]. Later explicit and factorized representations improve efficiency using voxel grids, multi-plane decompositions, or tensorized 4D structures [7, 40, 1, 8, 36], but still rely on costly volumetric sampling or neural decoding.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) instead adopts an explicit point-based representation with rasterization-oriented rendering [16]. Dynamic 3DGS methods further model temporal changes through deformation fields, Gaussian tracking, frame-wise updates, or pose-dependent Gaussian maps [43, 29, 25, 14, 49, 50, 52, 24]. Although these methods achieve high reconstruction quality and rendering speed, their large per-frame storage and limited compatibility with commodity video codecs make direct deployment for mobile volumetric video streaming challenging [43, 29, 24].

1.2 Efficient and Compact 3D Gaussian Representations

Despite efficient rasterization, 3DGS introduces substantial storage overhead because each Gaussian stores geometry, opacity, and view-dependent appearance attributes [16]. Existing compact 3DGS methods mainly reduce this cost through opacity- or contribution-aware pruning, vector quantization, entropy coding, codebook-based clustering, and context-adaptive prediction [18, 31, 33, 6, 2, 15]. These techniques show that Gaussian representations contain spatial and attribute redundancy and can be compressed without severely degrading rendering quality. However, they are designed for static scenes, where the representation is decoded once and reused across viewpoints. Dynamic Gaussian sequences further amplify the storage burden as geometry and appearance evolve over time. Recent methods therefore exploit temporal redundancy through keyframes, residual modeling, motion-aware updates, and memory-efficient 4D parameterizations [19, 48, 3, 46]. Streaming-oriented approaches employ adaptive layering and saliency-aware tiling to reduce transmission cost [11, 10]. Nevertheless, most methods optimize how the complete Gaussian sequence is compressed, without distinguishing primitives that remain stable over time. Our work instead separates stable Gaussians from residual-sensitive ones before dynamic encoding, avoiding repeated lossy compression of stable structures and reserving the dynamic stream for time-varying content.

1.3 Mobile Volumetric Video Streaming

Mobile volumetric video systems must jointly reduce network bandwidth, decoding overhead, and rendering cost on mobile devices. Early systems based on point clouds or meshes employ visibility-aware scheduling, adaptive transmission, view-dependent content selection, and edge-assisted processing to support interactive playback under constrained resources [13, 47, 12]. Recent 3DGS systems extend these ideas by adapting transmitted content, quality, or bitrate according to network conditions and user viewpoints [45, 37, 27, 11, 10, 44, 38]. SwinGS [28] further adopts a sliding-window design to limit memory consumption and support longer volumetric video sequences. Video-coded Gaussian streaming takes a complementary direction by exploiting commodity video hardware. V3[41] maps dynamic Gaussian attributes into 2D Gaussian videos, enabling H.264 compression, hardware decoding, and shader-based rendering on mobile devices. Vega [17] further improves full-scene mobile streaming through object-level selective computation and view-adaptive scheduling, while MobileGS and SEELE optimize client-side Gaussian processing and rasterization [5, 51]. Despite these advances, existing video-coded pipelines still treat all Gaussians as temporally varying signals and repeatedly pass them through frame-wise compression. This can unnecessarily expose stable background primitives to quantization noise and optimization-induced attribute drift. Our work instead isolates stable Gaussians before encoding, preserving them across frames while retaining compact dynamic streams for real-time mobile playback.

2 Preliminary

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [16] represents a scene as a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives G={gᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N. Each primitive is parameterized as

gᵢ=(pᵢ,qᵢ,sᵢ,αᵢ,cᵢ),

(1)

with pᵢ, qᵢ, sᵢ, αᵢ, and cᵢ describing its position, rotation, scale, opacity, and view-dependent color, respectively. The rotation and scale determine the spatial extent of a Gaussian through its covariance matrix. Under a viewing transformation W, the covariance is projected onto the image plane as

Σᵢ=RᵢSᵢSᵢᵀRᵢᵀ, Σ^′ᵢ=JWΣᵢWᵀJᵀ,

(2)

in which Rᵢ and Sᵢ are the rotation and scaling matrices, J is the Jacobian of the projective transformation, and Σ^′ᵢ gives the projected covariance. During rendering, the Gaussians overlapping a pixel are depth-sorted and accumulated through front-to-back alpha blending:

C=∑_i∈ℕcᵢα^′ᵢ∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-α^′ⱼ),

(3)

where ℕ contains the ordered Gaussians contributing to the pixel and α^′ᵢ is the corresponding projected opacity. This explicit representation enables efficient rasterization while maintaining high-quality novel-view rendering. For dynamic scenes, a volumetric video can therefore be viewed as a temporal sequence of these Gaussian attributes, whose values evolve from frame to frame.

Building on this explicit representation, V3[41] organizes dynamic 3DGS into frame groups for volumetric video streaming. The first frame of each group is reconstructed as a keyframe, and subsequent frames are optimized sequentially from the preceding Gaussian representation. Motion is first estimated for the Gaussian primitives, followed by fine-tuning of the remaining attributes to improve temporal consistency across frames. By maintaining a consistent set of primitives within each frame group, the attributes of the same Gaussian can be associated across consecutive frames rather than reconstructed independently at every time step. After training, the per-frame Gaussian attributes are packed into 2D attribute images for video coding. V3 applies Morton sorting before packing so that spatially neighboring Gaussians are placed at nearby image locations, improving the spatial coherence of the resulting attribute maps. The same ordering is retained across attribute images and consecutive frames, allowing corresponding pixel locations to represent the same Gaussian primitive over time. As a result, the evolution of Gaussian attributes is converted into temporally coherent image sequences that can be compressed using conventional video codecs such as H.264. On mobile devices, hardware video decoders recover the attribute maps for standard 3DGS rendering.

3 Motivation

In this section, we investigate why existing all-Gaussians video coding is poorly suited to complex full-scene volumetric video. This leads to our first research question.

3.1 RQ1. Is All-Gaussians Video Coding Effective for Full-Scene Content?

Effectiveness Analysis. Existing Gaussian-video pipelines treat the complete Gaussian representation as a frame-varying signal, which is well suited to human-centric content where many important primitives change together with the moving subject.
