We address this with a domain matching paradigm: at random training iterations, we replace the noisy irradiance map zₜ^E with the noisy cue zₜ^Eᶜᵘᵉ. This encourages denoising towards a probability path closer to the high-quality manifold and improves both RGB and irradiance generation. This design is fundamentally different from previous joint cross-modal modeling methods, which usually assume clean and reliable modalities during both training and inference. In contrast, our framework is explicitly designed for imperfect irradiance cues with domain discrepancies, which are common in practical relighting settings. It also differs from prior irradiance-conditioned methods that directly feed the estimated cue into the generator, making them more vulnerable to accumulated geometry and rendering errors.

    5.3. Hijacked asynchronous inference strategy

    In Section 5.1 we show how to construct the irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ, given an input video and a target lighting condition. In order to utilize it during inference, we design a hijacked conditional inference strategy that guides the sampling process towards the probability path indicated by the irradiance cue. We illustrate this process in Figure 3. Specifically, we obtain the noisy irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ_tₕ with Eq. 4, where tₕ is the hijack timestep. Before tₕ, at each timestep only the noisy RGB latents are updated while the irradiance latents remain fixed at Eᶜᵘᵉ_tₕ. After tₕ, the two modalities are denoised together. This strategy effectively utilizes low-frequency lighting prior provided by the noisy irradiance map, while removing high-frequency artifacts by joint denoising. The hyperparameter tₕ controls the amount of noise that is added to the irradiance cue, offering a flexible tradeoff between generation quality and lighting fidelity. In practice, we find that tₕ=0.6T works well for most cases. When the irradiance cue is reliable, a smaller tₕ helps preserve more high-frequency appearance details. When the cue is noisy or less aligned, a larger tₕ is preferable because it suppresses artifacts more aggressively.

    6. Experiments

    Implementation details.

    We fine-tune Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [(Wan et al., 2025)] for 12K steps at 832×480 resolution using a learning rate of 10⁻⁵ and batch size 16. Domain matching is applied only during the last 4K steps. We apply this second-stage training after the first-stage joint modeling has largely converged, and empirically find that 4K steps are sufficient for the model to adapt to the imperfect irradiance-cue distribution. To further mitigate the visual characteristics of synthetic training data, we adopt a noise augmentation strategy inspired by ReCamMaster [(Bai et al., 2025)]: a moderate level of noise (equivalent to 200–500 diffusion timesteps) is added to the conditional video latent during training, which discourages the model from relying on domain-specific synthetic cues and improves robustness at real-world inference time. We set the hijack timestep to tₕ=0.6T for every experiment and do not retune it case by case.

    Baselines

    We compare our method with the publicly available video relighting method DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)], UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)] and Light-X [(Liu et al., 2025a)]. Image relighting methods DiLightNet [(Zeng et al., 2024b)] and Neural-Gaffer [(Jin et al., 2024)] are also included. We adopt the Cosmos [(Agarwal et al., 2025)] implementation version of DiffusionRenderer for a fair comparison. These methods allow environment maps as control signals. We additionally include prompt-based relighting methods, including IC-Light [(Zhang et al., 2025b)], Light-A-Video [(Zhou et al., 2025)], TC-Light [(Liu et al., 2025b)]. For environment-map-conditioned methods we use the identical target HDR map; prompt-based methods instead receive best-effort captions derived from the target lighting, so exact direction and intensity cannot be guaranteed.

    Datasets

    We use the test subset of our synthetic dataset for quantitative evaluation. It contains 100 test cases: 50 static-lighting cases (SynthStatic) and 50 rotary-lighting cases (SynthDynamic), each with an input video, relit target, and target environment map. For qualitative comparison, test cases are sampled from the HumanVid [(Wang et al., 2024b)] dataset. Since there is no publicly available video relighting dataset for quantitative evaluation, we follow previous video relighting methods such as DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)] and UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)] by using our proposed synthetic dataset for the video benchmark. To test cross-dataset generalization independently of our synthetic renderer, we additionally evaluate static images from HumanOLAT [(Teufel et al., 2025)].

    Metrics.

    We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]. We also conduct a user study on visual quality and illumination accuracy. Following prior works [(Jin et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025; He et al., 2025)], we avoid per-channel rescaling and instead compare results directly with ground truth, enabling faithful evaluation of relighting fidelity.

    6.1. Evaluation

    Qualitative comparison

    Figures 5 and  6 compare vertical and horizontal cases, respectively; the latter includes SynthStatic examples. Prompt-based methods including IC-Light, TC-Light, and Light-A-Video produce appealing lighting styles, but cannot precisely control lighting direction or ambient color because text prompts are ambiguous. These methods often produce warm tones and can retain hard input shadows, as in the second case of Figure 5. Light-X and Neural Gaffer inherits much of the input lighting distribution and mainly modifies color tone, while DiLightNet produces low-quality results caused by inaccurate material estimates. DiffusionRenderer and UniRelight performs reasonably well in terms of light direction and color. However, inaccurate material estimation yields unrealistic skin and clothing textures (Figs. 6 and 5). It also causes identity drift, demonstrated on the third case of Figure 6. More importantly, implicit light transport modeling sometimes fails to produce physically correct results. In Fig. 5 (third case), DiffusionRenderer mistakes yellow ambient light for the main source, ignoring the actual moon light. In contrast, our method models light transport with guidance from the path-traced irradiance cue, facilitating physically accurate illumination control. Although trained on human-centric data, our method also generalizes to the cat example in Figure  6.

    Quantitative comparison

    Table 1 confirms the qualitative observation that DiffusionRenderer and UniRelight respond more faithfully to environment maps than the other baselines. We evaluate on 100 test cases in total, with 50 cases from SynthStatic and 50 from SynthDynamic. For prompt-based methods, we ask GPT 5.4 to describe the lighting in the ground truth video and use the caption as text prompt input. For image-based methods, we perform relighting frame by frame. Our method obtains the best PSNR and LPIPS on SynthStatic, while UniRelight obtains the best SSIM. On SynthDynamic, our method is best on all three metrics. The larger advantage under rotating illumination indicates that explicit irradiance guidance improves controllability when the target lighting changes over time.

    HumanOLAT evaluation

    We synthesize ground-truth relit images from HumanOLAT OLAT captures under 100 HDR environment maps. We apply the provided foreground masks before computing metrics and do not perform per-channel rescaling. Table 2 shows that our model, trained without HumanOLAT data, achieves the best performance among all evaluated methods. Qualitative comparison is presented in Figure 11

    User study

    A user study evaluated perceptual quality on in-the-wild videos. Participants viewed the relighting results, the input video, and the environment map, and rated methods from 1 to 5 on visual quality (VQ) and lighting fidelity (LF). The study involved 13 in-lab users, and average scores are reported in Table 1. We evaluate 15 indoor and outdoor test cases in total. Before the study, we explain that visual quality measures the overall perceptual realism, including artifacts and temporal stability, while lighting fidelity evaluates how well the generated result matches the target illumination in terms of light direction, shadow, and highlight consistency. Compared to baselines, our results are consistently preferred on both dimensions.

    Dynamic scenes with dynamic illumination

    Thanks to explicit light transport guidance from asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint modeling, our method naturally extends to dynamic scenes with dynamic illumination. Figure 7 shows results sampled every 10 frames. Our method faithfully follows the sun direction and produces physically plausible lighting effects.

    Runtime

    For an 81-frame, 832×480 video sampled with 50 diffusion steps on one NVIDIA A800 GPU, the full pipeline takes 223 s: 22.8 s for depth estimation, 38.2 s for mesh conversion, 18.8 s for Mitsuba rendering, and 141.9 s for neural generation (minor overhead accounts for the remaining time). Under the same evaluation setting, UniRelight, DiffusionRenderer, and Light-A-Video take 1077 s, 1629 s, and 1822 s, respectively. Thus, external reconstruction and rendering are not the main runtime bottleneck.

    7. Ablation study

    Qualitative ablation

    We conduct ablation study on our asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint modeling and domain matching strategy with qualitative results in Figure 10. Without the asynchronous joint modeling training paradigm, simply using the irradiance cue as control signal, the model fails to follow the light transport. Joint modeling alone does not sufficiently bridge the domain gap; domain matching is essential for producing pixel-aligned irradiance maps and physically plausible RGB results. Without it, the denoised irradiance maps exhibit black edges and blurred details, leading to suboptimal outputs. In contrast, the full recipe generates pixel-aligned RGB and irradiance images, producing physically accurate and visually plausible results.

    Quantitative ablation

    We report quantitative ablation results in Tables 3 and 4. We additionally train a no-irradiance variant that receives only the target HDR environment map under the same data and optimization protocol, analogous to HDR-conditioned implicit relighting. All ablation models are trained for 6K steps, with domain matching applied during the final 2K steps. HDR map conditioning does not provide pixel-aligned guidance for light distribution, which produces less accurate relighting results compared to irradiance conditioning. Joint modeling irradiance and RGB alone brings limited gains because the imperfect irradiance cue still causes a noticeable train-test mismatch. Introducing hijacked conditional generation and asynchronous timestep scheduling progressively improves both lighting fidelity and visual quality, while the domain matching strategy delivers the final performance boost by explicitly aligning the cue distribution with inference-time inputs. We also compare different modality embedding strategies and find that injecting the modality cue through the time embedding performs best, likely because it modulates the denoising process globally and reduces the ambiguity between RGB appearance and irradiance guidance.

    8. Discussion

    We present JointLight, a human-centric video relighting framework that jointly models RGB and irradiance asynchronously. We also introduce a high-quality human-centric multi-illumination synthetic dataset covering indoor and outdoor scenarios, paired with ground-truth irradiance maps. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model achieves state-of-the-art relighting quality and fidelity.

    Robustness to geometry errors

    Our method depends on monocular geometry only through the rendered irradiance cue. Because geometry is estimated independently per frame, errors do not accumulate as global reconstruction drift. Noise injection suppresses high-frequency defects such as jagged boundaries, holes, and aliased shadows, but cannot recover light transport that is absent from severely incorrect geometry. Aggressive subject or camera motion can also produce blur and occlusion errors. Incorrect depths or holes near discontinuities may distort the path-traced cue and can cause light leakage (the bottom-right case in Figure 9).

    Limitations and Future Work

    First, irradiance provides diffuse transport only and therefore cannot explicitly or physically control full specular transport. Video priors can synthesize plausible moderate highlights on skin and hair, but these effects are not guaranteed to follow the target illumination; polished metal, mirrors, and glass remain difficult. A failure case is shown in the bottom-right case of Figure 9. Second, suppressing high-frequency cue errors can also attenuate texture-rich appearance, occasionally over-smoothing fine facial details around the eyes and mouth. Future work could jointly reason about geometry, material, diffuse and specular transport, and use detail-preserving or preference-based post-training. Extending the control representation beyond environment maps to local spotlights or flashlights is another promising direction.

    Acknowledgements.

    This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62322210, 62561160115), the Beijing Major Science and Technology Project (No. Z251100008125009), the Royal Society (IEC \233596), and the Innovation Funding of ICT, CAS (No. E561100).

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 3DGS 综述把话说清了：渲染已有表示，和构建/更新/维护场景，是两笔不同的成本 ｜ Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Scene Reconstruction: Methods, Systems, and Trade-offs
item.description:
一句话：把 GS 场景重建分成五族并区分「渲染吞吐」与「场景构建/更新成本」，给出端到端管线的取舍地图。

要点：

  • 五族划分：单次生成、动态表示、效率与压缩、流式与沉浸系统、GS-SLAM（彼此有重叠）
  • 明确区分「只渲染」的吞吐与任务相关的场景生成、更新、跟踪、建图与优化成本
  • 把受控稀疏视角基准与各自的原始评测结合，梳理质量、延迟、显存与更新代价之间的跨族取舍

为什么值得看：工程上最容易踩的坑是把论文里的渲染 FPS 当成整条流水线成本；这篇综述给的是选型时的成本边界，而不是又一张 FPS 排行榜。

中文摘要：3DGS 自 2023 年提出以来，其显式且高度可配置的场景表示被迅速扩展到稀疏视角生成、动态重建、效率与压缩、流式传输以及 SLAM。这篇综述提醒一件常被混淆的事：高斯泼溅能实时渲染，但「渲染一个已有表示」和「构建、更新、维护场景本身」是完全不同的成本。作者把文献归成五族——单次生成、动态表示、效率与压缩、流式与沉浸式系统、GS-SLAM——并把它们串成一条端到端管线，同时把纯渲染吞吐与任务相关的生成、更新、跟踪、建图、优化代价分开统计，再用受控的稀疏视角基准结合各自的原始评测，找出跨族在质量、延迟、显存与更新成本上的取舍关系。对要选型的引擎团队来说，这比又一张 FPS 排行榜有用。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-13

本期推送：2026-10-25

Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Scene Reconstruction: Methods, Systems, and Trade-offs

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows for high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis. Since its inception in 2023, its explicit and highly configurable scene representation has been extended toward sparse-view generation, dynamic reconstruction, efficiency and compression, streaming, and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). Although Gaussian Splatting can provide real-time rendering, rendering an existing representation is distinct from constructing, updating, or maintaining the scene itself. In this survey, we synthesize current literature, categorize them and provide a connection of current approaches and tools towards an end-to-end pipeline. Explicitly, we categorize GS scene reconstruction into five overlapping families: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM. We distinguish render-only throughput from task-specific scene generation, update, tracking, mapping, and optimization costs, and combine controlled sparse-view benchmarking with native evaluations to identify cross-family quality, latency, memory, and update-cost trade-offs.

Keywords:

Gaussian Splatting , 3D Scene Representation , Novel View Synthesis , Neural Rendering , Multi-View Geometry

1 Introduction

Kerbl et al. [19] introduced 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) as an explicit scene representation capable of high-quality interactive novel-view rendering. Subsequent work rapidly extended this formulation beyond static per-scene reconstruction. Deformable 3DGS [67] and 4DGaussians [61] introduced temporal deformation and spatiotemporal representations, while later methods explored feed-forward sparse-view generation [4, 5], efficiency and compression, streaming, and Gaussian-based SLAM. These developments increasingly shift the systems bottleneck from rendering an existing representation toward constructing, updating, transmitting, or maintaining the Gaussian scene. This distinction is important for applications such as free-viewpoint video, immersive media, online mapping, and robotics. In these settings, interactive rendering alone is insufficient when scene construction, temporal updates, or map maintenance remain substantially slower than rasterization.

Several surveys have reviewed 3DGS from broader perspectives. Wu et al. [62] organize the field by 3D reconstruction, editing, and downstream applications; Fei et al. [10] use taxonomies based on characteristics and applications; and Bao et al. [2] examine optimization, applications, extensions, and recurring technical modules. More focused surveys address compression and compaction [1] and robotics [80]. As summarized in Table 1, our focus is different: we organize Gaussian Splatting as a reconstruction pipeline and study which task-specific costs limit real-time deployment.

In this survey, real-time is task specific. We distinguish render-only throughput from scene generation, dynamic or streaming updates, SLAM tracking and mapping, and offline optimization. These quantities are compared only when their unit of work and timing boundary are aligned, as defined in Section2.7.

We formulate real-time Gaussian scene reconstruction from the pipeline perspective illustrated in Figure1. We organize the literature into five overlapping families according to the stage containing the dominant contribution: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM. This pipeline-centric view exposes where geometry, pose estimation, temporal updates, memory, and rendering costs arise across otherwise different GS systems.

We summarize the scope, organization, and contributions of this survey as follows:

  • 1.

    Pipeline-centric taxonomy: We organize GS research into five overlapping families according to the dominant stage of the reconstruction pipeline, supported by a compact tag schema for structured comparison (Figures2 and 3).

  • 2.

    Task-specific real-time framework: We distinguish render-only throughput, scene generation, temporal updates, SLAM tracking and mapping, and offline optimization using explicit units of work and timing boundaries (Sections2.7, 4.2 and 4.3).

  • 3.

    Quantitative and algorithmic evaluation: We provide a controlled comparison of compatible sparse-view methods and complementary native evaluations across the remaining families, with explicit comparability boundaries and mechanism-level analysis (Section 6).

  • 4.

    Cross-family synthesis: We connect algorithmic choices to quality, latency, memory, update cost, and deployment suitability, and identify remaining barriers toward end-to-end real-time systems (Section 6 and Section7).

    • 2 Preliminaries

    Figure1 summarizes the end-to-end Gaussian Splatting reconstruction pipeline and where our five taxonomy families intervene. This section fixes terminology and notation, summarizes the core 3DGS representation and rasterization/compositing used for real-time rendering, and defines the training regimes, input/supervision assumptions, and the real-time criterion used throughout. We conclude with a compact tag schema used to structure the taxonomy and method comparisons.

    2.1 Scope and Terms

    We use Gaussian Splatting to refer to modern 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [19]: an explicit set of 3D Gaussian primitives parameterized in world space and rendered by fast (typically differentiable) screen-space splatting with rasterization/compositing. Under this scope, the primary object is a Gaussian scene representation (centers, covariances, opacities, and appearance parameters), and the key efficiency advantage comes from rasterizing a finite set of primitives rather than volumetric ray marching. We do not survey NeRFs [34] as a primary topic. We cite NeRF-related work only when necessary for context (e.g., datasets/metrics) or when a method explicitly transfers radiance-field ideas into Gaussian representations.

    Finally, we use real-time scene reconstruction in a task-specific sense rather than through a universal FPS threshold. Rendering, scene generation, dynamic or streaming updates, and SLAM are evaluated using their corresponding units of work and timing boundaries, as defined in Section2.7.

    2.2 Notations

    Table2 lists the main symbols used in the survey. For dynamic scenes, quantities are indexed by time t and the Gaussian set at time t is denoted Gₜ. Unless stated otherwise, each primitive is represented by (μⱼ,Σⱼ,αⱼ,cⱼ), where cⱼ may be RGB, spherical harmonics coefficients, or learned features depending on the method.

    2.3 Gaussian Representation

    Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as G={gⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^N, a set of N anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives in world coordinates. Each gⱼ is defined by a mean μⱼ∈ℝ³, covariance Σⱼ∈ℝ^3×3 (commonly parameterized via rotation and per-axis scales for stability), opacity αⱼ∈[0,1], and appearance parameters cⱼ. This explicit primitive-based representation enables high-throughput rasterization pipelines compared to radiance-field rendering [19].

    Methods primarily differ in (i) which parameters are optimized vs. predicted, and (ii) how time is modeled. Static pipelines often optimize all parameters per scene with SfM/MVS/depth-based initialization; dynamic extensions introduce time dependence via explicit per-frame parameters, deformation models, or static/dynamic partitions. Online/SLAM-style systems additionally constrain updates to bounded latency and control representation growth via pruning, keyframes, and local refinement.

    Representation complexity and real-time knobs

    Runtime and memory are dominated by the number of primitives N and the appearance bandwidth (e.g., SH degree or feature dimensionality). Dynamic/streaming settings add growth over time, so many systems explicitly regulate N and appearance parameters to meet real-time targets.

    Representation vs. serialization (file formats)

    Gaussian scenes may be stored in different encodings (e.g., PLY-like formats or .splat-style binaries). These typically change serialization/layout and attribute encoding (e.g., quantization, SH/features) rather than the underlying representation {(μⱼ,Σⱼ,αⱼ,cⱼ)}ⱼ₌₁^N.

    2.4 Rasterization

    Given camera intrinsics K and pose T=(R,t), each mean μⱼ projects to

    μ̂ⱼ=π (K,T;μⱼ)∈ℝ²,

    		(1)

    and its 3D covariance Σⱼ induces an elliptical screen-space footprint (2D covariance) Σ^2Dⱼ. Rendering composites projected splats in approximate front-to-back order using alpha/transmittance blending [19]. Modern implementations use GPU tiled rasterization and sorting so only splats overlapping a pixel/tile are processed, which is central to real-time performance [70]. Approximate visibility/sorting can cause artifacts in dense or dynamic regions [20], motivating improved compositing and hardware/system optimizations [73, 52, 12].

    2.5 Training

    We group common regimes by when optimization/learning happens: per-scene/per-sequence optimization (offline fitting), amortized feed-forward generation via pretrained models, and dynamic/online settings where temporal modeling and incremental updates impose bounded-latency constraints. Per-scene optimization fits {(μⱼ,Σⱼ,αⱼ,cⱼ)} for a specific sequence [19]; amortized methods predict Gaussians at inference time (optionally followed by brief test-time refinement) [63, 5, 4, 30]. Dynamic methods often introduce time-dependent parameterizations or deformations and are frequently optimized per sequence [61, 11, 67], while online/SLAM pipelines prioritize training-free or pretrained components at runtime with efficient map maintenance.

    2.6 Inputs and Supervision

    We categorize input modalities as multi-view captures, monocular video, and RGB-D or sensor-augmented streams (e.g., events). Pose assumptions range from known (calibration/SfM) to estimated/refined (tracked or jointly optimized) to pose-free. Supervision is often self-supervised via photometric consistency, but many pipelines incorporate pretrained priors (especially depth/MVS) to stabilize geometry and accelerate initialization.

    2.7 Task-Specific Real-Time Definition

    The term real-time is used differently across Gaussian Splatting methods. Rendering, scene generation, streaming updates, and SLAM correspond to different tasks and should therefore not share a single throughput definition. We use approximately 24 FPS only as a reference for interactive playback, not as a universal threshold for reconstruction or scene updates.

    Let all latency values be expressed in milliseconds. Render-only throughput is defined as

    rFPS=(1000)/(t_render),

    		(2)

    where t_render is the time required to render one frame from an existing Gaussian representation. For a reconstruction or update task, the pipeline latency can be written as

    tₚᵢₚₑ=tₚᵣₑ+tₚₒₛₑ+t_depth/fusion+tᵢₙᵢₜ+t_update+t_render,

    		(3)

    where only stages relevant to the evaluated task are included. The corresponding task throughput is

    R_T=(1000)/(t_T).

    		(4)

    Accordingly, we report scene throughput for feed-forward reconstruction, update throughput for dynamic and streaming methods, and tracking or mapping throughput for SLAM systems. Offline optimization is reported using training or optimization time rather than scenes per second. These quantities are compared only when the task, unit of work, and timing boundary are aligned.

    2.8 Summary of Tags

    To compare methods consistently across our taxonomy, we annotate each paper using a compact tag set capturing input assumptions, regime, temporal scope, and runtime setting. Table3 summarizes the master schema and family-specific extensions.

    3 Methodology

    We survey Gaussian Splatting (GS) research toward real-time scene reconstruction using the task-specific definitions in Section2.7. Our workflow is: (i) collect papers broadly, (ii) apply inclusion criteria aligned with the GS reconstruction pipeline, (iii) assign a pipeline-centric taxonomy with consistent tags, and (iv) interpret reported efficiency using end-to-end-aware conventions.

    3.1 Literature Collection and Inclusion Criteria

    We prioritize recent work (2023–2025) while retaining foundational baselines needed for context (datasets, metrics, and core dynamic/NVS references). Literature was identified primarily through Google Scholar and the proceedings of CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, NeurIPS, and ICLR. Seed queries included Gaussian splatting, Gaussian splatting for SLAM, efficient Gaussian splatting, fast Gaussian splatting, sparse-view Gaussian splatting, and zero-shot Gaussian splatting, together with closely related variants for dynamic reconstruction, streaming, compression, pose-free reconstruction, and real-time reconstruction. Reference lists of relevant papers were also inspected to identify related and foundational work (backward citation snowballing). We include methods whose primary scene representation is an explicit Gaussian-based model (or a direct extension) and that materially affect one or more stages of a GS reconstruction pipeline (initialization/generation, temporal modeling, map maintenance, streaming/delivery, compositing, or tracking-and-mapping). We exclude NeRF-style methods as a primary focus, citing them only when necessary for context or when they explicitly bridge into Gaussian representations. Duplicate versions and works outside the surveyed reconstruction/system scope are excluded; dataset, metric, and foundational papers are retained as supporting references rather than surveyed GS methods. Because the literature search evolved iteratively during preparation of the survey, intermediate retrieval and screening counts were not recorded prospectively and are therefore not reconstructed retrospectively.

    3.2 Tagging and Taxonomy Assignment

    Each paper is annotated using the master tag schema in Table 3 (input/pose/depth cues, regime, temporal scope, runtime setting, and efficiency levers). We assign each method to one primary family based on its dominant contribution, while noting meaningful overlaps when a method intervenes in multiple pipeline stages. The five families in Fig. 2 are constructed to reflect where methods intervene operationally in the end-to-end pipeline (Fig. 1), enabling consistent comparison across tables and sections.

    3.3 Interpreting Performance Claims

    To avoid conflating rendering speed with reconstruction throughput, runtime evidence is interpreted according to the task being measured rather than through a universal FPS or SPS quantity. Render-only results, scene generation, dynamic or streaming updates, SLAM, and offline optimization follow the timing boundaries defined in Section2.7. Results are treated as directly comparable only when the dataset, input protocol, resolution, hardware, unit of work, and timing boundary are sufficiently aligned; otherwise, they are treated as method-specific evidence. When code, pretrained models, or timing scripts are available, we prioritize these artifacts over high-level paper claims for interpreting runtime and memory. For methods evaluated in Section 6, repository configurations, checkpoints, native schedules, and evaluation procedures are used where available to establish the reported operating conditions.

    4 Datasets and Evaluation Protocols

    This section summarizes the datasets, quality metrics, and evaluation protocols used throughout the survey. Runtime comparisons follow the task-specific definitions introduced in Section 2.7.

    4.1 Datasets and Quality Metrics

    Datasets (representative regimes)

    Although datasets are not the main focus of this survey, they strongly influence what claims are comparable. Across the literature, benchmarks cluster into five recurring regimes. (i) Multi-view dome/studio captures provide calibrated multi-camera observations and controlled dynamics, commonly used for high-fidelity dynamic reconstruction (e.g., Technicolor Light Field [45], Neu3DV [27], Replay [48], NeRSemble [22], PKU-DyMVHumans [77], DiVa-360 [32]). (ii) Monocular/handheld sequences emphasize pose uncertainty, motion blur, and in-the-wild dynamics, often inherited from dynamic NeRF benchmarks (e.g., NSFF Dynamic [29], D-NeRF [42], Nerfies [40], HyperNeRF [39]) and more recent GS/video-generation settings (e.g., Splat4D [72]). (iii) Event+RGB settings target fast motion and low-light where conventional frames degrade, using event streams as additional supervision or cues (e.g., Dynamic EventNeRF [44], E-4DGS [11]). (iv) Outdoor/driving/drone captures evaluate scalability and SLAM-like conditions, often with LiDAR/SLAM pose supervision and dynamic agents (e.g., MTGS [28], DroneSplat [53], Wide-Range-4D [66]). (v) Synthetic/physics-based datasets provide controllable dynamics and/or ground-truth structure for stress-testing temporal modeling (e.g., Deep3D Mask Volume [31], PhysGaia [21], Hybrid 3D-4DGS [37], DynaSplat [7]).

    Image fidelity and temporal stability

    Most works report standard per-frame fidelity using PSNR, SSIM [59], and LPIPS [74], typically averaged over time for dynamic sequences. To reflect temporal stability, several papers additionally report flow-warped temporal errors or flow-based temporal discrepancy scores [6]. Some works also use video metrics such as FVD [55], although these are less consistently reported.

    4.2 Task-Specific Runtime Metrics

    Runtime is reported according to the task being measured. Render FPS (rFPS) refers only to rendering an existing Gaussian representation. Feed-forward methods use scene throughput, dynamic and streaming methods use update throughput, and SLAM methods use tracking or mapping throughput. Offline optimization is reported using training or optimization time. These quantities are compared only when they measure the same task under the same timing boundary.

    4.3 Evaluation Protocol

    Quantitative comparisons require aligned datasets, input settings, resolution, hardware, and timing boundaries. When these conditions are not aligned, results are treated as method-specific evidence rather than direct comparisons. We therefore report both quality and runtime together with the experimental conditions under which they were measured.

    5 Taxonomy

    We organize Gaussian Splatting work for real-time reconstruction into five pipeline-centric families, defined by the primary stage a method intervenes in (capture/training, representation, rendering, system delivery, or online estimation). Because many methods are multi-faceted, we allow secondary overlaps but assign each paper a single primary family based on its dominant technical contribution.

    Figure 3 shows the chronological development of representative methods across these families, illustrating how work following 3DGS progressively expanded toward amortized generation, temporal modeling, efficiency, streaming, and online mapping.

    Single-shot / amortized Gaussian generation

    Feed-forward construction of a usable Gaussian scene from one or few images, often using depth/MVS priors or learned regularizers, optionally followed by brief refinement. Poses may be known, refined, or pose-free, but the defining feature is replacing heavy per-scene iterative fitting with amortized inference from limited views.

    Dynamic representations beyond 4DGS

    Methods that treat time as a first-class variable in the scene model (e.g., time-conditioned parameters, deformation/warp fields, key-time primitives, canonical-plus-delta factorization) or explicitly mitigate dynamic failure modes such as ghosting, identity swaps, occlusion/disocclusion artifacts, and temporal flicker. The emphasis is modeling temporal change, not merely delivering or replaying content over time.

    Efficiency and compression

    Works whose central goal is reducing compute, memory, or storage/bandwidth while preserving real-time operation, via levers such as pruning/sparsification, quantization/packing, view-adaptive LoD selection, or system/hardware acceleration. We place a method here when efficiency is the primary objective rather than a side effect.

    Streaming and immersive video systems

    Long-duration capture and interactive free-viewpoint playback under latency/bandwidth constraints, enabled by explicit delivery mechanisms (progressive transmission, caching/tiling/segmenting, rate control, bandwidth-aware loading, or continual update protocols). The core contribution is system delivery and interactivity over time, not new temporal scene parameterizations.

    SLAM with Gaussian Splatting

    Online tracking-and-mapping where camera poses are estimated incrementally and the Gaussian map is updated under bounded latency/compute, typically using keyframes, map maintenance/pruning, robustness to blur/occlusions, and (when relevant) loop-consistency considerations. We place a method here when meeting tracking deadlines and maintaining a bounded-cost map are central to the design.

    6 Quantitative Evaluation and Synthesis

    6.1 Single-Shot and Sparse-View Generation

    For calibrated sparse-view methods, Gaussian construction can be expressed as depth inference followed by unprojection,

    μᵢ(u)=π⁻¹ (u,d̂ᵢ(u);Kᵢ,Tᵢ), (Σᵢ,αᵢ,cᵢ)=H_θ (fᵢ(u)).

    		(5)

    MVSplat [5] estimates d̂ᵢ from a plane-sweep cost volume,

    Cᵢ(u,dₖ)=Agg_m≠i⟨Fᵢ(u),W_m→i(Fₘ;dₖ)⟩, d̂ᵢ=∑ₖsoftmax(Cᵢ)ₖdₖ,

    		(6)

    so geometry is determined primarily by cross-view correspondence. DepthSplat [63] instead augments the multi-view matching representation with pretrained monocular depth features,

    C̃ᵢ=Φ_θ (Cᵢ,Fᵢᵐᵒⁿᵒ),

    		(7)

    before depth regression and Gaussian unprojection. This additional geometric prior corresponds to the highest PSNR/SSIM and lowest LPIPS in table5, but also increases model-stage latency and memory relative to MVSplat. pixelSplat [4] avoids committing directly to one depth by predicting pᵢ(d|u) and differentiably sampling

    dᵢ∼pᵢ(d|u), μᵢ(u)=π⁻¹(u,dᵢ;Kᵢ,Tᵢ).

    		(8)

    Its more flexible treatment of geometric ambiguity is accompanied by the largest construction latency and memory footprint in the controlled experiment. Thus, table5 shows that the mechanism used to estimate μⱼ directly affects both reconstruction quality and construction cost; in this experiment, augmenting multi-view matching with monocular depth features gives the strongest quality, while the lighter cost-volume formulation gives the lowest latency.

    The native methods in table6 remove the calibrated-pose assumption in different ways. Splatt3R [49] extends MASt3R [25] with a Gaussian prediction head, which can be summarized as

    (xⱼ, Δxⱼ, qⱼ, sⱼ, αⱼ, cⱼ)=H_θ(I₁,I₂), μⱼ=xⱼ+Δxⱼ,

    		(9)

    with Σⱼ obtained from the predicted rotation qⱼ and scale sⱼ. The scene is therefore produced directly from an uncalibrated pair without optimizing camera variables. InstantSplat  [9] instead uses dense stereo priors to initialize both geometry and cameras and then performs Gaussian Bundle Adjustment,

    \min_G, {Tᵢ}∑ᵢLₚₕₒₜₒ(Iᵢ,Î(G,Tᵢ)),

    		(10)

    jointly updating the Gaussian parameters and poses. This distinction is visible quantitatively: Splatt3R requires 1.10 s for measured construction/export, whereas InstantSplat uses 16.01 s for initialization followed by 35.02 s of optimization. Hence the former admits a construction throughput, while the latter is an optimization problem whose runtime depends on the refinement budget. In both cases, the much larger decoder-only rFPS reported in table5 remains a separate quantity from the cost of constructing G. Recent feed-forward generalists broaden this regime to unconstrained input views and unified geometry-to-Gaussian prediction, as exemplified by AnySplat and YoNoSplat [18, 68]. These systems relax capture assumptions, but move additional latency and memory pressure into their learned geometry backbones and cross-view fusion.

    6.2 Dynamic Representations

    Let qⱼ and sⱼ denote the rotation and scale parameterization of Σⱼ. Dynamic deformation can then be written as

    (Δμⱼ,Δqⱼ,Δsⱼ)=F_θ(μⱼ,t), μⱼ(t)=μⱼ+Δμⱼ,

    		(11)

    with the predicted rotation and scale determining Σⱼ(t). Deformable-3D-Gaussians [67] uses an MLP deformation field conditioned directly on canonical position and time. 4DGaussians [61] instead obtains the deformation from factorized spatio-temporal features, using a HexPlane-style  [3] 4D encoding followed by a lightweight decoder. Thus, the former places motion complexity in the continuous deformation network, whereas the latter shifts part of it into an explicit space–time feature structure. In table7, both reach similar quality on D-NeRF bouncingballs: 41.38 dB for Deformable-3D-Gaussians and 40.81 dB for 4DGaussians. These values show that both deformation parameterizations can represent the same synthetic motion regime at high fidelity. 4DGaussians additionally renders at 36.03 rFPS in the measured native setup, showing that the deformation representation can remain compatible with interactive rendering after optimization.

要点：

  • 五族划分：单次生成、动态表示、效率与压缩、流式与沉浸系统、GS-SLAM（彼此有重叠）
  • 明确区分「只渲染」的吞吐与任务相关的场景生成、更新、跟踪、建图与优化成本
  • 把受控稀疏视角基准与各自的原始评测结合，梳理质量、延迟、显存与更新代价之间的跨族取舍

为什么值得看：工程上最容易踩的坑是把论文里的渲染 FPS 当成整条流水线成本；这篇综述给的是选型时的成本边界，而不是又一张 FPS 排行榜。

中文摘要：3DGS 自 2023 年提出以来，其显式且高度可配置的场景表示被迅速扩展到稀疏视角生成、动态重建、效率与压缩、流式传输以及 SLAM。这篇综述提醒一件常被混淆的事：高斯泼溅能实时渲染，但「渲染一个已有表示」和「构建、更新、维护场景本身」是完全不同的成本。作者把文献归成五族——单次生成、动态表示、效率与压缩、流式与沉浸式系统、GS-SLAM——并把它们串成一条端到端管线，同时把纯渲染吞吐与任务相关的生成、更新、跟踪、建图、优化代价分开统计，再用受控的稀疏视角基准结合各自的原始评测，找出跨族在质量、延迟、显存与更新成本上的取舍关系。对要选型的引擎团队来说，这比又一张 FPS 排行榜有用。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-13

本期推送：2026-10-25

Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Scene Reconstruction: Methods, Systems, and Trade-offs

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) allows for high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis. Since its inception in 2023, its explicit and highly configurable scene representation has been extended toward sparse-view generation, dynamic reconstruction, efficiency and compression, streaming, and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). Although Gaussian Splatting can provide real-time rendering, rendering an existing representation is distinct from constructing, updating, or maintaining the scene itself. In this survey, we synthesize current literature, categorize them and provide a connection of current approaches and tools towards an end-to-end pipeline. Explicitly, we categorize GS scene reconstruction into five overlapping families: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM. We distinguish render-only throughput from task-specific scene generation, update, tracking, mapping, and optimization costs, and combine controlled sparse-view benchmarking with native evaluations to identify cross-family quality, latency, memory, and update-cost trade-offs.

Keywords:

Gaussian Splatting , 3D Scene Representation , Novel View Synthesis , Neural Rendering , Multi-View Geometry

1 Introduction

Kerbl et al. [19] introduced 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) as an explicit scene representation capable of high-quality interactive novel-view rendering. Subsequent work rapidly extended this formulation beyond static per-scene reconstruction. Deformable 3DGS [67] and 4DGaussians [61] introduced temporal deformation and spatiotemporal representations, while later methods explored feed-forward sparse-view generation [4, 5], efficiency and compression, streaming, and Gaussian-based SLAM. These developments increasingly shift the systems bottleneck from rendering an existing representation toward constructing, updating, transmitting, or maintaining the Gaussian scene. This distinction is important for applications such as free-viewpoint video, immersive media, online mapping, and robotics. In these settings, interactive rendering alone is insufficient when scene construction, temporal updates, or map maintenance remain substantially slower than rasterization.

Several surveys have reviewed 3DGS from broader perspectives. Wu et al. [62] organize the field by 3D reconstruction, editing, and downstream applications; Fei et al. [10] use taxonomies based on characteristics and applications; and Bao et al. [2] examine optimization, applications, extensions, and recurring technical modules. More focused surveys address compression and compaction [1] and robotics [80]. As summarized in Table 1, our focus is different: we organize Gaussian Splatting as a reconstruction pipeline and study which task-specific costs limit real-time deployment.

In this survey, real-time is task specific. We distinguish render-only throughput from scene generation, dynamic or streaming updates, SLAM tracking and mapping, and offline optimization. These quantities are compared only when their unit of work and timing boundary are aligned, as defined in Section2.7.

We formulate real-time Gaussian scene reconstruction from the pipeline perspective illustrated in Figure1. We organize the literature into five overlapping families according to the stage containing the dominant contribution: single-shot generation, dynamic representations, efficiency and compression, streaming and immersive systems, and Gaussian Splatting SLAM. This pipeline-centric view exposes where geometry, pose estimation, temporal updates, memory, and rendering costs arise across otherwise different GS systems.

We summarize the scope, organization, and contributions of this survey as follows:

  • 1.

    Pipeline-centric taxonomy: We organize GS research into five overlapping families according to the dominant stage of the reconstruction pipeline, supported by a compact tag schema for structured comparison (Figures2 and 3).

  • 2.

    Task-specific real-time framework: We distinguish render-only throughput, scene generation, temporal updates, SLAM tracking and mapping, and offline optimization using explicit units of work and timing boundaries (Sections2.7, 4.2 and 4.3).

  • 3.

    Quantitative and algorithmic evaluation: We provide a controlled comparison of compatible sparse-view methods and complementary native evaluations across the remaining families, with explicit comparability boundaries and mechanism-level analysis (Section 6).

  • 4.

    Cross-family synthesis: We connect algorithmic choices to quality, latency, memory, update cost, and deployment suitability, and identify remaining barriers toward end-to-end real-time systems (Section 6 and Section7).

    • 2 Preliminaries

    Figure1 summarizes the end-to-end Gaussian Splatting reconstruction pipeline and where our five taxonomy families intervene. This section fixes terminology and notation, summarizes the core 3DGS representation and rasterization/compositing used for real-time rendering, and defines the training regimes, input/supervision assumptions, and the real-time criterion used throughout. We conclude with a compact tag schema used to structure the taxonomy and method comparisons.

    2.1 Scope and Terms

    We use Gaussian Splatting to refer to modern 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [19]: an explicit set of 3D Gaussian primitives parameterized in world space and rendered by fast (typically differentiable) screen-space splatting with rasterization/compositing. Under this scope, the primary object is a Gaussian scene representation (centers, covariances, opacities, and appearance parameters), and the key efficiency advantage comes from rasterizing a finite set of primitives rather than volumetric ray marching. We do not survey NeRFs [34] as a primary topic. We cite NeRF-related work only when necessary for context (e.g., datasets/metrics) or when a method explicitly transfers radiance-field ideas into Gaussian representations.

    Finally, we use real-time scene reconstruction in a task-specific sense rather than through a universal FPS threshold. Rendering, scene generation, dynamic or streaming updates, and SLAM are evaluated using their corresponding units of work and timing boundaries, as defined in Section2.7.

    2.2 Notations

    Table2 lists the main symbols used in the survey. For dynamic scenes, quantities are indexed by time t and the Gaussian set at time t is denoted Gₜ. Unless stated otherwise, each primitive is represented by (μⱼ,Σⱼ,αⱼ,cⱼ), where cⱼ may be RGB, spherical harmonics coefficients, or learned features depending on the method.

    2.3 Gaussian Representation

    Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as G={gⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^N, a set of N anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives in world coordinates. Each gⱼ is defined by a mean μⱼ∈ℝ³, covariance Σⱼ∈ℝ^3×3 (commonly parameterized via rotation and per-axis scales for stability), opacity αⱼ∈[0,1], and appearance parameters cⱼ. This explicit primitive-based representation enables high-throughput rasterization pipelines compared to radiance-field rendering [19].

    Methods primarily differ in (i) which parameters are optimized vs. predicted, and (ii) how time is modeled. Static pipelines often optimize all parameters per scene with SfM/MVS/depth-based initialization; dynamic extensions introduce time dependence via explicit per-frame parameters, deformation models, or static/dynamic partitions. Online/SLAM-style systems additionally constrain updates to bounded latency and control representation growth via pruning, keyframes, and local refinement.

    Representation complexity and real-time knobs

    Runtime and memory are dominated by the number of primitives N and the appearance bandwidth (e.g., SH degree or feature dimensionality). Dynamic/streaming settings add growth over time, so many systems explicitly regulate N and appearance parameters to meet real-time targets.

    Representation vs. serialization (file formats)

    Gaussian scenes may be stored in different encodings (e.g., PLY-like formats or .splat-style binaries). These typically change serialization/layout and attribute encoding (e.g., quantization, SH/features) rather than the underlying representation {(μⱼ,Σⱼ,αⱼ,cⱼ)}ⱼ₌₁^N.

    2.4 Rasterization

    Given camera intrinsics K and pose T=(R,t), each mean μⱼ projects to

    μ̂ⱼ=π (K,T;μⱼ)∈ℝ²,

    		(1)

    and its 3D covariance Σⱼ induces an elliptical screen-space footprint (2D covariance) Σ^2Dⱼ. Rendering composites projected splats in approximate front-to-back order using alpha/transmittance blending [19]. Modern implementations use GPU tiled rasterization and sorting so only splats overlapping a pixel/tile are processed, which is central to real-time performance [70]. Approximate visibility/sorting can cause artifacts in dense or dynamic regions [20], motivating improved compositing and hardware/system optimizations [73, 52, 12].

    2.5 Training

    We group common regimes by when optimization/learning happens: per-scene/per-sequence optimization (offline fitting), amortized feed-forward generation via pretrained models, and dynamic/online settings where temporal modeling and incremental updates impose bounded-latency constraints. Per-scene optimization fits {(μⱼ,Σⱼ,αⱼ,cⱼ)} for a specific sequence [19]; amortized methods predict Gaussians at inference time (optionally followed by brief test-time refinement) [63, 5, 4, 30]. Dynamic methods often introduce time-dependent parameterizations or deformations and are frequently optimized per sequence [61, 11, 67], while online/SLAM pipelines prioritize training-free or pretrained components at runtime with efficient map maintenance.

    2.6 Inputs and Supervision

    We categorize input modalities as multi-view captures, monocular video, and RGB-D or sensor-augmented streams (e.g., events). Pose assumptions range from known (calibration/SfM) to estimated/refined (tracked or jointly optimized) to pose-free. Supervision is often self-supervised via photometric consistency, but many pipelines incorporate pretrained priors (especially depth/MVS) to stabilize geometry and accelerate initialization.

    2.7 Task-Specific Real-Time Definition

    The term real-time is used differently across Gaussian Splatting methods. Rendering, scene generation, streaming updates, and SLAM correspond to different tasks and should therefore not share a single throughput definition. We use approximately 24 FPS only as a reference for interactive playback, not as a universal threshold for reconstruction or scene updates.

    Let all latency values be expressed in milliseconds. Render-only throughput is defined as

    rFPS=(1000)/(t_render),

    		(2)

    where t_render is the time required to render one frame from an existing Gaussian representation. For a reconstruction or update task, the pipeline latency can be written as

    tₚᵢₚₑ=tₚᵣₑ+tₚₒₛₑ+t_depth/fusion+tᵢₙᵢₜ+t_update+t_render,

    		(3)

    where only stages relevant to the evaluated task are included. The corresponding task throughput is

    R_T=(1000)/(t_T).

    		(4)

    Accordingly, we report scene throughput for feed-forward reconstruction, update throughput for dynamic and streaming methods, and tracking or mapping throughput for SLAM systems. Offline optimization is reported using training or optimization time rather than scenes per second. These quantities are compared only when the task, unit of work, and timing boundary are aligned.

    2.8 Summary of Tags

    To compare methods consistently across our taxonomy, we annotate each paper using a compact tag set capturing input assumptions, regime, temporal scope, and runtime setting. Table3 summarizes the master schema and family-specific extensions.

    3 Methodology

    We survey Gaussian Splatting (GS) research toward real-time scene reconstruction using the task-specific definitions in Section2.7. Our workflow is: (i) collect papers broadly, (ii) apply inclusion criteria aligned with the GS reconstruction pipeline, (iii) assign a pipeline-centric taxonomy with consistent tags, and (iv) interpret reported efficiency using end-to-end-aware conventions.

    3.1 Literature Collection and Inclusion Criteria

    We prioritize recent work (2023–2025) while retaining foundational baselines needed for context (datasets, metrics, and core dynamic/NVS references). Literature was identified primarily through Google Scholar and the proceedings of CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, NeurIPS, and ICLR. Seed queries included Gaussian splatting, Gaussian splatting for SLAM, efficient Gaussian splatting, fast Gaussian splatting, sparse-view Gaussian splatting, and zero-shot Gaussian splatting, together with closely related variants for dynamic reconstruction, streaming, compression, pose-free reconstruction, and real-time reconstruction. Reference lists of relevant papers were also inspected to identify related and foundational work (backward citation snowballing). We include methods whose primary scene representation is an explicit Gaussian-based model (or a direct extension) and that materially affect one or more stages of a GS reconstruction pipeline (initialization/generation, temporal modeling, map maintenance, streaming/delivery, compositing, or tracking-and-mapping). We exclude NeRF-style methods as a primary focus, citing them only when necessary for context or when they explicitly bridge into Gaussian representations. Duplicate versions and works outside the surveyed reconstruction/system scope are excluded; dataset, metric, and foundational papers are retained as supporting references rather than surveyed GS methods. Because the literature search evolved iteratively during preparation of the survey, intermediate retrieval and screening counts were not recorded prospectively and are therefore not reconstructed retrospectively.

    3.2 Tagging and Taxonomy Assignment

    Each paper is annotated using the master tag schema in Table 3 (input/pose/depth cues, regime, temporal scope, runtime setting, and efficiency levers). We assign each method to one primary family based on its dominant contribution, while noting meaningful overlaps when a method intervenes in multiple pipeline stages. The five families in Fig. 2 are constructed to reflect where methods intervene operationally in the end-to-end pipeline (Fig. 1), enabling consistent comparison across tables and sections.

    3.3 Interpreting Performance Claims

    To avoid conflating rendering speed with reconstruction throughput, runtime evidence is interpreted according to the task being measured rather than through a universal FPS or SPS quantity. Render-only results, scene generation, dynamic or streaming updates, SLAM, and offline optimization follow the timing boundaries defined in Section2.7. Results are treated as directly comparable only when the dataset, input protocol, resolution, hardware, unit of work, and timing boundary are sufficiently aligned; otherwise, they are treated as method-specific evidence. When code, pretrained models, or timing scripts are available, we prioritize these artifacts over high-level paper claims for interpreting runtime and memory. For methods evaluated in Section 6, repository configurations, checkpoints, native schedules, and evaluation procedures are used where available to establish the reported operating conditions.

    4 Datasets and Evaluation Protocols

    This section summarizes the datasets, quality metrics, and evaluation protocols used throughout the survey. Runtime comparisons follow the task-specific definitions introduced in Section 2.7.

    4.1 Datasets and Quality Metrics

    Datasets (representative regimes)

    Although datasets are not the main focus of this survey, they strongly influence what claims are comparable. Across the literature, benchmarks cluster into five recurring regimes. (i) Multi-view dome/studio captures provide calibrated multi-camera observations and controlled dynamics, commonly used for high-fidelity dynamic reconstruction (e.g., Technicolor Light Field [45], Neu3DV [27], Replay [48], NeRSemble [22], PKU-DyMVHumans [77], DiVa-360 [32]). (ii) Monocular/handheld sequences emphasize pose uncertainty, motion blur, and in-the-wild dynamics, often inherited from dynamic NeRF benchmarks (e.g., NSFF Dynamic [29], D-NeRF [42], Nerfies [40], HyperNeRF [39]) and more recent GS/video-generation settings (e.g., Splat4D [72]). (iii) Event+RGB settings target fast motion and low-light where conventional frames degrade, using event streams as additional supervision or cues (e.g., Dynamic EventNeRF [44], E-4DGS [11]). (iv) Outdoor/driving/drone captures evaluate scalability and SLAM-like conditions, often with LiDAR/SLAM pose supervision and dynamic agents (e.g., MTGS [28], DroneSplat [53], Wide-Range-4D [66]). (v) Synthetic/physics-based datasets provide controllable dynamics and/or ground-truth structure for stress-testing temporal modeling (e.g., Deep3D Mask Volume [31], PhysGaia [21], Hybrid 3D-4DGS [37], DynaSplat [7]).

    Image fidelity and temporal stability

    Most works report standard per-frame fidelity using PSNR, SSIM [59], and LPIPS [74], typically averaged over time for dynamic sequences. To reflect temporal stability, several papers additionally report flow-warped temporal errors or flow-based temporal discrepancy scores [6]. Some works also use video metrics such as FVD [55], although these are less consistently reported.

    4.2 Task-Specific Runtime Metrics

    Runtime is reported according to the task being measured. Render FPS (rFPS) refers only to rendering an existing Gaussian representation. Feed-forward methods use scene throughput, dynamic and streaming methods use update throughput, and SLAM methods use tracking or mapping throughput. Offline optimization is reported using training or optimization time. These quantities are compared only when they measure the same task under the same timing boundary.

    4.3 Evaluation Protocol

    Quantitative comparisons require aligned datasets, input settings, resolution, hardware, and timing boundaries. When these conditions are not aligned, results are treated as method-specific evidence rather than direct comparisons. We therefore report both quality and runtime together with the experimental conditions under which they were measured.

    5 Taxonomy

    We organize Gaussian Splatting work for real-time reconstruction into five pipeline-centric families, defined by the primary stage a method intervenes in (capture/training, representation, rendering, system delivery, or online estimation). Because many methods are multi-faceted, we allow secondary overlaps but assign each paper a single primary family based on its dominant technical contribution.

    Figure 3 shows the chronological development of representative methods across these families, illustrating how work following 3DGS progressively expanded toward amortized generation, temporal modeling, efficiency, streaming, and online mapping.

    Single-shot / amortized Gaussian generation

    Feed-forward construction of a usable Gaussian scene from one or few images, often using depth/MVS priors or learned regularizers, optionally followed by brief refinement. Poses may be known, refined, or pose-free, but the defining feature is replacing heavy per-scene iterative fitting with amortized inference from limited views.

    Dynamic representations beyond 4DGS

    Methods that treat time as a first-class variable in the scene model (e.g., time-conditioned parameters, deformation/warp fields, key-time primitives, canonical-plus-delta factorization) or explicitly mitigate dynamic failure modes such as ghosting, identity swaps, occlusion/disocclusion artifacts, and temporal flicker. The emphasis is modeling temporal change, not merely delivering or replaying content over time.

    Efficiency and compression

    Works whose central goal is reducing compute, memory, or storage/bandwidth while preserving real-time operation, via levers such as pruning/sparsification, quantization/packing, view-adaptive LoD selection, or system/hardware acceleration. We place a method here when efficiency is the primary objective rather than a side effect.

    Streaming and immersive video systems

    Long-duration capture and interactive free-viewpoint playback under latency/bandwidth constraints, enabled by explicit delivery mechanisms (progressive transmission, caching/tiling/segmenting, rate control, bandwidth-aware loading, or continual update protocols). The core contribution is system delivery and interactivity over time, not new temporal scene parameterizations.

    SLAM with Gaussian Splatting

    Online tracking-and-mapping where camera poses are estimated incrementally and the Gaussian map is updated under bounded latency/compute, typically using keyframes, map maintenance/pruning, robustness to blur/occlusions, and (when relevant) loop-consistency considerations. We place a method here when meeting tracking deadlines and maintaining a bounded-cost map are central to the design.

    6 Quantitative Evaluation and Synthesis

    6.1 Single-Shot and Sparse-View Generation

    For calibrated sparse-view methods, Gaussian construction can be expressed as depth inference followed by unprojection,

    μᵢ(u)=π⁻¹ (u,d̂ᵢ(u);Kᵢ,Tᵢ), (Σᵢ,αᵢ,cᵢ)=H_θ (fᵢ(u)).

    		(5)

    MVSplat [5] estimates d̂ᵢ from a plane-sweep cost volume,

    Cᵢ(u,dₖ)=Agg_m≠i⟨Fᵢ(u),W_m→i(Fₘ;dₖ)⟩, d̂ᵢ=∑ₖsoftmax(Cᵢ)ₖdₖ,

    		(6)

    so geometry is determined primarily by cross-view correspondence. DepthSplat [63] instead augments the multi-view matching representation with pretrained monocular depth features,

    C̃ᵢ=Φ_θ (Cᵢ,Fᵢᵐᵒⁿᵒ),

    		(7)

    before depth regression and Gaussian unprojection. This additional geometric prior corresponds to the highest PSNR/SSIM and lowest LPIPS in table5, but also increases model-stage latency and memory relative to MVSplat. pixelSplat [4] avoids committing directly to one depth by predicting pᵢ(d|u) and differentiably sampling

    dᵢ∼pᵢ(d|u), μᵢ(u)=π⁻¹(u,dᵢ;Kᵢ,Tᵢ).

    		(8)

    Its more flexible treatment of geometric ambiguity is accompanied by the largest construction latency and memory footprint in the controlled experiment. Thus, table5 shows that the mechanism used to estimate μⱼ directly affects both reconstruction quality and construction cost; in this experiment, augmenting multi-view matching with monocular depth features gives the strongest quality, while the lighter cost-volume formulation gives the lowest latency.

    The native methods in table6 remove the calibrated-pose assumption in different ways. Splatt3R [49] extends MASt3R [25] with a Gaussian prediction head, which can be summarized as

    (xⱼ, Δxⱼ, qⱼ, sⱼ, αⱼ, cⱼ)=H_θ(I₁,I₂), μⱼ=xⱼ+Δxⱼ,

    		(9)

    with Σⱼ obtained from the predicted rotation qⱼ and scale sⱼ. The scene is therefore produced directly from an uncalibrated pair without optimizing camera variables. InstantSplat  [9] instead uses dense stereo priors to initialize both geometry and cameras and then performs Gaussian Bundle Adjustment,

    \min_G, {Tᵢ}∑ᵢLₚₕₒₜₒ(Iᵢ,Î(G,Tᵢ)),

    		(10)

    jointly updating the Gaussian parameters and poses. This distinction is visible quantitatively: Splatt3R requires 1.10 s for measured construction/export, whereas InstantSplat uses 16.01 s for initialization followed by 35.02 s of optimization. Hence the former admits a construction throughput, while the latter is an optimization problem whose runtime depends on the refinement budget. In both cases, the much larger decoder-only rFPS reported in table5 remains a separate quantity from the cost of constructing G. Recent feed-forward generalists broaden this regime to unconstrained input views and unified geometry-to-Gaussian prediction, as exemplified by AnySplat and YoNoSplat [18, 68]. These systems relax capture assumptions, but move additional latency and memory pressure into their learned geometry backbones and cross-view fusion.

    6.2 Dynamic Representations

    Let qⱼ and sⱼ denote the rotation and scale parameterization of Σⱼ. Dynamic deformation can then be written as

    (Δμⱼ,Δqⱼ,Δsⱼ)=F_θ(μⱼ,t), μⱼ(t)=μⱼ+Δμⱼ,

    		(11)

    with the predicted rotation and scale determining Σⱼ(t). Deformable-3D-Gaussians [67] uses an MLP deformation field conditioned directly on canonical position and time. 4DGaussians [61] instead obtains the deformation from factorized spatio-temporal features, using a HexPlane-style  [3] 4D encoding followed by a lightweight decoder. Thus, the former places motion complexity in the continuous deformation network, whereas the latter shifts part of it into an explicit space–time feature structure. In table7, both reach similar quality on D-NeRF bouncingballs: 41.38 dB for Deformable-3D-Gaussians and 40.81 dB for 4DGaussians. These values show that both deformation parameterizations can represent the same synthetic motion regime at high fidelity. 4DGaussians additionally renders at 36.03 rFPS in the measured native setup, showing that the deformation representation can remain compatible with interactive rendering after optimization.

item.title: 给原味 NeRF 补几何：从密度场取候选点发虚拟光线，外观不一致就压不透明度，Chamfer 降 30.8% ｜ Geometry Regularization for Vanilla NeRF via Self-Supervised Cross-Ray Consistency
item.description:
一句话：不加深度或法线监督，只靠跨光线颜色一致性约束隐式几何，Replica 八场景平均 Chamfer 距离降 30.8%。

要点：

  • 从密度场采样候选表面点，向不同方向发射虚拟光线并用 NeRF 渲其外观，按可见性加权比较颜色一致性
  • 外观预测不一致的候选点惩罚其不透明度，另加局部法线平滑项
  • 全部约束来自 NeRF 自身预测，不需要深度或表面法线的真值；Replica 八场景平均 Chamfer 距离比原味 NeRF 降 30.8%

为什么值得看：密度场几何发虚是 NeRF 落进引擎管线的老问题（做遮挡、做碰撞都不行）；用自监督一致性把形状和辐射解耦，不需要额外采集深度。

中文摘要：原味 NeRF 能把新视角合成得很好，但它密度场编码出的几何往往又噪又偏——因为同一组输入图像，可以被很多不同的形状与辐射组合解释。这篇工作给原味 NeRF 加了一条几何优化分支，靠自监督的跨光线一致性来消歧：从密度场采样候选表面点，在每个点上向不同方向发射虚拟光线，用 NeRF 网络渲染它们的外观，再按可见性加权比较这些光线的颜色是否一致；外观预测不一致的候选点会被压低不透明度，同时鼓励局部法线平滑。这些几何约束全部由 NeRF 自身预测导出，不需要任何深度图或表面法线真值。在 Replica 的八个场景上，该方法把平均 Chamfer 距离相对原味 NeRF 降低 30.8%，对需要从重建结果里取几何的引擎侧应用意义更大。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-25

Geometry Regularization for Vanilla NeRF via Self-Supervised Cross-Ray Consistency

© none

Abstract.

Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve high-quality novel-view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field. However, the geometry encoded by the density field of vanilla NeRF can be noisy and inaccurate, since different combinations of shape and radiance may explain the same input images. To reduce this ambiguity, we augment vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch based on self-supervised cross-ray consistency. Specifically, this branch samples candidate surface points from the density field, generates virtual rays that intersect at each point from different directions, and renders their appearance using the NeRF network. Based on the visibility-weighted color consistency across these rays, we constrain the implicit geometry. We further regularize the implicit geometry by penalizing opacity at candidates with inconsistent appearance predictions and encouraging local normal smoothness. These geometric constraints are derived from the NeRF predictions and require no ground-truth depth or surface-normal supervision. Experiments on eight Replica scenes show that the proposed method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% compared with vanilla NeRF.

Keywords:

neural radiance fields, implicit geometry, 3D reconstruction, cross-ray consistency

1. Introduction

Recovering 3D shape from 2D observations is a cornerstone problem of computer vision and graphics. This long-standing research topic supports various applications in AR, VR, games, movies, etc.[(Azinović et al., 2022; Boss et al., 2022)] With the advances of inverse graphics, differentiable renderer can be integrated in neural network pipelines, making it feasible to directly optimize the 3D geometric parameters using observed 2D images. Among various 3D geometry representations, implicit function represents 3D content continuously and without discretization. With its small memory footprint, implicit neural representation is popular in recent studies. One of the most successful approaches is NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)].

NeRF is a scene representation method presented by Mildenhall et al.[(Mildenhall et al., 2021)]. In that work, a deep neural network (typically, a multilayer perceptron, MLP) is applied to parameterize a continuous implicit function, which takes the position x∈ℝ³ and viewing direction d∈ℝ³ as input, and predicts the density σ(x)∈ℝ⁺ and view-dependent color c(x,d)∈ℝ³. Through differentiable volume rendering, dense colors from multiple 2D images can be used directly to optimize the neural radiance field. Encoding the information from multi-view 2D images, this powerful representation shows promising results in capturing complex scene structures and synthesizing 3D-consistent images with fine details. The superior rendering effects ignite research enthusiasm towards NeRF-like methods. Subsequent works include modification for dynamic scene modelling [(Li et al., 2021; Fang et al., 2022)], large-scale scene representation [(Tancik et al., 2022; Turki et al., 2022; Xiangli et al., 2022)], baking approaches for real-time rendering [(Hedman et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023a; Yariv et al., 2023)], encoding extra layers for scene understanding (e.g.  intrinsic [(Ye et al., 2022)] and semantic [(Zhi et al., 2021)] layers), and 3D-aware content or scene generation [(Gu et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023b)]. Although these approaches have shown impressive results for novel view synthesis, the 3D geometry extracted from the underlying volume density is far from satisfactory, usually suffering from noise and inaccuracy [(Yariv et al., 2021; Yariv et al., 2023)].

Neural implicit functions help circumvent the limitations about complex pipelines in classic depth-based multi-view stereo (MVS) [(Schönberger et al., 2016)] and expensive memory consumption in voxel-based approaches [(Ulusoy et al., 2015; Wang and Lu, 2019)]. However, it is still a fundamentally under-constrained problem to recover accurate geometry from 2D images, even for approaches based on differentiable rendering [(Barron et al., 2022)]. One of the main observations is the ambiguity between 3D shape and radiance, dubbed shape-radiance ambiguity [(Zhang et al., 2020)]. As illustrated in Figure 1, different surface hypotheses can reproduce similar training-view colors through view-dependent radiance. This ambiguity makes it difficult to recover the scene’s actual geometry from image agreement alone [(Zhang et al., 2020; Barron et al., 2022; Kutulakos and Seitz, 2000)].

A lot of effort has been dedicated to improve the 3D reconstruction quality of implicit neural representations. To put it briefly, there are works applying signed distance function (SDF) to model the 3D surface [(Niemeyer et al., 2020; Yariv et al., 2021; Yariv et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Yariv et al., 2023)], combining neural implicit field with explicit 3D representations such as voxel [(Liu et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021)] and polygon mesh [(Chen et al., 2023a; Munkberg et al., 2022)], optimizing sampling approach of ray marching [(Liu et al., 2020; Oechsle et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Rematas et al., 2022)], applying regularizers about smoothness and sparsity to the implicit field [(Mildenhall et al., 2021; Oechsle et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021)], adding priors about depth and structure to constrain the geometry [(Oechsle et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2022)], and using multi-view consistency as MVS-based reconstruction [(Darmon et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021)].

In this paper, we directly refine the implicit geometry of vanilla NeRF to reduce its shape-radiance ambiguity. We choose vanilla NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)] because its simple radiance-field representation supports complex scenes and arbitrary camera poses. However, as its geometry is represented only by volume density, the extracted surfaces often contain noise and inaccuracies. To improve the geometric fidelity, we build on the observation that the appearance of a surface point cannot vary arbitrarily across nearby viewpoints [(Kutulakos and Seitz, 2000)]. Existing neural reconstruction methods use this photo-consistency cue through feature matching or image warping between captured views [(Darmon et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021)]. We instead extend the NeRF architecture with a branch that samples candidate surface points, generates virtual viewpoints around them, and renders the corresponding cross-ray appearances. Based on these predictions, we obtain a self-supervised signal for optimizing the density field.

Contributions. We summarize the contributions as follows:

  • •

    We design a geometry-optimization branch for vanilla NeRF that derives geometric cues from the density field and integrates multi-view appearance constraints into the differentiable rendering pipeline.

  • •

    We propose visibility-weighted, self-supervised cross-ray consistency and penalize opacity at candidates whose rendered appearances disagree across virtual views.

  • •

    Experiments on eight Replica scenes show a 30.8% reduction in mean Chamfer distance relative to vanilla NeRF, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework in improving implicit geometry.

    • 2. Related Work

    2.1. 3D Geometric Representations

    3D geometry is commonly represented by volumes, point clouds, meshes, or implicit functions. Volumetric representations encode spatial structure directly [(Wang and Lu, 2019)], but their memory consumption often limits resolution. Point clouds are compact and flexible, although they lack an explicit neighborhood structure. Meshes are compatible with conventional graphics pipelines [(Yariv et al., 2023)], but changes in topology require modifying their connectivity. Implicit representations instead describe geometry through continuous functions, such as occupancy fields or signed distance fields (SDFs) [(Niemeyer et al., 2020; Yariv et al., 2021)]. Neural networks parameterize these functions without maintaining a dense spatial grid. We focus on the geometry encoded by implicit neural representations.

    2.2. Implicit Neural Representations

    NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)] represents a scene with a neural network that maps 3D positions and viewing directions to density and view-dependent color. Through differentiable volume rendering, it learns the radiance field directly from posed images. Its continuous representation supports novel-view synthesis without explicitly reconstructing a surface during training.

    Subsequent work extends this representation to dynamic scenes [(Li et al., 2021; Fang et al., 2022)], large-scale environments [(Turki et al., 2022; Xiangli et al., 2022; Tancik et al., 2022)], and scene understanding [(Zhi et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2022)]. Specifically, Li et al.[(Li et al., 2021)] model scene motion through forward and backward flow fields, while Fang et al.[(Fang et al., 2022)] use time-aware voxel features. For large environments, Mega-NeRF and Block-NeRF decompose scenes into local radiance fields, whereas BungeeNeRF progressively grows its representation. Semantic extensions jointly encode scene labels and appearance, and intrinsic models separate reflectance, shading, and residual components. Neural fields also support 3D-aware content generation [(Gu et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023b)]. However, high-quality rendered images do not ensure accurate geometry: the surfaces extracted from the underlying density field can still contain noise and inaccuracies [(Yariv et al., 2021; Yariv et al., 2023)]. We therefore focus on improving implicit geometry through neural rendering.

    2.3. Reconstruction through Neural Rendering

    Recovering geometry from images remains under-constrained because different combinations of shape and radiance can explain the same observations [(Zhang et al., 2020; Barron et al., 2022)]. Existing methods address this ambiguity through surface representations, sampling strategies, geometric priors, and multi-view constraints.

    One approach is to make the surface representation more explicit. Niemeyer et al.[(Niemeyer et al., 2020)] proposed Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR), which models shape with an occupancy network and differentiates the surface projection through implicit differentiation. VolSDF [(Yariv et al., 2021)] and NeuS [(Wang et al., 2021)] instead optimize SDF-based surfaces through volume rendering. DVR uses object masks during training, while SDF-based methods such as VolSDF and NeuS can reconstruct surfaces without mask supervision. In NeuS, the volume-rendering formulation reduces the geometric bias in the recovered zero-level set. Appropriate initialization and a bounding-sphere prior also guide its surface optimization [(Wang et al., 2021)]. UNISURF [(Oechsle et al., 2021)] unifies implicit surfaces and radiance fields and progressively narrows the sampling region around the estimated surface, allowing reconstruction without input masks.

    Hybrid representations combine neural fields with explicit spatial structures. Neural Sparse Voxel Fields (NSVF) [(Liu et al., 2020)] organizes local implicit fields in sparse voxels, which also restrict the sampling region during ray marching. Its sparse voxel structure avoids evaluating empty regions, and progressive optimization supports the recovery of finer scene geometry. Munkberg et al.[(Munkberg et al., 2022)] optimize a discrete SDF on a deformable tetrahedral grid and render the resulting mesh during training. Their framework estimates geometry, spatially varying materials, and lighting from posed images and object masks. For efficient rendering, MobileNeRF [(Chen et al., 2023a)] encodes appearance and opacity on polygon faces and bakes the result into textures, while BakedSDF [(Yariv et al., 2023)] optimizes a hybrid surface-volume representation for unbounded scenes and bakes it for rasterization. Such approaches modify the representation or rendering pipeline to connect neural reconstruction with explicit geometry.

    Besides the representation, geometric regularization and additional cues can improve reconstruction. NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)] injects noise into density predictions to regularize ambiguous regions. UNISURF [(Oechsle et al., 2021)] encourages local normal smoothness, and PlenOctrees [(Yu et al., 2021)] uses a sparsity prior to favor empty space in ambiguous regions. MonoSDF [(Yu et al., 2022)] incorporates monocular depth and normal estimates to constrain the surface. Based on predictions from general-purpose monocular estimators, these cues improve reconstruction quality and reduce optimization time. Guo et al.[(Guo et al., 2022)] apply planar constraints to wall and floor regions based on the Manhattan-world assumption. Semantic segmentation identifies these regions, and the constraints encourage their surface normals to follow parallel or orthogonal directions. Other approaches use direct geometric observations: Rematas et al.[(Rematas et al., 2022)] use lidar supervision to constrain reconstruction and limit ray-marching samples to a bounded region.
