These constraints reduce ambiguity by imposing smoothness, sparsity, or prior geometric information.

    Multi-view methods obtain geometric cues from agreement between captured images. MVSNeRF [(Chen et al., 2021)] builds plane-swept cost volumes for geometry-aware scene reasoning and combines them with volume rendering to reconstruct a radiance field from a small set of nearby views. NerfingMVS [(Wei et al., 2021)] uses learned depth priors, adapted with sparse structure-from-motion observations, to guide NeRF optimization. NeuralWarp [(Darmon et al., 2022)] combines image warping with volume rendering to optimize photo-consistency across source views. These methods use captured images or depth priors to constrain the geometry through multi-view observations. Direct photo-consistency methods must also account for source-view selection and visibility when comparing projections of the same 3D point.

    In this paper, we constrain the density field of vanilla NeRF through agreement among virtual rays rendered by the same network. Specifically, the cross-ray constraint compares appearance predictions around each candidate point, with visibility weights reducing the influence of occluded rays. This provides a self-supervised geometric constraint without image warping or additional depth, normal, or correspondence supervision in the training losses.

    3. Cross-Ray Consistency for Implicit Geometry Optimization

    Our framework extends vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch, as shown in Figure 2. The NeRF network still predicts density and view-dependent color from 3D positions and viewing directions. The added branch samples candidate surface points from the current density field, generates virtual viewpoints around them, and performs multi-view appearance rendering for rays passing through each point. Based on these predictions, we impose visibility-aware cross-ray consistency and geometric regularization to optimize the field.

    3.1. Overview and Cross-Ray Consistency

    A vanilla NeRF represents a scene with a function F_θ that maps a position x∈ℝ³ and viewing direction d∈ℝ³ to density σ_θ(x) and color c_θ(x,d):

    (1)

    F_θ(x,d)=(σ_θ(x),c_θ(x,d)).

    For a camera ray r(t)=o+td with ordered samples {tₖ}ₖ₌₁^K, volume rendering gives

    (2)Ĉ(r)=∑ₖ₌₁^KTₖαₖc_θ(r(tₖ),d),
    (3)αₖ=1-\exp(-σ_θ(r(tₖ))δₖ), Tₖ=∏_l

    where δₖ=tₖ₊₁-tₖ. The NeRF rendering branch minimizes the image reconstruction loss

    (4)

    L_rgb=∑_r∈ℝ∥Ĉ(r)-C(r)∥₂².

    Multi-view reconstruction commonly compares the projections of the same 3D point in captured images. Such methods must select source views, establish correspondences, and handle visibility [(Darmon et al., 2022)]. Our added branch instead generates a local bundle of virtual rays for each candidate surface point and renders every ray with the NeRF network. These rays intersect at the same point but differ in origin and direction. If the candidate lies on a stable surface, its appearance should remain similar across the visible rays in this local bundle. We therefore use their color disagreement as a self-supervised constraint, without image warping or ground-truth depth.

    3.2. Candidate Surface Sampling

    As illustrated in Figure 3(a), we combine random proposals with rendered-depth anchors to obtain candidate surface points. We first sample random points in a bounded scene volume V and query the current density field. With a fixed interval δ, we convert density to opacity,

    (5)

    α(x)=1-\exp(-σ_θ(x)δ).

    We then select candidate points from an intermediate opacity band:

    (6)

    S_rand={x∈V|α_\min<α(x)<α_\max}, α_\min=0.5, α_\max=0.95.

    We retain intermediate-opacity samples as surface candidates, excluding low-density samples and those with nearly saturated opacity.

    To complement the random candidates, we also obtain surface anchors from rendered training rays. Specifically, using the rendering weights in Equation (2), we define the unnormalized rendered-depth estimate t̂(r)=∑ₖTₖαₖtₖ. The corresponding anchor is

    (7)

    x_ray=o+t̂(r)d, S=S_rand∪S_ray.

    We apply the same opacity-band test to the rendered-depth anchors before adding them to S_ray. Based on the combined set S, we randomly retain a candidate batch for the geometry branch. The uniform proposals explore the current field, while the rendered-depth anchors provide candidates at surface locations estimated along the training rays.

    3.3. Cross-Ray Generation and Visibility Estimation

    Figure 3(b) illustrates the cross-ray construction. For each candidate xᵢ∈S, we first estimate a local surface direction from the opacity gradient:

    (8)

    nᵢ=-(∇ₓα(xᵢ))/(∥∇ₓα(xᵢ)∥₂+ε).

    This normal is computed on the fly from the radiance field rather than supplied as ground truth. We keep its computation in the automatic-differentiation graph so that cross-ray construction and normal smoothness can update the density field. Next, we sample uᵢⱼ∼U(S²) and form an auxiliary location

    (9)

    õᵢⱼ=xᵢ+l₀nᵢ+ruᵢⱼ.

    Here l₀ is a normal-direction bias: it shifts the isotropic perturbation ruᵢⱼ toward the estimated outward side of the candidate surface. The auxiliary location only determines the ray direction. Defining the normal-bias strength λₙ=l₀/r for r>0, we obtain

    (10)

    dᵢⱼ=(xᵢ-õᵢⱼ)/(∥xᵢ-õᵢⱼ∥₂)=-(λₙnᵢ+uᵢⱼ)/(∥λₙnᵢ+uᵢⱼ∥₂).

    Thus, the virtual-viewpoint directions depend on l₀ and r through their ratio. When λₙ=0, they are isotropic around the candidate; increasing λₙ continuously favors the estimated normal side without explicitly rejecting sampled directions. We independently draw lᵢⱼ∼U(l_\min,l_\max) to place the final ray origin:

    (11)

    oᵢⱼ=xᵢ-lᵢⱼdᵢⱼ, rᵢⱼ(t)=oᵢⱼ+tdᵢⱼ.

    The ratio λₙ therefore controls the angular normal bias, whereas lᵢⱼ controls the actual ray-origin distance. By construction, all rays indexed by j intersect at xᵢ. Standard volume rendering in Equation (2) gives their colors cᵢⱼ=Ĉ(rᵢⱼ).

    However, a generated ray may pass through another occupied region before reaching the candidate, as shown in Figure 3(c). To reduce the influence of such rays, we sample M points {pᵢⱼₖ}ₖ₌₁^M on the segment from oᵢⱼ to xᵢ and compute

    (12)αᵢⱼₖ=1-\exp(-σ_θ(pᵢⱼₖ)Δᵢⱼₖ),
    (13)mᵢⱼ=∑ₖ₌₁^Mαᵢⱼₖ,
    (14)wᵢⱼ=(1)/(1+\exp(β(mᵢⱼ-γ))), β=20, γ=1.10.

    Here mᵢⱼ is an accumulated opacity proxy, defined as the sum of per-sample opacities rather than physical transmittance. Based on this proxy, the sigmoid assigns a smaller weight to rays whose paths contain substantial density. We treat the estimated visibility weights as constants during back-propagation (stop gradients through wᵢⱼ), preventing the consistency loss from directly adjusting them to downweight rays with inconsistent color predictions.

    3.4. Geometry Regularization

    To measure the appearance agreement of the visible rays, let Dᵢ=\max(∑ⱼwᵢⱼ,η) with η=0.1 for candidate i. We then compute the visibility-weighted mean color and cross-ray variance as

    (15)μᵢ=(∑ⱼwᵢⱼcᵢⱼ)/(Dᵢ),
    (16)Vᵢ=(∑ⱼwᵢⱼ∥cᵢⱼ-μᵢ∥₂²)/(Dᵢ).

    The cross-ray consistency loss is the average variance over N candidates:

    (17)

    L_CRC=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^NVᵢ.

    We assume that a valid surface hypothesis should exhibit similar appearance across visible virtual views within the sampled local angular range. A large cross-view rendering discrepancy therefore provides negative evidence for occupancy at the candidate point. Minimizing color variance alone may change the appearance predictions while leaving unreliable density in place. We therefore use the visibility-weighted variance to penalize the candidate point’s opacity:

    (18)

    L_occ=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nsg(Vᵢ)α(xᵢ),

    where sg(·) denotes stop-gradient. The variance acts as a fixed weight in this term: a larger Vᵢ gives a stronger penalty on α(xᵢ). Stop-gradient prevents the penalty from being reduced by changing Vᵢ through this path.

    Although L_CRC is expressed through rendered colors, it also affects geometry. Specifically, each rendered color depends on density through opacity and transmittance in Equation (2), and the cross-ray directions depend on differentiable opacity gradients. In addition, Equation (18) directly penalizes the opacity of inconsistent candidates. The opacity-band test itself is discrete and provides no gradient; instead, it updates the candidate distribution as the field changes. Meanwhile, L_rgb keeps the predictions anchored to the captured images during refinement. This reasoning assumes that surface appearance varies modestly across the sampled local directions; strong specular effects may therefore penalize valid geometry.

    To further reduce high-frequency noise in the density field, we apply local normal smoothness. Given a random perturbation εᵢ∼U(-s/2,s/2)³ and x^′ᵢ=xᵢ+εᵢ,

    (19)

    Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^N∥n(xᵢ)-n(x^′ᵢ)∥₂.

    Here, s>0 denotes the side length of the cubic neighborhood used to sample local perturbations.

    3.5. Training Objective

    We combine RGB reconstruction from the NeRF path with the constraints from the geometry branch in the training objective

    (20)

    L=L_rgb+λ_cr(L_CRC+λ_occL_occ)+λₛₘLₛₘₒₒₜₕ.

    Here L_rgb maintains agreement with the captured images, while L_CRC supplies the cross-ray constraint. The occupancy and smoothness terms act on the geometry in complementary ways: one suppresses inconsistent density, and the other reduces local noise.

    Algorithm 1 summarizes one optimization update with a nonempty candidate batch. Specifically, the geometry branch uses the current field to select candidates, construct cross-rays, and render their colors. Based on these predictions, it evaluates the visibility-weighted losses and updates the shared network together with RGB reconstruction. The normal computation and appearance rendering remain differentiable, whereas the visibility weights and the variance used in the occupancy penalty are detached as described above.

    4. Experiments

    4.1. Implementation Details

    For the reported experiments, we initialize the NeRF network from a vanilla-NeRF checkpoint and continue optimization with the objective in Equation (20). In each geometry-optimization step, we draw 20,000 uniform proposals from the sampling volume, append rendered-depth anchors, apply the opacity-band filter, and randomly retain up to 100 candidates. We generate 15 cross-rays for each candidate. For the opacity and normal computations, we use δ=(10.0-0.1)/128 and ε=10⁻⁵, respectively. Unless noted below, we set r=0.15 and l₀=0.28, giving a default normal-bias strength of λₙ=l₀/r≈1.87. We also set (l_\min,l_\max)=(0.15,0.45), s=0.08, λ_cr=1.5×10⁻³, λ_occ=1.15, and λₛₘ=2.5×10⁻⁴.

    For visibility estimation, we place 32 uniform samples between 0.01lᵢⱼ and lᵢⱼ along each origin-to-candidate segment, including the endpoint, and set Δᵢⱼₖ=0.99lᵢⱼ/32. Cross-ray rendering uses near and far bounds of 0.1 and 10.0 meters. The continuation with the geometry branch starts at a learning rate of 1.15×10⁻⁴.

    Room 1 uses (l_\min,l_\max)=(0.125,0.30), λ_occ=0.8, and λₛₘ=2.5×10⁻³. Office 2 uses r=0.25, (l_\min,l_\max)=(0.08,0.70), s=0.10, λ_cr=1.05×10⁻³, and λ_occ=3.25; its scene-specific continuation starts at a learning rate of 1.25×10⁻⁴. These settings are fixed in the reported runs.

    For Office 2, we additionally suppress residual floating density with an auxiliary global sparsity penalty:

    (21)

    Lₛₚₐᵣₛₑ=1-𝔼_x∼V[\exp(-δₛReLU(σ_θ(x)))].

    The optimization objective for this scene is L+λₛₚLₛₚₐᵣₛₑ, where L is defined in Equation (20), λₛₚ=10⁻², and δₛ=0.01. This auxiliary term is not used for the other seven scenes.

    For the comparison in Table 1, both vanilla NeRF and our method are evaluated after 300,000 cumulative training iterations. When our run is initialized from a vanilla-NeRF checkpoint, its continuation iterations are counted within this total. Thus, both methods have the same iteration budget.

    All surface normals used during refinement are computed on the fly from opacity gradients; ground-truth normals are not used. For Replica scenes, the reference mesh determines an oriented 3D sampling volume, but does not enter the training losses. Ground-truth depth is reserved for evaluation. Thus, the losses use no ground-truth depth or normal supervision, although the sampling bounds still depend on reference geometry in the current experiments.

    4.2. Geometry Reconstruction Results

    Table 1 reports the Chamfer distance on eight Replica scenes at the matched 300,000-iteration budget. Compared with vanilla NeRF, our method improves six scenes and reduces the mean distance by 30.8%. Room 1 and Office 0 are the two scenes for which the distance increases.

    Figure 4 qualitatively compares the geometry extracted from the density fields with the ground-truth scene geometry. Although vanilla NeRF recovers the overall scene layout, its surfaces often contain pronounced noise and irregular deformations. After geometry optimization, several wall and furniture surfaces become smoother and more closely resemble the reference geometry. Specifically, the wall in Room 1 and the tabletops in Room 2 and Office 2 exhibit reduced surface irregularities. Together with the quantitative results, these comparisons demonstrate that the proposed geometry optimization can improve the geometric fidelity of NeRF’s underlying density field. The smoother wall in Room 1 is a local improvement, despite the higher scene-level Chamfer distance reported in Table 1.

    5. Conclusion and Discussion

    We proposed a framework that augments vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch. Specifically, the branch samples candidate surface points, generates virtual cross-rays through them, and renders their appearance from multiple viewpoints. Based on the visibility-weighted disagreement of these rendered colors, cross-ray consistency constrains the density field, while occupancy suppression and local normal smoothness reduce geometric noise. On eight Replica scenes, the method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% relative to vanilla NeRF.

    The current experiments use a reference mesh to define sampling bounds and scene-specific settings for Room 1 and Office 2. Future work should estimate the bounds from training cameras, isolate the effect of the added branch through an RGB-only continuation from the same checkpoint, and investigate appearance models that are less sensitive to specular surfaces.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：不加深度或法线监督，只靠跨光线颜色一致性约束隐式几何，Replica 八场景平均 Chamfer 距离降 30.8%。

要点：

  • 从密度场采样候选表面点，向不同方向发射虚拟光线并用 NeRF 渲其外观，按可见性加权比较颜色一致性
  • 外观预测不一致的候选点惩罚其不透明度，另加局部法线平滑项
  • 全部约束来自 NeRF 自身预测，不需要深度或表面法线的真值；Replica 八场景平均 Chamfer 距离比原味 NeRF 降 30.8%

为什么值得看：密度场几何发虚是 NeRF 落进引擎管线的老问题（做遮挡、做碰撞都不行）；用自监督一致性把形状和辐射解耦，不需要额外采集深度。

中文摘要：原味 NeRF 能把新视角合成得很好，但它密度场编码出的几何往往又噪又偏——因为同一组输入图像，可以被很多不同的形状与辐射组合解释。这篇工作给原味 NeRF 加了一条几何优化分支，靠自监督的跨光线一致性来消歧：从密度场采样候选表面点，在每个点上向不同方向发射虚拟光线，用 NeRF 网络渲染它们的外观，再按可见性加权比较这些光线的颜色是否一致；外观预测不一致的候选点会被压低不透明度，同时鼓励局部法线平滑。这些几何约束全部由 NeRF 自身预测导出，不需要任何深度图或表面法线真值。在 Replica 的八个场景上，该方法把平均 Chamfer 距离相对原味 NeRF 降低 30.8%，对需要从重建结果里取几何的引擎侧应用意义更大。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-25

Geometry Regularization for Vanilla NeRF via Self-Supervised Cross-Ray Consistency

© none

Abstract.

Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve high-quality novel-view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field. However, the geometry encoded by the density field of vanilla NeRF can be noisy and inaccurate, since different combinations of shape and radiance may explain the same input images. To reduce this ambiguity, we augment vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch based on self-supervised cross-ray consistency. Specifically, this branch samples candidate surface points from the density field, generates virtual rays that intersect at each point from different directions, and renders their appearance using the NeRF network. Based on the visibility-weighted color consistency across these rays, we constrain the implicit geometry. We further regularize the implicit geometry by penalizing opacity at candidates with inconsistent appearance predictions and encouraging local normal smoothness. These geometric constraints are derived from the NeRF predictions and require no ground-truth depth or surface-normal supervision. Experiments on eight Replica scenes show that the proposed method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% compared with vanilla NeRF.

Keywords:

neural radiance fields, implicit geometry, 3D reconstruction, cross-ray consistency

1. Introduction

Recovering 3D shape from 2D observations is a cornerstone problem of computer vision and graphics. This long-standing research topic supports various applications in AR, VR, games, movies, etc.[(Azinović et al., 2022; Boss et al., 2022)] With the advances of inverse graphics, differentiable renderer can be integrated in neural network pipelines, making it feasible to directly optimize the 3D geometric parameters using observed 2D images. Among various 3D geometry representations, implicit function represents 3D content continuously and without discretization. With its small memory footprint, implicit neural representation is popular in recent studies. One of the most successful approaches is NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)].

NeRF is a scene representation method presented by Mildenhall et al.[(Mildenhall et al., 2021)]. In that work, a deep neural network (typically, a multilayer perceptron, MLP) is applied to parameterize a continuous implicit function, which takes the position x∈ℝ³ and viewing direction d∈ℝ³ as input, and predicts the density σ(x)∈ℝ⁺ and view-dependent color c(x,d)∈ℝ³. Through differentiable volume rendering, dense colors from multiple 2D images can be used directly to optimize the neural radiance field. Encoding the information from multi-view 2D images, this powerful representation shows promising results in capturing complex scene structures and synthesizing 3D-consistent images with fine details. The superior rendering effects ignite research enthusiasm towards NeRF-like methods. Subsequent works include modification for dynamic scene modelling [(Li et al., 2021; Fang et al., 2022)], large-scale scene representation [(Tancik et al., 2022; Turki et al., 2022; Xiangli et al., 2022)], baking approaches for real-time rendering [(Hedman et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023a; Yariv et al., 2023)], encoding extra layers for scene understanding (e.g.  intrinsic [(Ye et al., 2022)] and semantic [(Zhi et al., 2021)] layers), and 3D-aware content or scene generation [(Gu et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023b)]. Although these approaches have shown impressive results for novel view synthesis, the 3D geometry extracted from the underlying volume density is far from satisfactory, usually suffering from noise and inaccuracy [(Yariv et al., 2021; Yariv et al., 2023)].

Neural implicit functions help circumvent the limitations about complex pipelines in classic depth-based multi-view stereo (MVS) [(Schönberger et al., 2016)] and expensive memory consumption in voxel-based approaches [(Ulusoy et al., 2015; Wang and Lu, 2019)]. However, it is still a fundamentally under-constrained problem to recover accurate geometry from 2D images, even for approaches based on differentiable rendering [(Barron et al., 2022)]. One of the main observations is the ambiguity between 3D shape and radiance, dubbed shape-radiance ambiguity [(Zhang et al., 2020)]. As illustrated in Figure 1, different surface hypotheses can reproduce similar training-view colors through view-dependent radiance. This ambiguity makes it difficult to recover the scene’s actual geometry from image agreement alone [(Zhang et al., 2020; Barron et al., 2022; Kutulakos and Seitz, 2000)].

A lot of effort has been dedicated to improve the 3D reconstruction quality of implicit neural representations. To put it briefly, there are works applying signed distance function (SDF) to model the 3D surface [(Niemeyer et al., 2020; Yariv et al., 2021; Yariv et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Yariv et al., 2023)], combining neural implicit field with explicit 3D representations such as voxel [(Liu et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021)] and polygon mesh [(Chen et al., 2023a; Munkberg et al., 2022)], optimizing sampling approach of ray marching [(Liu et al., 2020; Oechsle et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021; Rematas et al., 2022)], applying regularizers about smoothness and sparsity to the implicit field [(Mildenhall et al., 2021; Oechsle et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021)], adding priors about depth and structure to constrain the geometry [(Oechsle et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2022)], and using multi-view consistency as MVS-based reconstruction [(Darmon et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021)].

In this paper, we directly refine the implicit geometry of vanilla NeRF to reduce its shape-radiance ambiguity. We choose vanilla NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)] because its simple radiance-field representation supports complex scenes and arbitrary camera poses. However, as its geometry is represented only by volume density, the extracted surfaces often contain noise and inaccuracies. To improve the geometric fidelity, we build on the observation that the appearance of a surface point cannot vary arbitrarily across nearby viewpoints [(Kutulakos and Seitz, 2000)]. Existing neural reconstruction methods use this photo-consistency cue through feature matching or image warping between captured views [(Darmon et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021)]. We instead extend the NeRF architecture with a branch that samples candidate surface points, generates virtual viewpoints around them, and renders the corresponding cross-ray appearances. Based on these predictions, we obtain a self-supervised signal for optimizing the density field.

Contributions. We summarize the contributions as follows:

  • •

    We design a geometry-optimization branch for vanilla NeRF that derives geometric cues from the density field and integrates multi-view appearance constraints into the differentiable rendering pipeline.

  • •

    We propose visibility-weighted, self-supervised cross-ray consistency and penalize opacity at candidates whose rendered appearances disagree across virtual views.

  • •

    Experiments on eight Replica scenes show a 30.8% reduction in mean Chamfer distance relative to vanilla NeRF, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework in improving implicit geometry.

    • 2. Related Work

    2.1. 3D Geometric Representations

    3D geometry is commonly represented by volumes, point clouds, meshes, or implicit functions. Volumetric representations encode spatial structure directly [(Wang and Lu, 2019)], but their memory consumption often limits resolution. Point clouds are compact and flexible, although they lack an explicit neighborhood structure. Meshes are compatible with conventional graphics pipelines [(Yariv et al., 2023)], but changes in topology require modifying their connectivity. Implicit representations instead describe geometry through continuous functions, such as occupancy fields or signed distance fields (SDFs) [(Niemeyer et al., 2020; Yariv et al., 2021)]. Neural networks parameterize these functions without maintaining a dense spatial grid. We focus on the geometry encoded by implicit neural representations.

    2.2. Implicit Neural Representations

    NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)] represents a scene with a neural network that maps 3D positions and viewing directions to density and view-dependent color. Through differentiable volume rendering, it learns the radiance field directly from posed images. Its continuous representation supports novel-view synthesis without explicitly reconstructing a surface during training.

    Subsequent work extends this representation to dynamic scenes [(Li et al., 2021; Fang et al., 2022)], large-scale environments [(Turki et al., 2022; Xiangli et al., 2022; Tancik et al., 2022)], and scene understanding [(Zhi et al., 2021; Ye et al., 2022)]. Specifically, Li et al.[(Li et al., 2021)] model scene motion through forward and backward flow fields, while Fang et al.[(Fang et al., 2022)] use time-aware voxel features. For large environments, Mega-NeRF and Block-NeRF decompose scenes into local radiance fields, whereas BungeeNeRF progressively grows its representation. Semantic extensions jointly encode scene labels and appearance, and intrinsic models separate reflectance, shading, and residual components. Neural fields also support 3D-aware content generation [(Gu et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023b)]. However, high-quality rendered images do not ensure accurate geometry: the surfaces extracted from the underlying density field can still contain noise and inaccuracies [(Yariv et al., 2021; Yariv et al., 2023)]. We therefore focus on improving implicit geometry through neural rendering.

    2.3. Reconstruction through Neural Rendering

    Recovering geometry from images remains under-constrained because different combinations of shape and radiance can explain the same observations [(Zhang et al., 2020; Barron et al., 2022)]. Existing methods address this ambiguity through surface representations, sampling strategies, geometric priors, and multi-view constraints.

    One approach is to make the surface representation more explicit. Niemeyer et al.[(Niemeyer et al., 2020)] proposed Differentiable Volumetric Rendering (DVR), which models shape with an occupancy network and differentiates the surface projection through implicit differentiation. VolSDF [(Yariv et al., 2021)] and NeuS [(Wang et al., 2021)] instead optimize SDF-based surfaces through volume rendering. DVR uses object masks during training, while SDF-based methods such as VolSDF and NeuS can reconstruct surfaces without mask supervision. In NeuS, the volume-rendering formulation reduces the geometric bias in the recovered zero-level set. Appropriate initialization and a bounding-sphere prior also guide its surface optimization [(Wang et al., 2021)]. UNISURF [(Oechsle et al., 2021)] unifies implicit surfaces and radiance fields and progressively narrows the sampling region around the estimated surface, allowing reconstruction without input masks.

    Hybrid representations combine neural fields with explicit spatial structures. Neural Sparse Voxel Fields (NSVF) [(Liu et al., 2020)] organizes local implicit fields in sparse voxels, which also restrict the sampling region during ray marching. Its sparse voxel structure avoids evaluating empty regions, and progressive optimization supports the recovery of finer scene geometry. Munkberg et al.[(Munkberg et al., 2022)] optimize a discrete SDF on a deformable tetrahedral grid and render the resulting mesh during training. Their framework estimates geometry, spatially varying materials, and lighting from posed images and object masks. For efficient rendering, MobileNeRF [(Chen et al., 2023a)] encodes appearance and opacity on polygon faces and bakes the result into textures, while BakedSDF [(Yariv et al., 2023)] optimizes a hybrid surface-volume representation for unbounded scenes and bakes it for rasterization. Such approaches modify the representation or rendering pipeline to connect neural reconstruction with explicit geometry.

    Besides the representation, geometric regularization and additional cues can improve reconstruction. NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)] injects noise into density predictions to regularize ambiguous regions. UNISURF [(Oechsle et al., 2021)] encourages local normal smoothness, and PlenOctrees [(Yu et al., 2021)] uses a sparsity prior to favor empty space in ambiguous regions. MonoSDF [(Yu et al., 2022)] incorporates monocular depth and normal estimates to constrain the surface. Based on predictions from general-purpose monocular estimators, these cues improve reconstruction quality and reduce optimization time. Guo et al.[(Guo et al., 2022)] apply planar constraints to wall and floor regions based on the Manhattan-world assumption. Semantic segmentation identifies these regions, and the constraints encourage their surface normals to follow parallel or orthogonal directions. Other approaches use direct geometric observations: Rematas et al.[(Rematas et al., 2022)] use lidar supervision to constrain reconstruction and limit ray-marching samples to a bounded region. These constraints reduce ambiguity by imposing smoothness, sparsity, or prior geometric information.

    Multi-view methods obtain geometric cues from agreement between captured images. MVSNeRF [(Chen et al., 2021)] builds plane-swept cost volumes for geometry-aware scene reasoning and combines them with volume rendering to reconstruct a radiance field from a small set of nearby views. NerfingMVS [(Wei et al., 2021)] uses learned depth priors, adapted with sparse structure-from-motion observations, to guide NeRF optimization. NeuralWarp [(Darmon et al., 2022)] combines image warping with volume rendering to optimize photo-consistency across source views. These methods use captured images or depth priors to constrain the geometry through multi-view observations. Direct photo-consistency methods must also account for source-view selection and visibility when comparing projections of the same 3D point.

    In this paper, we constrain the density field of vanilla NeRF through agreement among virtual rays rendered by the same network. Specifically, the cross-ray constraint compares appearance predictions around each candidate point, with visibility weights reducing the influence of occluded rays. This provides a self-supervised geometric constraint without image warping or additional depth, normal, or correspondence supervision in the training losses.

    3. Cross-Ray Consistency for Implicit Geometry Optimization

    Our framework extends vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch, as shown in Figure 2. The NeRF network still predicts density and view-dependent color from 3D positions and viewing directions. The added branch samples candidate surface points from the current density field, generates virtual viewpoints around them, and performs multi-view appearance rendering for rays passing through each point. Based on these predictions, we impose visibility-aware cross-ray consistency and geometric regularization to optimize the field.

    3.1. Overview and Cross-Ray Consistency

    A vanilla NeRF represents a scene with a function F_θ that maps a position x∈ℝ³ and viewing direction d∈ℝ³ to density σ_θ(x) and color c_θ(x,d):

    (1)

    F_θ(x,d)=(σ_θ(x),c_θ(x,d)).

    For a camera ray r(t)=o+td with ordered samples {tₖ}ₖ₌₁^K, volume rendering gives

    (2)Ĉ(r)=∑ₖ₌₁^KTₖαₖc_θ(r(tₖ),d),
    (3)αₖ=1-\exp(-σ_θ(r(tₖ))δₖ), Tₖ=∏_l

    where δₖ=tₖ₊₁-tₖ. The NeRF rendering branch minimizes the image reconstruction loss

    (4)

    L_rgb=∑_r∈ℝ∥Ĉ(r)-C(r)∥₂².

    Multi-view reconstruction commonly compares the projections of the same 3D point in captured images. Such methods must select source views, establish correspondences, and handle visibility [(Darmon et al., 2022)]. Our added branch instead generates a local bundle of virtual rays for each candidate surface point and renders every ray with the NeRF network. These rays intersect at the same point but differ in origin and direction. If the candidate lies on a stable surface, its appearance should remain similar across the visible rays in this local bundle. We therefore use their color disagreement as a self-supervised constraint, without image warping or ground-truth depth.

    3.2. Candidate Surface Sampling

    As illustrated in Figure 3(a), we combine random proposals with rendered-depth anchors to obtain candidate surface points. We first sample random points in a bounded scene volume V and query the current density field. With a fixed interval δ, we convert density to opacity,

    (5)

    α(x)=1-\exp(-σ_θ(x)δ).

    We then select candidate points from an intermediate opacity band:

    (6)

    S_rand={x∈V|α_\min<α(x)<α_\max}, α_\min=0.5, α_\max=0.95.

    We retain intermediate-opacity samples as surface candidates, excluding low-density samples and those with nearly saturated opacity.

    To complement the random candidates, we also obtain surface anchors from rendered training rays. Specifically, using the rendering weights in Equation (2), we define the unnormalized rendered-depth estimate t̂(r)=∑ₖTₖαₖtₖ. The corresponding anchor is

    (7)

    x_ray=o+t̂(r)d, S=S_rand∪S_ray.

    We apply the same opacity-band test to the rendered-depth anchors before adding them to S_ray. Based on the combined set S, we randomly retain a candidate batch for the geometry branch. The uniform proposals explore the current field, while the rendered-depth anchors provide candidates at surface locations estimated along the training rays.

    3.3. Cross-Ray Generation and Visibility Estimation

    Figure 3(b) illustrates the cross-ray construction. For each candidate xᵢ∈S, we first estimate a local surface direction from the opacity gradient:

    (8)

    nᵢ=-(∇ₓα(xᵢ))/(∥∇ₓα(xᵢ)∥₂+ε).

    This normal is computed on the fly from the radiance field rather than supplied as ground truth. We keep its computation in the automatic-differentiation graph so that cross-ray construction and normal smoothness can update the density field. Next, we sample uᵢⱼ∼U(S²) and form an auxiliary location

    (9)

    õᵢⱼ=xᵢ+l₀nᵢ+ruᵢⱼ.

    Here l₀ is a normal-direction bias: it shifts the isotropic perturbation ruᵢⱼ toward the estimated outward side of the candidate surface. The auxiliary location only determines the ray direction. Defining the normal-bias strength λₙ=l₀/r for r>0, we obtain

    (10)

    dᵢⱼ=(xᵢ-õᵢⱼ)/(∥xᵢ-õᵢⱼ∥₂)=-(λₙnᵢ+uᵢⱼ)/(∥λₙnᵢ+uᵢⱼ∥₂).

    Thus, the virtual-viewpoint directions depend on l₀ and r through their ratio. When λₙ=0, they are isotropic around the candidate; increasing λₙ continuously favors the estimated normal side without explicitly rejecting sampled directions. We independently draw lᵢⱼ∼U(l_\min,l_\max) to place the final ray origin:

    (11)

    oᵢⱼ=xᵢ-lᵢⱼdᵢⱼ, rᵢⱼ(t)=oᵢⱼ+tdᵢⱼ.

    The ratio λₙ therefore controls the angular normal bias, whereas lᵢⱼ controls the actual ray-origin distance. By construction, all rays indexed by j intersect at xᵢ. Standard volume rendering in Equation (2) gives their colors cᵢⱼ=Ĉ(rᵢⱼ).

    However, a generated ray may pass through another occupied region before reaching the candidate, as shown in Figure 3(c). To reduce the influence of such rays, we sample M points {pᵢⱼₖ}ₖ₌₁^M on the segment from oᵢⱼ to xᵢ and compute

    (12)αᵢⱼₖ=1-\exp(-σ_θ(pᵢⱼₖ)Δᵢⱼₖ),
    (13)mᵢⱼ=∑ₖ₌₁^Mαᵢⱼₖ,
    (14)wᵢⱼ=(1)/(1+\exp(β(mᵢⱼ-γ))), β=20, γ=1.10.

    Here mᵢⱼ is an accumulated opacity proxy, defined as the sum of per-sample opacities rather than physical transmittance. Based on this proxy, the sigmoid assigns a smaller weight to rays whose paths contain substantial density. We treat the estimated visibility weights as constants during back-propagation (stop gradients through wᵢⱼ), preventing the consistency loss from directly adjusting them to downweight rays with inconsistent color predictions.

    3.4. Geometry Regularization

    To measure the appearance agreement of the visible rays, let Dᵢ=\max(∑ⱼwᵢⱼ,η) with η=0.1 for candidate i. We then compute the visibility-weighted mean color and cross-ray variance as

    (15)μᵢ=(∑ⱼwᵢⱼcᵢⱼ)/(Dᵢ),
    (16)Vᵢ=(∑ⱼwᵢⱼ∥cᵢⱼ-μᵢ∥₂²)/(Dᵢ).

    The cross-ray consistency loss is the average variance over N candidates:

    (17)

    L_CRC=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^NVᵢ.

    We assume that a valid surface hypothesis should exhibit similar appearance across visible virtual views within the sampled local angular range. A large cross-view rendering discrepancy therefore provides negative evidence for occupancy at the candidate point. Minimizing color variance alone may change the appearance predictions while leaving unreliable density in place. We therefore use the visibility-weighted variance to penalize the candidate point’s opacity:

    (18)

    L_occ=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Nsg(Vᵢ)α(xᵢ),

    where sg(·) denotes stop-gradient. The variance acts as a fixed weight in this term: a larger Vᵢ gives a stronger penalty on α(xᵢ). Stop-gradient prevents the penalty from being reduced by changing Vᵢ through this path.

    Although L_CRC is expressed through rendered colors, it also affects geometry. Specifically, each rendered color depends on density through opacity and transmittance in Equation (2), and the cross-ray directions depend on differentiable opacity gradients. In addition, Equation (18) directly penalizes the opacity of inconsistent candidates. The opacity-band test itself is discrete and provides no gradient; instead, it updates the candidate distribution as the field changes. Meanwhile, L_rgb keeps the predictions anchored to the captured images during refinement. This reasoning assumes that surface appearance varies modestly across the sampled local directions; strong specular effects may therefore penalize valid geometry.

    To further reduce high-frequency noise in the density field, we apply local normal smoothness. Given a random perturbation εᵢ∼U(-s/2,s/2)³ and x^′ᵢ=xᵢ+εᵢ,

    (19)

    Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^N∥n(xᵢ)-n(x^′ᵢ)∥₂.

    Here, s>0 denotes the side length of the cubic neighborhood used to sample local perturbations.

    3.5. Training Objective

    We combine RGB reconstruction from the NeRF path with the constraints from the geometry branch in the training objective

    (20)

    L=L_rgb+λ_cr(L_CRC+λ_occL_occ)+λₛₘLₛₘₒₒₜₕ.

    Here L_rgb maintains agreement with the captured images, while L_CRC supplies the cross-ray constraint. The occupancy and smoothness terms act on the geometry in complementary ways: one suppresses inconsistent density, and the other reduces local noise.

    Algorithm 1 summarizes one optimization update with a nonempty candidate batch. Specifically, the geometry branch uses the current field to select candidates, construct cross-rays, and render their colors. Based on these predictions, it evaluates the visibility-weighted losses and updates the shared network together with RGB reconstruction. The normal computation and appearance rendering remain differentiable, whereas the visibility weights and the variance used in the occupancy penalty are detached as described above.

    4. Experiments

    4.1. Implementation Details

    For the reported experiments, we initialize the NeRF network from a vanilla-NeRF checkpoint and continue optimization with the objective in Equation (20). In each geometry-optimization step, we draw 20,000 uniform proposals from the sampling volume, append rendered-depth anchors, apply the opacity-band filter, and randomly retain up to 100 candidates. We generate 15 cross-rays for each candidate. For the opacity and normal computations, we use δ=(10.0-0.1)/128 and ε=10⁻⁵, respectively. Unless noted below, we set r=0.15 and l₀=0.28, giving a default normal-bias strength of λₙ=l₀/r≈1.87. We also set (l_\min,l_\max)=(0.15,0.45), s=0.08, λ_cr=1.5×10⁻³, λ_occ=1.15, and λₛₘ=2.5×10⁻⁴.

    For visibility estimation, we place 32 uniform samples between 0.01lᵢⱼ and lᵢⱼ along each origin-to-candidate segment, including the endpoint, and set Δᵢⱼₖ=0.99lᵢⱼ/32. Cross-ray rendering uses near and far bounds of 0.1 and 10.0 meters. The continuation with the geometry branch starts at a learning rate of 1.15×10⁻⁴.

    Room 1 uses (l_\min,l_\max)=(0.125,0.30), λ_occ=0.8, and λₛₘ=2.5×10⁻³. Office 2 uses r=0.25, (l_\min,l_\max)=(0.08,0.70), s=0.10, λ_cr=1.05×10⁻³, and λ_occ=3.25; its scene-specific continuation starts at a learning rate of 1.25×10⁻⁴. These settings are fixed in the reported runs.

    For Office 2, we additionally suppress residual floating density with an auxiliary global sparsity penalty:

    (21)

    Lₛₚₐᵣₛₑ=1-𝔼_x∼V[\exp(-δₛReLU(σ_θ(x)))].

    The optimization objective for this scene is L+λₛₚLₛₚₐᵣₛₑ, where L is defined in Equation (20), λₛₚ=10⁻², and δₛ=0.01. This auxiliary term is not used for the other seven scenes.

    For the comparison in Table 1, both vanilla NeRF and our method are evaluated after 300,000 cumulative training iterations. When our run is initialized from a vanilla-NeRF checkpoint, its continuation iterations are counted within this total. Thus, both methods have the same iteration budget.

    All surface normals used during refinement are computed on the fly from opacity gradients; ground-truth normals are not used. For Replica scenes, the reference mesh determines an oriented 3D sampling volume, but does not enter the training losses. Ground-truth depth is reserved for evaluation. Thus, the losses use no ground-truth depth or normal supervision, although the sampling bounds still depend on reference geometry in the current experiments.

    4.2. Geometry Reconstruction Results

    Table 1 reports the Chamfer distance on eight Replica scenes at the matched 300,000-iteration budget. Compared with vanilla NeRF, our method improves six scenes and reduces the mean distance by 30.8%. Room 1 and Office 0 are the two scenes for which the distance increases.

    Figure 4 qualitatively compares the geometry extracted from the density fields with the ground-truth scene geometry. Although vanilla NeRF recovers the overall scene layout, its surfaces often contain pronounced noise and irregular deformations. After geometry optimization, several wall and furniture surfaces become smoother and more closely resemble the reference geometry. Specifically, the wall in Room 1 and the tabletops in Room 2 and Office 2 exhibit reduced surface irregularities. Together with the quantitative results, these comparisons demonstrate that the proposed geometry optimization can improve the geometric fidelity of NeRF’s underlying density field. The smoother wall in Room 1 is a local improvement, despite the higher scene-level Chamfer distance reported in Table 1.

    5. Conclusion and Discussion

    We proposed a framework that augments vanilla NeRF with a geometry-optimization branch. Specifically, the branch samples candidate surface points, generates virtual cross-rays through them, and renders their appearance from multiple viewpoints. Based on the visibility-weighted disagreement of these rendered colors, cross-ray consistency constrains the density field, while occupancy suppression and local normal smoothness reduce geometric noise. On eight Replica scenes, the method reduces the mean Chamfer distance by 30.8% relative to vanilla NeRF.

    The current experiments use a reference mesh to define sampling bounds and scene-specific settings for Room 1 and Office 2. Future work should estimate the bounds from training cameras, isolate the effect of the added branch through an RGB-only continuation from the same checkpoint, and investigate appearance models that are less sensitive to specular surfaces.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 稀疏视角 3DGS 就是个 few-shot 问题：把高斯当神经元，用 dropout 与 early stopping 治过拟合 ｜ Rethinking Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting: A Few-Shot Learning Perspective on Overfitting Prevention
item.description:
一句话：换视角看稀疏视角 3DGS：用深度学习正则化那一套（伪视角、dropout、早停）系统治过拟合，拿下赛道第一。

要点：

  • 把每个高斯图元看作一个神经元，于是 3DGS 优化可以直接套用深度学习的正则化框架
  • 数据侧：光流引导的伪视角合成，加相机与场景联合优化，从稀缺观测里造更有效的监督
  • 训练侧：运动感知 dropout 加 early stopping 抑制过拟合，同时保住动态场景稳定性；SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 稀疏视角赛道第一名

为什么值得看：稀疏输入是手机拍一圈、无人机绕一圈的真实场景，过拟合就是几何塌陷；把已有正则化手段按 few-shot 的思路组合，比新造表示更省事。

中文摘要：稀疏视角下的新视角合成对 AR/VR 与实时通信都很关键，却很难：3DGS 在稠密视角下很强，输入一变稀疏就过拟合、几何退化。现有做法要么只管数据质量、要么只管训练正则，缺少统一且可解释的框架。这篇工作换了个切入角度：把稀疏视角 3DGS 当成 few-shot 学习问题，把每个高斯图元看作一个神经元，从而把深度学习里成熟的正则化手段系统搬过来。具体分两条线：数据侧用光流引导的伪视角合成，配合相机与场景联合优化，从稀缺观测里造出更有效的监督；训练侧用运动感知 dropout 与 early stopping 压过拟合，同时保持动态场景的稳定性。在 SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 体积视频挑战赛的稀疏视角数据集上，该方法超过优化式与前馈式基线，并拿下该赛道第一名。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-25

Rethinking Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting:
A Few-Shot Learning Perspective on Overfitting Prevention

© none

Abstract.

Sparse-view novel view synthesis (NVS) is essential for AR/VR and real-time communication applications, yet remains challenging when reconstructing 3D scenes from limited viewpoints. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) excels in dense-view scenarios, it suffers from overfitting and geometry degradation under sparse inputs. Current approaches often tackle these problems from a local perspective, addressing either data quality or training regularization individually, lacking a unified and interpretable framework for systematic improvement. We introduce a new perspective that reframes sparse-view 3DGS from a few-shot learning viewpoint, treating each Gaussian primitive as a neuron and leveraging deep learning regularization techniques. Under this unified framework that systematically connects 3DGS optimization with deep learning regularization principles, our approach generates more effective supervision from scarce observations through two strategies: (1) data-related supervision enrichment via optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and joint camera–scene optimization; and (2) training-time regularization via motion-aware dropout and early stopping, which suppress overfitting while preserving dynamic-scene stability. Extensive experiments on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 volumetric video challenge sparse-view dataset demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art optimization-based and feed-forward baselines. Our system won first place in the sparse-view track of the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 challenge.

Keywords:

3D Gaussian Splatting, sparse-view synthesis, few-shot learning

1. Introduction

Sparse-view novel view synthesis (NVS) aims to reconstruct a renderable 3D scene from a small number of input viewpoints, a capability that is critical for AR/VR and real-time communication applications. Recent advances in differentiable rendering—most notably Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)—have driven substantial progress; in dense-view settings, 3DGS in particular offers fast convergence and high rendering efficiency and has been widely adopted [(Kerbl et al., 2023)]. However, under sparse inputs, even 3DGS often overfits the limited viewpoints, resulting in geometry degradation and unstable, artifact-prone appearance.

Existing approaches address the sparse viewpoint problem through various strategies—synthesizing pseudo-views, incorporating external depth supervision, and applying training regularization [(Bao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Smith et al., 2024)]—but lack a unified perspective. This motivates us to seek a principled viewpoint that organizes these strategies within a single methodology. We therefore ask: if each Gaussian primitive could be treated as a neuron, can we borrow the well-established regularization toolkit from deep learning? This question leads us to reframe sparse-view 3DGS from a few-shot learning perspective, making deep learning regularization principles directly applicable.

In deep learning, Ying et al. [(Ying, 2019)] attribute overfitting to three causes—noisy data, excessive model capacity, and insufficient data. We argue that a corresponding mapping to sparse-view 3DGS challenges is: camera miscalibration introduces noise, excessive and entangled Gaussians lead to overfitting and co-adaptation, and limited viewpoints provide insufficient supervision. Correspondingly, the four canonical overfitting prevention strategies in deep learning—early stopping, model reduction, data augmentation, and regularization—naturally apply to 3DGS to address these challenges. We therefore group them into the two pillars that structure our method: Supervision Enhancement (data-related) and Training Regularization (model-training-related).

Our approach instantiates these pillars through: (1) Supervision Enhancement: data expansion via optical flow-guided pseudo-view synthesis and data augmentation via joint camera–scene optimization; (2) Training Regularization: motion-aware dropout (restricted to static regions to handle dynamic scenes) paired with early stopping.

Contributions. Our work makes the following contributions:

  • •

    To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to provide a principled reframing of sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting as a few-shot learning problem by interpreting each Gaussian primitive as a computational unit. This perspective yields an interpretable link between graphics optimization and well-established generalization mechanisms in deep learning.

  • •

    We instantiate the Supervision Enhancement component via a supervision scheme tailored to limited viewpoints that (i) synthesizes pseudo-views through optical flow, and (ii) performs adaptive joint camera–scene optimization based on reprojection error.

  • •

    We instantiate the Training Regularization component by coupling motion-aware dropout—selectively applied to static Gaussians—with early stopping, effectively reducing co-adaptation under sparse inputs.

  • •

    Experiments on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 sparse-view dataset demonstrate improvements over both feed-forward and optimization-based methods across quantitative metrics and visual quality.

    • 2. Methodology

    Our overall algorithm is illustrated in Figure 2. Following the deep learning perspective outlined in the introduction, we organize our approach into two complementary categories: Supervision Enhancement and Training Regularization. This unified framework addresses the three fundamental causes of overfitting in sparse-view 3DGS: noisy data (corresponding to camera miscalibration), insufficient data, and excessive model capacity. In the following subsections, we detail each component.

    2.1. Supervision Enhancement

    To address insufficient supervision and noisy data in sparse-view 3DGS, we enhance the training data through two strategies: pseudo-view synthesis addresses insufficient data, while joint camera–scene optimization addresses noisy data.

    2.1.1. Optical Flow Guided Pseudo-view Synthesis

    Given a predicted depth map D with intrinsics (fₓ,f_y,cₓ,c_y), we synthesize a nearby view by applying a small in-plane translation t=(tₓ,t_y,0)^⊤. The induced pixel shifts are

    (1)u(x)=fₓ(-tₓ)/D(x), v(x)=(f_y(-t_y))/(D(x)).

    Rendering the translated pose produces Ĩ, which we warp back via differentiable sampling:

    (2)I_w(x)=Ĩ (x+\beginbmatrixu(x) v(x)\endbmatrix).

    This optical-flow parameterization explicitly reasons about horizontal and vertical displacements, providing extra robustness along the vertical axis when the training views lie roughly on the same horizontal ring (a common sparse-view setting where vertical supervision is weak). Over the valid pixel set V (visible and in-bounds), we measure the Charbonnier photometric consistency as

    (3)Lₚₕₒₜₒ=(1)/(|V|)∑_x∈V√∥I_w(x)-I_gt(x)∥₂²+ε,

    where ε>0 is a small constant.

    To regularize depth and the induced flow, we adopt total variation (TV) regularization for both depth and flow fields, along with edge-aware smoothing to preserve depth discontinuities at image edges. The final geometric objective combines the photometric consistency loss with these regularization terms:

    (4)L_geo=λ_geoLₚₕₒₜₒ
    (5)+λ_dL_depth-TV+λ_fL_flow-TV+λₑL_edge,

    where L_depth-TV and L_flow-TV are total variation terms that encourage smoothness in depth and flow fields, respectively, and L_edge is an edge-aware term that reduces smoothing at image edges. The hyperparameters are λ_geo,λ_d,λ_f,λₑ>0.

    2.1.2. Joint Camera–Scene Optimization

    Camera poses are part of the input data; when their calibration is inaccurate, they act as noise that degrades sparse-view reconstructions. To address this, we jointly optimize both camera poses and scene geometry based on reprojection error. We parameterize camera poses using SO(3) rotations and ℝ³ translations (SO3xR3), allowing the optimization to correct calibration errors while simultaneously refining the 3D Gaussian scene representation. To avoid unnecessary optimization when camera calibration is already accurate, we selectively enable camera pose optimization only for sequences with high reprojection errors, which indicates potential calibration issues. The camera optimizer is activated after an initial warmup period and frozen before geometric constraints are applied, ensuring stable convergence. This selective joint optimization effectively reduces the impact of noisy camera parameters on sparse-view reconstruction while preserving well-calibrated camera poses.

    2.2. Training Regularization

    To address excessive model capacity and prevent overfitting, we employ two regularization strategies: motion-aware dropout and early stopping.

    2.2.1. Motion-Aware Dropout

    Dropout requires that different subsets of Gaussians, after being dropped, yield comparable outcomes. However, this consistency assumption is often violated under fast motion. We therefore restrict dropout to static regions only. To define static and dynamic regions, we leverage dense initialization that combines optical flow estimation (PDCNet[(Truong et al., 2023)]) and multi-view point cloud reconstruction (OpenMVS[(cdcseacave, 2023)]). PDCNet provides a complete point cloud covering both static and dynamic regions, while OpenMVS, relying on multi-view consistency, primarily produces static point clouds. We compute the distance from each point in the PDCNet point cloud to the nearest point in the OpenMVS point cloud. Points close to OpenMVS (within a threshold) are assigned as static, while distant points are labeled as dynamic.

    During training, we apply motion-aware dropout: for each Gaussian, we determine whether it lies in a dynamic region based on the initial definition. Gaussians in dynamic regions are excluded from dropout to preserve rendering quality, while only static-region Gaussians are subject to dropout regularization. This selective application maintains the consistency assumption for dropout while protecting dynamic regions.

    2.2.2. Early Stopping

    To prevent overfitting, we employ early stopping based on validation metrics. We determine the optimal early-stopping point by evaluating checkpoints throughout training and computing rankings on novel view synthesis metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). The optimal stopping point is determined as the checkpoint with the lowest average rank across all three metrics. This stopping criterion is determined using a validation sequence and then applied consistently across all experiments.

    2.3. Training Objective and Optimization

    The overall training objective combines rendering loss, geometric objective, and camera pose regularization. We optimize training under sparse views by combining early stopping and motion-aware dropout to stabilize convergence and improve efficiency.

    Rendering Loss Let Î be the rendered image and I_gt the ground truth. We adopt a standard combination of ℓ₁ and SSIM:

    (6)L_render=λ₁ ∥Î-I_gt∥₁+λ_SSIM (1-SSIM(Î,I_gt)).

    Geometric Objective The geometric objective L_geo combines photometric consistency with depth and flow regularization, as detailed in Section 2.1.1.

    Camera Regularization The camera regularization term L_cam constrains the deviation of optimized camera poses from their initial values, preventing excessive pose modifications.

    Overall Objective The complete training objective is a weighted sum of all three components:

    (7)Lₜₒₜₐₗ=λ_renderL_render+λ_geoL_geo+λ_camL_cam,

    where λ_render, λ_geo, and λ_cam are the weights for the rendering loss, geometric objective, and camera regularization, respectively.

    3. Experiments

    3.1. Experimental Settings

    Dataset and Evaluation Protocol We evaluate our method on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 Volumetric Video Challenge sparse-view track dataset [(Yu et al., 2025)]. The dataset consists of 2 validation sequences (with full 16 camera viewpoints) and 5 test sequences (with 8 camera viewpoints), each containing 300 frames. All quantitative comparisons reported in this paper are conducted on the validation sequences, where we use 8 training views for reconstruction and evaluate on 8 novel test views. Test sequences are reserved for challenge submissions. Metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) are computed on foreground regions only across all novel views.

    Implementation Details All experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA A100 40GB GPU, with the training phase of each run taking roughly three minutes (preprocessing time is excluded). Although the nominal schedule budgets 30k optimization steps, we monitor PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on a held-out validation sequence and consistently trigger early stopping around step 5k.

    Hyperparameters For the rendering loss, we set λ₁=0.8 and λ_SSIM=0.2. The geometric objective weights are: λ_geo=0.8, λ_d=0.05 (depth TV), λ_f=0.1 (flow TV), and λₑ=0.05 (edge-aware). Camera optimization is enabled for sequences with reprojection error exceeding 1.0, activated at step 3,000 and frozen at step 4,000. Motion-aware dropout uses a factor of 0.1 for static Gaussians, with motion detection threshold of 0.8. The geometric constraint starts at iteration 500 with translation range (0.05,0.2).

    3.2. Comparison with SOTA Methods

    Our comparative study covers state-of-the-art optimization-based and feed-forward methods, specifically: 1the base 3DGS method [(Kerbl et al., 2023)]; 2a representative self-supervised pseudo-data approach, Binocular3DGS [(Han et al., 2024)]; 3a representative feed-forward method, GPS-Gaussian [(Zheng et al., 2024)]; 4the state-of-the-art for sparse reconstruction, SparseGS [(Xiong et al., 2025)]. Quantitative comparisons are reported in Table 1, while qualitative results are visualized in Figures 1 and 3.

    4. Conclusion

    Conclusion We reframe sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting from a few-shot learning perspective and organize the solution around two pillars: Supervision Enhancement (optical-flow pseudo views plus joint camera–scene optimization) and Training Regularization (motion-aware dropout plus early stopping). Together with a stabilized training objective, this unified methodology delivers consistent quantitative and qualitative gains on the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 sparse-view benchmark.

    Limitations and Future Work The current pipeline still assumes moderate motion when synthesizing pseudo views and extremely rapid human dynamics can violate this assumption. Future work will explore explicit motion compensation or learned pose priors to better align highly dynamic sequences.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：换视角看稀疏视角 3DGS：用深度学习正则化那一套（伪视角、dropout、早停）系统治过拟合，拿下赛道第一。

要点：

  • 把每个高斯图元看作一个神经元，于是 3DGS 优化可以直接套用深度学习的正则化框架
  • 数据侧：光流引导的伪视角合成，加相机与场景联合优化，从稀缺观测里造更有效的监督
  • 训练侧：运动感知 dropout 加 early stopping 抑制过拟合，同时保住动态场景稳定性；SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 稀疏视角赛道第一名

为什么值得看：稀疏输入是手机拍一圈、无人机绕一圈的真实场景，过拟合就是几何塌陷；把已有正则化手段按 few-shot 的思路组合，比新造表示更省事。

中文摘要：稀疏视角下的新视角合成对 AR/VR 与实时通信都很关键，却很难：3DGS 在稠密视角下很强，输入一变稀疏就过拟合、几何退化。现有做法要么只管数据质量、要么只管训练正则，缺少统一且可解释的框架。这篇工作换了个切入角度：把稀疏视角 3DGS 当成 few-shot 学习问题，把每个高斯图元看作一个神经元，从而把深度学习里成熟的正则化手段系统搬过来。具体分两条线：数据侧用光流引导的伪视角合成，配合相机与场景联合优化，从稀缺观测里造出更有效的监督；训练侧用运动感知 dropout 与 early stopping 压过拟合，同时保持动态场景的稳定性。在 SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 体积视频挑战赛的稀疏视角数据集上，该方法超过优化式与前馈式基线，并拿下该赛道第一名。

item.title: 50V50 战斗中 Lua 一直高耗时：先分清「持续高频」还是「单帧峰值」，别只看调用次数
item.description:
一句话：一条 Lua 路径从每帧 100+ 次涨到 300+ 次，另一条在个别帧打到 24,000 次，两者的排查路径完全不同。

要点：

  • 持续高频调用要看它占了多少 CPU：某条路径从每帧 100 多次涨到 300 次以上，先查有没有多余的重复更新
  • 瞬时峰值要结合该帧实际耗时判断：另一条路径在个别帧出现约 24,000 次调用，可能只是合理的一次性集中处理
  • 高频 Lua 与 C#/Unity API 交互要考虑合并调用；寻路与路径更新评估能否从每帧改成按需，优化后用同条件对比耗时与 FPS

为什么值得看：多人战斗的卡顿常被归给「Lua 慢」，实际问题要么是每帧重复执行、要么是跨层调用放大开销；按耗时而非调用次数排优先级，才不会优化错地方。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：UWA 博客（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-25

多人战斗中Lua持续高耗时，是瞬时峰值还是高频调用在作祟

  • 作者：admin
  • /
  • 时间：3天前
  • /
  • 浏览：202 次
  • /
  • 分类：厚积薄发

    • 1）多人战斗中Lua持续高耗时，应优先排查什么
    2）战斗后期温度和功耗下降，判断CPU是否降频

    这是第497篇UWA技术知识分享的推送，精选了UWA社区的热门话题，涵盖了UWA问答、社区帖子等技术知识点，助力大家更全面地掌握和学习。

    UWA社区主页：community.uwa4d.com
    UWA QQ群：793972859

    本次推送的实战案例来自于使用UWA服务的项目的真实且典型的问题。UWA将关键线索、定位路径与处理建议整理成了可复用的案例笔记，便于大家快速对照、排查自身项目中的同类问题。

    实战案例

    Q：在50V50的多人战斗测试中，帧率持续偏低，CPU耗时主要集中在Lua逻辑。进一步查看函数堆栈，发现部分函数存在持续高频调用，也有个别函数在单帧出现大量调用。面对这种情况，应该优先排查瞬时调用峰值，还是持续高频调用？

    A：应结合函数的实际CPU耗时及其对帧率的影响确定排查优先级，而不能仅凭调用次数判断。对于持续低帧率，应优先关注长期占用较多CPU时间的调用路径；对于偶发卡顿，则应重点检查与卡顿帧对应的瞬时调用峰值。

    从函数调用情况来看，主要存在两类现象：

  • 持续高频调用：某条Lua调用路径从每帧100多次增加至300次以上，且相关节点耗时占比较高，需要检查是否存在不必要的重复更新；

  • 瞬时调用峰值：另一条Lua调用路径在个别帧出现约24,000次调用，需要结合对应帧的实际耗时，判断是否造成卡顿。

    建议重点排查以下两个方面：
    1. 检查函数耗时与调用频率
    沿调用堆栈定位主要耗时节点，结合调用次数判断问题是来自重复执行，还是单次执行耗时较高。例如部队寻路、路径更新等逻辑，检查是否需要每帧执行，能否改为按需更新。对于瞬时峰值，则应结合具体操作确认集中调用是否合理；

    • 2. 检查Lua跨层调用
    如果高频调用涉及Lua与C#或Unity API之间的交互，需要关注重复调用产生的开销，评估是否能够合并调用或集中处理部分逻辑。优化后，在相同测试条件下对比Lua函数耗时、调用次数及FPS，确认持续开销是否下降，同时检查是否仍存在明显的单帧卡顿。

    需要注意，Development包及较多Lua函数打点可能引入额外开销，建议在相同采集条件下验证优化效果。

    实战案例

    Q：在长时间多人战斗测试中，CPU温度明显高于GPU，设备功耗也处于较高水平。但随着战斗进行，后半段的温度和功耗反而下降，部分CPU核心频率也出现波动。这是否意味着CPU发生了降频，应该如何判断？

    A：温度和功耗下降既可能是业务负载减少，也可能与温控降频有关，不能仅凭曲线变化判断，需要结合CPU频率、各模块耗时和具体业务逻辑进行分析判断。

    测试中，部分设备CPU温度比GPU高出十几度，设备功耗约为5W，后半段则出现温度、功耗下降及部分CPU核心频率波动的现象。

    建议从以下三个方面排查：
    1. 对照CPU频率与FPS

    重点关注承担游戏主线程任务的CPU核心，检查其频率是否持续下降，以及同期FPS是否出现明显变化。需要注意，单个核心的频率波动不一定代表温控降频，也可能与正常调频或线程调度有关；

    2. 对比相近负载下的模块耗时
    CPU降频可能影响多个CPU侧模块的执行效率。在UI更新频率、粒子特效规模等业务条件相近的情况下，可以对比UI、粒子系统等模块的CPU耗时。如果多个模块的耗时明显增加，则需要结合设备热状态及线程调度情况，进一步判断是否存在温控或功耗限制；

    3. 排查战斗过程中的业务负载变化
    温度和功耗下降也可能是实际计算量减少所致，需要确认前后战斗状态是否发生变化。例如，部分战斗玩法存在伤兵机制，随着战斗推进，部分单位不再参与战斗，寻路、AI决策等逻辑的计算量随之减少，CPU负载也可能降低。

    建议对照温度下降前后的参战单位数量及相关函数调用次数，确认是否存在明显的业务负载变化。

    综合来看，温度和功耗下降不能直接认定为CPU降频，应结合CPU频率、FPS及相近负载下的模块耗时，区分硬件性能受限与业务计算量减少的影响，必要时通过相同业务负载下的对照测试进一步验证。

item.title: 卡在 Shader.CreateGPUProgram 的那一帧，现在能直接下钻到变体明细
item.description:
一句话：把「背帧号、切页面、猜资源」这几段断掉的排查链路接上：卡顿帧直连 Shader 变体与 Call Tree。

要点：

  • 定位到 Shader.CreateGPUProgram 的卡顿帧后，可直接调出该帧的 Shader 变体明细（Shader / Pass / Keywords 与耗时），需 Android Development 包并开 Log Shader Compilation
  • 自定义函数组里的函数若有下层堆栈，可就地点详情跳到 Call Tree，省掉跨页面横跳
  • GC 模块新增 GarbageCollector.CollectIncremental 独立耗时曲线，看增量 GC 与常规 GC.Collect 不必再去堆栈里手搜

为什么值得看：Shader 变体爆炸和 GC 抖动是 Unity 线上性能的两大固定成本，工具能把「哪一帧碰到哪些变体」显示出来，才算真正可归因。

中文摘要：版本将上线、新角色与特效刚合入，回归测试第一跑就卡了一下，打开 UWA GOT Online 报告，Shader.CreateGPUProgram 赫然在列——但知道函数名只是痛苦的开始：这一帧到底碰到哪一批 Shader 变体？这次更新把几条常断的链路接上了。定位到该函数的卡顿帧后，可以直接调出这一帧的 Shader 变体明细，包含具体 Shader、Pass、Keywords 与对应耗时，拿着明细去核对本轮新增的材质或特效即可（该能力目前覆盖 Android APP 的 Development 包，需开启 Log Shader Compilation）。其次，自定义函数组里的函数若有下层堆栈，直接在当前页点详情就能跳到对应堆栈页面，热点圈定与 Call Tree 追溯连成一条线。另外 GC 模块补了独立的 GarbageCollector.CollectIncremental 耗时曲线，MCP 侧也支持调取报告截图、网格渲染利用率表与按需提取指定关卡数据。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：UWA 博客（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-25

深挖Shader变体明细，下钻自定义函数堆栈：性能排查链路再升级

  • 作者：admin
  • /
  • 时间：3天前
  • /
  • 浏览：208 次
  • /
  • 分类：万象更新

    • 版本准备上线，新角色、材质和战斗特效刚合入，回归测试第一跑就在场景里卡了一下。打开UWA GOT Online报告，老面孔Shader.CreateGPUProgram赫然在列。问题看似有了方向，但这往往是痛苦的开始：这一帧到底碰到了哪一批Shader变体？

    以往我们只能拿着函数名去海量的项目资源里盲猜，这轮更新后，几条经常断掉的排查链路，终于接上了。

    穿透CreateGPUProgram，卡顿帧直连Shader变体明细

    现在定位到Shader.CreateGPUProgram的卡顿帧后，可以直接调出这一帧的Shader变体明细，包含具体的Shader、Pass、Keywords以及对应耗时。

    拿着这份明细，直接去核对本轮新增的特效或材质资源即可。精准锁定问题源头，不用再从整个项目的Shader库里大海捞针。（注：该能力目前覆盖Android APP的Development包，需开启Log Shader Compilation。）

    查热点不断档，自定义函数组原地展开Call Tree

    战斗或UI逻辑大改后，自定义函数组里的某个函数开销突然飙升。以前查这种情况，得先硬记下异常帧号，再切到CPU模块去查调用栈。现在，只要自定义函数组中的函数存在下层堆栈，直接在当前页面点击“详情”就能跳转至对应堆栈页面。

    省去跨页面的来回横跳，热点圈定和Call Tree追溯终于连成了一条线。

    免搜堆栈，GC模块新增Incremental增量耗时曲线

    长时间跑测时常会遇到GC波动。现在，GC模块中直接补充了独立的GarbageCollector.CollectIncremental CPU耗时趋势图。

    看似只是轻量的细节补充，在日常排查中却极其高频，对比观察增量GC与常规GC.Collect的执行情况时，再也不用专门去堆栈里手动搜了，看上下两张图表趋势即可。

    还原“案发现场”，MCP支持截图获取与场景按需提取

  • 截图获取与AI诊断：短时卡顿光看数据不够直观。现在MCP可调取报告截图与网格渲染利用率表，将画面与数据同步喂给AI，快速定位最需优化的Mesh资源。

  • 场景数据按需提取：针对多场景重度报告，MCP支持定向提取指定关卡数据，直接调取目标关卡快速完成横向对比。

    • 更多更新与体验优化

  • 自定义面板配置自动记忆：同项目自定义变量配置后支持跨报告生效，查看新报告无需重复勾选；

  • 全面适配Lua 5.5：Unity SDK现已兼容，无缝衔接原有性能采集流程。

    • 线索中断往往最让人抓狂。从Shader变体下钻到MCP现场还原，这次更新抹平了“切页面、背帧号、猜资源”的缝隙。顺着一条线索一挖到底，让性能排查直达根源。

    最后说两句：

    我们深知，在项目期引入或尝试一个新工具是有决策成本的。

    工具的价值，不仅在于它能算得多快，更在于它能不能真的融入团队的日常流转中，帮大家准时下班。

    但如果它能每天帮你省下半小时的查Bug时间，这笔账就绝对划算。为了让大家能毫无负担地验证这波“AI+性能优化”的疗效，我们为大家准备了专属福利：
    联系商务同学，即可直接申请「两周GOT Online免费试用」与「专家一对一诊断名额」。不管你们现在卡在什么性能瓶颈上，UWA 的技术专家会陪着你们跑通测试，直击问题！

    关于UWA

    UWA是一家创业十年的高新技术企业，作为游戏行业的深耕者，UWA始终专注于为使用Unity、Unreal引擎的开发者提供丰富的优化产品，帮助开发者高效解决开发问题、定位性能瓶颈、提供解决方案，已支持超过一万款游戏项目。还打造了技术博客、问答、学堂等社区产品，为开发者提供便利和高效的支持。线上培训和线下教育的新业务，满足行业对人才培育的需求。

    文章标签：got online

item.title: 《我的世界》渲染管线现代化：RenderDragon 拆开游戏逻辑与绘制，DragonFX 一次编写到处跑
item.category: 公众号·游戏AI编程与图形渲染
item.description:
一句话：老引擎做 PBR 升级的真实约束：玩法手感一点不能动，材质靠自动管线量产，光线传输用廉价近似。

要点：

  • 原版光照是 CPU 在方块网格里做「墨水扩散」，火把与天空光直接烘进顶点，跨平台与画质诉求逼着推倒重来
  • 新框架 RenderDragon 把游戏逻辑与底层绘制解绑，另自研着色语言 DragonFX 做到一次编写、到处运行
  • Vibrant Visuals 转向物理渲染，但昼夜更替、刷怪、红石反馈都按原样保留；树叶透光在漫反射里近似，最大穿透深度卡在 1 个方块

为什么值得看：这是「不能改玩法、不能崩性能、还要上 PBR」的教科书案例：抽象层先行、着色语言自研、材质靠自动化管线补产能，最后用一条硬指标（穿透深度 1 格）把性能钉住。

中文摘要：该账号的分享卡片梳理了《我的世界》渲染团队的升级思路：原版光照全靠 CPU 在方块网格里做类似墨水扩散的计算，火把和天空光直接烘焙进顶点；玩家同时要跨平台和画质，团队只能推倒重来。他们做了 RenderDragon 新框架，把游戏逻辑与底层绘制彻底解绑，又自研着色语言 DragonFX，做到一次编写、到处运行。新出的 Vibrant Visuals 全面转向物理渲染，为了不破坏老玩家的肌肉记忆，新光照必须保住昼夜更替、怪物刷怪、红石反馈的原有表现；美术侧靠自动化管线一口气产出三千多张材质贴图。最省的一手是树叶透光：直接在漫反射里做近似，把最大穿透深度死死卡在 1 个方块，画面保住了，设备也没被拖垮。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：公众号·游戏AI编程与图形渲染（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-18

本期推送：2026-10-25

刚看完《我的世界》渲染团队的分享，他们给游戏画面升级这事儿，真不是换个贴图那么简单。 原版的光照全靠 CPU 在方块网格里“墨水扩散”，火把和天空光直接烘焙进顶点。但玩家既要跨平台，又要画质，团队只能推倒重来。他们搞了个叫 RenderDragon 的新框架，把游戏逻辑和底层绘制彻底解绑。接着又自研了 DragonFX 着色语言，做到“一次编写，到处运行”。 新出的 Vibrant Visuals 包全面转向物理渲染。为了不破坏老玩家的肌肉记忆，团队硬是给新光照加了限制：昼夜更替、怪物刷怪、红石反馈，全得按原样保留。美术这边也没闲着，靠着自动化管线，一口气产出了三千多张材质贴图。 最绝的是树叶透光效果。为了省性能，他们直接在漫反射里做近似，把最大穿透深度死死卡在 1 个方块。既保住了画面，又没拖垮设备。 经典游戏的现代化，从来不是把旧砖拆光，而是给老地基接上新管线。

item.title: 着色器跟着下载一起到：Advanced Shader Delivery 铺到 AMD/Intel/NVIDIA/Qualcomm，首启编译从几分钟变几秒 ｜ Advanced Shader Delivery is Available Now Across Hardware and Coming Soon to Other Storefronts
item.description:
一句话：把预编译着色器在下载时交付，直接消掉首启编译时间与着色器卡顿；UE 5.8.4 已能集成，Unity 要等 2027。

要点：

  • 随游戏下载交付预编译着色器，减少总加载时间、游戏中着色器卡顿与功耗；COD:MW4 首启编译从几分钟缩到几秒
  • 已覆盖 Windows 11 24H2+ 上的 RDNA1–4、Arc B / Core Ultra 2–3、全系 RTX 与 RTX Spark、Snapdragon X2
  • 分发面扩到 Epic Games Store 与 Steam（Fortnite 后续更新接入）；开发者收集 SODB 上传商店，UE 5.8.4 已可集成，Unity 计划 2027

为什么值得看：着色器卡顿这笔老账正从「引擎侧异步编译/预热」转到「分发侧预编译」，构建管线要开始产出、版本化并随包管理 SODB。

中文摘要：微软宣布 Advanced Shader Delivery（ASD）已在 Windows 生态上广泛可用，覆盖 AMD、Intel、NVIDIA 与 Qualcomm 的显卡。它要解决的是 PC 生态的老问题：着色器编译发生在玩家机器上，导致首次启动漫长、游戏中随机卡顿并多耗电。ASD 的做法是在下载游戏时就把预编译好的着色器一并交付，官方以 Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 为例，首启编译从典型 PC 上的几分钟缩到几秒，左下角还会显示「Precompiled shaders installed」。硬件要求是 Windows 11 24H2 及以上：AMD RDNA 1–4（Adrenalin 26.6.1+）、Intel Arc B 系列与 Core Ultra 2/3、全系 RTX 与 RTX Spark、Qualcomm Snapdragon X2。分发面也扩大：将从 Microsoft Store 与 XBOX PC 应用扩展到 Epic Games Store 与 Steam，Fortnite 后续更新接入。对开发者而言要做的是收集 state object database（SODB）并上传商店；UE 5.8.4 已支持集成，Unity 侧要等到 2027。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：DirectX Dev Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-10-23

本期推送：2026-10-25

A few weeks ago, we announced that Advanced Shader Delivery (ASD) is available for Gears of War: E-Day and teased that the feature is coming to devices across Windows 11. Today, we’re proud to announce that Advanced Shader Delivery is broadly available across the Windows ecosystem on devices powered by AMD, Intel, Nvidia, and Qualcomm!

ASD addresses a PC ecosystem wide challenge by delivering shaders at download of a title- reducing overall loading time, reducing shader stutter in game, and saving on power consumption. Check out the system requirements below for supported hardware and graphics drivers.

What’s next?

We’re also excited to announce that ASD will soon expand beyond the Microsoft Store and XBOX PC app to the Epic Games Store and Steam to deliver a better Windows gaming experience to more players! Epic Games will also roll out ASD support in an upcoming update for Fortnite.

For game developers, we’re continuing to make it easier to enumerate and compile state objects. Our upcoming October Agility SDK release includes important improvements such as partial programs, which will more efficiently compile complex state objects in different configurations.

Today: Advanced Shader Delivery Comes to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4

We are also excited to showcase Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 as a great example of ASD working across devices. With ASD, shader compilation at first launch takes just a few seconds, compared to several minutes on a typical PC without ASD.

To experience ASD for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, install the XBOX PC app before downloading.  For the best experience for ASD across all supported titles, make sure your graphics drivers are up to date.

Call to Action

If you’re a game developer looking to solve shader compilation, take a look at our documentation on how to integrate ASD for your title. Here, you’ll find instructions on how to collect state object databases (SODB) and upload them to game storefronts to support pre-compilation for your title today.

For those using Unreal Engine 5.8.4 to develop their title, the ability to integrate SODBs into the process is available today. Here is a link to their documentation on how to easily build an SODB into the process.

For those using Unity, SODB integration will be available in 2027!

System Requirements:

OS: Windows 11 24H2 or higher

AMD:

GPUs supported:AMD RDNA ™ 1, RDNA 2, RDNA 3, RDNA 3.5, RDNA 4 architectures

Driver version:Adrenalin 26.6.1 or higher

Intel:

GPUs supported:Intel® Arc B-Series: B570, B580, Intel® Core™ Ultra Series 2, Intel® Core™ Ultra Series 3

Min driver version:32.0.101.9150 or higher

Nvidia:

GPUs supported:All RTX GPUs and RTX Spark

Driver version:621.01 or higher

Qualcomm:

GPUs supported:Qualcomm® Snapdragon® X2 Series

Driver version:2026.08.3 or higher

Feedback?

For feedback on the Advanced Shader Delivery experience, you can let us know via our DirectX Discord.

Category

  • Advanced Shader Delivery
  • DirectX

    • Author

    Join the discussion.

    Sort by :Newest

  • Hi Wendy, whats the expected behavior with an Optimus config?

    The Xbox app loads on the Low Power device in this scenario and users are reporting that supported games such as Gears E-day aren't showing the Precompiled shaders message.

    Should it be getting shaders for all present gpu's in the system?

    if that is the intent, is there a bug where an unsupported driver causes the download to fail on All devices?

    Edit: There is a bug in Gaming Services which does exactly this, if an unsupported adapter (old driver, or possibly no asd package for this driver) the whole request is destroyed and...

    Hi Wendy, whats the expected behavior with an Optimus config?

    The Xbox app loads on the Low Power device in this scenario and users are reporting that supported games such as Gears E-day aren’t showing the Precompiled shaders message.

    Should it be getting shaders for all present gpu’s in the system?

    if that is the intent, is there a bug where an unsupported driver causes the download to fail on All devices?

    Edit: There is a bug in Gaming Services which does exactly this, if an unsupported adapter (old driver, or possibly no asd package for this driver) the whole request is destroyed and there is no fail through onwards to other devices in the system.

    This also widens the issue to any system with an active igp with pre-asd drivers.

    • Stay informed

    Get notified when new posts are published.Follow this blog
