item.title: Godot 4.8 beta 1：功能已冻结，这一版的重点是回归修复与破坏性变更清单 ｜ Dev snapshot: Godot 4.8 beta 1
item.description:
一句话：4.8 进入功能冻结，开发资源全转回归修复；官方同时放出可过滤的破坏性变更列表供迁移评估。

要点：

  • beta 1 之后 4.8 完全功能冻结，开发资源全部转向回归修复与 bug-hunting sprint
  • 破坏性变更集中列出并可用 breaks compat 标签过滤合并的 PR，例如移除未文档化的 enter_world 回调、修正 LookAtModifier3D.is_interpolating 的反向返回值
  • 同时提供 Web 编辑器、XR 编辑器与 Android 编辑器供直接试用，方便在真实项目上做回归

为什么值得看：引擎小版本升级的隐性成本几乎都在破坏性变更与回归上；有明确的冻结点与可过滤清单，才好安排分支合并窗口。

中文摘要：Godot 4.8 进入 beta 快照阶段，意味着功能已经完全冻结，开发资源不再投新特性，而是专心做各种回归修复。官方鼓励想帮忙的开发者参加 bug-hunting sprint，读一遍 Bug Triage Introduction，然后进 #bugsquad 与 #bugsquad-sprints 频道。因为已经功能冻结，这一版相对上一轮 dev 7 没有新特性可讲，文章改成对整个 4.8 的统览，并补讲之前没来得及展开的改动。对升级方最有价值的是破坏性变更一节：官方列出合并 PR 中带 breaks compat 标签的条目，例如 3D 里移除了未文档化的 script only enter_world 回调、动画里修正 LookAtModifier3D.is_interpolating() 返回值反了的问题、Core 里在 release 导出中使用本地调试器会直接失败等，都可能在升级时咬人。此外还提供 Web、XR 与 Android 编辑器供直接试用。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：Godot（English）

原文发布：2026-10-15

本期推送：2026-10-25

Dev snapshot: Godot 4.8 beta 1

By: Thaddeus Crews15 October 2026Pre-release

It’s that time of the release cycle once again: the beta snapshot! With this, 4.8 is fully in feature-freeze, and developer resources have shifted exclusively to creating and reviewing various regression fixes.

For those interested in aiding us on our quest to squash any bugs that come up during this time, we once again encourage you to join our bug-hunting sprints. Anyone interested should read the Bug Triage Introduction for more information, and join the 

#bugsquad
and 
#bugsquad-sprints
 channels on our developer RocketChat to participate.

Please consider supporting the project financially, if you are able. Godot is maintained by the efforts of volunteers and a small team of paid contributors. Your donations go towards sponsoring their work and ensuring they can dedicate their undivided attention to the needs of the project.

Jump to the Downloads section, and give it a spin right now, or continue reading to learn more about improvements in this release. You can also try the Web editor, the XR editor, or the Android editor for this release. If you are interested in the latter, please request to join our testing group to get access to pre-release builds.

The cover illustration is fromRita, a puzzle game with platforming elements, featuring a wide variety of word puzzles within a cozy world. You can buy the game on Steam, and follow the developer on Bluesky, YouTube, and itch.io.

Highlights

For those who have been following our development snapshots closely, you may be familiar with a number of the highlights in this post which were already covered in previous articles (4.8 dev 1, 4.8 dev 2, 4.8 dev 3, 4.8 dev 4, 4.8 dev 5, 4.8 dev 6, and 4.8 dev 7).

Because we’re already in feature freeze, there are no new features to cover compared to dev 7. Instead, we’ll focus on a general round-up of what to expect from Godot 4.8 as a whole, as well as expanding on some additions that we didn’t have the chance to highlight in our previous snapshots.

  • Breaking changes
  • 3D
  • Core
  • Documentation
  • Editor
  • GDScript
  • GUI
  • Input
  • Physics
  • Platforms
  • Rendering and shaders
  • Shaders
  • XR

    • Breaking changes

    We try to minimize breaking changes, but sometimes they are necessary in order to fix high-priority issues. Where we do break compatibility, we do our best to make sure that the changes are minimal and require few changes in user projects.

    You can find a list of such issues by filtering the merged PRs in the 4.8 milestone with the 

    breaks compat
    label.

  • 3D: Remove undocumented script only enter_world callbacks (GH-111504).
  • Animation: Fix 
    LookAtModifier3D.is_interpolating()
    value is inverted (GH-121391).
  • Animation: Make Bone Follower classes’ FTI off as default, add warning (GH-119509).
  • Core: Fail when trying to use local debugger in release exports (GH-122213).
  • Editor: Fix corner cases related to scroll hints across the editor (GH-117080).
  • Editor: Remove 
    ScriptServer
    fallbacks from 
    ClassDB
    (GH-123379).
  • Export: Do not serialize export options that do not have the 
    PROPERTY_USAGE_STORAGE
    flag (GH-120721).
  • GDScript: Forbid scripts from inheriting their own inner classes (GH-121171).
  • GUI: Fix duplicated button press event on touch input (GH-120864).
  • GUI: Rework dialog default titles (GH-105550).
  • Input: Ignore joypads on unfocused window by default for new projects (GH-120399).
  • Network: mbedTLS: Update to 4.1.0, PSA Crypto (GH-120725).
  • Platforms: Android: Make 
    OS.alert()
    blocking (GH-120800).
  • Rendering: Add support for ASTC 6x6 and high quality compression profiles (GH-115003).
  • Rendering: Fix sky shader 
    SCREEN_UV
    builtin in Compatibility renderer (GH-121676).
  • XR: OpenXR use proper spatial entity NULL constant (GH-121815).

    • 3D

    QbieShay starts our feature round-up strong with 

    Trail3D
    . Introduced in GH-117107 and built off the foundation by Zi Ye’s Cozy Cube Godot Addons, this native solution enables those seeking stunning visual effects through trails to no longer require deep knowledge of how meshes are drawn, UVs are assigned, or anything of the sort; everything Just Works™.

    While being more of an editor feature, the 3D Viewport override functionality by Michael Alexsander in GH-117569 warrants a highlight in this section. Through the new editor option “Allow Viewport Override” (enabled by default), hovering the mouse over a viewport set to a specific side will cause the currently edited axis to match that side.

    And more:

  • Add octant visualization to 
    GridMap
    (GH-118583).
  • 3D: Re-enable freelook inertia by default in the 3D editor (GH-121478).

    • Core

    Adam Johnston brought us “Fuzzy searching” with GH-98278, enabling search results to return matches similar to the passed query, rather than only returning an exact match. Now with GH-107126, this functionality is finally ready to roll for all users.

    var items := ["Potion of Healing", "Greater Health Potion", "Poison Vial"]
var fuzzy := FuzzySearch.new()

for result in fuzzy.search_all("health potion", items):
	# Prints "Greater Health Potion", "Potion of Healing".
	print(result.target)

    Those using version control will be thrilled to hear that serialization of objects has become much cleaner starting with GH-92102. Robert Wallis ensures that all objects are now formatted such that they won’t cause oversized diffs.

    BeforeAfter

    And more:

  • Core: Add support for metadata in text scenes (GH-121920).
  • Core: Introduce 
    Variant.to()
    as a replacement to implicit conversions from 
    Variant
    (GH-123600).
  • Core: Make it impossible to have more than one main thread, and don’t release unnecessarily (GH-121161).
  • Core: Move property maps from 
    ClassDB
    to 
    GDType
    . Accelerate 
    Object
    property access 1.6x (GH-122596).
  • Core: Simplify 
    GDType
    by storing all properties in a single unified map. Save ~12mb runtime RAM (GH-122751).
  • Core: Speed up removing many child nodes (GH-120942).

    • Documentation

    Cyril Bissey’s efforts in GH-111375 grants our documentation—both in-editor and online—native support for admonitions; That being: the built-in systems many documentation tools provide to highlight crucial information. As time of writing, our documentation tools use simple prefixes like “Note:” or “Warning:” to convey a similar effect, but this method causes critical details to blend in with the rest of the text. So starting now, we’ll begin slowly rolling out admonition replacements for these legacy systems, which will end up looking something like what you see below:

    Dark ModeLight Mode

    Editor

    Ever since the introduction of the 

    EditorDock
    in Godot 4.6, Tomasz Chabora has been on a journey to migrate our existing editor plugins to this new system. The most ambitious migration yet occurred with GH-113051, which converts the main screen itself into a dock. This is a very fundamental change to how the editor is handled, but the benefits that are immediately available are more than worth it.

    As a result of these changes:

  • The main screen editors aren’t tied to specific plugins anymore, instead being regular 
    EditorDock
    s.
  • Main screen docks have their own editor setting for tab style.
  • All main screens can be closed.
  • All main screens can float.
  • The only exception is Game, as custom behavior is currently tightly integrated with 
    WindowWrapper
    .

    • Complimenting the new structure of our editor are new and improved toolbars for our various main screens. Jayden Sipe delivered three fantastic overhauls to the Game, 2D, and 3D panels with GH-118664, GH-121080, and GH-121065 respectively. All three being spearheaded by the same creative vision ensures a uniform style; one which heavily emphasizes usability and clarity in comparison to the prior implementations.

    BeforeAfter
    Game
    2D
    3D

    Mikael Hermansson delivers the ability to drag-toggle visibility in the scene tree editor with GH-118634. Now when toggling the visibility of a given node, the newly toggled state can be applied to any subsequent nodes when dragging the mouse across them.

    It’s never been easier to make a title more accessible to users across multiple languages, thanks to the use of pseudolocalization. Tomasz Chabora, seeking to further expand the utility and awareness of our language hot-swap functionality, enabled pseudolocalization within the editor itself in GH-119443. This simple toggle simulates changes that might take place during localization, allowing any issues that would come from that process to be recognized as early as possible in development.

    Hugo Locurcio’s work in GH-99725 brought a long-desired QOL addition to the inspector: auto-expansion of resources. While most of our inspector items automatically revealed themselves when initialized, resources always existed as an unfortunate blindspot. As demonstrated below, this will no longer be the case!

    DexterFstone made it possible to play a scene from the file system directly in GH-111941. Now any scene can be played from the file system’s context menu alone; no extra steps required!

    Jayden returns with two more editor goodies in GH-119103, aiming to expand the QOL for our 

    FileSystem
    logic. The first of these features is the ability to zoom in/out of the window with a mouse’s scrollwheel. By simply holding 
    Ctrl
    while hovering over a 
    FileSystem
    window, the contents will either grow or shrink upon scrolling the mouse up or down respectively.

    Next up is glob-based searching. Sometimes you want to find a type of file or something with a specific prefix, without necessarily narrowing it down to a specific file. By utilizing glob-based search, now your results can explicitly capture whatever use-case you desire.

    Michael Alexsander keeps the editor train rolling with another highly-requested feature: runtime manipulation of 

    CanvasItem
    s! Thanks to his work in GH-122510, the following functionality is now fully integrated within Godot 4.8 (lifted verbatim from the original PR):

  • Movement, resizing, rotation, scaling, and pivot modification of 
    CanvasItem
    s, together with its own toolbar.
  • Full undo/redo support, unified in the editor’s undo/redo manager.
  • Added the ability to open scenes by double-clicking them in the game. Just like how it’s done in the editor.
  • Improved remote shortcut handling. Which is now funneled into a single debugger message, and triggers the pressed visual on the buttons.
  • Improved mouse cursor updates in the editor. Now they trigger immediately rather than after an action is taken with the mouse again.

    • We’ll end our editor highlights with symbol renaming, an experimental feature brought to us by Tomasz with GH-117949. With this, renaming a symbol will properly propogate that logic across the project, uniformly applying the rename where relevant.

    And more:

  • Add an option to run the project upgrade tool when updating to a new Godot version (GH-119466).
  • Add Clear Project Cache option (GH-120093).
  • Add replace preview to Find in Files (GH-122659).
  • Add toggle button for texture preview metadata overlay (GH-117216).
  • Automatically create default resources in the editor for many objects (GH-88647).
  • Clean and simplify 
    Inspector
    header (GH-117499).
  • Embed the game view in the main editor window as the default (GH-120736).
  • Fix metadata formatting in inspector (GH-108878).
  • List monitor resolutions and refresh rates in editor Copy System Info (GH-122809).
  • Make main screen dock colors more readable (GH-122903).
  • Show doc tooltips in quick settings (GH-121278).
  • Show enum integer values in inspector tooltips (GH-102734).
  • Show inspector warning on deprecated properties (GH-121364).
  • Turn the script method outline into a 
    Tree
    (GH-121534).
  • Use VHS Circle as the default editor color picker shape (GH-110615).

    • GDScript

    Courtesy of Malcolm Anderson in GH-119588, the debugging process for GDScript will become much more streamlined thanks to the direct and immediate information provided by underlined warnings. While you would previously have a line with a warning/error be highlighted if a problem existed, it highlighted the entire line, which both obfuscated the problem and risked multiple issues being hidden if they existed on the same line. With these changes, only the relevant portions of a given line will be underlined. For instance, the following codeblock would’ve previously been highlighted in its entirety:

    And more:

  • Disallow strings as comments (GH-121833).
  • Fix shutdown crash when 
    ScriptInstance
    references its owner (GH-121762).
  • Improve performance for Syntax Highlighting (GH-123320).
  • Make language shutdown more crash resilient (GH-120976).

    • GUI

    Every developer knows the struggle of text container constraints all too well. No matter how reasonable you think your font scale is, or what kind of variable text you believe can make it in, a translation string or player input will inevitably break those bounds. Even if you actively and thoroughly filter all input length at all times, that’s still a lot of code upkeep and boilerplating across different areas of your project to achieve the desired effect.

    Ismail Ivanov is one of many who felt this struggle of our text container constraints, and decided to do something about it. GH-116791 grants 

    Label
    and 
    RichTextLabel
    resize-to-fit functionality, utilizing three newly-added properties: 
    auto_font_size
    , 
    min_font_size
    , and 
    max_font_size
    .

    One of the most common requests we’ve seen for improving 

    Tree
    functionality is the ability to support “sticky items”. That is: the ability for a given line to stick to the top if it represents a foldable region. Koliur Rahman is no stranger to integrating popular editor requests, so it was only a matter of time before they delivered the desired functionality in GH-115697.

    And more:

  • Add 
    format
    property to SpinBox and deprecate 
    prefix
    /
    suffix
    (GH-103998).
  • Add new default algorithm of automatic focus strategy for 
    Control
    nodes (GH-120631).
  • Audio: Add theme sound items and playback on common UI events (GH-111455).
  • TabBar: Add options for tab sizing strategy (GH-113385).
  • Use OS taskbar progress when 
    ProgressDialog
    is shown (GH-121505).

    Many of our existing GUI items have received native touch support in 4.8, warranting a separate input-focused section dedicated to showcasing their new functionality. All of the following featured items come courtesy of Anish Kumar.

item.content:encoded:
一句话：4.8 进入功能冻结，开发资源全转回归修复；官方同时放出可过滤的破坏性变更列表供迁移评估。

要点：

  • beta 1 之后 4.8 完全功能冻结，开发资源全部转向回归修复与 bug-hunting sprint
  • 破坏性变更集中列出并可用 breaks compat 标签过滤合并的 PR，例如移除未文档化的 enter_world 回调、修正 LookAtModifier3D.is_interpolating 的反向返回值
  • 同时提供 Web 编辑器、XR 编辑器与 Android 编辑器供直接试用，方便在真实项目上做回归

为什么值得看：引擎小版本升级的隐性成本几乎都在破坏性变更与回归上；有明确的冻结点与可过滤清单，才好安排分支合并窗口。

中文摘要：Godot 4.8 进入 beta 快照阶段，意味着功能已经完全冻结，开发资源不再投新特性，而是专心做各种回归修复。官方鼓励想帮忙的开发者参加 bug-hunting sprint，读一遍 Bug Triage Introduction，然后进 #bugsquad 与 #bugsquad-sprints 频道。因为已经功能冻结，这一版相对上一轮 dev 7 没有新特性可讲，文章改成对整个 4.8 的统览，并补讲之前没来得及展开的改动。对升级方最有价值的是破坏性变更一节：官方列出合并 PR 中带 breaks compat 标签的条目，例如 3D 里移除了未文档化的 script only enter_world 回调、动画里修正 LookAtModifier3D.is_interpolating() 返回值反了的问题、Core 里在 release 导出中使用本地调试器会直接失败等，都可能在升级时咬人。此外还提供 Web、XR 与 Android 编辑器供直接试用。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：Godot（English）

原文发布：2026-10-15

本期推送：2026-10-25

Dev snapshot: Godot 4.8 beta 1

By: Thaddeus Crews15 October 2026Pre-release

It’s that time of the release cycle once again: the beta snapshot! With this, 4.8 is fully in feature-freeze, and developer resources have shifted exclusively to creating and reviewing various regression fixes.

For those interested in aiding us on our quest to squash any bugs that come up during this time, we once again encourage you to join our bug-hunting sprints. Anyone interested should read the Bug Triage Introduction for more information, and join the 

#bugsquad
and 
#bugsquad-sprints
 channels on our developer RocketChat to participate.

Please consider supporting the project financially, if you are able. Godot is maintained by the efforts of volunteers and a small team of paid contributors. Your donations go towards sponsoring their work and ensuring they can dedicate their undivided attention to the needs of the project.

Jump to the Downloads section, and give it a spin right now, or continue reading to learn more about improvements in this release. You can also try the Web editor, the XR editor, or the Android editor for this release. If you are interested in the latter, please request to join our testing group to get access to pre-release builds.

The cover illustration is fromRita, a puzzle game with platforming elements, featuring a wide variety of word puzzles within a cozy world. You can buy the game on Steam, and follow the developer on Bluesky, YouTube, and itch.io.

Highlights

For those who have been following our development snapshots closely, you may be familiar with a number of the highlights in this post which were already covered in previous articles (4.8 dev 1, 4.8 dev 2, 4.8 dev 3, 4.8 dev 4, 4.8 dev 5, 4.8 dev 6, and 4.8 dev 7).

Because we’re already in feature freeze, there are no new features to cover compared to dev 7. Instead, we’ll focus on a general round-up of what to expect from Godot 4.8 as a whole, as well as expanding on some additions that we didn’t have the chance to highlight in our previous snapshots.

  • Breaking changes
  • 3D
  • Core
  • Documentation
  • Editor
  • GDScript
  • GUI
  • Input
  • Physics
  • Platforms
  • Rendering and shaders
  • Shaders
  • XR

    • Breaking changes

    We try to minimize breaking changes, but sometimes they are necessary in order to fix high-priority issues. Where we do break compatibility, we do our best to make sure that the changes are minimal and require few changes in user projects.

    You can find a list of such issues by filtering the merged PRs in the 4.8 milestone with the 

    breaks compat
    label.

  • 3D: Remove undocumented script only enter_world callbacks (GH-111504).
  • Animation: Fix 
    LookAtModifier3D.is_interpolating()
    value is inverted (GH-121391).
  • Animation: Make Bone Follower classes’ FTI off as default, add warning (GH-119509).
  • Core: Fail when trying to use local debugger in release exports (GH-122213).
  • Editor: Fix corner cases related to scroll hints across the editor (GH-117080).
  • Editor: Remove 
    ScriptServer
    fallbacks from 
    ClassDB
    (GH-123379).
  • Export: Do not serialize export options that do not have the 
    PROPERTY_USAGE_STORAGE
    flag (GH-120721).
  • GDScript: Forbid scripts from inheriting their own inner classes (GH-121171).
  • GUI: Fix duplicated button press event on touch input (GH-120864).
  • GUI: Rework dialog default titles (GH-105550).
  • Input: Ignore joypads on unfocused window by default for new projects (GH-120399).
  • Network: mbedTLS: Update to 4.1.0, PSA Crypto (GH-120725).
  • Platforms: Android: Make 
    OS.alert()
    blocking (GH-120800).
  • Rendering: Add support for ASTC 6x6 and high quality compression profiles (GH-115003).
  • Rendering: Fix sky shader 
    SCREEN_UV
    builtin in Compatibility renderer (GH-121676).
  • XR: OpenXR use proper spatial entity NULL constant (GH-121815).

    • 3D

    QbieShay starts our feature round-up strong with 

    Trail3D
    . Introduced in GH-117107 and built off the foundation by Zi Ye’s Cozy Cube Godot Addons, this native solution enables those seeking stunning visual effects through trails to no longer require deep knowledge of how meshes are drawn, UVs are assigned, or anything of the sort; everything Just Works™.

    While being more of an editor feature, the 3D Viewport override functionality by Michael Alexsander in GH-117569 warrants a highlight in this section. Through the new editor option “Allow Viewport Override” (enabled by default), hovering the mouse over a viewport set to a specific side will cause the currently edited axis to match that side.

    And more:

  • Add octant visualization to 
    GridMap
    (GH-118583).
  • 3D: Re-enable freelook inertia by default in the 3D editor (GH-121478).

    • Core

    Adam Johnston brought us “Fuzzy searching” with GH-98278, enabling search results to return matches similar to the passed query, rather than only returning an exact match. Now with GH-107126, this functionality is finally ready to roll for all users.

    var items := ["Potion of Healing", "Greater Health Potion", "Poison Vial"]
var fuzzy := FuzzySearch.new()

for result in fuzzy.search_all("health potion", items):
	# Prints "Greater Health Potion", "Potion of Healing".
	print(result.target)

    Those using version control will be thrilled to hear that serialization of objects has become much cleaner starting with GH-92102. Robert Wallis ensures that all objects are now formatted such that they won’t cause oversized diffs.

    BeforeAfter

    And more:

  • Core: Add support for metadata in text scenes (GH-121920).
  • Core: Introduce 
    Variant.to()
    as a replacement to implicit conversions from 
    Variant
    (GH-123600).
  • Core: Make it impossible to have more than one main thread, and don’t release unnecessarily (GH-121161).
  • Core: Move property maps from 
    ClassDB
    to 
    GDType
    . Accelerate 
    Object
    property access 1.6x (GH-122596).
  • Core: Simplify 
    GDType
    by storing all properties in a single unified map. Save ~12mb runtime RAM (GH-122751).
  • Core: Speed up removing many child nodes (GH-120942).

    • Documentation

    Cyril Bissey’s efforts in GH-111375 grants our documentation—both in-editor and online—native support for admonitions; That being: the built-in systems many documentation tools provide to highlight crucial information. As time of writing, our documentation tools use simple prefixes like “Note:” or “Warning:” to convey a similar effect, but this method causes critical details to blend in with the rest of the text. So starting now, we’ll begin slowly rolling out admonition replacements for these legacy systems, which will end up looking something like what you see below:

    Dark ModeLight Mode

    Editor

    Ever since the introduction of the 

    EditorDock
    in Godot 4.6, Tomasz Chabora has been on a journey to migrate our existing editor plugins to this new system. The most ambitious migration yet occurred with GH-113051, which converts the main screen itself into a dock. This is a very fundamental change to how the editor is handled, but the benefits that are immediately available are more than worth it.

    As a result of these changes:

  • The main screen editors aren’t tied to specific plugins anymore, instead being regular 
    EditorDock
    s.
  • Main screen docks have their own editor setting for tab style.
  • All main screens can be closed.
  • All main screens can float.
  • The only exception is Game, as custom behavior is currently tightly integrated with 
    WindowWrapper
    .

    • Complimenting the new structure of our editor are new and improved toolbars for our various main screens. Jayden Sipe delivered three fantastic overhauls to the Game, 2D, and 3D panels with GH-118664, GH-121080, and GH-121065 respectively. All three being spearheaded by the same creative vision ensures a uniform style; one which heavily emphasizes usability and clarity in comparison to the prior implementations.

    BeforeAfter
    Game
    2D
    3D

    Mikael Hermansson delivers the ability to drag-toggle visibility in the scene tree editor with GH-118634. Now when toggling the visibility of a given node, the newly toggled state can be applied to any subsequent nodes when dragging the mouse across them.

    It’s never been easier to make a title more accessible to users across multiple languages, thanks to the use of pseudolocalization. Tomasz Chabora, seeking to further expand the utility and awareness of our language hot-swap functionality, enabled pseudolocalization within the editor itself in GH-119443. This simple toggle simulates changes that might take place during localization, allowing any issues that would come from that process to be recognized as early as possible in development.

    Hugo Locurcio’s work in GH-99725 brought a long-desired QOL addition to the inspector: auto-expansion of resources. While most of our inspector items automatically revealed themselves when initialized, resources always existed as an unfortunate blindspot. As demonstrated below, this will no longer be the case!

    DexterFstone made it possible to play a scene from the file system directly in GH-111941. Now any scene can be played from the file system’s context menu alone; no extra steps required!

    Jayden returns with two more editor goodies in GH-119103, aiming to expand the QOL for our 

    FileSystem
    logic. The first of these features is the ability to zoom in/out of the window with a mouse’s scrollwheel. By simply holding 
    Ctrl
    while hovering over a 
    FileSystem
    window, the contents will either grow or shrink upon scrolling the mouse up or down respectively.

    Next up is glob-based searching. Sometimes you want to find a type of file or something with a specific prefix, without necessarily narrowing it down to a specific file. By utilizing glob-based search, now your results can explicitly capture whatever use-case you desire.

    Michael Alexsander keeps the editor train rolling with another highly-requested feature: runtime manipulation of 

    CanvasItem
    s! Thanks to his work in GH-122510, the following functionality is now fully integrated within Godot 4.8 (lifted verbatim from the original PR):

  • Movement, resizing, rotation, scaling, and pivot modification of 
    CanvasItem
    s, together with its own toolbar.
  • Full undo/redo support, unified in the editor’s undo/redo manager.
  • Added the ability to open scenes by double-clicking them in the game. Just like how it’s done in the editor.
  • Improved remote shortcut handling. Which is now funneled into a single debugger message, and triggers the pressed visual on the buttons.
  • Improved mouse cursor updates in the editor. Now they trigger immediately rather than after an action is taken with the mouse again.

    • We’ll end our editor highlights with symbol renaming, an experimental feature brought to us by Tomasz with GH-117949. With this, renaming a symbol will properly propogate that logic across the project, uniformly applying the rename where relevant.

    And more:

  • Add an option to run the project upgrade tool when updating to a new Godot version (GH-119466).
  • Add Clear Project Cache option (GH-120093).
  • Add replace preview to Find in Files (GH-122659).
  • Add toggle button for texture preview metadata overlay (GH-117216).
  • Automatically create default resources in the editor for many objects (GH-88647).
  • Clean and simplify 
    Inspector
    header (GH-117499).
  • Embed the game view in the main editor window as the default (GH-120736).
  • Fix metadata formatting in inspector (GH-108878).
  • List monitor resolutions and refresh rates in editor Copy System Info (GH-122809).
  • Make main screen dock colors more readable (GH-122903).
  • Show doc tooltips in quick settings (GH-121278).
  • Show enum integer values in inspector tooltips (GH-102734).
  • Show inspector warning on deprecated properties (GH-121364).
  • Turn the script method outline into a 
    Tree
    (GH-121534).
  • Use VHS Circle as the default editor color picker shape (GH-110615).

    • GDScript

    Courtesy of Malcolm Anderson in GH-119588, the debugging process for GDScript will become much more streamlined thanks to the direct and immediate information provided by underlined warnings. While you would previously have a line with a warning/error be highlighted if a problem existed, it highlighted the entire line, which both obfuscated the problem and risked multiple issues being hidden if they existed on the same line. With these changes, only the relevant portions of a given line will be underlined. For instance, the following codeblock would’ve previously been highlighted in its entirety:

    And more:

  • Disallow strings as comments (GH-121833).
  • Fix shutdown crash when 
    ScriptInstance
    references its owner (GH-121762).
  • Improve performance for Syntax Highlighting (GH-123320).
  • Make language shutdown more crash resilient (GH-120976).

    • GUI

    Every developer knows the struggle of text container constraints all too well. No matter how reasonable you think your font scale is, or what kind of variable text you believe can make it in, a translation string or player input will inevitably break those bounds. Even if you actively and thoroughly filter all input length at all times, that’s still a lot of code upkeep and boilerplating across different areas of your project to achieve the desired effect.

    Ismail Ivanov is one of many who felt this struggle of our text container constraints, and decided to do something about it. GH-116791 grants 

    Label
    and 
    RichTextLabel
    resize-to-fit functionality, utilizing three newly-added properties: 
    auto_font_size
    , 
    min_font_size
    , and 
    max_font_size
    .

    One of the most common requests we’ve seen for improving 

    Tree
    functionality is the ability to support “sticky items”. That is: the ability for a given line to stick to the top if it represents a foldable region. Koliur Rahman is no stranger to integrating popular editor requests, so it was only a matter of time before they delivered the desired functionality in GH-115697.

    And more:

  • Add 
    format
    property to SpinBox and deprecate 
    prefix
    /
    suffix
    (GH-103998).
  • Add new default algorithm of automatic focus strategy for 
    Control
    nodes (GH-120631).
  • Audio: Add theme sound items and playback on common UI events (GH-111455).
  • TabBar: Add options for tab sizing strategy (GH-113385).
  • Use OS taskbar progress when 
    ProgressDialog
    is shown (GH-121505).

    • Input

    Many of our existing GUI items have received native touch support in 4.8, warranting a separate input-focused section dedicated to showcasing their new functionality. All of the following featured items come courtesy of Anish Kumar.

    Starting with GH-119706’s two-for-one package deal, both 

    TextEdit
    and 
    CodeEdit

item.title: 仿真数据不落盘直接进 UE5：改一个 ANARI-USD 设备，把场景图流给引擎渲染 ｜ Bridging In-Situ Visualization to Game Engines: From ParaView Catalyst via ANARI to Unreal Engine
item.description:
一句话：在 ANARI 层截住 USD 场景图，经 ZeroMQ 流进 UE5 插件，数千万粒子点云可边到边渲染。

要点：

  • 修改的 ANARI-USD 设备在 ANARI 层于内存中捕获 USD 场景图，通过内嵌 ZeroMQ broker 传给可视化客户端
  • JuSync 中间件与配套 UE5 插件边收边解析几何，运行时直接路由到引擎渲染组件，收到即可自由移动相机
  • 在 Jülich 的 JURECA-DC 超算上以自由电子激光仿真的数千万粒子点云演示；设计与仿真解耦，客户端可随时接入或断开

为什么值得看：HPC 仿真的后处理瓶颈往往在写盘与搬运；用引擎无关的 USD 当交换格式、把引擎当渲染前端，是让引擎进入科学可视化的可行接口设计。

中文摘要：在机（in-situ）高性能计算仿真会产生海量数据，但这些数据很难流进游戏引擎做交互式可视化。这篇论文给出了一条不落盘的管线：仿真数据经 ParaView 的 ANARI 渲染接口，由一个改造过的 ANARI-USD 设备在 ANARI 层把 USD 场景图在内存里捕获下来，再通过内嵌的 ZeroMQ broker 把这份引擎无关的 USD 数据流给可视化客户端；客户端侧是 JuSync 中间件加一个 Unreal Engine 5 插件，边接收边解析几何，运行时直接路由进引擎渲染组件，数据一到就能自由移动相机。因为设计上把仿真执行与可视化负载解耦，客户端任何时候接入或断开都不影响仿真本身。作者在 Forschungszentrum Jülich 的 JURECA-DC 超算上，用自由电子激光仿真的数千万粒子点云演示了整条链路。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：arXiv·引擎架构（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-25

Bridging In-Situ Visualization to Game Engines : From ParaView Catalyst via ANARI to Unreal Engine

Abstract

In-situ high-performance computing (HPC) simulations produce massive datasets that remain difficult to stream into game engines for interactive visualization. We present an in-situ, disk-free pipeline that couples simulation data to Unreal Engine 5 through ParaView’s ANARI rendering API. A modified ANARI-USD device captures Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graphs in memory at the ANARI layer and streams the engine-agnostic USD format through an embedded ZeroMQ broker to visualization clients, where JuSync, middleware with a companion Unreal Engine 5 plugin, parses the geometry as it arrives and routes it to engine rendering components at runtime, producing scenes that are camera-navigable once received. The decoupled design keeps simulation execution independent of visualization load, and clients may connect or disconnect at any time. The pipeline is demonstrated on the JURECA-DC supercomputer at Forschungszentrum Jülich, streaming Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation data with point clouds of tens of millions of particles.

Index Terms:

In-Situ, ANARI, Scientific visualization, Unreal Engine, Real-time rendering, HPC, Streaming

I Introduction

ParaView, paired with its Catalyst framework, is one of the standard tools for in-situ analysis on HPC clusters, keeping data in memory without writing to disk. ParaView targets scientific analysis, whereas interactive presentation is the domain of a complementary tool — a modern game engine. Rendering simulation data inside realistic, contextually accurate environments — for example, a reconstructed laboratory facility — has the potential to increase scientific insight by letting researchers explore their results as they would look in the real world. Game engines such as Unreal Engine 5 are built for exactly these capabilities: immersive virtual reality (VR) navigation, realistic lighting, custom annotations, and multi-user collaboration. However, Unreal Engine’s built-in USD support and Datasmith [1] import data from files on disk, not from live streaming in memory.

This work bridges that gap by streaming USD scene graphs directly from ParaView to visualization clients, disk-free, yielding scenes that are interactable on the client once the payload is received. Because JuSync operates at the USD level, the streamed data could in principle feed rendering engines other than Unreal Engine, though only the Unreal Engine 5 client is demonstrated in this work.

As shown in Figure 1, the pipeline moves data from the simulation on the HPC cluster through ParaView and a memory-only ANARI-USD device, across the network via ZeroMQ, and into the JuSync middleware before finally rendering in Unreal Engine. The dashed line separates the cluster-side processing from the client-side visualization.

Following the pipeline in Figure 1, three gaps appear along the data path. First, on the simulation side, the simulation produces particle data that ParaView processes in-situ and ANARI-USD converts into USD scene graphs in memory. However, those graphs stay on the cluster and are not sent over a network. Second, on the client side, even if the USD payload is streamable, Unreal Engine cannot consume it directly at runtime. The scene graph must be parsed, converted to triangulated geometry, and routed to engine-specific rendering components for which no standard tool exists. Finally, the transport must keep the simulation running independently of network conditions or client speed.

These challenges are addressed with two components, illustrated in Figure 1. The ANARI-USD device is extended with a memory tracking layer and an embedded ZeroMQ transport that streams USD scene graphs directly from RAM; the broker is designed to support multiple visualization clients. JuSync [2] is presented as a standalone C++ middleware that receives the streamed USD over ZeroMQ and parses it into runtime geometry. Together, these form a complete disk-free path from ParaView to Unreal Engine. The additions are confined to a modified ANARI-USD device and the JuSync client plugin; the simulation, ParaView, and the Unreal Engine core itself require no code changes.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A memory-only ANARI-USD serialization path that streams standardized USD scene graphs from ParaView over ZeroMQ, enabling a disk-free path to a game engine that is engine-agnostic at the USD boundary.

  • •

    JuSync, an engine-agnostic C++ middleware with a companion UE5 plugin, bridging the gap between streamed USD scene graphs and runtime Unreal Engine geometry.

    • For results and evaluation:

  • •

    An end-to-end evaluation of the pipeline on the JURECA-DC supercomputer using a Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation with point clouds of tens of millions of particles. The pipeline itself is not limited to FEL and works with any ParaView-compatible input.

    • II State of the Art

    II-AParaView-to-External-Renderer Pipelines

    Several recent pipelines share the goal of bridging ParaView’s scientific data processing with a game engine. These pipelines face a common set of challenges: they must transfer scene data produced by ParaView’s visualization pipeline to a rendering environment that operates on a different runtime, often on a different machine, without introducing prohibitive latency.

    InsitUE [3] addresses this with a Catalyst2-compatible hybrid workflow that streams simulation results directly into Unreal Engine. It supports both in-situ and in-transit operation, allows bidirectional steering of visualization parameters, and uses a custom TCP/UDP socket communication protocol with TCP for the control plane and UDP for the data plane. InsitUE couples a Catalyst2/Conduit path to a pair of components — its Catalyst implementation and its Unreal plugin — and additionally offers bidirectional simulation steering, which we do not provide. The two systems differ chiefly in the interchange format: InsitUE transfers geometry as Conduit mesh blueprints, whereas our pipeline emits USD scene graphs in memory at the ANARI layer, a format that existing USD-capable renderers can ingest. ZeroMQ then delivers these graphs to a client that consumes USD alone, though only the Unreal Engine client is demonstrated here. The sort-last in-transit approach by Nealey et al. [4] uses SENSEI [5] to move data to staging nodes, where ParaView Catalyst extracts PLY mesh geometry that is forwarded to Unreal Engine over WebSockets, demonstrating near-real-time visualization of distributed simulation data. Kitware has demonstrated VTK rendering within Unity [6] using a direct VTK-to-Unity bridge. A ParaView-to-Unity VR pipeline has been developed for cosmological particle data, extracting VTK geometry from ParaView and importing it into Unity for immersive cluster analysis [7]. Outside the game-engine domain, ParaView has been used with Blender to generate augmented reality (AR) models from finite element simulation data [8], where ParaView extracts surface geometry and Blender handles rendering and export. The NVIDIA Omniverse ParaView Connector [9] takes a different approach: it uses the ANARI-USD device to write USD stages to shared storage, which Omniverse then watches and ingests, allowing Omniverse’s rendering engine to access ParaView-generated scenes without tight coupling.

    Across these pipelines, scene data reaches the engine in a representation tied to the data path—VTK or Conduit geometry mapped by a dedicated bridge, PLY meshes over WebSockets, or USD stages written to shared storage—each a reasonable fit for its own goal. We instead standardize the interchange on USD captured in memory at ParaView’s ANARI layer, removing the shared-filesystem round-trip and confining engine-specific work to a thin client plugin. We chose USD for practical, not superiority, reasons: it describes a full scene (hierarchy, transforms, materials, and metadata) rather than geometry alone; it is what the ANARI-USD device already emits, so no producer-side conversion is needed; and its open-source support across renderers underpins the engine-agnostic boundary. Beyond reaching a game engine, a standard scene format also keeps the payload inspectable and reusable, which aids debugging and reproducibility. Decoupling producers from consumers is the design aim elaborated in Section IV. We do not claim to remove every constraint of the surveyed systems: like them, we demonstrate a single renderer (Unreal Engine); unlike InsitUE, we provide no simulation steering; and in our evaluation, forwarding latency currently dominates end-to-end time (Section V).

    II-BANARI as a Rendering Abstraction

    The Khronos ANARI specification [10] defines a device-based rendering abstraction that decouples applications from specific rendering backends such as OSPRay and NVIDIA VisRTX. Applications issue rendering commands through the ANARI API, and any conformant backend device translates them into its native rendering operations. This design allows visualization applications like ParaView to switch between external rendering backends without code changes.

    The ANARI-USD device (NVIDIA’s AnariUsdDevice) [9] can serve as such an external “rendering” backend. Even though it does not render any image, it produces USD scene descriptions from the ANARI rendering commands. It receives ANARI scene graphs from ParaView’s rendering pipeline and writes the resulting USD stages to shared storage, where applications such as NVIDIA Omniverse can ingest them for interactive visualization. The device handles geometry conversion, material assignment, and scene graph construction automatically, making the ParaView-to-USD path transparent to the user.

    This work builds on the same ANARI-USD device but replaces the disk-based write path with memory-only serialization and ZeroMQ streaming. The ANARI scene graph is captured from an in-memory serialization path, stored in a per-rank memory buffer (one buffer per MPI process), and streamed over the network. This enables scene transfer to external rendering engines without shared filesystem access, while retaining all the benefits of the ANARI abstraction layer.

    II-CIn-Situ Data Movement

    Moving simulation data to visualization consumers with minimal overhead is a core challenge in in-situ workflows. ParaView Catalyst Live [11] provides real-time streaming of in-memory VTK data to a live ParaView GUI connection, enabling interactive exploration during simulation execution. Catalyst-ADIOS2 [12] integrates ADIOS2 [13] with ParaView Catalyst for in-transit streaming, supporting data reduction and transfer over high-speed interconnects. It uses ADIOS2’s staging engines to move data between simulation and visualization nodes without writing intermediate files. Ascent [14] takes a flyweight approach, providing a lightweight in-situ library that minimizes the simulation-side integration burden while supporting multi-stage analysis pipelines. Inshimtu [15] provides a lightweight shim between simulation codes and ParaView, adapting simulation data structures for visualization consumption without requiring the simulation to link against ParaView’s libraries. It handles data format conversion and memory management, allowing ParaView to connect to simulations that would otherwise require custom instrumentation. Serviz [16] proposes a shared in-situ visualization service that runs alongside the simulation and serves visualization data to multiple consumers on demand. By decoupling producers from consumers, Serviz allows different visualization tools to connect to the same simulation independently.

    This project uses ParaView Catalyst for data movement from the simulation to the ParaView side. On the client side of the pipeline presented here, JuSync receives streamed USD payloads from a modified ANARI-USD device, parses them with TinyUSDZ, and routes the resulting geometry to rendering components, including Epic’s LiDAR Point Cloud plugin [17] and the RealtimeMesh plugin [18], which support runtime updates from streaming data sources.

    III Free Electron Laser Undulator Simulation

    As the in-situ data source for our pipeline, we use a Free Electron Laser (FEL) undulator simulation originally developed as a mini-application in the IPPL (Independent Parallel Particle Layer) framework [19, 20]. IPPL is a massively parallel high-performance computing library providing parallel data structures and operator primitives for performance-portable particle-mesh methods, with primary applications in beam/plasma physics and cosmology. The FEL simulation models the propagation of an electron beam through a periodic undulator magnet array, generating coherent X-ray radiation as beam particles oscillate and interact with their self-consistent electromagnetic fields. The code supports configurable particle and mesh resolutions, producing datasets with particle positions and velocity vectors for up to billions of particles, as well as electromagnetic field data on uniform refined grids. In the near future, this will allow simulations to abandon the approximate modelling via macroparticles and instead simulate real electrons. In a recent update, IPPL was instrumented with the Catalyst API to support direct in-situ export of its core data structures [21] enabling any IPPL-based simulation to serve as a data source for our visualization pipeline with minimal integration effort.

    The FEL simulation was selected as the demonstration case because it represents a scientifically significant and computationally challenging regime, rooted in the specific nature of its real-world experimental counterpart. There is considerable interest in the particle accelerator community in better understanding electron beam dynamics, in particular the coupled processes of intrabeam scattering and microbunching. Current standard simulation codes encounter difficulties in capturing these phenomena at the accuracy required [22]: at the Swiss Free Electron Laser, intrabeam scattering has been observed to degrade beam quality, suppressing microbunch formation and reducing achievable photon beam brightness. This effect was not predicted by prior simulations and motivates the need for advanced simulation models and analysis, capable of studying these processes in finer detail. Accurately modeling Coulomb collisions between electrons, which lie at the root of intrabeam scattering, requires abandoning the macroparticle approximation [23] in favour of tracking real electrons. At the scale of a realistic accelerator, this pushes the total particle count to order O(10⁹), producing datasets too large to reasonably write and store to disk. This makes the FEL simulation a prime example of a high-performance scientific code unsuited to rely on traditional post-processing workflows and instead benefitting directly from modern in-situ analysis — enabling detailed 3D visualization that captures in full the phenomena advanced models are designed to resolve.

    The FEL undulator simulation is therefore integrated into the pipeline via the IPPL–Catalyst interface, coupling the simulation directly to ParaView without intermediate file I/O. At each user-defined timestep, particle positions, velocity vectors, and electromagnetic field data are passed in-situ to ParaView [24] through Catalyst, which constructs visual representations and feeds the resulting scene graph to the modified ANARI-USD device.

    IV Pipeline Architecture

    IV-ASimulation Layer

    The pipeline works with any ParaView-compatible input. This work demonstrates it using the FEL simulation described in Section III, which produces particle positions and velocity vectors that are made available to ParaView through an in-situ workflow using ParaView Catalyst. The FEL simulation can push millions of particles per timestep, limited only by available resources.

    The simulation and ParaView run concurrently on dedicated node pools, with the simulation generating particle data while ParaView constructs and updates the visualization pipeline and the modified ANARI-USD device produces in-memory USD stages (deployment, as shown in Figure 2). The specific node counts and rank layout used for evaluation are given in Section V.

    IV-BParaView and ANARI Integration

    ParaView performs visualization-oriented data processing. In the evaluation setup, the FEL particle data is processed as point clouds and rendered directly as points; ParaView’s Glyph filter would convert particle positions into sphere glyphs only if triangulated mesh geometry were required, a mode not exercised in this evaluation. To decouple visualization construction from the rendering backend, ParaView interfaces with ANARI, which provides a device-based rendering abstraction that allows different rendering devices to be used, such as VisRTX, OSPRay, or ANARI-USD. The ANARI-USD device implements this interface by producing USD scene descriptions from ANARI rendering commands rather than generating rasterized images. Importantly, ParaView itself remains unchanged; all pipeline-specific modifications are confined to the ANARI-USD device.

    IV-CUSD Memory Streaming

    The ANARI-USD device for ParaView supports MPI where each rank produces USD scene graphs independently. By default, each committed stage is serialized to disk, adding filesystem I/O to the per-timestep path at multi-node scale. The modification introduces a tracking layer on the device’s existing in-memory serialization path: each committed USD stage is captured into a per-rank memory store as a serialized buffer, with an XXH3-128 hash computed on each payload for fast change detection. The disk write step is bypassed entirely.

    On top of this, a ZeroMQ transport layer streams the in-memory buffers across the interconnect to visualization clients (protocol summarized in Figure 3). On each worker rank, a DEALER socket connects to a broker on rank 0. The broker runs two ROUTER sockets: one for worker connections and one for client connections. The broker aggregates file metadata from all workers into a unified reference table, while the actual USD payload data remains distributed in the per-rank memory stores. When a client requests a file, the broker routes the request to the appropriate worker rank, which streams the data back through the broker in configurable chunks (default 4 MB). Chunking keeps per-transfer memory bounded and predictable on the client while adding negligible framing overhead, and the granular flow lets parsing and streaming overlap. The chunk size is set primarily as a fault-tolerance granularity: because the link crosses an external SSH tunnel, a drop mid-transfer costs at most the remainder of the in-flight dataset, and a reconnected client resumes from the broker’s dataset table with hash-based dedup skipping datasets already received.

    This memory-only approach removes any dependence on the parallel filesystem from the data path: ANARI rendering commands are converted by the USD bridge and serialized into per-rank memory stores, and shared files are relayed through the broker to clients without ever touching disk. The broker itself holds only the aggregated file list; the USD payload data remains distributed in the per-rank memory stores until a client pulls it.

    IV-DJuSync Middleware

    JuSync [2] is a standalone C++ middleware that receives USD payloads from the modified ANARI-USD device via ZeroMQ streaming (data flow in Figure 4). Each payload is parsed with TinyUSDZ [25] for lightweight, dependency-free USD parsing. The geometry module extracts mesh primitives into an internal representation, converting them into engine-ready buffers with required coordinate transforms (e.g., right-handed to left-handed system conversion) and triangulation. Texture data are decoded via the STB [26] library, with gradients extracted for transfer-function mapping. The middleware exposes a C API intended for use by other rendering engines, with background threads handling parse operations asynchronously.

    IV-EDecoupled Architecture

    The modifications are confined to the ANARI-USD device (tracking layer and ZeroMQ streaming) and the JuSync middleware; the simulation, ParaView, and Unreal Engine themselves require no code changes. Deployment nevertheless requires building and linking the modified ANARI-USD device, running the ZeroMQ broker, and installing the JuSync UE5 plugin (Appendix), rather than the stock ParaView/Unreal stack alone. Because JuSync sits at the USD level, any simulation that feeds into ParaView can be streamed to Unreal Engine without code modifications to the simulation or ParaView. The architecture provides decoupling along four independent axes. (i) Producer/consumer decoupling: the simulation and ParaView continue running regardless of whether a client is connected, and clients can join or leave at any time. (ii) HPC/client decoupling: the Unreal instance requires only TinyUSDZ for lightweight USD parsing rather than the full OpenUSD stack or ParaView’s binary dependencies. (iii) Simulation/rendering decoupling: ParaView handles scientific data processing and visualization construction, while Unreal Engine handles real-time rendering and interaction. (iv) Simulation/visualization decoupling: the asynchronous ZeroMQ transport is designed so that USD payload transmission does not block the simulation, because the broker buffers messages independently of client timing.

    IV-FUnreal Engine Plugin Integration

    A companion UE5 runtime plugin [2] incorporates the JuSync middleware. On startup, it initializes the C middleware library, connects to the ZeroMQ broker, and receives USD payloads through the C API. Received data are dispatched to Unreal Engine’s rendering components on the game thread.

    Point cloud data from particle simulations are routed through Epic’s LiDAR Point Cloud plugin [17], which provides dynamic level-of-detail (LOD) scaling, global point budget control, and runtime insertion capabilities for large-scale particle datasets. Mesh data are streamed into URealtimeMeshComponent for interactive triangulated geometry. Both rendering paths update at runtime without intermediate file I/O. DaVinCo [27], a collaborative multi-user VR/desktop visualization application developed by Forschungszentrum Jülich, provides the rendering environment driven by this plugin.

    V Results and Evaluation

    V-ASetup

    Evaluation was conducted on the JURECA-DC system at Forschungszentrum Jülich (dc-cpu partition). A 60-node allocation exercised the full pipeline at a representative multi-node HPC configuration, within the dc-cpu partition’s practical limits. 52 nodes ran the FEL simulation and eight ran pvserver for ParaView processing (64 MPI worker ranks). The 52/8 split is a chosen trade-off rather than a tight quota: more simulation nodes shorten the FEL particle calculation, while more pvserver nodes give ParaView more workers for serializing and streaming USD, smoothing delivery to the client; we made no attempt to tune for optimal utilization, as the goal was multi-node scale rather than peak throughput. The client machine, equipped with an Intel Core i9-14700HX and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090, ran Unreal Engine and connected via SSH tunnel (-L 5556:127.0.0.1:5556) to the ZeroMQ broker on MPI rank 0. Measurements focus on the client-side arrival path: each dataset size was streamed through the full pipeline and timed across the dataset-listing, receive, and parse stages, with transfer throughput and host memory usage recorded alongside. Cluster-side ANARI-USD serialization and per-frame rendering times were not captured and are not reported. Unless stated otherwise, reported times refer to the client-side arrival path over the external SSH-tunnel link, where network delivery dominates the wall-clock budget. The pipeline operates independently of whether the simulation on the HPC runs on CPU or GPU: it consumes whatever data ParaView produces in-situ, and the same path applies to any simulation feeding into ParaView via Catalyst, regardless of compute backend. The pipeline was also exercised on standard ParaView example datasets (mesh and point-cloud sources); those runs are not reported here, as the evaluation focuses on the production FEL use case.

    V-BVisualization Results

    Figure 5 shows the full view of the FEL particle beam as rendered in ParaView from the raw point cloud, colored by velocity magnitude. The electron beam is initialized with a continuous particle distribution along all axes. As the beam traverses the undulator magnet array, the onset of microbunching becomes visible: particles self-organize into separated, periodically spaced microbunches along the direction of propagation, as revealed in the zoomed-in view in Figure 6. Figure 7 shows the same data streamed through the pipeline and rendered in Unreal Engine via DaVinCo as a scene that is camera-navigable once received, using Epic’s LiDAR Point Cloud plugin for point-based rendering. Figure 8 provides a close-up of the streamed point cloud, demonstrating interactive examination of the microbunching structure with free camera navigation. Finally, Figure 9 shows an alternate level in Unreal Engine illustrating the rendering quality a game engine offers, with physically-based reflections and environment lighting; it is included to motivate the game-engine presentation environment rather than to claim a faithful reconstruction of a facility.

    V-CThroughput and Point Scaling

    We measured the full pipeline across six dataset sizes ranging from 2 million to 80 million points on the fixed 60-node deployment of Section V (52 simulation / 8 pvserver nodes), varying only the payload size. Table I reports the per-run stage times across these sizes, and Figure 10 shows the time to stream, parse, and list payloads as a function of point count for this fixed configuration. The total serialized USD payload grows from 0.12 GB (2 million points) to 4.77 GB (80 million points), and the mean per-worker-rank share grows from 1.8 MB to 74.6 MB (Table II). The number of 4 MB transfer chunks sent to the client stays nearly flat (2121 to 2202) because, across this range, every per-rank USD dataset is below the 4 MB chunk size and is sent as a single chunk; the count therefore mirrors the point-cloud actor count, which is set by scene structure and is essentially constant across the range (2088–2147). Within this range, the 40× growth in point count is absorbed as larger per-chunk size rather than more chunks. This flatness is range-specific, not structural: at the measured serialization density (≈60 MB per million points), per-rank datasets reach the 4 MB boundary near 150–160 M total points, beyond which oversized datasets are split into additional chunks and the count grows with total payload. The chunk size itself is configurable. All simulation points are forwarded, with no subset.

    Two factors dominate end-to-end time. First, the transit leg dominates the wall-clock budget: receive occupies the large majority of total time, and parse runs concurrently with it. Parsing operates at chunk granularity as data flows in rather than after the whole payload is assembled, which is why the reported parse time tracks receive so closely instead of exceeding it: parsing keeps pace with streaming and terminates a moment after the final chunk is processed. Second, receive and parse time scale nearly linearly with point count, paralleling the linear-scaling reference in Figure 10. The transit leg is request-based: throughput stays within a narrow 5.9–16.1 MB/s band across all sizes rather than tracking size, so the total time is governed by data volume and the per-chunk transit path. The band itself is bound by the round-trip latency of each 4 MB chunk relayed through the broker and SSH tunnel, not by the client’s nominal line rate: the peak observed is well under 1% of the workstation’s 2 Gbit/s link. Throughput rises modestly with size as larger payloads keep more chunks in flight.

    The dataset-listing stage is a fixed overhead: it stays at ≈15.2 s in every run regardless of size (the flat series in Figure 10). This is the broker’s metadata round-trip to rank 0: JuSync must enumerate the per-worker dataset tables (∼ 2,700 dataset handles in a full run) before requesting payloads, and this enumeration does not scale with payload size. Spawn time, by contrast, reflects point-cloud actor creation from the streamed data; Table I reports its nominal scaling, growing from roughly 6.6 s at 2 million points toward ≈22 s at 80 million points. In this evaluation, no meshes or triangles are created; only point clouds are streamed.

    V-DMemory Profile

    Host memory (RAM) usage rises with data volume, from 26.5 GB at 2 million points to 30.4 GB at 80 million points, and correlates at 0.79 with point count. Because the pipeline stores serialized USD stages in per-rank memory stores on the HPC side and accumulates parsed geometry on the client, the host footprint grows roughly with the streamed data volume. The correlation is below the near-perfect values seen for time because the baseline includes the fixed Unreal Engine runtime footprint, which dilutes the data-driven portion.

    The modest absolute growth over a 40× range in point count (≈ 4 GB for the client side) shows that the streamed representation remains compact relative to the point count, consistent with the fixed-cost memory model of the two application hosts. GPU memory rose with the point count over the 2–10 million range (≈2.8 GB at 2 million to ≈4.7 GB at 10 million) and stayed well within the RTX 5090’s 32 GB budget; measurements at larger sizes were not reliable and are therefore omitted. Memory was not the binding constraint: the dominant resource at large scale is the transit time established above, and the runtime cost of interactivity is GPU processing of the growing point cloud, not memory pressure.

    V-ELimitations

    Several aspects of the evaluation bound the current claims and motivate the future work below.

    Transit-bound latency. The 5.9–16.1 MB/s throughput band is measured over the SSH-tunnel between the client Unreal instance and the cluster; it reflects the per-4 MB-chunk request/response latency relayed through the broker, not the raw link or an intrinsic pipeline limit. Client-side arrival time is dominated by this serialized chunk path. Interactivity is asserted qualitatively (payloads are renderable and camera-navigable once received).

    Metadata round-trip. The ≈15.2 s dataset-listing stage does not scale with payload size. It reflects the broker enumerating ∼ 2,700 per-worker dataset handles at rank 0 before payload transfer, so it becomes the dominant share of end-to-end time for small payloads. The gap between datasets requested and datasets transferred in a run is not data loss: each USD dataset carries an XXH3-128 fingerprint, and datasets whose hash is unchanged from the previous timestep are skipped by the client rather than retransmitted (an intentional diff-aware deduplication). Across sizes this skipped roughly 19–20% of the ≈ 2,700 notified datasets, and every dataset that was actually transferred completed with 100% success and zero errors.

    Spawn cost reflects rebuilds, not raw sizing. The Spawn column in Table I reports the nominal scaling of Unreal Engine’s point-cloud actor creation rather than a raw per-size measurement. Raw spawn timing was non-monotonic because it follows the diff-aware deduplication: when only a few datasets change, the client updates an existing LiDAR point-cloud actor in place (cheap); when many actors must be rebuilt from new data, spawn cost rises. The reported Spawn values therefore reflect the intended Unreal actor-creation behavior at scale and should not be read as exact per-run measurements.

    GPU memory logging. VRAM was only reliably captured on the 2–10 million subset; larger runs produced inconsistent GPU-memory readings and are excluded. Only a bound (well within the RTX 5090’s 32 GB) is claimed for GPU memory.

    No server-side or frame-time benchmark. The cost of ANARI-USD serialization on the cluster and per-frame rendering time on the client were not instrumented; the evaluation characterizes the client arrival path (dataset-listing, receive, parse) and memory use, and no head-to-head comparison against the default disk-writing path is reported. The client and broker logs do record the total payload, per-rank byte share, and chunk counts, which are reported in Table II.

    Chunk count assumes a uniform split. The Chunks column equals the number of transferred datasets only because every per-rank USD dataset is below the 4 MB chunk size, which holds for the uniform point-cloud split used here (mean per-dataset size at most ≈2.12 MB at 80 M points). Per-run logs record dataset counts but not the maximum single-dataset size, so a non-uniform split containing a dataset larger than 4 MB would add chunks; this is not observed for the reported data. The near-constant count is an artifact of the evaluated range: per-rank datasets cross the 4 MB boundary near 150–160 M total points, after which the count scales in step with payload; no dataset or payload size is structurally capped by the chunking scheme.

    VI Conclusion

    This paper presented and evaluated an in-situ streaming pipeline that couples ParaView-based scientific processing to Unreal Engine through ANARI, USD, and ZeroMQ, exercised on a multi-node HPC deployment. By serializing USD stages directly into per-rank memory and streaming them over the ZeroMQ broker, the memory-only ANARI-USD device removes filesystem I/O from the per-timestep path, and JuSync parses the streamed geometry asynchronously and routes it to Unreal Engine’s LiDAR Point Cloud plugin. Splitting producers from consumers lets clients connect or disconnect at any time without disturbing the simulation. Because the streamed payloads are expressed as USD, the path is in principle open to rendering targets beyond Unreal Engine, though only the Unreal client is demonstrated here.

    End-to-end evaluation on the 60-node JURECA-DC allocation: a live FEL in-situ simulation at 2–80 million particles was delivered over a disk-free path from the cluster to an Unreal Engine client, with near-linear growth in receive and parse time across the transit leg, sustained throughput in a 5.9–16.1 MB/s band, and a small, bounded host memory footprint on the RTX 5090 client. Payloads are interactable on the client once received, though arrival latency is set by the external transit link rather than by pipeline processing. The memory-only design removes the parallel filesystem from the data path, so HPC-side processing is not the scaling limit; end-to-end latency is instead governed by the external transit leg, identified as the target of future work (Section VII).

    VII Future Work

    Several directions would extend the capabilities and scalability of the current pipeline:

  • •

    USD time-sampled stages—persistent stages with time-sampled attributes reduce retransmission overhead versus discrete full payloads per timestep.

  • •

    Delta-based updates—transmit only changed geometry attributes rather than full USD payloads, improving bandwidth efficiency when timestep-to-timestep changes are small.

  • •

    Volume processing—support for USD volume data in JuSync (currently mesh and point clouds only).

  • •

    Additional rendering engines—the JuSync C API can target other USD-capable tools beyond Unreal Engine 5, such as NVIDIA Omniverse, three.js, or custom viewers.

  • •

    Digital twin for OPALX—apply the pipeline to a live in-situ digital twin of the particle accelerators at PSI using OPALX [28]. Its multi-resolution simulations stream beam and field data into a contextual Unreal replica for operational monitoring and interactive steering.

  • •

    Cross-platform evaluation—validate the pipeline on additional HPC systems and interconnect technologies beyond JURECA-DC.

  • •

    Single-GPU and multi-GPU rendering boundaries—characterize where Unreal Engine on the single RTX 5090 client reaches its limits as the streamed point-cloud budget grows, and outline multi-GPU clients for the larger data sets motivating this work.

  • •

    Forwarding-path throughput—the measured 5.9–16.1 MB/s band is bound by the per-chunk relay over the SSH tunnel; push-based transfer, compression, a direct interconnect, or an in-cluster client would lift this ceiling. This is the precondition for the O(10⁹)-particle regime.

  • •

    Progressive / LOD streaming—exploit the LiDAR Point Cloud plugin’s dynamic level-of-detail to render a coarse representation while payloads arrive, providing early interactivity instead of waiting for the full transfer.

  • •

    Simulation steering and multi-user collaboration—steering a running simulation by adjusting parameters between payloads, and multi-user collaborative visualization over the broker’s multiple simultaneous connections. The DaVinCo viewer [27] already supports a collaboration model, not yet exercised with this pipeline.

    • （参考文献见原文。）

    Acknowledgments

    We gratefully acknowledge the Bundesministerium für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt (BMFTR) and the Ministerium für Kultur und Wissenschaft des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen (MWK-NRW) for funding this work in the project InHPC-DE through the Gauss Centre for Supercomputing e.V. Computing resources were provided by the Jülich Supercomputing Centre. S.A.T.K. is funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation. The authors disclose that a generative AI language tool assisted with language editing of this manuscript; all scientific content, measurements, and claims are solely the authors’ work.

    Reproducibility Appendix

    The following notes provide sufficient information to reproduce the pipeline on a comparable setup.

  • (a)

    Repositories:

  • •

    JUSYNC: https://github.com/FZJ-JSC/jusync (middleware with C API and UE5 plugin).

  • •

    ANARI-USD (ZMQ-enabled): https://github.com/staticx-g7/ANARI-USD (ANARI-USD with the memory-only serialization and embedded ZeroMQ transport used here).

  • (b)

    Build the ANARI-USD device: Build ParaView against the ANARI SDK, then build the ANARI-USD device from the repository above; point ParaView’s ANARI backend at it so the USD renderer is available.

  • (c)

    Launch ParaView with the ANARI-USD device: Start pvserver with MPI as needed and configure the ANARI/USD environment before launching:

    ⬇exportANARI_LIBRARY=’usd’exportANARI_USD_SERIALIZE_LOCATION=$SCRATCH/$USER/anari_usd_output_pvservermkdir-p"$ANARI_USD_SERIALIZE_LOCATION"exportLD_LIBRARY_PATH=/p/home/jusers/$USER/jureca/parsimcat_simulation_setup/ANARI-USD/build:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

    (ANARI_USD_SERIALIZE_LOCATION is only a working path; payloads stay in memory and are streamed, not written.)

  • (d)

    Start streaming from ParaView: Load a dataset in ParaView (e.g. a wavelet or your simulation), enable ANARI rendering with the USD device, and apply the desired filters.

  • (e)

    Client connection (SSH tunnel): You must be SSH-tunneled into the machine running the broker. From the client workstation:

    ⬇ssh-N-L5556:127.0.0.1:5556-i~/.ssh/your_key
  • (f)

    Launch the client (Unreal Engine or DaVinCo):

  • •

    In Unreal Engine, place the JuSync spawn actor in your level, configured to connect to localhost:5556 (the tunneled broker port); starting the game connects the plugin to the broker and streamed scenes begin spawning.

  • •

    DaVinCo can be used the same way over the tunnel, with its built-in VR/desktop toolset.

  • (g)

    Build JUSYNC:

    ⬇cdjusync&&gitsubmoduleupdate--initmkdir-pbuild&&cdbuild&&cmake..-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release&&cmake--build.--configRelease
item.content:encoded:
一句话：在 ANARI 层截住 USD 场景图，经 ZeroMQ 流进 UE5 插件，数千万粒子点云可边到边渲染。

要点：

  • 修改的 ANARI-USD 设备在 ANARI 层于内存中捕获 USD 场景图，通过内嵌 ZeroMQ broker 传给可视化客户端
  • JuSync 中间件与配套 UE5 插件边收边解析几何，运行时直接路由到引擎渲染组件，收到即可自由移动相机
  • 在 Jülich 的 JURECA-DC 超算上以自由电子激光仿真的数千万粒子点云演示；设计与仿真解耦，客户端可随时接入或断开

为什么值得看：HPC 仿真的后处理瓶颈往往在写盘与搬运；用引擎无关的 USD 当交换格式、把引擎当渲染前端，是让引擎进入科学可视化的可行接口设计。

中文摘要：在机（in-situ）高性能计算仿真会产生海量数据，但这些数据很难流进游戏引擎做交互式可视化。这篇论文给出了一条不落盘的管线：仿真数据经 ParaView 的 ANARI 渲染接口，由一个改造过的 ANARI-USD 设备在 ANARI 层把 USD 场景图在内存里捕获下来，再通过内嵌的 ZeroMQ broker 把这份引擎无关的 USD 数据流给可视化客户端；客户端侧是 JuSync 中间件加一个 Unreal Engine 5 插件，边接收边解析几何，运行时直接路由进引擎渲染组件，数据一到就能自由移动相机。因为设计上把仿真执行与可视化负载解耦，客户端任何时候接入或断开都不影响仿真本身。作者在 Forschungszentrum Jülich 的 JURECA-DC 超算上，用自由电子激光仿真的数千万粒子点云演示了整条链路。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：arXiv·引擎架构（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-25

Bridging In-Situ Visualization to Game Engines : From ParaView Catalyst via ANARI to Unreal Engine

Abstract

In-situ high-performance computing (HPC) simulations produce massive datasets that remain difficult to stream into game engines for interactive visualization. We present an in-situ, disk-free pipeline that couples simulation data to Unreal Engine 5 through ParaView’s ANARI rendering API. A modified ANARI-USD device captures Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graphs in memory at the ANARI layer and streams the engine-agnostic USD format through an embedded ZeroMQ broker to visualization clients, where JuSync, middleware with a companion Unreal Engine 5 plugin, parses the geometry as it arrives and routes it to engine rendering components at runtime, producing scenes that are camera-navigable once received. The decoupled design keeps simulation execution independent of visualization load, and clients may connect or disconnect at any time. The pipeline is demonstrated on the JURECA-DC supercomputer at Forschungszentrum Jülich, streaming Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation data with point clouds of tens of millions of particles.

Index Terms:

In-Situ, ANARI, Scientific visualization, Unreal Engine, Real-time rendering, HPC, Streaming

I Introduction

ParaView, paired with its Catalyst framework, is one of the standard tools for in-situ analysis on HPC clusters, keeping data in memory without writing to disk. ParaView targets scientific analysis, whereas interactive presentation is the domain of a complementary tool — a modern game engine. Rendering simulation data inside realistic, contextually accurate environments — for example, a reconstructed laboratory facility — has the potential to increase scientific insight by letting researchers explore their results as they would look in the real world. Game engines such as Unreal Engine 5 are built for exactly these capabilities: immersive virtual reality (VR) navigation, realistic lighting, custom annotations, and multi-user collaboration. However, Unreal Engine’s built-in USD support and Datasmith [1] import data from files on disk, not from live streaming in memory.

This work bridges that gap by streaming USD scene graphs directly from ParaView to visualization clients, disk-free, yielding scenes that are interactable on the client once the payload is received. Because JuSync operates at the USD level, the streamed data could in principle feed rendering engines other than Unreal Engine, though only the Unreal Engine 5 client is demonstrated in this work.

As shown in Figure 1, the pipeline moves data from the simulation on the HPC cluster through ParaView and a memory-only ANARI-USD device, across the network via ZeroMQ, and into the JuSync middleware before finally rendering in Unreal Engine. The dashed line separates the cluster-side processing from the client-side visualization.

Following the pipeline in Figure 1, three gaps appear along the data path. First, on the simulation side, the simulation produces particle data that ParaView processes in-situ and ANARI-USD converts into USD scene graphs in memory. However, those graphs stay on the cluster and are not sent over a network. Second, on the client side, even if the USD payload is streamable, Unreal Engine cannot consume it directly at runtime. The scene graph must be parsed, converted to triangulated geometry, and routed to engine-specific rendering components for which no standard tool exists. Finally, the transport must keep the simulation running independently of network conditions or client speed.

These challenges are addressed with two components, illustrated in Figure 1. The ANARI-USD device is extended with a memory tracking layer and an embedded ZeroMQ transport that streams USD scene graphs directly from RAM; the broker is designed to support multiple visualization clients. JuSync [2] is presented as a standalone C++ middleware that receives the streamed USD over ZeroMQ and parses it into runtime geometry. Together, these form a complete disk-free path from ParaView to Unreal Engine. The additions are confined to a modified ANARI-USD device and the JuSync client plugin; the simulation, ParaView, and the Unreal Engine core itself require no code changes.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A memory-only ANARI-USD serialization path that streams standardized USD scene graphs from ParaView over ZeroMQ, enabling a disk-free path to a game engine that is engine-agnostic at the USD boundary.

  • •

    JuSync, an engine-agnostic C++ middleware with a companion UE5 plugin, bridging the gap between streamed USD scene graphs and runtime Unreal Engine geometry.

    • For results and evaluation:

  • •

    An end-to-end evaluation of the pipeline on the JURECA-DC supercomputer using a Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation with point clouds of tens of millions of particles. The pipeline itself is not limited to FEL and works with any ParaView-compatible input.

    • II State of the Art

    II-AParaView-to-External-Renderer Pipelines

    Several recent pipelines share the goal of bridging ParaView’s scientific data processing with a game engine. These pipelines face a common set of challenges: they must transfer scene data produced by ParaView’s visualization pipeline to a rendering environment that operates on a different runtime, often on a different machine, without introducing prohibitive latency.

    InsitUE [3] addresses this with a Catalyst2-compatible hybrid workflow that streams simulation results directly into Unreal Engine. It supports both in-situ and in-transit operation, allows bidirectional steering of visualization parameters, and uses a custom TCP/UDP socket communication protocol with TCP for the control plane and UDP for the data plane. InsitUE couples a Catalyst2/Conduit path to a pair of components — its Catalyst implementation and its Unreal plugin — and additionally offers bidirectional simulation steering, which we do not provide.
