    Appendix A Further Comparisons

    Sec. 4 compares against font-generation models and general-purpose image generators. Here we include additional comparisons with three recent methods that are particularly relevant to our setting. B-LoRA [10] and ZipLoRA [24], like ours, use low-rank adapters to separate what is depicted from how it is rendered, while Abstraction in Style (AiS) [19] explicitly models structural abstraction as part of stylization. Fig. 13 shows the B-LoRA and ZipLoRA results next to ours for the same sketch and style; AiS is discussed separately below.

    B-LoRA.

    B-LoRA leverages LoRA to implicitly separate the style and content of a single image by jointly learning the LoRA weights of two specific SDXL blocks, which can then be used as independent components. We use the official implementation and settings, which we verified by reproducing the authors’ published example. The content adapter is trained on the structural sketch and the style adapter on six training examples of the style, matching the other reference-based baselines. As Fig. 13 (left) shows, the style block carries only the palette and texture of the style: the geometric style is lost, and the structure of the sketch is replaced by hallucinated, unrelated content, because a thin line drawing provides little reconstruction signal.

    ZipLoRA.

    ZipLoRA merges independently trained style and subject LoRAs by learning per-column merger coefficients that minimize their interference. As no official implementation exists, we implement it on our own backbone, which isolates the merging strategy: the content adapter is our UGL and the style adapter is a Style LoRA trained without the UGL, as in the Non-hierarchical ablation (Sec. 12). Both adapters are frozen and only the coefficients are optimized, with the paper’s hyperparameters. With all coefficients at one, the two adapters are simply added, which is exactly the Non-hierarchical configuration of our ablation study; sampling uses its sketches, prompts, seeds and guidance. The learned coefficients scale down both adapters, averaging 0.39-0.48 for the UGL and 0.24-0.52 for the Style LoRA across the three styles. As Fig. 13 (right) shows, the result follows the sketch, but the conflict between structure and style remains, only in a milder form: style-specific details such as the pictogram tile and the wedge-shaped terminals of the display font are weakened. Training the Style LoRA with the UGL active, as we do, avoids the conflict altogether.

    Abstraction in Style (AiS). AiS is designed specifically for styles in which abstraction extends beyond color and texture to geometric and structural deformation. AiS explicitly separates structural abstraction from visual stylization in two stages: it first transforms the target into an intermediate abstraction proxy that reflects the structural tendencies of the reference style, and then renders this proxy into the final stylized output. Both stages are learned from a small set of visual exemplars through its Visual Analogy Transfer framework. This makes AiS particularly relevant to our setting, as it is one of the few recent methods that explicitly treats structural reinterpretation as part of style transfer.

    Fig. 14 compares AiS with our method on three styles: two pictogram sets and a sculptural style. We train AiS on the same style references and use the structural sketch as the abstraction target. AiS captures the visual appearance of each style, but on the pictogram styles its outputs do not reliably follow the sketch: across the scripts, strokes are rearranged, omitted, or fused, while the runner pose is only loosely preserved. On the sculptural style, whose exemplars are themselves single continuous strokes, AiS follows the sketch more closely, though it renders every glyph as one uniform tube. This reflects AiS’s design: its abstraction proxy follows structural tendencies learned from the references rather than the geometry of a specific target. Our method follows each sketch closely while preserving the same style traits, including the tile deformation and stroke bands of the orange set.

    Appendix B Dual Classifier-Free Guidance

    Our generator is conditioned on two inputs: a sketch image c_I of the target geometry and a text caption c_T that carries the style token. Conventional text-conditioned classifier-free guidance (CFG) [16] has a single scale: it amplifies the caption, while the sketch enters both branches as an ordinary, unamplified condition, so the strength of the geometric conditioning cannot be controlled. We therefore adopt the compositional guidance of InstructPix2Pix [3], which separates the two conditions into terms with independent scales.

    Null conditions.

    CFG requires the network to model the unconditional branches, so during training each sample is assigned to one of the four conditioning branches listed in Table 2: most samples keep both conditions, one in five drops the style caption, and a small share drops the sketch or both. The image null ∅_I is the complete absence of reference tokens, i.e. the model’s native text-to-image mode, rather than a blank or noise image, and the text null ∅_T is the empty prompt.

    Guidance.

    Let v_θ(zₜ,c_I,c_T) denote the predicted velocity at noise level t. Each sampling step evaluates the unconditional, geometry-conditioned, and fully conditioned branches of Table 2 (the style-only branch is not used at sampling) and combines them as

    ṽ_θ(zₜ,c_I,c_T) =v_θ(zₜ,∅_I,∅_T)(1)
    +s_I[v_θ(zₜ,c_I,∅_T)-v_θ(zₜ,∅_I,∅_T)]
    +s_T[v_θ(zₜ,c_I,c_T)-v_θ(zₜ,c_I,∅_T)].

    The first bracket moves the prediction toward the sketch and is scaled by the geometry scale s_I; the second adds the contribution of the style token on top of the sketch and is scaled by the style scale s_T. With s_I=s_T, the two brackets merge into one and the rule becomes single-scale CFG on the joint condition (c_I,c_T). Values of s_I above 1 amplify the geometric conditioning independently of the style scale. In practice we use s_I∈[4,6] and s_T∈[2,3] (Sec. 4).

    Reading the two levers.

    Fig. 15 jointly sweeps the two guidance scales for a held-out sketch of a “3”. The grid makes the roles of the two guidance signals and their characteristic failure modes clear.

    With no sketch guidance (s_I=0, top row), the sketch is effectively ignored: increasing s_T strengthens the style but does not recover the geometry of a “3”. At s_I=1, a coherent letterform emerges, but with incorrect geometry, and strong style guidance can further distort its shape.

    At the other extreme, strong sketch guidance (s_I=8, bottom row) reliably preserves the geometry but weakens the appearance signal. Increasing s_T restores the red tubular style, though gradients and translucency remain muted. The intermediate regime (s_I=6, third row) provides the best balance, recovering the correct “3” while preserving the inflated volume and warm gradient of the exemplars. We therefore choose our operating point in this regime.

    Appendix C Geometry Enrichment Engine: Details

    This appendix details the construction of the geometry-enriched training corpus used to train UGL (Sec. 3.2).

    Generating unfamiliar geometries.

    We begin with 80 base glyphs (Latin letters, Latin Extended letters, and digits) shared across 16 fonts and treat them as raw geometric material. We expand this initial vocabulary using two simple structural operations: component removal, which removes a structural part of a glyph, and merging, which combines components from two glyphs. The operations are applied iteratively, allowing newly generated shapes to participate in subsequent operations. As illustrated in Fig. 4 of Sec. 3.2, the resulting forms quickly depart from recognizable characters, producing a much broader distribution of coherent but unfamiliar geometries.

    We represent each sequence of structural operations as a geometric recipe. Importantly, a recipe is defined independently of a particular font and can therefore be applied to corresponding glyphs across multiple fonts. This produces related geometric constructions realized in different styles. Beyond increasing geometric diversity, this correspondence is what allows us to separate the structural information conveyed by a sketch from the style of its target realization.

    A GEE recipe is a sequence of component-removal and merging operations, with both operations applied one to three times. The output of one step is the input of the next. Both operations share a first step, graph extraction, described next.

    Graph extraction.

    Editing a glyph’s outline directly is fragile, since a removal or a join depends on local contour details that differ from style to style. Both operators therefore act on the glyph’s underlying stroke structure, which we extract as a graph; Fig. 5 of Sec. 3.2 illustrates the steps. Starting from the glyph (a), we compute its medial axis transform, which gives the centerline of every stroke together with the radius of the maximal inscribed disk at each point, a local estimate of stroke thickness (b). Treating the axis pixels as a graph, we prune the short branches caused by serifs and other stylistic contour details, retaining the dominant stroke structure (c). Chains of pixels between meeting points are then collapsed into single edges, junctions become nodes and stroke ends become tips (d). Finally, each edge is classified (e). An edge between two junctions is a bar, and an edge from a junction to a tip is a leg. Because these roles do not depend on the exact contour of a style, an operation on these graphs can be replayed across styles.

    Structural correspondence.

    A recipe names the component it edits, but only within the style on which it was defined. To apply the same edit consistently across styles, we must identify the corresponding component in each style. We represent the selected component using a compact descriptor consisting of its type (bar or leg), the orientation of the chord connecting its endpoints, its midpoint normalized by the glyph’s bounding box, and its arc length relative to glyph size. For each other style, we compare this descriptor with all removable components of the same type and select the component with the smallest weighted distance, provided that the distance is below a matching tolerance. If no component falls below this tolerance, the recipe is not applied to that style. A recipe is retained only if at least a minimum number of styles remain (we configured as 6).

    Component removal.

    Fig. 6 of Sec. 3.2 illustrates the process step by step. Given the extracted graph, we aim to remove exactly one structural component, such as a leg or bar, while keeping the rest of the outline unchanged and reconstructing the cut in the font’s own terminal style (a). The component to be removed is described by its structural attributes in the graph. In each style, we use these attributes to identify the corresponding component, so that the same component is removed consistently across styles. Removing only the skeleton associated with the component’s edge is not sufficient, since part of its medial axis may also belong to the junction. To avoid leaving an artificial bulge, we remove medial-axis points near the junction within a radius slightly smaller than its inscribed-disk radius (b). This creates a small gap, which we reconnect with a straight stroke that smoothly bridges the surviving branches. We remove pixels belonging to the deleted limb while preserving those shared with surviving strokes. We then fill small junction concavities using the convex hull of the surviving strokes (c). The removal is defined as a pixel mask, but the output must be vectorized. We therefore trace the removal region into a smooth contour and subtract it from the original glyph outline (d). Geometry outside the edited region is preserved exactly. The newly exposed cut boundary has no counterpart in the original glyph. To reconstruct it in a style-consistent way, we search other glyphs from the same font for a matching outline segment, after normalizing for position, scale, and rotation. We then fit this donor segment to the exposed boundary and insert it into the cut region. The result is a glyph with one structural component removed while preserving the original outline wherever possible (e).

    Merging.

    Fig. 7 of Sec. 3.2 illustrates the process. The connection between the two glyphs is described through structural attributes of their graphs. These attributes identify where the guest should attach to the host and allow the corresponding connection to be found across styles. We begin with two glyphs from the same style: a guestgₐ (a) and a hostg_b (b). Our goal is to attach the guest to the host so that they form a single coherent glyph. The merge has two stages. First, we augment the pair,

    ĝₐ=augment(gₐ), ĝ_b=augment(g_b),

    to generate multiple candidate configurations. The host may be mirrored, while the guest may be also rotated and scaled. These choices are randomly sampled when the recipe is created. In Fig. 7(c), for example, the host is unchanged while the guest is mirrored and rotated by 270^∘. We then merge the augmented pair,

    merge(ĝₐ,ĝ_b).

    On the guest, the connection is anchored at a stroke end facing the host, marked by the red dot in Fig. 7(c). On the host, we select the stroke end facing the guest; if none exists, we use the nearest skeleton point (Fig. 7(d)). The guest is then translated so that the two connection points align. We keep only merges that form a coherent single shape, with a localized overlap at the junction and no narrow gaps or small enclosed holes, as shown in Fig. 7(e). A merge recipe is retained only if it succeeds across a minimum number of styles, ensuring that the structural relation transfers consistently. Small fragments extending beyond the seam are removed to produce the final glyph, as shown in Fig. 7(f).

    Style-suppressed structural sketches.

    For each generated glyph, we extract a structural sketch from its medial axis. A raw medial axis, however, can retain local characteristics of the font from which it was extracted, allowing the conditioning sketch to inadvertently reveal style. We therefore simplify the extracted structure by pruning small branches associated with local stylistic details and approximating the remaining structure with a limited set of Bézier curves. During training, we additionally apply random modifications to these curves. Together, these operations preserve the dominant structure while making residual stylistic cues unreliable.

    We now describe the style-suppressing operations in more detail.

    Pruning. We first remove branches that are more likely to arise from outline decoration than from genuine stroke structure. Pruning is defined relative to the local stroke width rather than by an absolute length threshold. In an initial pass, branches shorter than 0.4 stroke widths are removed. This suppresses small decorative spurs without systematically eliminating genuinely short structural components. Serifs require separate treatment. At a serif terminal, the medial axis often splits into two short branches on opposite sides of the stroke. Removing either branch independently would shorten the stroke rather than remove only its decoration. We distinguish such serif pairs from genuine bifurcations using the line segment joining the two branch tips. If this segment lies entirely inside the glyph, the branches are treated as the two prongs of a serif. If it exits the glyph, as between the upper arms of a Y, the branches are treated as genuine structure and retained. A detected serif pair is replaced by a single branch between the two prongs, preserving the full stroke extent while discarding the terminal shape. In our fonts, serif branches span at most approximately one stroke width, whereas genuine structural limbs typically span two to five stroke widths. We therefore merge a pair only when both branches are shorter than 1.5 stroke widths. A final pruning pass removes branches shorter than 0.9 stroke widths, except where such a branch independently captures a substantial part of the glyph structure.

    Representational bottleneck. We next approximate the pruned medial axis with a limited number of cubic Bézier curves. This sparse representation acts as an explicit information bottleneck rather than merely a compact encoding. A limited number of smooth curves can preserve the coarse glyph geometry, including stroke paths, curvature, and connectivity, while lacking the capacity to reproduce fine stylistic irregularities inherited from the original outline. Curve fitting is performed adaptively. The axis is initially represented by a single cubic Bézier curve and is subdivided at the point of maximum fitting error only when needed. Capacity is therefore allocated preferentially to regions that require additional geometric detail. Across our data, a glyph is represented by approximately ten curves on average and by at most 12. If this capacity is exceeded, the least significant cues are discarded as intended. The subdivision tolerance is expressed relative to stroke thickness. Because the medial axis is defined by its distance to the glyph boundary, constraining the fitting error in this way keeps the approximation geometrically consistent with the glyph interior. The resulting representation is deliberately lossy while remaining faithful to the underlying stroke geometry.

    Although pruning and curve compression remove much of the stylistic information, they cannot guarantee complete invariance. A sufficiently expressive model may still exploit residual correlations between the conditioning sketch and the target style. We therefore introduce two training-time mechanisms in UGL to make such residual information unreliable.

    Perturbation during training. During training, each conditioning stroke is randomly perturbed while the corresponding target glyph remains unchanged. The model therefore does not observe a single exact skeleton as the unique conditioning representation of a target. Large-scale structure is preserved, while small local details become unreliable as predictive features. The curve representation allows us to perturb strokes structurally rather than at the pixel level. We deform the interior of each curve while keeping its endpoints fixed, preserving junctions and overall connectivity. Perturbation magnitude is scaled by curve length and correlated along the stroke, causing the stroke to bend smoothly as a whole rather than introducing high-frequency local noise. Each interior control point is displaced by a Gaussian whose standard deviation is a fraction of the curve’s chord length, capped at twice that deviation so that a curve cannot fold back on itself. We resample this fraction uniformly for every sample at every epoch, from [0.10,0.20] when training UGL and from [0.03,0.08] when training a Style LoRA (Table 3), so the model sees a range of sketch precision rather than one fixed noise level.

    Cross-style pairing.

    To further prevent the sketch from serving as a style condition, we exploit the cross-font correspondence provided by the geometric recipes. Rather than always pairing a target glyph with its own extracted sketch, we can condition it on a sketch extracted from another font generated by the same recipe. Although their precise medial axes may differ, the sketch and target share the same underlying construction while belonging to different styles. This cross-style pairing discourages UGL from using the conditioning sketch to infer the target style.

    Together, geometry enrichment, style suppression, and cross-style pairing produce a broad training distribution in which structural sketches primarily communicate geometry rather than shape identity or style. Training UGL on this corpus encourages it to follow the supplied structure, providing the universal geometry prior required for open-form transfer.

    Appendix D Training details

    Both adapters are LoRA modules [17] on the attention projections of the FLUX.2-klein-base-4B transformer [2] (80 linear layers); the backbone, the VAE and the Qwen3 text encoder stay frozen, the text encoder in 8-bit. UGL uses rank 192 with α=192; every Style LoRA uses rank 32 with α=32 and is trained with UGL attached as a frozen adapter, never merged. Both stages use AdamW-8bit (learning rate 10⁻⁴, constant after a linear warm-up, β=(0.9,0.999), weight decay 0.01, ε=10⁻⁶), an EMA of the adapter weights with decay 0.99, gradient checkpointing, and a flow-matching objective at 256×256 for both the target and the sketch condition. Adapter weights are stored in fp16. Table 3 lists the per-stage settings.

    Appendix E Additional Results

    Figure 16: Sculptural and decorative styles on pose and glyph sketches. Each row is one structural sketch (left): four pose sketches (top) and five glyph sketches (bottom); each column is one style, shown by three reference examples at the top.

    Appendix F VLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation

    We employ a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation framework to assess generated results in the open-set regimes, where no unique paired ground truth exists: for a target structure outside the style’s own shape family there is no single correct rendering to compare against, so paired metrics such as LPIPS and SSIM are undefined. The judge is asked instead whether the requested structure is depicted and whether it is realized in the demonstrated geometric design language.

    Each judged candidate is presented as a single composite image with labeled panels: a top row of K=6 style references, and a bottom row holding the target structural sketch and the candidate. References are drawn only from the style’s training rows, so the judge never sees the ground-truth target of the case it is grading. All panels are rendered at 256×256 on a common canvas, and nothing in the image or the prompt identifies the method that produced the candidate.

    We score each candidate absolutely rather than in pairs. This has two consequences we rely on: the resulting scalar does not depend on which baselines happen to be included in the comparison, and there is no left–right position bias to mitigate. To remove the remaining ordering effect, the six style references are shuffled per case with a fixed per-case permutation. The judge is instructed to return a single JSON object conforming to a strict response schema, which prevents the answer from drifting into prose and bounds the output length.

    The response to the example query illustrates the two axes being scored independently. Geometry is 4 rather than 5 because the judge locates two nameable departures from the sketch before scoring it: the rider is given the head the sketch leaves implicit, and the bicycle frame is redrawn cleaner than the tangle of strokes it was traced from. Style is 4 because the candidate carries the references’ badge, weight and figure convention onto a sport none of them shows, while stopping short of being mistaken for one of them. Both flags are false: the candidate reproduces no shown reference, and it is not the sketch passed through unstyled.

    F.1 Judge Configuration

    We use the same judge configuration for the entire evaluation: all reported numbers come from gemini-3.1-pro-preview with a structured response schema and medium media resolution. Each candidate is judged in a single pass. Scores are aggregated hierarchically, matching the rest of our protocol: samples within a case, cases within a style, then styles weighted equally.

    Appendix G User Study

    G.1 User Study Setup

    We complement the VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation with a human preference study. Unlike the judge, which scores each candidate absolutely, the study is pairwise: participants see two results for the same input and indicate which one is better. Relative judgments are easier for non-expert participants to make consistently than absolute ratings, and they directly answer the question of interest, namely whether our results are preferred over those of each baseline.

    Each question is presented as a single composite image with labeled panels: a top row with the style references and the structural sketch, and a bottom row with two results, A and B. One result is ours and the other is produced by a baseline, both generated for the same style and the same sketch. All panels, including the two results, are rendered at the same size on a common canvas, so that the native output resolution of a method is not revealed, and nothing in the image or the text identifies the method behind a result.

    The study contains 12 questions: three for each of the four baselines (MX-Font, FontDiffuser, Gemini, and GPT-Image), each on a different style, covering black-and-white fonts, decorative fonts, and pictogram styles. The sketches span held-out glyphs, non-Latin glyphs, human poses, and symbols. For each question, participants answer three multiple-choice items, on style, structure, and overall preference, each with the options Result A, Result B, and About the same.

    To control for ordering and position effects, we prepare four editions of the questionnaire. Each edition shuffles the order of the questions, never placing the same baseline in two consecutive questions, and randomizes which side shows our result. Within every edition our result appears as A in exactly half of the questions, and the side assignment is mirrored between editions, so that any preference for a side cancels out. Participants reach the study through a single link that assigns them to one of the editions at random. Responses are anonymous, and each participant answers one edition.

    The example illustrates why the two axes are asked separately. Both results depict a recognizable treble clef, so the structure item mainly asks whether the particular structure of the sketch is preserved, such as its proportions, the spiral around the stem, and the hooked tail. The style item asks something different: whether the result carries the distinctive traits of the references, such as the rounded, asymmetric blue tile, the bold white strokes with rounded ends, and the thin parallel lines that accompany the figures, rather than merely sharing their colors.

    Before the first question, participants are shown one worked example in the same layout, with the intended answers marked and a one-line explanation of each. Its two results are not method outputs: one is a letter of a reference font and the other is the same letter in a plain serif font, so the intended answers are unambiguous and do not bias participants toward any method.

    G.2 Aggregation

    For each baseline and each of the three items, we report the percentage of votes that prefer our result, prefer the baseline’s result, or rate the two as about the same, pooled over participants, editions, and the three questions of that baseline. Significance is assessed with a two-sided exact binomial test against 50% on the decisive votes, i.e., after discarding About the same answers. In total, 32 participants completed the study.

item.title: 测语言世界模型别只测预测准不准：CivWorldBench 用策略游戏记录好的内部状态考「猜隐藏状态」与「预测干预」 ｜ CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds
item.description:
一句话：建在多智能体策略游戏引擎上，1900 个决策点、475 个世界，分关联预测／信念推断／干预预测三级。

要点：

  • 基于带内部状态记录的多智能体策略游戏引擎构建，可做受控观测与成对的干预 rollout
  • 475 个世界共 1,900 个决策点，分三级任务：关联预测、隐藏信念推断、干预结果预测
  • 存下的轨迹让中间预测可核对；agent 试玩实验检验这些世界模型能力能否真的用于决策

为什么值得看：世界模型要做引擎的「想象器」，就得能推断看不见的状态并预测干预后果；这套三级任务把这两件事分开了，正好对应引擎里状态与规则的分界。

中文摘要：语言模型越来越多被用于预测未来，于是需要更全面的世界模型评测：不能只看预测准确度，还要看它能不能推断隐藏状态、能不能预测干预后果。真实世界的预测基准拿不到隐藏状态真值，也做不了受控实验，因此作者构建了 CivWorldBench——建立在带内部状态记录的多智能体策略游戏引擎之上，具备受控观测与成对的干预 rollout。它包含 475 个世界、共 1,900 个决策点，分三级任务：关联预测、信念推断、干预预测；受控观测与参考预测器让能力差距可以归因，专家脚手架与经验上限估计则给分数提供参照。存档轨迹使中间预测可核对，agent 试玩实验进一步检验这些世界模型能力是否可用于决策。评测面板覆盖 11 个不同能力档位的前沿语言模型，综合分与真实世界预测榜单的相关性高于与通用能力指数的相关性。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-12

本期推送：2026-10-25

CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds

Abstract

The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments for evaluating intervention predictions. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Controlled observations and reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities are usable for decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models spanning different capability levels. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and further motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.

Code:https://github.com/Leon-Francis/CivWorldBench

1 Introduction

Language models increasingly support forecasting and decision-making in multi-agent systems. They simulate agent populations [(Park et al., 2023; Piatti et al., 2024; Piao et al., 2025)], forecast geopolitical and economic events [(Halawi et al., 2024; Karger et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026)], negotiate [(Meta Fundamental AI Research Diplomacy Team (FAIR) et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024)], and act in digital, social, and physical environments [(Zhu and Cai, 2026)]. These applications require a world model that predicts observable dynamics, infers relevant hidden state, and anticipates the consequences of interventions [(Chen et al., 2026; Chu et al., 2026)]. Forecasting is the observable output of such a world model: a forecast commits implicitly to beliefs about hidden state and dynamics, but its accuracy alone does not establish that these beliefs are correct [(Vafa et al., 2024)], and intervention prediction further requires mechanism assumptions beyond observed associations [(Pearl, 2009; Bareinboim et al., 2022)].

Existing benchmarks each isolate part of this problem. Real-world forecasting benchmarks such as ForecastBench [(Karger et al., 2025)] resolve against genuine outcomes but provide no latent-state ground truth and no alternative trajectories, so belief and dynamics errors cannot be separated. Causal-reasoning benchmarks test inference from statistical descriptions [(Jin et al., 2024)] or interactive discovery in synthetic laboratories [(Yang et al., 2026a)], and SocietyBench forecasts social events on anonymized timelines [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. None of them pairs forecasting, hidden-state inference, and intervention prediction on the same recorded multi-agent dynamics. Game-agent benchmarks such as CivRealm and BALROG [(Qi et al., 2024; Paglieri et al., 2025)] score an acting policy, entangling world knowledge with planning and execution. Isolating world-model capabilities therefore requires prediction tasks with verifiable hidden states and intervention outcomes, plus controls for observation limits and stochasticity.

We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on the Freeciv game engine.111 Freeciv is an open-source turn-based strategy game, https://www.freeciv.org. Civilizations expand, research, trade, cooperate, and compete under recorded rules and latent behavioral parameters. Figure1 illustrates how textual observation histories support three task levels: L1 association forecasting (Quantity, Event), L2 belief inference (Trait, Rules), and L3 intervention prediction (Intervene). The benchmark contains 475 worlds, 1,900 decision points, and 18,499 prompts. Global, egocentric, and out-of-distribution settings separate observation limits from configuration shifts. Saved checkpoints enable paired intervention, control, and placebo rollouts, and re-seeded futures measure engine stochasticity. Floor, Expert, and Ceiling references contextualize performance, and the Sandbox-World Forecasting Index (SWFI) aggregates reference-normalized scores across levels and settings.

Our evaluation of eleven language models identifies distinct capability profiles. SWFI correlates with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a forecasting-specific proxy. Within the benchmark, association forecasting rankings do not consistently reflect belief and intervention capabilities. Most models predict intervention directions above chance while estimating effect magnitudes poorly. Process verification identifies intermediate errors missed by final-answer scores, and the strongest model in the process study improves effect prediction through structured reasoning. Agent-play results show that useful advice is not identified by association forecasting alone.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we enable attributable evaluation through a structured multi-agent benchmark with controlled observations, paired intervention outcomes, and task-specific reference predictors. Second, we make answers and intermediate predictions verifiable against recorded engine states and rollouts, including Table and Code reasoning protocols. Third, we assess whether these capabilities are usable in agent decision-making and how they relate to real-world forecasting. Engine patches and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/Leon-Francis/CivWorldBench. The benchmark data release is in preparation.

2 The CivWorldBench Environment

CivWorldBench uses Freeciv to combine multi-agent dynamics with recorded hidden states, controlled observations, and executable interventions. Each world contains 3–10 AI civilizations that expand, research, trade, form alliances, and fight over hundreds of turns.

2.1 State, dynamics, and observations

A world w∼W is an engine instance with state sₜ=(xₜ,zₜ;θ_w), where xₜ contains reportable map, city, unit, economic, technological, and diplomatic fields, the hidden dynamic state zₜ includes attitudes and internals, and θ_w contains fixed personality traits and world parameters. Formally, each world is a partially observable Markov decision process (S,A,T,Ω,Oᵥ) without a reward, since the benchmark evaluates prediction rather than control. Each built-in agent i follows a policy πᵢ that maps its observation O_ego(i)(sₜ)∈Ω to an action in A, and the joint actions together with the random innovation uₜ induce the transition sₜ₊₁=T(sₜ,{πᵢ},uₜ). The evaluated world model is a map f(o_≤t₁,{πᵢ})↦(b(z_t₁,θ_w), p̂(s_t₁+h)) from the observation history and the agents’ current policies to a belief over the hidden state and a forecast of the future state under those policies.

The world model’s input at t₁ is three-frame history o_≤t₁=(o_t₁-2Δ,o_t₁-Δ,o_t₁,narrative,policies) with Δ=40 turns, or 20 when t₁<81, where each frame oₜ=Oᵥ(sₜ) is a text report. The global view v=omni renders reportable fields across civilizations, and the egocentric view v=ego(i) is the engine’s own fog-of-war rendering for agent i. The narrative summarizes observed events in five-turn blocks, and the policies give each agent’s research aim and course of action, such as its expansion or war posture. The output is elicited as quantile forecasts, event probabilities, and hidden-state beliefs, as Section3 specifies. AppendixC gives the formal definitions.

2.2 Behavioral validity of hidden targets

Hidden state includes personality traits that shape strategic preferences, diplomatic attitudes that influence relations between civilizations, and world parameters governing disaster frequency, city growth, and research speed. L2 infers traits and world parameters, and L3 additionally intervenes on attitudes. In Freeciv’s default AI, several traits had little or no effect and war was rarely reversed. We apply 5 source patches to activate these traits, initialize contact at peace, and permit ceasefires. AppendicesD and K document the modifications.

2.3 World generation

Table1 summarizes the two world sets. The basic set fixes the ruleset and difficulty across three map classes while varying hidden parameters and generated worlds. The generalization set jointly varies the ruleset, AI difficulty, map size, civilization count, hidden-parameter ranges, and team play: 128 worlds use the classic ruleset, which changes the unit, building, and technology sets, five difficulty levels appear, and 60 worlds play in teams, so the shift affects game dynamics rather than only the map. Each world contributes four decision points, and collection runs beyond the reporting budget to record forecast targets. Median Quantity prompt lengths are 17.9K, 47.6K, and 78.1K tokens for the basic map classes.

2.4 Interventions

An intervention applies an edit m to a saved checkpoint before continuing the simulation. Each eligible checkpoint produces four arms: an unedited control, a repeated recheck, a real edit, and a matched placebom₀ with negligible or mechanism-irrelevant impact. Real-arm outcomes are compared with the rerun control rather than the mainline, and placebos measure responses to nominal edits. Reloads and edits can alter random-number consumption, so branch differences retain stochastic variation, as SectionD.3 documents.

3 Tasks and Evaluation Settings

The three levels query different components of the process in Section2: L1 predicts future observables xₜ₊ₕ, L2 infers the static hidden parameters θ_w, and L3 predicts xₜ₊ₕ after an external edit to sₜ. Table2 summarizes the five tasks.

L1: Association.

Quantity requests five quantiles for eleven quantities at two budget-dependent horizons, listed in AppendixE. Six quantity families, namely economy, scale, technology–culture, military, diplomacy, and overall score, receive equal weight. Event requests probabilities for ten binary event templates, including city capture, wonder completion, and alliance formation, and a distribution over the future score leader.

L2: Belief.

Trait ranks civilizations on aggression, expansion, trade, and building preference. Rules classifies disaster frequency, growth speed, and research speed into three bins each, subject to evidence requirements. Both tasks use recorded engine values as ground truth.

L3: Intervention.

Eleven operators modify treasury, research points, cities, government access, map visibility, personality traits, attitudes, or disaster frequency. The model receives the history and edit description, then re-answers Quantity within the operator’s target and horizon range. Capture compares the predicted shift from the model’s own control answer with the realized shift between engine branches. Direction assesses sign agreement, and specificity measures response selectivity between real and placebo edits.

Settings.

Omni-ID uses the basic worlds with global observations. Ego uses the same worlds through one civilization’s view, with questions scoped to contacted civilizations. Omni-OOD applies global observations to the generalization worlds, whose rulesets, AI difficulty, map sizes, civilization counts, hidden-parameter ranges, and team structures differ from the basic set, separating restricted information from shifts in world dynamics. Table17 reports information ablations.

4 Evaluation Protocol and Research Questions

4.1 Scores

Quantity forecasting. For each cell c, indexed by world, decision point, civilization, quantity, and horizon, let y be the engine target and q̂=(q̂_τ)_τ∈T the predicted quantiles at T={0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.9}. Quantile loss (QL) approximates the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) [(Gneiting and Raftery, 2007)]:

QL(q̂,y)=(2)/(|T|)∑_τ∈Tρ_τ (φ(y)-φ(q̂_τ)), ρ_τ(u)=(τ-1[u<0])u,

(1)

where ρ_τ is the pinball loss and 1[·] the indicator. The transform φ(x)=sign(x)\log(1+|x|) applies to treasury and population levels and culture increments, and is the identity otherwise. The normalized cell loss is ℓ_c=QL(q̂,y)/σᵥ, where σᵥ>0 is the fixed corpus scale for quantity v, equal to one for log-transformed quantities. Enemy and ally counts instead use the absolute error of the predicted median.

For eligible cells ℂ_wf of family f in world w, let ℓ_c,ref denote trend-reference loss. World–family skill S_wf and the Quantity score S_QNT are

S_wf=clip_[-1,1] (1-(∑_c∈ℂ_wfℓ_c)/(∑_c∈ℂ_wfℓ_c,ref)), S_QNT=(1)/(|W|)∑_w∈W(1)/(|F_w|)∑_f∈F_wS_wf,

(2)

where F_w contains families with positive reference loss, W contains worlds with at least one such family, and vertical bars denote cardinality.

Event forecasting.Event averages Brier gain [(Brier, 1950; Murphy, 1988)]G=Brier(p_ref,y)-Brier(p̂,y) for model probability p̂, reference probability p_ref, and outcome y. Binary items use Brier(p,y)=(p-y)² for event probability p and y∈{0,1}, referenced to the supplied task-cell rate. Leader items use multiclass loss ∑ⱼ(pⱼ-1[y=j])², where pⱼ is the probability that civilization j leads and y the realized leader, with current-leader persistence as reference.

Hidden-state inference.Trait uses pairwise ranking accuracy, and Rules averages classification accuracy equally across rule parameters.

Intervention prediction. For cell c of quantity v, let q̂_m,0.5 and yₘ denote the predicted median and engine outcome under edit m. Subscript ctrl denotes the unedited control. Predicted and realized effects are d̂_c=[φ(q̂_m,0.5)-φ(q̂_ctrl,0.5)]/σᵥ and d_c=[φ(yₘ)-φ(y_ctrl)]/σᵥ. For an operator’s eligible cells ℂ with nonzero realized effect d_c, Capture is

C=1-(∑_c∈ℂ|d̂_c-d_c|)/(∑_c∈ℂ|d_c|),

(3)

clipped to [-1,1] before averaging equally over operators with at least three eligible cells. No-effect and exact predictions score 0 and 1. Direction measures sign agreement among nonzero responses on these cells, counting missing answers as failures and weighting operators by eligible moved-cell counts.

Let s̄ᵣₑₐₗ and s̄ₚₗ denote mean |d̂_c| under real edits and matched placebos across valid cells and operators, including unchanged-truth cells. Valid-response Specificity is

Spec_valid=clip_[-1,1] (1-(s̄ₚₗ)/(s̄ᵣₑₐₗ)),

(4)

defined when s̄ᵣₑₐₗ>0 and both arms have valid shifts. It measures selectivity, not correctness, and should be interpreted alongside Capture.

Reference adjustment. Trait, Rules, and Direction report S_adj=c(a-b)/(c-b) for raw accuracy a, baseline b, and reference ceiling c, which maps the baseline to zero without changing the ceiling or the model ordering. Missing or unparseable answers receive task-specific failure penalties, as specified in AppendixF.

4.2 Reference lines and composite index

Reference lines.Floor defines metric-specific origins, with Capture’s clipped lower endpoint -1. Expert adds domain knowledge and a tool-assisted harness under the same observations, without hidden test state, future outcomes, or random seeds. The conceptual Ceiling assumes complete simulator state and engine knowledge, but not future random draws.

Composite index. For model m, setting s, and metric k, let xₘₛₖ be the score, with floor fₛₖ and ceiling cₛₖ. Completion is rₘₛₖ=(xₘₛₖ-fₛₖ)/(cₛₖ-fₛₖ), a fraction that tables report as a percentage. To define the Sandbox-World Forecasting Index (SWFI), let Sₑᵥₐₗ={\textscOmni-ID,\textscEgo,\textscOmni-OOD} and K_ℓ contain Quantity and Event at level ℓ=1, Trait and Rules at ℓ=2, and Capture, Direction, and Specificity at ℓ=3. Then

SWFI(m)=100/9∑_s∈Sₑᵥₐₗ∑_ℓ=1³(1)/(|K_ℓ|)∑_k∈K_ℓrₘₛₖ.

(5)

Metrics are weighted equally within levels, then across levels and settings. Weights and reference scales are fixed independently of external leaderboards, and completion and SWFI are not clipped.

4.3 Research questions

RQ1, validity. Do information controls, reference lines, and external forecasting associations support the evaluation? RQ2, limits. Where do current models fall short across task levels? RQ3, process. How does intermediate prediction quality relate to final answers, and how do reasoning protocols affect intervention prediction? RQ4, utility. Can world models improve agent decisions, and which capability profiles indicate utility?

4.4 Models and inference

We evaluate eleven language models with thinking enabled at model-specific effort settings recorded in AppendixM. Open-weight models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, hereafter Flash-Next, cover the full grid. Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, hereafter Opus and Sol, use medium reasoning effort on 190 shared frozen decision points, 10% of the benchmark, to bound API cost. This subset is stratified to match the full benchmark’s composition by split, world size, budget, ruleset, decision time, and operator, one anchor per world, so subset scores estimate the same quantities as the full grid. Expert uses Sol on the same anchors with a manual combining engine rules and regularities from 447 disjoint worlds. The Artificial Analysis (AA) Intelligence Index v4.3 [(Artificial Analysis, 2026)] provides a general-capability reference. The reported evaluations consumed about 3,600 H20-equivalent GPU-hours of open-weight inference, 5,000 CPU core-hours of engine simulation, and $2,500 of closed-model API calls.

5 Benchmark Validity and Model Capabilities

Table3 summarizes the main results, with full setting-wise results in Table14. We examine evaluation validity (RQ1), then identify model limitations and directions for improvement across task levels (RQ2).

5.1 Do the tasks and metrics support valid evaluation? (RQ1)

Insight 1: Information controls and engine checks support validity. Re-seeded rollouts in SectionG.1 retain uncertainty despite complete state information, motivating distributional scoring. Figure3 shows that removing history reduces forecasting performance, whereas study notes and privileged future narratives improve it, demonstrating evidence sensitivity. Construction checks in SectionG.4 detect no leakage or consistency violations, and replay diagnostics in SectionG.5 justify factual-rerun controls.

Insight 2: Reference lines locate the deficit in the models.Table3 shows that Expert reaches 51% of Ceiling, against 29% for the best model, so knowledge and harness support reveal substantial headroom under fixed observations, and the headroom lies in the models rather than in noisy targets. Branch noise lowers the Capture Ceiling to +0.39 but cannot make a model negative, since predicting no effect scores 0. Nine of eleven models nonetheless score below -0.3 in Omni-ID, while Expert reaches +0.13 and study notes raise Flash-Next by +0.24 on paired cells in SectionH.3. Models shift forecasts as much under placebo as under real edits in Table24, so their negative scores reflect over-reaction. For Trait the limit is the evidence: a privileged observer reaches only 0.59, so the task measures recovery of a weak but real signal, on which Expert and Sol still separate from models at chance.

Insight 3: Sandbox scores track real-world forecasting.Figure3 shows positive correlations between SWFI and forecasting scores on ForecastBench [(Karger et al., 2025)], Metaculus FutureEval [(Metaculus, 2026)], and Prophet Arena [(Prophet Arena, 2026)], with r=0.79–0.95 over panels of four to six matched models, and a model-level permutation test pooling the panels gives r=0.73 with p=0.009. These exceed SWFI’s correlation of r=0.76 with the AA general-capability index, and Table13 shows the belief components nearly uncorrelated with AA. SWFI thus tracks forecasting-specific ability rather than general capability alone, which supports CivWorldBench as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability.

5.2 Where do current world models fall short? (RQ2)

Insight 1: Association forecasting strength does not reliably extend to belief inference and intervention prediction.Table3 shows that GLM-5.3 leads the model panel in quantity forecasting, yet its trait score is below chance. Both GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 lag behind Sol in belief inference and intervention direction. Such reversals recur across the panel, so association forecasting rankings do not consistently reflect belief and intervention capabilities.

The process analysis in Section6 traces this gap to intermediate states, which models often mispredict even when their final answers are accurate and whose quality tracks intervention performance. The usability study in Section7 further suggests that agent performance is more closely associated with L2 and L3 capabilities than with L1 forecasting alone, motivating evaluation beyond observation.

Insight 2: Effect prediction remains a shared weakness across models.Table3 shows above-chance intervention direction for most models. Yet nearly all models have negative capture across settings, below the zero-effect baseline. Figure4 shows informative direction predictions alongside widely dispersed effect magnitudes. Among correct-direction predictions, some medians approach 100%, while interquartile ranges span underestimation and overestimation. SectionH.4 reports coverage and conditional results across settings, including 17–35% of correct-direction predictions in Omni-ID, and up to 44% in Omni-OOD, exceeding twice the realized magnitude. These errors arise from over-reaction to edits rather than from target noise. A single global rescaling cannot correct errors that fall on both sides of the truth, so effect magnitudes must be calibrated conditional on the world state.

6 Process Verification and Prediction Quality

Recorded trajectories and engine ground truth make intermediate predictions verifiable, linking process quality to intervention prediction and structured reasoning to process supervision (RQ3).

6.1 Tasks and experimental settings

We evaluate Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma 4 31B, and Kimi K3 on 190 anchors, 10% of the benchmark, and GPT-5.6 Sol on a 30-anchor subset, each under three reasoning protocols. Free uses unrestricted reasoning without a prescribed process score. Table predicts prescribed intermediate states before answering, and Code generates a stochastic simulator, executed across 50 random seeds to yield intermediate predictions and final-answer distributions. Both are scored against engine truth at the same prescribed intermediate cells, with process quality defined as intermediate-state skill over the trend reference. AppendixI details the protocols.

6.2 How does process quality relate to prediction performance? (RQ3)

Insight 1: Strong final-answer performance can accompany weak intermediate forecasts.Figure5a shows that 4.7–9.5% of matched predictions exceed the final-answer reference without exceeding the intermediate-state reference, across models and both structured protocols. Final-answer evaluation therefore misses intermediate prediction errors, motivating separate process verification.

Insight 2: Process quality is positively associated with L3 intervention prediction performance.Figure5b shows that higher L3 process quality accompanies greater Capture completion across models. This association supports process verification as a complementary diagnostic and intermediate-state forecasting as a route to stronger intervention prediction. SectionI.3 reports uncertainty.

Insight 3: Structured reasoning can improve intervention prediction.Figure5c shows Table gains over Free increasing with SWFI. Sol benefits from both structured protocols and improves most with Code. Tables expose intermediate states for verification, while code connects them through executable dynamics. These results motivate world-model process supervision on states and intervention-induced changes, for which CivWorldBench provides a multi-agent counterpart to the verified executable worlds of [Wang et al. (2026a)].

7 World-Model Capabilities and Decision Utility

We assess whether world-model forecasts and advice improve agent decisions and how these gains relate to benchmark capability profiles (RQ4).

7.1 Experimental setup and evaluation

A fixed Flash-Next agent plays turns 60–210 in 76 worlds, either without world-model assistance or with forecasts and advice from Flash-Next or Kimi K3 to inform plan revisions. A local study compares original, self-reviewed, and assisted plans at matched decision points in 36 validation worlds, using Flash-Next, Kimi, Sol, and Opus as advisers. Each plan undergoes four 20-turn executions without further strategic consultation. Both studies compare the engine’s civilization score within worlds, as AppendixN details.

7.2 Do better world models support better decisions? (RQ4)

Insight 1: World models can support agent decision-making.Figure6 traces score gains over turns 60–210, with positive mean gains for both assisted conditions at turn 210. In the local study, selecting plans on trial executions and evaluating them on held-out executions, adding WM-generated plans improves selection by 2.36 score points over choosing among original and self-reviewed plans only, so advice expands the set of useful alternatives. The case studies show what useful advice consists of: Opus corrects the agent’s reading of a conditional loss probability as a certainty and redirects its remaining gold to one fortified defender, saving two cities, whereas Sol’s precautionary tax increase buys defenses against a threat that never materializes and costs research. Useful advice therefore hinges on reading the opponent’s intentions and the state-specific cost of a precaution, which are belief and intervention judgments rather than trend extrapolation. Figures13 and 14 illustrate how specific recommendations change decisions.

Insight 2: Decision-oriented evaluation should extend beyond association forecasting.Table4 shows larger estimated decision gains for Opus and Sol than Kimi despite lower L1 scores, and these two advisers also lead the panel in belief inference and intervention direction. Decision utility thus tracks the capabilities that association forecasting leaves unmeasured. This motivates evaluating hidden-state inference and action-conditioned effect prediction alongside association forecasting.

8 Conclusion

CivWorldBench evaluates forecasting, hidden-state inference, and intervention prediction in multi-agent worlds with engine-verifiable targets. Its composite score tracks real-world forecasting more closely than general capability, while level diagnostics expose weaknesses hidden by observational accuracy: intermediate-state errors, poorly calibrated effects, and advice utility that forecasting alone does not explain. These findings prioritize state representation, effect calibration, and verifiable process supervision. Taken together, the results characterize current language models as competent trend extrapolators but weak causal simulators of multi-agent worlds, and the benchmark supplies the hidden-state and intervention targets needed to train the latter. AppendixB discusses limitations.

AI use statement

Generative AI tools, including Claude and Codex, assisted implementation and manuscript polishing, and were used for retrieval and discovery, such as finding related work and checking bibliographic details, which the authors then verified against the original sources. Language models also produced the forecasts, reasoning, executable predictors, and advice evaluated in the experiments. These outputs are distinct from the ground-truth states and outcomes generated by the game engine. Expert-harness and mechanism-card uses are documented with their experimental protocols. The authors are responsible for the implementation, analyses, and manuscript writing.

Ethics statement

The study involves no human participants. Benchmark trajectories use engine-controlled agents, and the usability study introduces language-model-controlled decisions within the same simulated environment. Freeciv is distributed under the GPL, whose requirements apply to engine modifications. Benchmark performance does not validate policy recommendations for human societies. The icons used in our figures are sourced from Flaticon222https://www.flaticon.com and are free for personal and commercial purposes with attribution.

Reproducibility statement

Scoring and analysis code, engine patches, and build instructions are available at https://github.com/Leon-Francis/CivWorldBench. The benchmark data release, including frozen questions, targets, and model predictions, is in preparation. AppendixM records evaluation configurations and result provenance. AppendixG specifies reference-line estimation, and AppendixD documents the collection pipeline and validation checks.
