Appendix A Related Work

World-model evaluation and intervention prediction.

WorldPrediction evaluates action and action-sequence selection from video states [(Chen et al., 2025)], while [Li et al. (2026)] survey text world models for agents. Corr2Cause tests causal inference from statistical descriptions [(Jin et al., 2024)], while CausaLab supports interactive causal discovery in synthetic laboratories [(Yang et al., 2026a)]. These studies examine dynamics prediction and mechanism recovery under different task formulations. CivWorldBench evaluates forecasting, hidden-state inference, and intervention prediction within the same multi-agent dynamics. Recorded trait and rule values provide inference targets, while paired engine rollouts measure intervention outcomes under controlled observations.

Real-world and social forecasting.

ForecastBench evaluates forecasts of future events [(Karger et al., 2025)]. Prophet Arena separates event collection, prediction, and evaluation in a live forecasting pipeline [(Yang et al., 2026b)], while [Lu (2025)] compares model forecasts with expert predictions on Metaculus questions. SocietyBench evaluates social-event forecasting on anonymized, date-shifted timelines [(Wang et al., 2026b)], and SWM-Bench uses prediction-market trajectories to evaluate collective belief transitions [(Yu et al., 2026)]. CivWorldBench complements these outcome-based evaluations with recorded hidden states and repeated stochastic futures. SectionG.3 relates its composite scores to real-world forecasting through matched-model comparisons.

Multi-agent environments and decision utility.

SOTOPIA evaluates social interaction [(Zhou et al., 2024)], while social world models explicitly represent other agents’ mental states [(Zhou et al., 2025)]. CivRealm and BALROG assess decision-making agents through game interaction [(Qi et al., 2024; Paglieri et al., 2025)]. End-to-end performance combines dynamics knowledge, planning, and action execution. CivWorldBench separately evaluates an observer of engine-controlled civilizations, then holds the acting model fixed when comparing world-model advisers. This design connects prediction diagnostics to decision utility while controlling the agent’s execution capabilities.

Process verification and executable worlds.

[Rahmani (2026)] distinguishes action-generation errors from state-propagation errors in code world models. Verifier-driven executable models also support planning in ARC-AGI-3 by checking simulated transitions against previous observations [(Rodionov, 2026)]. Code as Worlds uses verified executable worlds to derive physical-reasoning supervision [(Wang et al., 2026a)]. CivWorldBench extends process evaluation to stochastic multi-agent trajectories, checking Table and Code predictions at shared intermediate states and relating their quality to final intervention forecasts. These targets support studying supervision for both state prediction and intervention-induced changes.

Appendix B Limitations

Scope.

All dynamics come from one engine and its built-in AI. The generalization set changes the ruleset, difficulty, map, civilization count, hidden-parameter ranges, and team structure, but remains within that engine. The benchmark does not test transfer to other simulators or to human societies.

References and targets.

The Trait and Direction ceilings are computed on identifiable subsets, namely trait gaps of at least 60 and cells with |d_c|>σ_c, so completion in these columns is conservative, and the Capture ceiling in SectionG.2 assumes Gaussian branch divergence. Intervention targets include the reload-path divergence measured in SectionG.5. This divergence bounds attainable Capture but cannot produce negative scores, which Section5 attributes to the models. Traits are only weakly identifiable from 80 turns of behavior, even for a privileged observer, whose accuracy is 0.59, so Trait scores should be read against that observer. Expert is a language model with a manual and tools, not a human baseline.

External and downstream evidence.

The matched forecasting panels contain four to six models, and a general-capability index is also correlated with the same leaderboards, so proxy validity rests on the component-level evidence in Table13 as much as on the composite. The process study covers five models, and agent play uses one actor in benchmark worlds. Their model-level association and full-game gain intervals include zero, as AppendicesI and N report.

Appendix C Formal definition

World and observation.

In the process (S,A,T,Ω,Oᵥ) of Section2, a world w∼W specifies a ruleset, map, agent population, difficulty, hidden parameters, and team layout. The action set A collects the engine commands available to an agent, and Ω is the space of rendered reports. Determinism conditional on an engine random stream does not imply that an edited reload consumes that stream identically to an unedited run. The rendered policies {πᵢ} describe current aims rather than future commitments.

Queries.

The world model f(o_≤t₁,{πᵢ}) answers four query types. With g a visible quantity of one agent, e an event predicate on a trajectory segment, and m an operator on states, they are

\textscQuantity:P(g(s_t₁+h)|o_≤t₁,{πᵢ})reported as five quantiles,
\textscEvent:P(e(s_t₁:t₁+h)=1|o_≤t₁,{πᵢ})for binary items,
\textscTrait,\textscRules:P(θₖ|o_≤t₁)as a ranking or a bin, policies withheld,
\textscIntervene:P(g(s_t₁+h^′)|o_≤t₁,{πᵢ}, do(s_t₁←m(s_t₁))),

where s^′ follows T from m(s_t₁) under the unchanged policies, and θₖ denotes a queried trait or world parameter in θ_w. Mainline trajectories provide forecast targets, recorded hidden fields provide belief targets, and rerun arms provide intervention targets. Realized branch differences are not noise-free conditional average treatment effects. Matched placebos measure response to negligible or mechanism-irrelevant edits, while the model’s own no-intervention forecast defines its predicted effect.

References.

A reference predictor is a fixed map r(o_≤t₁). Persistence uses the current value, while the trend reference extrapolates the two most recent frames. The conceptual ceiling knows T and s_t₁ but not future u. Re-seeded reruns approximate its forecasting loss. The information sets of the ceiling and expert references are

ŷ_ceil∈\arg\min_ŷ𝔼[ℓ(ŷ,Y)|s_t₁,T],
ŷₑₓₚₑᵣₜ=h_H(o_≤t₁;K),

where K denotes expert knowledge and H the harness. The ceiling has complete state information, while the expert retains the model’s rendered history and adds knowledge and computation. The process evidence in Section6 consists of claims about g(s_τ), t₁<τ

Appendix D Corpus construction and engine patches

D.1 World generation

The evaluation corpus contains 475 worlds with four nominal decision points per world. The basic set fixes the ruleset to civ2civ3 and difficulty to hard, with 75 worlds in each of three map and population classes. The generalization set jointly varies ruleset, difficulty, map, civilization count, hidden parameters, and team structure. Table1 summarizes the map, population, and budget ranges. Hidden-parameter ranges are wider than in the development pool. The resulting shift does not require every OOD world to be harder than every ID world.

Mainline collection saves every turn and runs beyond the reporting budget to provide future targets. The reporting budgets are 400, 800, and 1,200 turns. Decision points are distributed from turn 60 to the reporting endpoint. Budget-specific forecast horizons and the final post-filtering prompt inventory are defined separately in AppendixE.

D.2 Engine and ruleset modifications

The benchmark uses Freeciv 3.1.6 with five source patches that make selected behavioral parameters effective and permit changes in diplomatic relations. Table5 summarizes their roles. Ruleset modifications widen trait ranges and enable domestic and intercontinental trade. Illness variants alter generation but their suffixes are not shown in model observations. The corpus and all intervention arms were collected with the resulting image, tagged freeciv-server:3.1.6-v2. The optional alliance-threshold patch is unapplied, and the later task-persistence patch enters only the agent-play image of AppendixN, not the benchmark engine.

Development checks tested diplomatic transitions, trait sensitivity, rule identifiability, team-game completion, and intervention persistence before model evaluation. They establish behavioral variation, while the final evidence gates define which inference questions are asked.

D.3 Replacements and branch collection

Three worlds were replaced after crashes or premature termination prevented target collection. Only their replacements enter the final question set.

Figure7 shows the four branches collected from each eligible checkpoint. Collection produces an unedited factual rerun, a factual recheck, a real intervention, and a matched placebo. Branches are saved every turn. Validation checks the applied edit, save continuity, and factual/recheck agreement over comparable saved states. Successful short runs contribute only horizons with recorded truth. Failed engine states are retried under recorded settings, including anchor-level reseeding where needed, and their control arms are regenerated consistently. The branch metadata records these deviations. No model prediction is used to select a retry.

Matching factual and recheck digests verifies replay, not shared randomness after an edit. End-turn settings, save frequency, reload behavior, and interventions can change subsequent random-number consumption. SectionG.5 reports placebo and reseeding diagnostics.

D.4 Integrity and provenance

Each world and branch record identifies the engine configuration, initial state, intervention, observation window, and available targets. The question verifier checks scoped leakage and consistency constraints before scoring. SectionG.4 reports these checks. Versioned checksums distinguish changes to experimental inputs from changes to scoring or presentation.

Appendix E Question construction

E.1 Observation windows and question scopes

Each question is associated with a world, decision turn, task, and observation condition. With the frame spacing of Section2, an anchor at turn 60 uses turns 20, 40, and 60. A narrative summarizes intervening events without including events after the anchor. The egocentric viewer is the median-scoring living civilization at that decision point. Its question scope includes itself and living civilizations it has contacted.

Belief questions omit the rendered policies because policy fields can reveal their hidden targets, and truth fields remain outside the model-facing prompt.

E.2 Numerical forecasts

Quantity requests the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of each eligible quantity. Treasury, population, city count, total city size, military and civilian unit counts, and enemy and ally counts are levels. Score, culture, and technology targets are increments from the decision point. Repeated Future Technology advances do not increase the technology count. Forecast horizons are 60/120, 120/250, and 200/300 turns for reporting budgets of 400, 800, and 1,200 turns, respectively.

Unavailable engine targets are not imputed. Constant culture in classic-rule worlds and technology increments after all technologies are known are excluded by the scorer’s eligibility rules. These exclusions are distinct from missing model answers, which receive the penalties specified in AppendixF.

E.3 Events and supplied base rates

Binary templates describe occurrences within a horizon or comparisons between the initial and final state. Leader items instead request a categorical distribution over civilizations. The first filter retains binary template–budget–horizon–decision-turn cells with empirical rates between 0.1 and 0.9. A second pass checks the reference cells actually used by each evaluation setting. Cells with at least 200 items use the setting-specific empirical rate. Sparse cells fall back to the corresponding corpus cell, which must also contain at least 200 items and satisfy the same rate filter. The final reference is therefore determined before model scoring, not by its valid outputs.

Each retained binary question prints its reference rate. Leader items retain their original categorical format and current-leader persistence reference. Intervention event prompts use the same reference-cell machinery. These rates are in-sample benchmark statistics supplied equally to all models, not estimates from an independent training set.

E.4 Hidden traits and world rules

Trait questions rank civilizations separately on aggression, expansion, trade, and building preference. Each ranking includes every rankable civilization exactly once and permits predicted ties. True ties are excluded from pairwise scoring. A scope with fewer than two rankable civilizations has no trait-ranking question.

World-rule questions classify disaster frequency, growth cost, and research cost into three bins. Disaster bins are at most 12, 13–40, and above 40. Growth- and research-cost bins are at most 82, 83–117, and above 117. Lower costs correspond to faster growth or research. Growth questions require at least one observed city-size change, and research questions require at least two completed technologies within the observation window. Egocentric evidence gates use the viewer’s evidence rather than inaccessible foreign events. Disaster questions have no additional event-count gate. Illness is not a benchmark target.

E.5 Intervention prompts and eligibility

An intervention prompt retains the history and describes the edit. Visible-state edits also update the affected current observation. Numerical and event subquestions are separate prompts, and a no-intervention control prompt is added when the required horizon or question set differs from the ordinary forecast. Each intervention is paired with this explicit control or the ordinary forecast, matching the target variables and horizons.

Table6 lists the numerical scoring targets. Standard budget horizons are used when they fall inside an operator’s declared band. Otherwise the longest resolved arm horizon in that band is selected. The available arm horizons are 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 200, 250, and 300 turns. The target mask is fixed before inspecting a model’s errors.

Real and placebo edits share their operator family but differ in magnitude or mechanism. For example, city-destruction arms remove large versus small cities. City count is excluded from their numerical target mask because both edits remove the same number of cities. Likewise, the government-enabling and placebo technology grants each add one technology, so their numerical target is a downstream score change rather than the identical count increment. Four single-trait operators replace the earlier composite-trait edit. Their collected modifiers are +90 for real edits and +3 for placebos. An accepted edit need not produce a favorable or nonzero downstream effect in every state. Main capture uses truth-moved cells, whereas specificity retains both moved and unmoved response cells.

Appendix F Metrics

Quantity aggregation.

The headline Quantity score pools model and reference losses within each world and quantity family before taking the ratio in Equation2. Families with zero reference loss are omitted. Valid families are averaged within each world, followed by equal weighting of worlds. Enemy and ally counts use the absolute error of the predicted median rather than the five-quantile loss in Equation1. The appendix’s family breakdown additionally equalizes variables within each family before averaging worlds. It is a diagnostic and its columns need not average to the headline Quantity score. The constants and variable transforms are shared across compared conditions. Pooling reduces sensitivity to small per-cell denominators but does not eliminate sensitivity when aggregate reference loss is small.

Events and hidden attributes.

Event gain combines calibration and discrimination, without identifying them separately. The template plot uses a Brier skill ratio only as a diagnostic. Trait averages pairwise ordering accuracy over four traits. Predicted ties receive half credit and true ties are excluded. Rules averages accuracies over the three rule parameters equally. Its majority reference and observer reference use the same parameter weights, rather than weights proportional to question counts.

Baselines for the reference adjustment.

The adjustment in Section4 uses b=0.5 for trait and direction accuracy and, for rules, the equal-parameter majority accuracy on the complete truth set, independent of a model’s missing or unparseable answers. Table7 reports the underlying accuracies.

Missing or unparseable outputs.

We retain required answer cells that a model omits or renders unparseably and count them as failed predictions, using the same policy for every model. For Quantity, a missing cell contributes twice its reference loss to the model-loss accumulator before the existing family aggregation and clipping. A wholly missing family therefore receives skill -1. The same rule uses the MAE reference for diplomacy. Families with zero reference loss remain undefined. Missing binary event probabilities receive Brier loss 1, and missing leader distributions receive multiclass Brier loss 2. Missing trait orderings and categorical labels receive zero accuracy. These penalties do not impute a forecast. For intervention capture, a missing arm or control prediction in cell c contributes 2|d_c| to the effect-error numerator, and its direction is counted as incorrect. For specificity, let r be the fraction of required response cells with valid arm and control predictions. We report r Spec_valid-(1-r), with score -1 when no responses are valid. Here Spec_valid is the valid-response selectivity score in Equation4. An all-valid set retains the original statistic. Raw loss and calibration diagnostics still require actual predictions. Incomplete experiments are reported at their available evaluation scope. Entirely unrun anchors are not counted as failed model attempts.

Interventions.

Capture uses truth-moved cells, d_c≠0, of the target civilization within each operator’s declared variable set and horizon band, applying the failure convention above. Zero predicted responses are excluded from the direction denominator. Correctness and selectivity use different denominators, so a specificity of 1 can accompany inaccurate real-arm predictions, and negative capture can accompany above-chance direction accuracy. For reference ceiling c_Capture, the completion percentage is 100(C+1)/(c_Capture+1), not the improvement over a no-effect prediction, which attains C=0 inside this display interval.

Paired analyses and uncertainty.

The paired analyses in Section5 intersect valid cells within each comparison and retain the original aggregation, truth, and reference losses. A cell is indexed by world, decision point, operator and arm when relevant, civilization, target, and horizon. Repeated event items with the same scored key retain their source-order occurrence index, assigned before validity filtering. The ablation builders preserve this order. Paired cells must have identical ground truth. Missing predictions are excluded jointly, so the paired estimate is conditional on common valid outputs and is not a missingness-adjusted full-run estimate. Quantity and Event intervals resample worlds jointly between conditions with 1,000 replicates and seed 2026. For capture, exponential world weights give a paired Bayesian bootstrap that keeps the eligible operator set fixed. If any included operator has only one world, no between-world interval is reported. These intervals do not quantify variation across repeated model calls, and the exploratory comparisons are not adjusted for multiple testing.

Appendix G Validation, reference lines, and evaluation noise

G.1 Repeated-future reference protocol

We sample 92 decision points stratified by evaluation set and turn budget. Each contributes 8 re-seeded reruns saved every turn, combined with a historical factual rerun to form the nine-member reference ensemble. The mainline’s rank among the nine trajectories has mean probability integral transform 0.49, compared with 0.5 under exchangeability. Fair CRPS and fair Brier losses correct for finite ensemble size. We report comparisons against mainline truth, leave-one-out comparisons against rerun truth, and an ensemble evaluated with the benchmark scorer. Leave-one-out estimates are the primary event reference because reload behavior can change the event distribution relative to the uninterrupted mainline.

Reload triggers AI government re-evaluation, changing the government-event distribution. Ten-turn saves also miss brief treasury-to-zero events, shifting their reference from -0.43 to +0.29 with per-turn recording. The historical factual member retains ten-turn evaluation, leaving a residual resolution mismatch. These template-specific distribution shifts remain despite the near-central aggregate rank. In Ego, the full-checkpoint observer remains a privileged reference rather than the Bayes limit of the rendered history.

G.2 Reference definitions and interpretation

G.2.1 Information sets of the numerical ceiling

Repeated futures approximate the forecast loss of the conceptual Ceiling, while the other columns use privileged observers, noise models, or an algebraic endpoint. Trait and rule observers infer labels from privileged behavioral evidence with target fields withheld, so their scores characterize empirical recoverability rather than proven information limits.

G.2.2 Trait and rule references

The trait observer is leave-world-out ridge regression on 33 privileged behavior statistics from the 80 turns preceding the decision point. Its accuracy ranges from 0.56–0.62 across traits, averaging 0.59 over all unequal pairs. Restricting true trait gaps to at least 40 raises the four-trait mean to 0.63, with a per-trait range of 0.59–0.66, and gaps of at least 60 raise it to 0.66. The displayed 0.66 is this well-separated-pair reference, whereas the model scores include all eligible unequal pairs. The accuracies in this paragraph precede the main table’s reference adjustment. The improvement with larger trait gaps indicates that behavioral evidence is more informative for strongly separated dispositions. The rule observer inverts growth and research-cost formulas where evidence is available and uses a leave-world-out classifier on disaster counts per city-turn for the remaining parameter. Disaster accuracy is 0.79 / 0.59 / 0.72. Averaging the three parameter references equally yields 0.93 / 0.86 / 0.90.

G.2.3 Intervention noise model

Let d_c be the observed real-arm effect and σ_c the root-mean-square placebo effect for the corresponding operator and quantity. The direction reference uses Φ(√\max(d_c²-σ_c²,0)/σ_c), where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. It is 0.71 / 0.71 / 0.68 over all moved cells and about 0.92 on the 48% (basic) / 42% (generalization) of moved cells with |d_c|>σ_c, whereas models are scored on all moved cells. The capture reference assumes centered Gaussian divergence and exact prediction of the underlying mechanism, so expected absolute residual error is σ_c√2/π. Substituting this into the operator-level capture ratio gives 1-∑_cσ_c√2/π/∑_c|d_c|, then the operator macro-average +0.39 / +0.39 / +0.30. Cell pooling gives +0.29 / +0.29 / +0.20, illustrating the effect of operator weighting. These estimates assume Gaussian divergence and transferable placebo variance. Completion expresses progress along the resulting reference scale.

G.2.4 Construction of the expert reference

The published Expert reference combines GPT-5.6 Sol with the frozen v3.3 manual and a tool-assisted harness on the shared 190-anchor sample.

Additional expert knowledge.

The v3.3 manual summarizes game rules, default-AI logic, engine patches, and empirical regularities from non-benchmark worlds. It covers growth and research formulas, behavioral cues for hidden targets, forecast intervals, and intervention reasoning, without target-world answers or model scores.

Harness and information boundary.

An independent agent handles each anchor–condition pair using the manual, canonical observations, task prompts, and a fixed answer inventory. It maintains working notes, uses Python for calculations, and answers sequentially to coordinate factual and intervention predictions. Access is restricted to this input pack, excluding external data, prior predictions, scores, hidden state, and future outcomes. The harness adds computation and multi-step reasoning without changing the evaluated world’s information boundary.

Validation and interpretation.

Table14 reports the combined effect of expert knowledge, tools, and reasoning resources under the same observations. Evaluation uses the fixed v3.3 manual and input packs, with answer inventories checked before scoring and standard penalties for missing or unparseable cells. Later manual revisions and expanded-information pilots are excluded.

G.3 Association with real-world forecasting performance

External associations.

Table9 shows positive Pearson and Spearman correlations between SWFI and matched-model forecasting scores across all reported tracks. Agreement in both score variation and ranking supports the use of CivWorldBench as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability.

Evaluation scope.

All comparisons use the same scores, missing-answer penalties, and reference scales as Tables3 and 14. The analysis uses 1,900 anchors for open models and 190 for Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol. Gemini 3.7 Flash, GPT-6 Astra, GLM-5.3 Flash, and Hunyuan Hy3 add evaluations on the same 60 anchors under the same scoring policy. Both subsets are stratified to match the full benchmark’s composition, as described in Section4, so the three sample sizes estimate the same quantities at different precision. As a check, SWFI recomputed on the 60 anchors is 27.5 for Sol against 27.7 on its 190 anchors, and 25.1 for Kimi K3 against 21.9 on the full grid. Neither difference changes either model’s rank among the matched models on any panel. The assisted expert is excluded as a non-independent model.

Expansion and matching protocol.

Weights and scales were fixed before evaluating the four additional models, selected for external overlap and API access. Leaderboard eligibility was refined during exploratory analysis after inspecting existing results. Table10 lists exact model identities, local scores, and eligible matches. Each model contributes one observation, with multiple external configurations handled as described below.

External sources and configurations.

ForecastBench [(Karger et al., 2025; ForecastBench, 2026)] uses the September 22, 2026 organizer tables for Tournament Overall and Preliminary Dataset. Preliminary remains provisional, and the two tracks overlap. Eligible rows retain their search/code and reasoning configurations. For multiple eligible variants, Table9 reports all correlation combinations. The main-text figure correlates each model’s median external score across configurations.

Metaculus FutureEval [(Metaculus, 2026)] uses the archived leaderboard PDF dated September 23, 2026 and its log-score-based Avg Score. All five matches use AskNews variants, although Opus and GPT reasoning levels differ from the local medium settings. Matching distinguishes Gemma 26B from Gemma 31B.

Prophet Arena [(Prophet Arena, 2026)] uses the Fixed Context SKILL snapshot retrieved September 23, 2026 at 16:17 China Standard Time, with six exact model matches. SKILL is the fitted market-anchored parameter θ. Retired models retain their last scores. Evidence and inference budgets can differ within the shared track. FutureX is excluded because a common-framework comparison could not be established.

Sensitivity and uncertainty.

Pearson correlation measures linear association, while Spearman correlation measures rank agreement. Each comparison uses models with observed scores on both benchmarks.

Table11 shows that Preliminary and FutureEval retain strong correlations after each model is removed, while Tournament is more sensitive to model removal. The reported ranges cover leave-one-model-out estimates and eligible configurations. Exact two-sided permutation tests are exploratory and unadjusted for multiple comparisons. With four matched models the smallest attainable two-sided p is 0.083, so the Tournament panel cannot reach significance at any correlation. The pooled test in Section5 standardizes each panel’s external scores, pools the 20 model–panel pairs over 10 distinct models, and permutes SWFI across models so that a model’s pairs move together, with 200,000 draws. It gives r=0.73 and p=0.009, and r=0.73 with p=0.006 after dropping the Tournament panel, which overlaps Preliminary. The SWFI–AA correlation over eleven models has permutation p=0.007. These analyses condition on observed scores and model panels, leaving external score uncertainty, decoding variation, and model-family dependence outside their uncertainty estimates.

The AA Intelligence Index v4.3 [(Artificial Analysis, 2026)] provides a general-capability reference for the eleven main-table models, excluding the assisted expert. Table13 reports its association with each metric, where the forecasting and Capture columns track the index and the belief columns do not. Table12 separately compares SWFI and AA against the same forecasting outcomes on matched models.

G.4 Evidence sensitivity and construction checks

Question targets are computed from recorded engine states and trajectories. Automated validation covers 1,900 decision points and 22,763 prompts, including 4,264 intervention-event prompts excluded from the reported task inventory. No violations were detected in the tested constraints. The checks cover hidden-key and future-turn leakage, observer scope, event-cell eligibility, hidden-rule evidence gates, intervention horizon bands and arm pairing, and the task-specific presence of policy summaries. SectionH.3 reports the paired evidence-sensitivity ablations.

G.5 Noise sources and reload checks

Uncertainty arises from future engine randomness, ambiguity in partially observed state, reload and temporal-resolution effects, and finite evaluation samples. Repeated futures address the first source, privileged observers characterize the second under their stated information sets, and replay checks address the third. World bootstraps estimate sampling uncertainty across worlds conditional on the recorded model outputs.

All intervention truths use rerun factual arms from the same saved checkpoint rather than the uninterrupted mainline. Saves are taken every turn so short-lived events are not missed. The RNG-sharing diagnostic compares 141,250 placebo cells with 11,091 re-seeded cells: mean normalized absolute divergence is 0.116 versus 0.259, and 56.1% of placebo cells have zero divergence. Only 3,752 of 28,968 compared saved turns, or 13.0%, have identical digests. The low digest agreement shows that edited and unedited runs can follow different random streams. The divergence means describe different cell populations, so the comparison is descriptive. Placebo rollouts characterize variation introduced along the edit and reload path. Intervention errors therefore reflect both effect-estimation error and stochastic branch divergence.

Appendix H Full results

H.1 Complete three-setting results

Table14 reports all seven metrics in Omni-ID, Ego, and Omni-OOD, using the score sources and references of Table3. SWFI averages the three settings. The expert uses the shared 190-anchor sample and the knowledge and harness specified in SectionG.2.4, with the same failure penalties as other models.

H.2 Detailed model profiles

Figure8 compares the six quantity families across all models and settings. Overall-score increments remain difficult despite positive skill on many stock quantities. The diagnostic equalizes variables within families as specified in AppendixF. Tables15 and 16 further show that hidden-target recovery varies across attributes. Table14 shows model-dependent changes under OOD shift: Flash-Next improves in quantity forecasting, Opus 5 changes little, and Gemma 4 declines. The OOD set changes rulesets and trajectory budgets without matching ID difficulty or selecting worlds to enforce a particular score ordering.

H.3 Information ablations and three-game study notes

Paired design.

The Flash-Next ablations use 60 basic worlds, or 240 anchors, in Omni-ID, except the primer, which covers 40 worlds. Each row of Table17 uses its own common valid cells and paired world-bootstrap interval, so baselines can differ across rows. The conditions remove history or thinking, add generic rules, supply privileged future narratives, or add study notes. Future narratives provide an information control rather than a deployable forecast input.

Study input and notes.

The one-shot study uses three independently seeded, 3-civilization, 400-turn games outside the evaluation corpus. Each is summarized at turns 60, 145, 230, 315, and 400, with intervening narratives. The 411,688-character input produces an 11,221-character note reused across 1,624 evaluation prompts. No model parameters are updated, and the note is not revised during evaluation.

Forecasting gains.

Table17 shows a paired quantity gain of +0.086 with interval [+0.061, +0.111]. Notes also improve event Brier gain from -0.034 to -0.015. This event comparison uses the no-base-rate protocol, including eligible leader items. Supplying base rates is a separate condition that reaches +0.012 from the same baseline.

Table18 shows similar gains for real and placebo capture, both remaining below zero. Notes also change the no-intervention forecast. Thus, learned context improves forecasting broadly, while selective responses to intervention mechanisms remain difficult.

H.4 Intervention breakdowns and mechanism cards

Direction-conditioned magnitude distributions.

Figure4 examines effect magnitudes among correct-sign predictions under the main score’s real-arm, target-variable, horizon-band, and truth-movement rules. Predicted and realized effects use the transformed, normalized differences in Section4.1. Eligible cells exclude undefined control-relative loss ratios, including zero-loss control forecasts, with counts in Table22. Diagnostic direction accuracy is the cell-weighted fraction of correct signs among valid nonzero responses. The main score additionally penalizes missing answers and weights operator scores by eligible-cell counts. Tables19, 20 and 21 report missing and zero responses separately. Relative magnitude is |δ̂|/|δ|, where δ̂ and δ denote predicted and realized effects. Figure medians and 25th–75th percentile bars summarize its distribution across correct-sign cells, with 100% denoting a magnitude match. Ratios are cell-weighted and unclipped, with linearly interpolated quantiles. Additional bins classify predictions below half, within a factor of two, or above twice the realized magnitude, using inequalities in the same scoring space. The conditional score S₊ applies the clipped equal-operator Capture formula to correct-sign cells, retaining operators with at least three such cells.

Conditional results.

Table23 shows that near-matching medians coexist with broad magnitude distributions across settings. In Omni-ID, six of eleven models have negative S₊ estimates, with intervals entirely below zero for gpt-oss, Gemma, and DeepSeek. For these models, magnitude errors persist even when the direction is correct. GLM-5.3 has positive S₊ with an interval above zero, while its main Capture remains negative and its direction intervals exceed chance in all three settings. Its conditional improvement illustrates the contribution of wrong-direction predictions to overall error. A correct-sign prediction above twice the realized magnitude has greater absolute error than a zero-effect prediction. Table22 shows that these overshoots persist, at lower frequencies, after removing effects at or below each operator’s lower quartile before conditioning on correct signs. Underestimation and overestimation therefore remain relevant beyond the smallest effects, motivating state-conditioned magnitude calibration.

Sampling and interpretation.

The magnitude bars describe dispersion across predictions, and intervals follow AppendixF. Model-specific samples and correct-sign subsets differ, so these comparisons diagnose within-model errors. Conditioning also changes the cells and operators included in S₊ relative to main Capture. The targets are realized stochastic branch differences, and future calibration studies should evaluate gains on held-out worlds.

item.title: 20 个模型在《杀戮尖塔》打到最高难度：第一幕能追平专家，越往后越掉队 ｜ SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
item.description:
一句话：给模型完整的商业游戏本体做长程策略评测：前沿模型超启发式基线、追平普通玩家，但远落后专家。

要点：

  • 让模型玩完整的商业卡牌构筑游戏 Slay the Spire，早期决策决定长期结果，测的是真正的长程策略
  • 20 个大模型在最高难度下：前沿模型超过启发式基线、追平普通人类玩家，但与专家差距随对局变长而扩大
  • 把所有游戏术语做自洽改名后性能下降，说明部分表现来自对这款游戏的先验知识；跨局写下的记忆常错且过度保守，没能提升表现

为什么值得看：「模型会玩游戏」和「模型会规划」是两件事；把整局切片成战斗级与战役级来看，才能看出它在哪一层掉队。

中文摘要：agentic 大模型已经能处理复杂任务，但长程的策略推理研究不足：多数 agent 基准短且情节化，长任务的表现也很难拆成记忆知识、推理与运气。SpireBench 让模型完整地玩商业卡牌构筑游戏《杀戮尖塔》，在这款游戏里早期决策决定长期成败。作者测试了 20 个大语言模型在最高难度下的表现：前沿模型能超过启发式基线、追平普通玩家的平均水平，但离专家仍差很远，而且差距随对局推进而拉大——最强模型在第一幕的胜率与专家相当，之后就掉队。区分强弱的关键是每场战斗打得好不好，而所有模型都对整局的风险判断失误，宁可保血也不愿花血变强。把所有游戏术语做一次自洽的改名后，模型表现下降，说明部分能力来自对这款游戏的先验知识；模型也不会从自己跨局写下的记忆中变强，那些记忆常常是错的且过度保守。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-08

本期推送：2026-10-25

SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire

Abstract

Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game’s highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) progress has been rapid, with high scores on tests of a wide range of general-intelligence-aligned skills [(Sajadieh et al., 2026)], and LLMs increasingly act as autonomous agents over extended periods [(Brohi et al., 2025)]. However, single-step competence does not necessarily translate into reliable performance over many sequential decisions, a shortfall termed the horizon gap[(Chen et al., 2026)]. Performance on long tasks is also hard to dissect: does a model rely on stored knowledge or on reasoning [(Lowe, 2024)], and can it store and effectively use long-term memories? How is it impacted by stochasticity?

Existing evaluations leave these questions open. Agentic benchmarks [(Yehudai et al., 2026)] are mostly short-horizon, with little carried between episodes; game benchmarks [(Paglieri et al., 2025)] rarely hand a model every decision a player makes, or ask whether performance reflects prior knowledge, reasoning or luck; and reported memory gains [(Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024)] usually come with an external check on what was learned.

We introduce SpireBench, built on the commercial game Slay the Spire (StS), which combines tactical combat, deck construction and route planning over 56 floors (Fig. 1). It is turn-based, fully describable in text, and its choices involve weighing short-term gains over long term success at multiple time horizons, making it well suited for a long-horizon benchmark (Appx.A). Unlike previous work on benchmarking StS [(Bateni and Whitehead, 2024; Park et al., 2026)], SpireBench interacts directly with all aspects of the game, and allows for separating knowledge from reasoning.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    A harness for the complete original game. Agents play the unmodified commercial game through our harness, making every decision a human player makes (a first) and seeing the same information as a human player would. We allow the model to return a whole turn’s actions as multiple tool calls in one response, and the harness reports the effect of each action back to the model. Against its other variants on the same models and seeds, it plays further and costs less per floor (Table2).

  • •

    A benchmark at the game’s highest difficulty, calibrated against human data. We evaluate 20 LLMs at Ascension 20 on the same ten held-out seeds, with cost and reasoning spend. For a human performance reference we use Mega Crit’s released telemetry (206 k A20 Ironclad runs) and the run histories of 4 expert streamers. Frontier models beat rule-based and symbolic baselines and the average human player, yet remain far from expert play. The benchmark tracks the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but is among the least predictable from other evaluations.

  • •

    Knowledge ablation with reskin. We reskin the entire game with a holistically consistent theme, separating prior knowledge of the game from reasoning about its rules. Hiding the real names costs performance, concentrated in a few models. Random and permuted control mappings show that the cost comes from the knowledge attached to familiar names, not from reading unfamiliar ones.

  • •

    Memory mechanisms, and what the models write. We allow models to write notes and memories within their run and between runs with various methods. No memory formation between runs is able to improve play. Reading the banks shows why: 17% of memories are false, advice to be cautious outnumbers advice to take risks seven to one, reinforcing existing tendencies, and nothing prunes errors.

  • •

    Analysis of model understanding and failures. We probe the models to predict future game states to evaluate their understanding of play, demonstrating that more performant models are better able to predict near-term game states, but not capable of predicting long-term success. Comparing model in-game choices against humans, the best models are too conservative, failing to amortize their risk profile across the run into earlier sections so they do not take the risks needed to outpace the game’s difficulty curve.

    • 2 Background

    Slay the Spire is a seminal roguelike deck-builder game, in which players have to balance decision making over several horizons (Fig. 1). In combat turns the player draws a hand from a deck of cards and spends a limited pool of energy to attack, block, or build effects that scale over turns; between fights they add and sometimes remove cards from a deck, and pick a route through a map of nodes (consisting of fights, elite fights, events, shops, and rests — Fig. 1 middle row). Decisions are taken under uncertainty and compound: a card once taken usually stays in the deck across the run, and threats met very late in the game must be prepared for early. A core component is balancing risk, since riskier options early yield the growth that the rising difficulty curve demands (Fig.1). These are properties shared with other long tasks agents face (Appx.A).

    2.1 Related work

    Slay the Spire. Analyses of the game measure its mix of luck and skill [(Andersson et al., 2023; Nam and Rerkjirattikal, 2023)] and the complexities of its map uncertainty [(Bazzaz and Cooper, 2025)]. MiniStS [(Bateni and Whitehead, 2024)] tests LLMs on 8 cards and 5 isolated encounters, evaluating micro-play but no macro-level deck-building. The twelve-game benchmark Orak[(Park et al., 2026)] drives the real game through the CommunicationMod harness [(ForgottenArbiter and others, 2019)], but its LLM plays only combat and card rewards, at Ascension 0 on one seed, with a rule-based bot doing the rest. In another approach, Bottled AI, a symbolic AI was handcrafted to play the game [(Bottled AI contributors, 2022)]. While it does not support every card or event, it does report high performance. Finally, in concurrent and most comparable work, AgenticSTS [(Cheng et al., 2026)], plays complete runs of the sequel Slay the Spire 2. However, the sequel is still in early access with fortnightly balance patches, making it unsuited for benchmarking purposes, and AgenticSTS only plays the game at its lowest difficulty, and was mainly tested with one model. Overall, no existing evaluation has an LLM make every decision in the released game, tests it at the highest difficulty, studies more than a few models, compares against human play, or controls for the models’ prior knowledge of the game. SpireBench plays Slay the Spire at its highest difficulty (A20) across many more models (20). We evaluated model performance against extensive human telemetry, with a controlled reskin; to our knowledge, ours is the first harness giving a model the complete original game.

    Games as benchmarks. Deep reinforcement learning reached superhuman play in Atari, Go, chess and shogi [(Mnih et al., 2015; Silver et al., 2016; Silver et al., 2018)] and hard-exploration games [(Ecoffet et al., 2021)] by training on the game. LLM agents are evaluated untrained, in NetHack, Crafter and Minecraft [(Küttler et al., 2020; Hafner, 2022; Wang et al., 2024)], benchmark suites [(Paglieri et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024a)] and commercial games from frames [(Zhang et al., 2025)], mostly on simplified states or partial games and rarely with learning across runs. The nearest deck-builder benchmark, BalatroBench [(Coder, 2026)], has shorter horizons and only the basic difficulty; earlier deck-construction work searches whole decks before play [(García-Sánchez et al., 2016)].

    Long-horizon benchmarks. Tool-use, web and agentic benchmarks [(Jimenez et al., 2024; Mialon et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b)] are mostly tens of steps long; others lengthen the horizon by task duration [(Kwa et al., 2025)], execution length [(Sinha et al., 2026)] or a simulated business over tens of millions of tokens [(Backlund and Petersson, 2025)]. Trading [(Li et al., 2025a)] is long but has a fixed action space. In contrast, a Slay the Spire agent builds the action space it gets to act in later.

    Memory across episodes. Agents with persistent memory [(Park et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023)] have previously been found to improve across episodes [(Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Majumder et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025)] given an external check on what is stored; without one, models struggle to self-correct [(Huang et al., 2024)] and propagate errors in stored experience [(Xiong et al., 2026)]. We test memory on a long, stochastic task with no such check.

    Reskinning. Renaming entities but not mechanics probes memorization against reasoning: nonsense predicates [(Valmeekam et al., 2023)], changed rules [(Wu et al., 2024b)], isomorphic worlds [(Gu et al., 2026)], masked names [(Hu et al., 2026)], renamed security tasks [(Honarvar et al., 2026)] and re-textured game objects [(Dubey et al., 2018)]; other benchmarks generate environments a model cannot have seen [(Costarelli et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b)]. Our reskin covers the whole game with names evoking each mechanic, with random and permuted controls (Sec.3), paired within seed.

    3 Methods

    Agent harness. Agents play the released game through CommunicationModPlus, our fork of CommunicationMod [(ForgottenArbiter and others, 2019)], which exchanges JSON states and text commands and adds snapshots around each enemy’s turn. The harness holds one conversation per floor, shared by a combat, its rewards, and the post-floor reflection. See Figs.5 and B in the appendix for an overview and example floor.

    A cached system prompt holds the task instructions, a compendium of the game’s rules and items, and the memory bank (Sec.3); each floor adds the act map, the run’s notes and the player’s state. The model acts only through tool calls, interleaving reasoning with action [(Yao et al., 2023)], and may return a whole turn’s actions in one response (multi-action); they run in order up to the first that fails, and each state change is returned as the result of the call that caused it.

    Our multi-action implementation asks the model to plan the turn before acting and needs fewer calls: a turn costs one response and one pass over the context, where one action per call pays for both again at every card. This is non-trivial to work with since the action space can shift during a turn; we ask models to internalize these changes to make correct tool calls, and interrupt the action queue if an unpredictable event occurs. MiniStS makes one call per action [(Bateni and Whitehead, 2024)]; Orak's agent may return several actions but spends three calls on each decision (reflection, planning, action), shows only the state they leave, re-plans only once they are spent, and leaves every mid-fight card interaction selection to its rule bot [(Park et al., 2026)]; AgenticSTS submits combat as a plan and rebuilds the prompt for every decision by retrieval [(Cheng et al., 2026)]. Table2 compares the designs and measures ours against its variants and Orak on the same models and seeds. Ours sees what a human player sees, without strategic steering. It plans a route each act, forecasts at the end of each floor its chances of surviving the act and winning the run, and may predict its HP when it ends a turn. Reasoning is kept across turns wherever the provider allows, and no response reached the output ceiling (Sec.B.2).

    Notes and memory. After each floor the model may write, overwrite or delete free-form run notes under keys of its choosing. After each run it consolidates them into its persistent memory bank one operation at a time (save, delete or finish); the bank enters every later run’s system prompt, so a read-write cohort is a chain played in seed order. We conduct memory ablation experiments to investigate the utility of this schema (Sec.B.3).

    Knowledge reskin. Unless stated otherwise every run is reskinned: each game-specific name the model can see is replaced by a name from a hand-written internally-consistent mapping themed around tabletop RPGs. We do this so we can evaluate the model’s ability to reason about the game, ablating as much prior information about rules of thumb for how to play StS which it may have seen in pretraining as possible. The model’s own text is not renamed, so a real game name it writes or thinks is evidence of recognition of the base game. We conduct ablation experiments to evaluate the effect of this thematic renaming compared to the original or a randomized rename vocabulary (Sec.B.4).

    Models and reasoning settings. We evaluate hosted models from Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Z.ai, and open-weight Qwen, Nemotron and gpt-oss models on our own hardware. Table1 runs each at its highest reasoning setting (grey, beside its name), resolved to the nearest level the provider supports at or above the request (Sec.C.1).

    Evaluation protocol. Every main result is on the Ironclad at Ascension 20, the hardest difficulty, on the same ten seeds—freshly minted both to prevent hyperparameter optimization against model/seed pairs used during preliminary experiments, and so that model providers cannot have trained on our earlier results on these seeds [(Sainz et al., 2023)]. A cohort is one model under one configuration on these seeds; each table cell is one cohort, validated by the analysis code (Sec.C.2). We score a run by the acts it clears (Act 4 ends with the Heart) and also report the floor it reaches. A run clears Acts 1 and 2 by beating their (randomly selected) bosses; Act 3 by beating two random bosses; and Act 4 by killing the Corrupt Heart. The act k win rate is the share of runs that cleared Act k; mean acts cleared (0–4), is our headline summary. Floor is the final floor reached. A frontier cohort can cost hundreds of dollars (Table33), so ten seeds is a budget decision, too few to reliably order neighbouring models but sufficient for broader trends.

    Baselines and cost. Three non-LLM policies play the same seeds without seeing names: pick first option and pick random option bracket the models from below; BottledAI[(Bottled AI contributors, 2022)] is a hand-written symbolic player (Sec.C.5).

    Human references at the same setting, scored alike, are the run histories of four expert streamers (Table1) and 206,082 finished runs of the game’s telemetry, released by Mega Crit. Human games are not matched cohorts against the LLM seeds (Appx.D).

    4 Results

    Performance and cost. Our benchmark results are shown in Table1. We will first consider baseline, symbolic, and human comparisons. Always picking the first option or picking a random option. Neither baseline reaches very far even into the first act. The BottledAI symbolic model [Bottled AI contributors (2022)] can beat act 1, but goes no further. In contrast, even the average human player in a 200,000 runs human dataset reaches and wins the final act 4% of the time. Top level players comfortably reach 50+% winrates. This illustrates that the game is non-trivial, and has a very high skill ceiling.

    In our LLM cohort, the strongest models are Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, and only Sol kills the Heart (the final boss), once; they are also among the most expensive, per run and per floor (Fig.2(a)). Mid-tier models outperform Bottled AI but not the average human, and four models never clear an act, no better than the random-choice policy. Performance tracks the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (Fig.2(b)), but reasoning spent does not buy play: GPT-6 Astra thinks least per floor (3.3k tokens) and clears 1.50 acts, while Nemotron 3 Nano Omni thinks most (34.0k) and clears none.

    Comparison with human players. The strongest models clear more acts than the average Ascension 20 Ironclad run in Mega Crit's telemetry (0.73) and than players with over 1000 hours (0.92), but far fewer than the four streamers (2.5–3.1 acts). The gap opens as the run lengthens (Tables1 and 4): the three strongest models win 90% of their Act 1 runs, as the streamers do (85–92%), but 40–50% of Act 2 against 65–78%, and 0–20% of Act 3 against 56–71%. Consequently, the models have a drastically lower win rate for the full game (Act 4) at 0–10% against 46–65%. These results are a demonstration of the horizon gap of [Chen et al. (2026)], exhibited within a single task.

    How the models spend a run. The models play Act 1 cautiously. They fight 0.9–1.4 elites, against 2.0 for the telemetry population and 2.6 for the streamers, rest at 57–75% of rest sites against 23% and 9%, and rest at 31% of the rest sites they enter with at least 70% HP, where the population does so at 2% and the streamers never, upgrading a card instead, a permanent boon for the rest of the game. At the Act 1 boss the top four models hold a median 90% of their maximum HP, the streamers 53% (Fig.3; Sec.E.1). Since the transition to the next act restores 75% of missing HP, HP carried to the end of an act keeps only a quarter of its value; the scarce resource is floors in which to outgrow enemies that scale as the game progresses. Human runs that play Act 1 as the models do clear Act 2 in 15% of cases, against 38% for runs that fight more elites and rest less (Table13), and in the models' own runs upgrading rather than resting predicts clearing Act 2 (r=0.56, 49 runs). Experience does not change this: over a chain, rest and elite rates move no differently from no-memory runs; the banks advise caution seven times as often as risk; and the four strongest models record the end-of-act heal correctly yet still rest in 21 of the 32 late-act decisions that weigh it. The route explains only about a fifth of the gap to the streamers; the rest is how the fights are played.

    Strong models fight better. What separates the models is neither the route (Sec.E.1) nor, much, the deck. Agreement with human card picks barely rises with model strength (Spearman ρ=0.16), no model builds its deck for the act boss the map shows, and the one deck-building signal is taking area-damage cards (46% of Act 1 offers for the top four models, 20% for the bottom tier; ρ=0.76). The fights separate them. The top four take 8.2 damage per Act 1 hallway fight, the bottom tier 14.0 (ρ=-0.87, 19 models; Table14). Every tier spends the same energy and blocks the same share of incoming damage; the strong models turn the energy into damage (7.5 against 5.8 per energy spent on attacks, ρ=0.91), rarely block on a turn when no enemy attacks (6% against 31%) and never miss a lethal play in hand (0% against 8.7%), so they kill a turn sooner and are hit less. The difference holds on the same encounter of the same seed, including the first six floors, before the decks diverge, and about three quarters of the top–bottom gap in Act 1 boss wins (94% against 19%) is not explained by the state in which the models arrive.

    Relation to public LLM benchmarks. Across 30 model and effort points, mean acts cleared tracks the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index closely (Pearson r=0.82, Spearman ρ=0.89; Fig.2(b)), but the public evaluations behind it, among them GPQA Diamond [(Rein et al., 2024)] and SciCode [(Tian et al., 2024)], are strongly correlated with each other too [(Burnell et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2024)]. Among them SpireBench is one of the least substitutable (Table18 in Appx.H): the other evaluations predict 50% of its variance for a held-out model, against 85% for Humanity's Last Exam [(Center for AI Safety et al., 2026)], consistent with lmgame-Bench, where a game probes a blend of capabilities that other benchmarks test in isolation [(Hu et al., 2026)]. Of the agentic evaluations, only Terminal-Bench 4.0 adds information beyond knowledge and reasoning scores (Table19).

    The harness moves scores as much as neighbouring models differ. On the same models and seeds (Table2), Orak's harness, whose rule bot plays every non-combat floor, reaches 3.3 fewer floors than ours and clears 0.15 fewer acts, a gap as large as that between many neighbouring models, and its own failures ended 11 of the 70 seeds. The comparison uses eight mostly weaker models, which clear 0.20 acts on those seeds with our harness and 0.04 with Orak's; its effect on frontier models is untested. Orak spends 85% fewer tokens per floor but costs only 31% less: most of our input is cached. One action per response needs 3.0 more calls per floor, costs 23% more and loses 0.07 acts, a loss that disappears when choices are also made by number (+0.00 acts), so cost is the robust advantage of multi-action. One conversation for the whole run costs 22% more per floor, loses 0.06 acts and raises tool-call errors from 0.8 to 2.2 per 100 calls [(Liu et al., 2024a; Sinha et al., 2026)].

    Memory does not compound. Agents that accumulate experience across episodes are reported to improve with it [(Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Majumder et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Suzgun et al., 2026)]; ours do not, nor did the episodic store of [Cheng et al. (2026)] in StS2 (6/10 wins with and without it). Consolidating a run's notes into a memory bank or writing a compact summary has no impact on the number of acts won (see Fig.17 and Table27). Carrying the notes from during the run forward verbatim without a memory consolidation or compaction phase does slightly better (+0.06 acts): the rewriting adds nothing, much as iterative rewriting of an agent's context erodes its detail [(Zhang et al., 2026)]. Without an external check on what is stored, models do not reliably correct their own reasoning [(Huang et al., 2024)], and agents propagate the errors they store [(Xiong et al., 2026)]. A run gives one delayed, noisy outcome for hundreds of decisions, so nothing verifies a consolidated memory, and the bank grows run on run (Fig.19). Moreover, in the final banks 17% of memories are false, mostly generalizations from a single run, and models whose banks hold more errors of their own clear fewer acts (Spearman ρ=-0.67, permutation p=0.002, n=20; Table20). Nothing prunes them: over the 200 runs the models opt to delete only 30 memories.

    Prior knowledge is part of the score. Renaming or altering a familiar task has exposed reliance on memorized content [(Valmeekam et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024b; McCoy et al., 2024)], while capture-the-flag agents are largely robust to renaming [(Honarvar et al., 2026)]. Our result lies between. Hiding the real names costs 0.14 acts and 11 points of Act 1 win rate, pooled over 12 model configurations (11 models) and every paired seed (Table29; per model with all 10 seeds, Table3), concentrated in a few: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash falls from 0.80 acts to 0.30 and GPT-5.6 Luna from 0.60 to 0.10 (Table30). Nonsense names cost least (0.01 acts), so unfamiliar words are not the difficulty; the two permuted mappings, which give each entity the name (real or themed) of another, cost about as much as the themed one (0.10 and 0.12). A familiar name pulls a model towards what it usually means although the prompt states the rules [(McCoy et al., 2024)]: the signature of knowledge acquired in training, which contamination studies seek in static benchmarks [(Golchin and Surdeanu, 2024)] and we show by intervention. The reskin hides names, not the game: in 125 of the 190 themed runs of Table1 with full logs (Gemma 4 E4B has none), from 18 of 19 models, the model recognizes Slay the Spire or a real entity the reskin replaced, yet recognition does not buy back the cost (Spearman ρ=0.18, permutation p=0.62; Table21).

    Models forecast the next turn, not the consequences for the rest of the run. Larger models are reported to be well calibrated on questions they can answer [(Kadavath et al., 2022)], while confidence stated in words tends to be overconfident [(Xiong et al., 2024)]; here the horizon decides which holds. Models that forecast the next turn's HP well clear more acts (Spearman ρ=-0.84 between error and acts; Table16). This forecast measures the fight-reading skill above: on turns where the intents shown determine the next HP exactly, the bottom tier still mispredicts it 31% of the time and the top four 0.5%. Forecasts of surviving the act are poorly calibrated: the four models that never clear an act give themselves a 55–76% chance, about as much as the four strongest (59–74%), whose forecasts are followed by surviving the act 63–76% of the time (Fig.14 in Appx.G), and they barely sharpen as the act nears its end (Fig.15). Card-reward policy, failures in the reasoning traces and tool-call errors are analysed in Appx.H (Tables22, 24 and 23).

    5 Discussion

    Our findings consistently demonstrate that agentic models fail to calibrate risk correctly over the long-term. Where the outcome is a turn or a fight away, the strongest models are competent: they win the first act as often as streamers do, win almost every ordinary fight and forecast the next turn well, though they still lose more HP in each fight than humans do. At the time horizon of an act or a run away, they fall behind: the gap to the streamers opens from Act 2, boss fights decide where each model stops, forecasts of surviving an act barely sharpen; moreover, what a model writes down for later runs does not compound. Our findings are indicative of the horizon gap of [Chen et al. (2026)], but within one task whose time scales share a single pool of resources. Measured as a time horizon [(Kwa et al., 2025)], the fall is a step: every model succeeds on at least 87% of its turns and falls below 50% between a fight and a run, for most models already at the act (Table17). The difficulty is not how long a model can keep going: it is fighting well enough to afford risk, and spending early floors on growth whose payoff comes an act later, which no model learns from its own runs. Any agent planning over a long, stochastic task with one delayed outcome needs memories checked against outcomes and forgotten when wrong, forecasts that sharpen as the stakes approach, and a harness that plays the whole task (Sec.5).

    Four findings confirm mechanisms that prior work demonstrated outside games. The harness is part of the score, as for other agents [(Kapoor et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024)]. Unverified memory does not compound wherever the outcome is delayed and noisy over many decisions, as in most open-ended deployments; where a verifier exists, such as tests for code, the reported gains should hold. Long contexts cost performance[(Liu et al., 2024a; Sinha et al., 2026)]. Calibration degrades with the horizon in any task whose outcomes resolve at several distances.

    Limitations.The ordering of models is measured on one character in a turn-based game played from parsed text; other characters, genres, real-time control or perception would weight the decisions differently. The size of the reskin cost depends on how much of this game each model saw in training, and the reskin hides names but not familiarity with deck-builders, so it is a lower bound. The human comparison is not seed-matched. Ten seeds per cohort cannot order neighbouring models, and providers can change the model behind an identifier without notice.
