    Appendices

    Appendix A Why Slay the Spire

    Slay the Spire is a seminal game that helped establish the roguelike deck-builder genre, and the properties that make it hard are those that make any long task hard for an agent.

    Every choice recurs. A card added to the deck on the second floor is drawn again in every later fight, so it has to be useful not only against the next enemy but against the act bosses an hour later, and a bad addition cannot simply be undone: card removals are limited opportunities and the deck starts with cards (Strikes) which the player would already benefit from removing, so adding a bad card puts the player down a card removal for the rest of the game. The consequences of a decision are therefore spread thinly over hundreds of later ones—this is the credit-assignment problem of long-horizon execution, where small per-step errors compound over the length of a task [(Sinha et al., 2026)]. The only verdict on the run as a whole, a win or a loss, comes at its end.

    An archetype is not a deck. Players learn named strategies, such as building around Strength or around exhausting cards, but each run offers a random array of cards and relics based on its seed. A plan must be devised as the run unfolds rather than determined in advance, and the agent has to judge when to commit to a plan and when to abandon it. A card's worth also depends on the cards and relics already held: a card that scales with Strength is weak in a deck with no source of Strength and strong in one with several, so cards cannot be valued one at a time.

    The agent builds its own action space. In combat, the actions open to the player on a turn are the cards in hand, and the hand is drawn from a deck the player assembled. Every card reward, purchase, removal and upgrade therefore decides which actions will exist in later fights: the agent chooses not only its moves but the set of moves it will later choose among. This is a sharper form of what an agent does when it builds a library of skills or tools for later use [(Wang et al., 2024)], with the difference that here the library is also a liability, since every card added is one more card that may be drawn in place of the one that was needed. Even a single turn is a small planning problem, because the order of plays matters: an attack does half as much again to an enemy made Vulnerable first, so Bash is played before the Strikes it sets up.

    Each fight tests the deck differently. A deck is not good or bad in general but against a particular fight. Groups of enemies call for damage that hits all of them; long fights against enemies that grow stronger call for cards that scale, while short ones call for damage up front; and some enemies punish a kind of play outright: Gremlin Nob gains Strength whenever a Skill is played, the Awakened One whenever a Power is played, and the Time Eater takes over the turn once a set number of cards has been played. A card bought to pass one of these checks can weaken the deck against another, and every card added dilutes the draws for all of them, so the player must decide which checks the deck has to pass, which it can afford to scrape through, and in what order the run will set them.

    Risk is amortized over the run. HP, gold, potions and the deck form one irreversible pool that carries from floor to floor. Taking an elite fight costs HP now for a relic that pays out over every later fight; resting at a campfire recovers HP at the price of an upgrade. The right choice depends on what the rest of the run will demand, so the agent must price present resources against a future it can only estimate, and how well it does so shows in how well calibrated those estimates are.

    The challenges ahead are known in kind but not in detail. Each act draws its fights from a fixed pool, and the map shows the types of room ahead, so a player who remembers what the act's elites and bosses do can build the deck to meet them; one who does not meets each as a surprise. Doing well therefore needs memory across runs as well as within one, which is the setting in which memory mechanisms for LLM agents are proposed [(Park et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023)] but seldom tested over long, stochastic episodes.

    Some of the game is fixed and some is dealt. Within a fight, each enemy shows its intended action for the coming turn, and enemies follow move patterns that can be learned, so the threat on the current turn is known exactly and a turn can be planned as a deterministic puzzle. What the player will draw next turn, which cards a reward will offer, and what an unknown room holds are random; the player knows which cards are in the draw pile but not their order. The map is visible from the start of each act, but not what will be on offer along a route. A good player therefore treats different parts of the same decision differently, solving what is fixed and pricing what is dealt, and an agent has to tell the two apart, neither gambling on a turn whose outcome it could have computed nor planning the run as though the draws were known. The models we test divide along this line: they forecast the next turn's HP far better than their chance of surviving the act (Sec.4).

    These properties are the parts of the horizon gap [(Chen et al., 2026)] that short benchmarks cannot reach, and a single run of the game, about an hour of human play, sits at the task lengths on which agent progress is now charted [(Kwa et al., 2025)]. The game also has three practical properties that make it a good testbed. It is turn-based and fully described in text, so what is tested is decision-making rather than perception or reaction time. Its outcomes mix skill with luck in a measured proportion [(Trojanowski and Andersson, 2021)], and its maps pose genuine route decisions under uncertainty [(Bazzaz and Cooper, 2025)], so a fixed set of seeds gives a paired, repeatable comparison. And it has a large, well-documented population of human players, from general game telemetry to expert streamers, against which models can be placed.

    Appendix B Harness

    Figure5 gives an overview of the components of the harness. Figure6 follows the messages exchanged between the game, the harness and the model through the four points at which the harness calls the model: the start of an act, each combat turn, the end of a floor and the end of a run (Sections3 and 3). The subsections then describe the game interface, the agent harness, notes and memory and the knowledge reskin, and Sec.B.5 lists every feature of the harness that the model can see.

    B.1 Game interface

    Our fork of CommunicationMod [(ForgottenArbiter and others, 2019)], CommunicationModPlus, adds a file-based channel that survives restarts of the game’s Java process, tracking of the three keys that unlock Act 4, and intermediate state snapshots around each enemy’s turn, from which the harness attributes damage, block and status changes to the enemy that caused them. Every run loads the same mod list: BaseMod, StSLib, CommunicationModPlus, rngFix, permNeow (a Neow blessing on every run), SuperFastMode (animation speed only), RelicStats and fast_multicast. None changes the rules a human plays by. Each run executes in an isolated game profile, and every act boss is marked as seen, so each run’s seed, and not the profile’s history, picks the act bosses.

    B.2 Agent harness

    Each call carries a cached system prompt in two parts. The first is stable across runs: task instructions and a compendium of the game’s rules, keywords, status effects, cards, relics and potions with their effects. The second is stable within a run: the memory bank (Sec.3). The first user message of a floor adds the act map, the run’s notes, a history of the floors played so far and the player’s current state (HP, gold, deck, relics, potions and keys). In combat, each turn’s message reports what each of the model’s actions did, what each enemy did, and the full state at the start of the new turn. Outside combat the message describes the current screen and its legal choices.

    The tools are: playing a card or a sequence of cards, ending the turn, using or discarding a potion, choosing an option by index or by name, choosing a map node, planning a route, taking notes, predicting the floor’s outcome, and the end-of-run memory operations. The full tool set is sent on every call, so that the cached prefix never changes, and an action illegal on the current screen is refused with an explanation. By default the model may return several actions in one response (multi-action), and the harness executes them in order, stopping at the first that fails. At the start of each act the model is asked for a route plan over the whole act map. At the end of each floor it is asked for its chance of surviving the current act and of winning the run, and may reflect and update its notes; when it ends a turn it may also predict its HP at the start of the next turn and at the end of the fight.

    Two principles shaped the harness. The model is shown what a human player sees and nothing more: the prompts describe the task on the current screen without steering towards a strategy (they never say, for instance, to check first whether an enemy can be killed this turn), and the system prompt holds only the documentation a player has in the game itself, namely its tutorial, tips and compendium. And the model is asked to do as much as possible per call, to keep cost down. Many combat actions have a deterministic effect, so the model plans the whole turn and returns every action it wants in one response, up to the first whose outcome is random. MiniStS makes one call per action and re-prompts with the new state [(Bateni and Whitehead, 2024)]. Orak’s agent may also return several actions at once, but spends three calls on each decision (reflection, planning, then the actions) and shows the model only the state its actions leave [(Park et al., 2026)]. Multi-action play asks the model to hold the intervening states in mind, which is harder. Batching also helped play in our preliminary runs. Because the model had to plan the whole turn before acting, it committed to a plan, and it did not spend reasoning deriving the same plan again after each action when that action had revealed nothing new. On the main seeds, one action per response needs 3.0 more calls per floor, costs 23% more and clears 0.07 fewer acts (Table2). So that it can still see what each action did, the harness diffs the game state between actions and returns each change as the result of the tool call that caused it, with enemies’ turns attributed enemy by enemy. A call that names a card imprecisely is resolved where the intended card is unambiguous, and otherwise answered with a “did you mean” suggestion rather than executed.

    Names, not indices.

    The model refers to what it acts on by name: a card by the name it is shown under (play_card(card_name="Bash", enemy_index=0)), and an event option, rest-site action, shop item or card on a selection screen by its label (choose_by_name(name="Rest")). Arguments are passed by name too, never by position. Only enemies, card rewards and the reward list are chosen by index, which is shown beside each entry. There are two reasons for this.

    The first is batching. A batch is written against the state at the start of the turn, but the hand changes while the batch runs: every card played moves the positions of the others, and cards are drawn, created, upgraded and moved by the plays themselves. A position in the hand goes stale after the first change, but a name still identifies the same card. A batch can therefore play a card that an earlier call in it creates, and it can answer, in the same call, a choice that a card opens (the card that Armaments upgrades, the card that Headbutt puts back), through target_card_names. This is what lets the model play a whole turn in one response without giving up any of the game’s mechanics. How Orak handles the same cases is in Sec.B.7.

    The second is reliability. In preliminary runs, weaker models sometimes reasoned their way to one option and then gave the index of another. A name states the intended option in the call itself, so it cannot pick a different option by mistake. A name that matches nothing is refused with a suggestion (Sec.B.5). On the main seeds this concern did not show up: with one action per response, the models tested chose no worse by index than by name (Table2).

    B.3 Notes and memory

    Run notes are rendered back to the model as tags. The memory ablation (Table27) varies the mechanism while holding everything else fixed. Consolidate (xml) is the default of Sec.3. Keep notes copies each run’s notes into the bank verbatim, with no consolidation call, so it keeps persistence but removes the rewriting. None discards the notes at the end of each run. In the compact arms the model instead writes a single prose summary through a one-argument compact tool, overwriting it at the end of every floor and, when consolidating, at the end of every run. Every prompt that asks the model to write something down includes the same generic guidance: distil insights rather than log events, and record what went well, what went wrong and what the model wishes it had known. It names nothing specific to the game.

    A cohort with a read-write bank is a chain. Seed k starts from the bank that seed k-1 left behind, so the seeds are played in order and a cohort’s bank is never shared with any other configuration: each bank is partitioned by model, character, the full configuration tag and the seed list.

    B.4 Knowledge reskin

    The names replaced are those of cards, relics, potions, enemies, events, powers and keywords, the character, and the map’s node labels. Names are replaced through placeholders, so that one replacement can never trigger another, and each replacement evokes the original’s effect rather than its name. The harness’s own text (the system prompt, state descriptions and tool results) is renamed; the model’s own text is not, so a real game name in a note is evidence of recognized prior knowledge rather than something to be laundered.

    The five mappings of the reskin ablation (Table29) are all generated in the same format, so that only the mapping file changes between arms. None shows the real names. Themed is the default. Random replaces every word with a pronounceable nonsense word, consistently, so that multiword names keep their shared structure. Permuted gives each entity the real name of a different entity of the same kind (cards within their colour and type), which is coherent but actively misleading. Permuted and themed applies the same permutation in the themed vocabulary. The permuted mappings keep every rule word that the themed mapping leaves unrenamed, so the arms differ only in the names. Table4 gives examples.

    B.5 Model-facing features

    This subsection lists everything the harness does that the model can see, beyond the outline in Sec.B.2. The harness never makes a strategic choice for the model. When it acts by itself, there is only one legal action, or the action has no strategic content. When it corrects a call, it either resolves the call where the intent is unambiguous or refuses it with an explanation. Quoted messages are given as the model receives them, before renaming.

    What the model is shown.

  • •

    Map. The act map is drawn with labelled nodes (Monster(5,2): floor 5, column 2). Burning elites, which carry the Emerald Key, are marked, and the act boss is named. The current floor is marked >> and the reachable next nodes *. On map screens the model may revise its route plan before choosing.

  • •

    Player overview. HP, gold, keys, the deck (identical copies merged as 3x Strike), relics with their descriptions and counters (e.g. (2/3), (USED)), and potions. It is omitted from a message when nothing in it has changed.

  • •

    Combat turn. Each enemy is shown with its index, HP, Block, intent (e.g. Attack for 6x2) and powers with their current descriptions. Dead enemies are removed and the rest renumbered. The player’s HP, Block, energy, powers, stance and orbs are shown, and the hand lists one card per line with cost, type, whether it targets and why it cannot be played. The draw, discard and exhaust piles are listed in full when they are relevant (on a new turn, after a change or a reshuffle, or when a card in hand refers to that pile) and as counts otherwise.

  • •

    Card names. Cards are referred to by name, not hand position. Copies that differ get a qualifier, e.g. [Strike (0 cost)] when an effect (e.g. Snecko Eye, Mummified Hand) has changed a cost, and so does a card whose value has grown past its base (Ritual Dagger, Genetic Algorithm).

  • •

    Effects. The result of each tool call is the change in game state that call caused, e.g. “Played Bash. Energy -2 (3→1). Enemy [0] Jaw Worm HP -8 (40→32); Vulnerable +2.” Cards drawn, created and exhausted are named. Between turns, the next message reports the end of the player’s turn, then one line per acting enemy, then the end of the round (powers/statuses decaying or expiring) and the start of the new turn (Block kept, start-of-turn relics, reshuffles). These are split using game-state snapshots from the mod (Sec.B.1). Where several effects land together (the end of a fight, a room, a selection screen), the harness reports the net change without naming a cause, leaving the attribution to the model, which can see its relics.

  • •

    Non-combat screens. Each screen lists its legal choices with what the model needs to choose: shop prices with (can’t afford) and the card-removal price; the HP a rest would heal; card, relic and potion rewards as one numbered list; event options with (DISABLED) marked; and the Match and Keep board. Each choice is confirmed with what it changed, e.g. “Chose to rest. HP +24 (…)”.

  • •

    History. One line per floor played so far (room type, encounter, turns taken, HP and gold change, cards added, upgraded and removed, relics gained), with the act’s route plan and the run notes.

    • Reading the model’s calls.

  • •

    Lenient matching. Card, potion, relic and option names are matched case-insensitively, with brackets, stray quotes and parentheses, and non-breaking spaces removed. A qualified name matches if its qualifiers match the card’s current values. A bare name resolves to the upgraded copy when only that copy is in hand (Bash→Bash+), but not the reverse. Numbers given as strings are converted. Under the reskin, names are mapped back to the game’s names and checked against what is on screen.

  • •

    Copies. If the copy of a card that a call names has left the hand by the time the call runs, the harness plays an identical copy that is still in hand, and refuses the call only if there is none.

  • •

    Deferred plays. A card named before it exists (one an earlier call in the batch will create or upgrade) is looked up again when its call comes up, and refused only if it is still missing then.

  • •

    Targets. An attack or potion that needs a target gets the only living enemy when there is one, and is refused otherwise. Enemy indices refer to the list the model was shown, not the game’s internal one. If a targeted enemy has died, the refusal says that the remaining enemies have been renumbered.

  • •

    Pre-targeted selections. A card that makes the player choose another card (Armaments, Headbutt, a discard) can name its target in the same call (target_card_names). The harness then makes the choice on the selection screen that opens and reports what was picked, so the batch continues without a further call to the model. Similarly, choose_by_name(name, target_name) buys a card removal, or picks Smith or Toke at a rest site, and then names the card in a single tool call.

  • •

    Aliases.choose_by_name("skip") or ("leave") means skip, and ("proceed") means proceed. A number given as a name is treated as an index. Phrases like “remove” map to the shop’s card removal. An event option can also be named by its effect text when exactly one option matches.

  • •

    Calls written as text. When a response contains no tool call, the harness reads calls written in its text: function-call notation (play_card(card_name="Strike")), JSON objects in the shapes models commonly use, a bare argument object that fits exactly one expected tool, or key: value lines when one tool is required. It reads the reasoning only when there is no visible text, and then only the final draft of the turn. It does not read a response that was cut off. A recovered call is executed like any other and counted as an error in Table23.

    • Corrections and refusals.

    A refused call costs nothing in the game. Its result says why, and usually what would be accepted:

  • •

    Did you mean. A card not in hand is refused with the cards that are, plus the closest name in hand if one is close enough (fuzzy match, similarity at least 0.6), with an example call: “Did you mean ‘Strike (1 cost)’? Example: play_card(card_name="Strike (1 cost)", enemy_index=0)”. Names that match more than one card are refused with the candidates. In preliminary runs, these suggestions stopped models from repeating the same refused call.

  • •

    Wrong tool or screen. A tool that does nothing on the current screen is refused with the tools that do: “not available on {SCREEN}. Valid tools here: […]”. The same applies to an action the game reports as unavailable (e.g. too little energy), to a disabled event option, and to an unaffordable shop item.

  • •

    Energy check.end_turn takes, as a required argument, the energy the model expects to have left. If the model ends its turn with more energy than it declared while a card in hand is still playable, the end of turn is refused: “Rejected end_turn: declared expected_energy_remaining=E, but you actually have A energy. Your turn plan didn’t match what happened…”. The model can then play more cards or end the turn again. This catches a model that has lost track of its own turn. For example, the relic Nunchaku gives an energy for every tenth Attack played; a model that does not notice the tenth Attack coming would end its turn with energy it could have spent. These miscounts are reported as tool errors (Table23).

  • •

    Actions the game would ignore. The game silently ignores some actions, which would leave the harness waiting for a state change that never comes. These are refused before they are sent: buying or picking up a potion with every potion slot full, drinking a potion the game marks as unusable here, taking a potion under Sozu, and buying a second card removal in one shop visit. The refusal names what is possible instead.

  • •

    Event fallback. If a named choice matches no option on an event, the event is shown again with both indices and labels, and choose_by_index is offered. Events whose options share a label (Memory Stone) are numbered from the start.

  • •

    Malformed arguments. A required argument left as a … placeholder, a missing argument, or a text argument under the wrong name is refused with an example of the correct call. A note given under a sibling field name is accepted, and the confirmation says so.

  • •

    No tool call. A response with no executable call gets one retry: “Your reply contained no tool call. Text describing a call, whether JSON or play_card(…) notation, is not a call. Call one or more of these tools now: …”. The model’s own reasoning is quoted back above this message. If the response was cut off at the length limit, the message says that nothing in it was executed.

  • •

    Game errors. An error from the mod is passed on as “Action failed: {error}. Choose a different action.”, with the player’s remaining energy added for an unplayable card. The harness does not retry the action itself.

  • •

    Repeated failure. After two batches in a row on the same screen with every call refused, the full screen state is sent again with the available tools.

    • Batches and interruptions.

    The model’s calls are executed one at a time, and the state is read after each. The rest of the batch is dropped, with a result for every dropped call, when:

  • •

    a call is refused (“Skipped: an earlier action in your batch was rejected… Your planned sequence is stale…”);

  • •

    cards are drawn or created mid-turn that the plan could not have foreseen (cards that fetch a named card do not count);

  • •

    an enemy’s intent changes to a different move;

  • •

    a Lightning orb hits a random enemy while more than one is alive;

  • •

    a selection screen opens that the plan did not account for;

  • •

    the fight or the floor ends.

    • Calls after end_turn are dropped as stale. Note writes always run. A batch with a single card play gets a reminder to send the whole turn in one response, unless that card draws cards or creates random ones, which the model cannot plan past. A card that makes the player choose another card does not excuse the batch, since the choice can be named in the same call. The exemption is decided from the card’s text: a card whose text says it draws, is random or has the player choose is exempt, which among Ironclad and colourless choice cards exempts Dual Wield and Discovery.

    Actions the harness takes by itself.

  • •

    Ending the turn when no card is playable and no potion usable (“No more playable options. Turn ended automatically.”).

  • •

    Single legal choices. The harness takes an event window with one option, a single reachable map node, and a selection screen where the number of eligible cards equals the number to pick. The skipped event windows are shown to the model at the start of its next call, with what they changed.

  • •

    Screens with no choice. The harness proceeds when proceeding is the only action, confirms a selection once the model has picked, opens chests (except with Cursed Key), and enters a shop it has walked into. It leaves a shop when nothing is affordable, or after 30 actions in it.

  • •

    Rewards with no trade-off. Gold, stolen gold and the Emerald Key are collected automatically, as are potions when they all fit. Each card reward is opened in the background so that its cards appear in the one reward list the model chooses from.

  • •

    Waiting for the game to deal the opening hand, finish a transform, or show a purchase before reporting it, so a reported effect is never one the game has not yet applied.

    • Guards.

    Ten consecutive failed model calls, or ten consecutive responses with no executable game action, end the run as a harness failure, and it is resumed from its autosave. Over the main runs (190 runs and 36,486 model calls) the first fired three times, each when an API account ran out of credit, and the second 16 times, all for Grok 4.6 on five of its seeds, each after ten responses that chose an option with an empty name. Transient API errors are retried with exponential backoff (five retries by default); 48 calls (0.13%) still failed after their retries. Authentication, billing and quota errors stop the whole seed queue rather than skipping the seed, because a skipped seed would change the memory every later seed in a read-write chain starts from; this happened twice. play_combo repeats a card sequence for an infinite combo, up to 1,000 times or until a pass changes nothing; it was called 149 times, and neither limit was reached. Reflection is capped at 20 turns and consolidation at 200; the longest took 13 and 47. When a conversation outgrows the model’s context window, the oldest turns of the floor are dropped (always keeping the floor’s first message and the latest turn) and a note tells the model how many were removed. This happened on 154 calls (0.4%), all from two models with 128k-token windows: Nemotron 3 Nano Omni (139 of its 708 calls, in every run) and gpt-oss-120b (15 calls, in three runs).

    B.6 What the model receives

    The excerpts below are quoted verbatim from Claude Opus 5's first run of the main cohort, so names appear as the model saw them under the themed reskin (“room” for floor, Guard for Block, Artifacts for relics).

    System prompt.

    A short preamble states the task, followed by the compendium: the game's rules and tips (42 points adapted from the game's own tutorial and loading-screen tips), its keywords and status effects, and the character's cards, the colourless, status and curse cards, and every relic and potion with its effect. On the first seed, before any memory exists, this is 30,715 characters, and with the tool definitions about 18,000 tokens. The memory bank is appended as it grows; by the tenth seed this model's system prompt had reached 227,089 characters.

    Tools.

    Seventeen tools are sent on every call (required arguments marked *): play_card(card_name*, enemy_index, target_card_names), play_combo(card_names*, enemy_index), end_turn(expected_energy_remaining*, predicted_hp_after_turn, predicted_hp_after_fight), use_potion(potion_name*, enemy_index), discard_potion(potion_name*), choose_by_index(choice_index*), choose_by_name(name*, target_name), choose_path(choice_index*), skip(), plan_route(route*, notes*), predict(act_win_probability*, run_win_probability*), save_note(key*, note*), delete_note(key*), finish_reflection(), save_memory(key*, memory*), delete_memory(key*), finish_consolidation().

    A combat turn.

    The message that opens a turn, here turn 3 of an elite fight on floor 8. The effect of each card played on the previous turn has already been returned as the result of its own tool call (e.g. “Played Trip Attack. Energy -2 (4→2). Enemy [2] Bolt Sprite HP -8 (41→33); Ward cleared.”).

    Lines longer than the page are wrapped with an indent; the text is otherwise as sent.

    End of a floor.

    After the floor's last screen the model is asked to reflect, then to forecast:

    End of the run.

    The consolidation message carries the run's result and final state, each act's full map, route plan and path taken, the history of every floor and the run notes, and ends:

    B.7 Coverage compared with Orak and Bottled AI

    Orak's own rule bot plays the map, events, shops, rest sites, chests, boss relics, Neow and potions, so its model decides combat and card rewards only. Even within a fight its model decides less than ours. Orak asks the model only when a card can be played, so every card choice that a card or potion opens mid-fight (Armaments, True Grit+, Dual Wield, Headbutt, Exhume, an Attack Potion) goes to the rule bot, which picks from a fixed card ranking rather than the fight at hand: the best-ranked card to upgrade or copy, the worst-ranked to exhaust, and, since the flag that would select the best is never set, the worst-ranked card for Headbutt and Exhume. The model is not told which card was chosen, and the rest of its planned turn is dropped. Orak's agent returns several actions at once, as ours does, but plays each card by its position in the hand as shown when the model decided, so a response cannot play a card that arrives mid-turn. Queued actions keep executing through draws and random effects, re-resolved by card identity so a shifted hand still plays the intended card, but the model sees what was drawn only once its queue is spent; Orak's paper describes the state as returned after each action, where its code returns it after the queue. Ours puts every such choice to the model, lets a card-targeting card name its target in the same call, and interrupts the queue when cards are drawn or created, orbs evoke at random or an enemy's intent changes, naming what changed [(Park et al., 2026)].

    Game coverage.

    Table5 goes through the game by feature. It refines the Model plays and Choices columns of Table2, and adds Bottled AI. Orak’s model sees no orbs, stance, potions or card piles, so a Defect under Orak plays its orb cards without seeing the orbs they make. Orak builds on spirecomm, a Python client for CommunicationMod whose last commit predates the Watcher, and so cannot play the Watcher at all; our harness adds the Watcher to spirecomm itself. Orak’s rule bot never chooses Recall at a rest site, so it never collects the Ruby Key and can never reach Act 4.

    Card coverage.

    Table6 estimates how much of the game each harness lets its player use in full. For Orak, a card counts as unsupported if playing it opens a choice (either version, so Armaments counts although Armaments+ upgrades every card without asking). Orak’s rule bot makes those choices, not the model. 33 cards open a choice when played, among them Headbutt, Warcry, Dual Wield and Exhume, and every card that has the player pick a card to discard, scry or keep, or pick one of three. Bottled AI plays only cards its combat simulator models, and treats any other card as one it can never play. Its gaps are mostly cards that open a choice or have a random effect (Armaments, Headbutt, Discovery, Infernal Blade), plus a few powers (Brutality, Combust, Rupture). Our harness passes every selection a card opens to the model, so every card is supported. The count covers playing a card, not how well a player uses it.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：给模型完整的商业游戏本体做长程策略评测：前沿模型超启发式基线、追平普通玩家，但远落后专家。

要点：

  • 让模型玩完整的商业卡牌构筑游戏 Slay the Spire，早期决策决定长期结果，测的是真正的长程策略
  • 20 个大模型在最高难度下：前沿模型超过启发式基线、追平普通人类玩家，但与专家差距随对局变长而扩大
  • 把所有游戏术语做自洽改名后性能下降，说明部分表现来自对这款游戏的先验知识；跨局写下的记忆常错且过度保守，没能提升表现

为什么值得看：「模型会玩游戏」和「模型会规划」是两件事；把整局切片成战斗级与战役级来看，才能看出它在哪一层掉队。

中文摘要：agentic 大模型已经能处理复杂任务，但长程的策略推理研究不足：多数 agent 基准短且情节化，长任务的表现也很难拆成记忆知识、推理与运气。SpireBench 让模型完整地玩商业卡牌构筑游戏《杀戮尖塔》，在这款游戏里早期决策决定长期成败。作者测试了 20 个大语言模型在最高难度下的表现：前沿模型能超过启发式基线、追平普通玩家的平均水平，但离专家仍差很远，而且差距随对局推进而拉大——最强模型在第一幕的胜率与专家相当，之后就掉队。区分强弱的关键是每场战斗打得好不好，而所有模型都对整局的风险判断失误，宁可保血也不愿花血变强。把所有游戏术语做一次自洽的改名后，模型表现下降，说明部分能力来自对这款游戏的先验知识；模型也不会从自己跨局写下的记忆中变强，那些记忆常常是错的且过度保守。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-08

本期推送：2026-10-25

SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire

Abstract

Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game’s highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) progress has been rapid, with high scores on tests of a wide range of general-intelligence-aligned skills [(Sajadieh et al., 2026)], and LLMs increasingly act as autonomous agents over extended periods [(Brohi et al., 2025)]. However, single-step competence does not necessarily translate into reliable performance over many sequential decisions, a shortfall termed the horizon gap[(Chen et al., 2026)]. Performance on long tasks is also hard to dissect: does a model rely on stored knowledge or on reasoning [(Lowe, 2024)], and can it store and effectively use long-term memories? How is it impacted by stochasticity?

Existing evaluations leave these questions open. Agentic benchmarks [(Yehudai et al., 2026)] are mostly short-horizon, with little carried between episodes; game benchmarks [(Paglieri et al., 2025)] rarely hand a model every decision a player makes, or ask whether performance reflects prior knowledge, reasoning or luck; and reported memory gains [(Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024)] usually come with an external check on what was learned.

We introduce SpireBench, built on the commercial game Slay the Spire (StS), which combines tactical combat, deck construction and route planning over 56 floors (Fig. 1). It is turn-based, fully describable in text, and its choices involve weighing short-term gains over long term success at multiple time horizons, making it well suited for a long-horizon benchmark (Appx.A). Unlike previous work on benchmarking StS [(Bateni and Whitehead, 2024; Park et al., 2026)], SpireBench interacts directly with all aspects of the game, and allows for separating knowledge from reasoning.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    A harness for the complete original game. Agents play the unmodified commercial game through our harness, making every decision a human player makes (a first) and seeing the same information as a human player would. We allow the model to return a whole turn’s actions as multiple tool calls in one response, and the harness reports the effect of each action back to the model. Against its other variants on the same models and seeds, it plays further and costs less per floor (Table2).

  • •

    A benchmark at the game’s highest difficulty, calibrated against human data. We evaluate 20 LLMs at Ascension 20 on the same ten held-out seeds, with cost and reasoning spend. For a human performance reference we use Mega Crit’s released telemetry (206 k A20 Ironclad runs) and the run histories of 4 expert streamers. Frontier models beat rule-based and symbolic baselines and the average human player, yet remain far from expert play. The benchmark tracks the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but is among the least predictable from other evaluations.

  • •

    Knowledge ablation with reskin. We reskin the entire game with a holistically consistent theme, separating prior knowledge of the game from reasoning about its rules. Hiding the real names costs performance, concentrated in a few models. Random and permuted control mappings show that the cost comes from the knowledge attached to familiar names, not from reading unfamiliar ones.

  • •

    Memory mechanisms, and what the models write. We allow models to write notes and memories within their run and between runs with various methods. No memory formation between runs is able to improve play. Reading the banks shows why: 17% of memories are false, advice to be cautious outnumbers advice to take risks seven to one, reinforcing existing tendencies, and nothing prunes errors.

  • •

    Analysis of model understanding and failures. We probe the models to predict future game states to evaluate their understanding of play, demonstrating that more performant models are better able to predict near-term game states, but not capable of predicting long-term success. Comparing model in-game choices against humans, the best models are too conservative, failing to amortize their risk profile across the run into earlier sections so they do not take the risks needed to outpace the game’s difficulty curve.

    • 2 Background

    Slay the Spire is a seminal roguelike deck-builder game, in which players have to balance decision making over several horizons (Fig. 1). In combat turns the player draws a hand from a deck of cards and spends a limited pool of energy to attack, block, or build effects that scale over turns; between fights they add and sometimes remove cards from a deck, and pick a route through a map of nodes (consisting of fights, elite fights, events, shops, and rests — Fig. 1 middle row). Decisions are taken under uncertainty and compound: a card once taken usually stays in the deck across the run, and threats met very late in the game must be prepared for early. A core component is balancing risk, since riskier options early yield the growth that the rising difficulty curve demands (Fig.1). These are properties shared with other long tasks agents face (Appx.A).

    2.1 Related work

    Slay the Spire. Analyses of the game measure its mix of luck and skill [(Andersson et al., 2023; Nam and Rerkjirattikal, 2023)] and the complexities of its map uncertainty [(Bazzaz and Cooper, 2025)]. MiniStS [(Bateni and Whitehead, 2024)] tests LLMs on 8 cards and 5 isolated encounters, evaluating micro-play but no macro-level deck-building. The twelve-game benchmark Orak[(Park et al., 2026)] drives the real game through the CommunicationMod harness [(ForgottenArbiter and others, 2019)], but its LLM plays only combat and card rewards, at Ascension 0 on one seed, with a rule-based bot doing the rest. In another approach, Bottled AI, a symbolic AI was handcrafted to play the game [(Bottled AI contributors, 2022)]. While it does not support every card or event, it does report high performance. Finally, in concurrent and most comparable work, AgenticSTS [(Cheng et al., 2026)], plays complete runs of the sequel Slay the Spire 2. However, the sequel is still in early access with fortnightly balance patches, making it unsuited for benchmarking purposes, and AgenticSTS only plays the game at its lowest difficulty, and was mainly tested with one model. Overall, no existing evaluation has an LLM make every decision in the released game, tests it at the highest difficulty, studies more than a few models, compares against human play, or controls for the models’ prior knowledge of the game. SpireBench plays Slay the Spire at its highest difficulty (A20) across many more models (20). We evaluated model performance against extensive human telemetry, with a controlled reskin; to our knowledge, ours is the first harness giving a model the complete original game.

    Games as benchmarks. Deep reinforcement learning reached superhuman play in Atari, Go, chess and shogi [(Mnih et al., 2015; Silver et al., 2016; Silver et al., 2018)] and hard-exploration games [(Ecoffet et al., 2021)] by training on the game. LLM agents are evaluated untrained, in NetHack, Crafter and Minecraft [(Küttler et al., 2020; Hafner, 2022; Wang et al., 2024)], benchmark suites [(Paglieri et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024a)] and commercial games from frames [(Zhang et al., 2025)], mostly on simplified states or partial games and rarely with learning across runs. The nearest deck-builder benchmark, BalatroBench [(Coder, 2026)], has shorter horizons and only the basic difficulty; earlier deck-construction work searches whole decks before play [(García-Sánchez et al., 2016)].

    Long-horizon benchmarks. Tool-use, web and agentic benchmarks [(Jimenez et al., 2024; Mialon et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024; Koh et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b)] are mostly tens of steps long; others lengthen the horizon by task duration [(Kwa et al., 2025)], execution length [(Sinha et al., 2026)] or a simulated business over tens of millions of tokens [(Backlund and Petersson, 2025)]. Trading [(Li et al., 2025a)] is long but has a fixed action space. In contrast, a Slay the Spire agent builds the action space it gets to act in later.

    Memory across episodes. Agents with persistent memory [(Park et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023)] have previously been found to improve across episodes [(Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Majumder et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025)] given an external check on what is stored; without one, models struggle to self-correct [(Huang et al., 2024)] and propagate errors in stored experience [(Xiong et al., 2026)]. We test memory on a long, stochastic task with no such check.

    Reskinning. Renaming entities but not mechanics probes memorization against reasoning: nonsense predicates [(Valmeekam et al., 2023)], changed rules [(Wu et al., 2024b)], isomorphic worlds [(Gu et al., 2026)], masked names [(Hu et al., 2026)], renamed security tasks [(Honarvar et al., 2026)] and re-textured game objects [(Dubey et al., 2018)]; other benchmarks generate environments a model cannot have seen [(Costarelli et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b)]. Our reskin covers the whole game with names evoking each mechanic, with random and permuted controls (Sec.3), paired within seed.

    3 Methods

    Agent harness. Agents play the released game through CommunicationModPlus, our fork of CommunicationMod [(ForgottenArbiter and others, 2019)], which exchanges JSON states and text commands and adds snapshots around each enemy’s turn. The harness holds one conversation per floor, shared by a combat, its rewards, and the post-floor reflection. See Figs.5 and B in the appendix for an overview and example floor.

    A cached system prompt holds the task instructions, a compendium of the game’s rules and items, and the memory bank (Sec.3); each floor adds the act map, the run’s notes and the player’s state. The model acts only through tool calls, interleaving reasoning with action [(Yao et al., 2023)], and may return a whole turn’s actions in one response (multi-action); they run in order up to the first that fails, and each state change is returned as the result of the call that caused it.

    Our multi-action implementation asks the model to plan the turn before acting and needs fewer calls: a turn costs one response and one pass over the context, where one action per call pays for both again at every card. This is non-trivial to work with since the action space can shift during a turn; we ask models to internalize these changes to make correct tool calls, and interrupt the action queue if an unpredictable event occurs. MiniStS makes one call per action [(Bateni and Whitehead, 2024)]; Orak's agent may return several actions but spends three calls on each decision (reflection, planning, action), shows only the state they leave, re-plans only once they are spent, and leaves every mid-fight card interaction selection to its rule bot [(Park et al., 2026)]; AgenticSTS submits combat as a plan and rebuilds the prompt for every decision by retrieval [(Cheng et al., 2026)]. Table2 compares the designs and measures ours against its variants and Orak on the same models and seeds. Ours sees what a human player sees, without strategic steering. It plans a route each act, forecasts at the end of each floor its chances of surviving the act and winning the run, and may predict its HP when it ends a turn. Reasoning is kept across turns wherever the provider allows, and no response reached the output ceiling (Sec.B.2).

    Notes and memory. After each floor the model may write, overwrite or delete free-form run notes under keys of its choosing. After each run it consolidates them into its persistent memory bank one operation at a time (save, delete or finish); the bank enters every later run’s system prompt, so a read-write cohort is a chain played in seed order. We conduct memory ablation experiments to investigate the utility of this schema (Sec.B.3).

    Knowledge reskin. Unless stated otherwise every run is reskinned: each game-specific name the model can see is replaced by a name from a hand-written internally-consistent mapping themed around tabletop RPGs. We do this so we can evaluate the model’s ability to reason about the game, ablating as much prior information about rules of thumb for how to play StS which it may have seen in pretraining as possible. The model’s own text is not renamed, so a real game name it writes or thinks is evidence of recognition of the base game. We conduct ablation experiments to evaluate the effect of this thematic renaming compared to the original or a randomized rename vocabulary (Sec.B.4).

    Models and reasoning settings. We evaluate hosted models from Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Z.ai, and open-weight Qwen, Nemotron and gpt-oss models on our own hardware. Table1 runs each at its highest reasoning setting (grey, beside its name), resolved to the nearest level the provider supports at or above the request (Sec.C.1).

    Evaluation protocol. Every main result is on the Ironclad at Ascension 20, the hardest difficulty, on the same ten seeds—freshly minted both to prevent hyperparameter optimization against model/seed pairs used during preliminary experiments, and so that model providers cannot have trained on our earlier results on these seeds [(Sainz et al., 2023)]. A cohort is one model under one configuration on these seeds; each table cell is one cohort, validated by the analysis code (Sec.C.2). We score a run by the acts it clears (Act 4 ends with the Heart) and also report the floor it reaches. A run clears Acts 1 and 2 by beating their (randomly selected) bosses; Act 3 by beating two random bosses; and Act 4 by killing the Corrupt Heart. The act k win rate is the share of runs that cleared Act k; mean acts cleared (0–4), is our headline summary. Floor is the final floor reached. A frontier cohort can cost hundreds of dollars (Table33), so ten seeds is a budget decision, too few to reliably order neighbouring models but sufficient for broader trends.

    Baselines and cost. Three non-LLM policies play the same seeds without seeing names: pick first option and pick random option bracket the models from below; BottledAI[(Bottled AI contributors, 2022)] is a hand-written symbolic player (Sec.C.5).

    Human references at the same setting, scored alike, are the run histories of four expert streamers (Table1) and 206,082 finished runs of the game’s telemetry, released by Mega Crit. Human games are not matched cohorts against the LLM seeds (Appx.D).

    4 Results

    Performance and cost. Our benchmark results are shown in Table1. We will first consider baseline, symbolic, and human comparisons. Always picking the first option or picking a random option. Neither baseline reaches very far even into the first act. The BottledAI symbolic model [Bottled AI contributors (2022)] can beat act 1, but goes no further. In contrast, even the average human player in a 200,000 runs human dataset reaches and wins the final act 4% of the time. Top level players comfortably reach 50+% winrates. This illustrates that the game is non-trivial, and has a very high skill ceiling.

    In our LLM cohort, the strongest models are Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, and only Sol kills the Heart (the final boss), once; they are also among the most expensive, per run and per floor (Fig.2(a)). Mid-tier models outperform Bottled AI but not the average human, and four models never clear an act, no better than the random-choice policy. Performance tracks the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (Fig.2(b)), but reasoning spent does not buy play: GPT-6 Astra thinks least per floor (3.3k tokens) and clears 1.50 acts, while Nemotron 3 Nano Omni thinks most (34.0k) and clears none.

    Comparison with human players. The strongest models clear more acts than the average Ascension 20 Ironclad run in Mega Crit's telemetry (0.73) and than players with over 1000 hours (0.92), but far fewer than the four streamers (2.5–3.1 acts). The gap opens as the run lengthens (Tables1 and 4): the three strongest models win 90% of their Act 1 runs, as the streamers do (85–92%), but 40–50% of Act 2 against 65–78%, and 0–20% of Act 3 against 56–71%. Consequently, the models have a drastically lower win rate for the full game (Act 4) at 0–10% against 46–65%. These results are a demonstration of the horizon gap of [Chen et al. (2026)], exhibited within a single task.

    How the models spend a run. The models play Act 1 cautiously. They fight 0.9–1.4 elites, against 2.0 for the telemetry population and 2.6 for the streamers, rest at 57–75% of rest sites against 23% and 9%, and rest at 31% of the rest sites they enter with at least 70% HP, where the population does so at 2% and the streamers never, upgrading a card instead, a permanent boon for the rest of the game. At the Act 1 boss the top four models hold a median 90% of their maximum HP, the streamers 53% (Fig.3; Sec.E.1). Since the transition to the next act restores 75% of missing HP, HP carried to the end of an act keeps only a quarter of its value; the scarce resource is floors in which to outgrow enemies that scale as the game progresses. Human runs that play Act 1 as the models do clear Act 2 in 15% of cases, against 38% for runs that fight more elites and rest less (Table13), and in the models' own runs upgrading rather than resting predicts clearing Act 2 (r=0.56, 49 runs). Experience does not change this: over a chain, rest and elite rates move no differently from no-memory runs; the banks advise caution seven times as often as risk; and the four strongest models record the end-of-act heal correctly yet still rest in 21 of the 32 late-act decisions that weigh it. The route explains only about a fifth of the gap to the streamers; the rest is how the fights are played.

    Strong models fight better. What separates the models is neither the route (Sec.E.1) nor, much, the deck. Agreement with human card picks barely rises with model strength (Spearman ρ=0.16), no model builds its deck for the act boss the map shows, and the one deck-building signal is taking area-damage cards (46% of Act 1 offers for the top four models, 20% for the bottom tier; ρ=0.76). The fights separate them. The top four take 8.2 damage per Act 1 hallway fight, the bottom tier 14.0 (ρ=-0.87, 19 models; Table14). Every tier spends the same energy and blocks the same share of incoming damage; the strong models turn the energy into damage (7.5 against 5.8 per energy spent on attacks, ρ=0.91), rarely block on a turn when no enemy attacks (6% against 31%) and never miss a lethal play in hand (0% against 8.7%), so they kill a turn sooner and are hit less. The difference holds on the same encounter of the same seed, including the first six floors, before the decks diverge, and about three quarters of the top–bottom gap in Act 1 boss wins (94% against 19%) is not explained by the state in which the models arrive.

    Relation to public LLM benchmarks. Across 30 model and effort points, mean acts cleared tracks the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index closely (Pearson r=0.82, Spearman ρ=0.89; Fig.2(b)), but the public evaluations behind it, among them GPQA Diamond [(Rein et al., 2024)] and SciCode [(Tian et al., 2024)], are strongly correlated with each other too [(Burnell et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2024)]. Among them SpireBench is one of the least substitutable (Table18 in Appx.H): the other evaluations predict 50% of its variance for a held-out model, against 85% for Humanity's Last Exam [(Center for AI Safety et al., 2026)], consistent with lmgame-Bench, where a game probes a blend of capabilities that other benchmarks test in isolation [(Hu et al., 2026)]. Of the agentic evaluations, only Terminal-Bench 4.0 adds information beyond knowledge and reasoning scores (Table19).

    The harness moves scores as much as neighbouring models differ. On the same models and seeds (Table2), Orak's harness, whose rule bot plays every non-combat floor, reaches 3.3 fewer floors than ours and clears 0.15 fewer acts, a gap as large as that between many neighbouring models, and its own failures ended 11 of the 70 seeds. The comparison uses eight mostly weaker models, which clear 0.20 acts on those seeds with our harness and 0.04 with Orak's; its effect on frontier models is untested. Orak spends 85% fewer tokens per floor but costs only 31% less: most of our input is cached. One action per response needs 3.0 more calls per floor, costs 23% more and loses 0.07 acts, a loss that disappears when choices are also made by number (+0.00 acts), so cost is the robust advantage of multi-action. One conversation for the whole run costs 22% more per floor, loses 0.06 acts and raises tool-call errors from 0.8 to 2.2 per 100 calls [(Liu et al., 2024a; Sinha et al., 2026)].

    Memory does not compound. Agents that accumulate experience across episodes are reported to improve with it [(Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Majumder et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Suzgun et al., 2026)]; ours do not, nor did the episodic store of [Cheng et al. (2026)] in StS2 (6/10 wins with and without it). Consolidating a run's notes into a memory bank or writing a compact summary has no impact on the number of acts won (see Fig.17 and Table27). Carrying the notes from during the run forward verbatim without a memory consolidation or compaction phase does slightly better (+0.06 acts): the rewriting adds nothing, much as iterative rewriting of an agent's context erodes its detail [(Zhang et al., 2026)]. Without an external check on what is stored, models do not reliably correct their own reasoning [(Huang et al., 2024)], and agents propagate the errors they store [(Xiong et al., 2026)]. A run gives one delayed, noisy outcome for hundreds of decisions, so nothing verifies a consolidated memory, and the bank grows run on run (Fig.19). Moreover, in the final banks 17% of memories are false, mostly generalizations from a single run, and models whose banks hold more errors of their own clear fewer acts (Spearman ρ=-0.67, permutation p=0.002, n=20; Table20). Nothing prunes them: over the 200 runs the models opt to delete only 30 memories.

    Prior knowledge is part of the score. Renaming or altering a familiar task has exposed reliance on memorized content [(Valmeekam et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024b; McCoy et al., 2024)], while capture-the-flag agents are largely robust to renaming [(Honarvar et al., 2026)]. Our result lies between. Hiding the real names costs 0.14 acts and 11 points of Act 1 win rate, pooled over 12 model configurations (11 models) and every paired seed (Table29; per model with all 10 seeds, Table3), concentrated in a few: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash falls from 0.80 acts to 0.30 and GPT-5.6 Luna from 0.60 to 0.10 (Table30). Nonsense names cost least (0.01 acts), so unfamiliar words are not the difficulty; the two permuted mappings, which give each entity the name (real or themed) of another, cost about as much as the themed one (0.10 and 0.12). A familiar name pulls a model towards what it usually means although the prompt states the rules [(McCoy et al., 2024)]: the signature of knowledge acquired in training, which contamination studies seek in static benchmarks [(Golchin and Surdeanu, 2024)] and we show by intervention. The reskin hides names, not the game: in 125 of the 190 themed runs of Table1 with full logs (Gemma 4 E4B has none), from 18 of 19 models, the model recognizes Slay the Spire or a real entity the reskin replaced, yet recognition does not buy back the cost (Spearman ρ=0.18, permutation p=0.62; Table21).

    Models forecast the next turn, not the consequences for the rest of the run. Larger models are reported to be well calibrated on questions they can answer [(Kadavath et al., 2022)], while confidence stated in words tends to be overconfident [(Xiong et al., 2024)]; here the horizon decides which holds. Models that forecast the next turn's HP well clear more acts (Spearman ρ=-0.84 between error and acts; Table16). This forecast measures the fight-reading skill above: on turns where the intents shown determine the next HP exactly, the bottom tier still mispredicts it 31% of the time and the top four 0.5%. Forecasts of surviving the act are poorly calibrated: the four models that never clear an act give themselves a 55–76% chance, about as much as the four strongest (59–74%), whose forecasts are followed by surviving the act 63–76% of the time (Fig.14 in Appx.G), and they barely sharpen as the act nears its end (Fig.15). Card-reward policy, failures in the reasoning traces and tool-call errors are analysed in Appx.H (Tables22, 24 and 23).

    5 Discussion

    Our findings consistently demonstrate that agentic models fail to calibrate risk correctly over the long-term. Where the outcome is a turn or a fight away, the strongest models are competent: they win the first act as often as streamers do, win almost every ordinary fight and forecast the next turn well, though they still lose more HP in each fight than humans do. At the time horizon of an act or a run away, they fall behind: the gap to the streamers opens from Act 2, boss fights decide where each model stops, forecasts of surviving an act barely sharpen; moreover, what a model writes down for later runs does not compound. Our findings are indicative of the horizon gap of [Chen et al. (2026)], but within one task whose time scales share a single pool of resources. Measured as a time horizon [(Kwa et al., 2025)], the fall is a step: every model succeeds on at least 87% of its turns and falls below 50% between a fight and a run, for most models already at the act (Table17). The difficulty is not how long a model can keep going: it is fighting well enough to afford risk, and spending early floors on growth whose payoff comes an act later, which no model learns from its own runs. Any agent planning over a long, stochastic task with one delayed outcome needs memories checked against outcomes and forgotten when wrong, forecasts that sharpen as the stakes approach, and a harness that plays the whole task (Sec.5).

    Four findings confirm mechanisms that prior work demonstrated outside games. The harness is part of the score, as for other agents [(Kapoor et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024)]. Unverified memory does not compound wherever the outcome is delayed and noisy over many decisions, as in most open-ended deployments; where a verifier exists, such as tests for code, the reported gains should hold. Long contexts cost performance[(Liu et al., 2024a; Sinha et al., 2026)]. Calibration degrades with the horizon in any task whose outcomes resolve at several distances.

    Limitations.The ordering of models is measured on one character in a turn-based game played from parsed text; other characters, genres, real-time control or perception would weight the decisions differently. The size of the reskin cost depends on how much of this game each model saw in training, and the reskin hides names but not familiarity with deck-builders, so it is a lower bound. The human comparison is not seed-matched. Ten seeds per cohort cannot order neighbouring models, and providers can change the model behind an identifier without notice.

    Appendices

    Appendix A Why Slay the Spire

    Slay the Spire is a seminal game that helped establish the roguelike deck-builder genre, and the properties that make it hard are those that make any long task hard for an agent.

    Every choice recurs. A card added to the deck on the second floor is drawn again in every later fight, so it has to be useful not only against the next enemy but against the act bosses an hour later, and a bad addition cannot simply be undone: card removals are limited opportunities and the deck starts with cards (Strikes) which the player would already benefit from removing, so adding a bad card puts the player down a card removal for the rest of the game. The consequences of a decision are therefore spread thinly over hundreds of later ones—this is the credit-assignment problem of long-horizon execution, where small per-step errors compound over the length of a task [(Sinha et al., 2026)]. The only verdict on the run as a whole, a win or a loss, comes at its end.

    An archetype is not a deck. Players learn named strategies, such as building around Strength or around exhausting cards, but each run offers a random array of cards and relics based on its seed. A plan must be devised as the run unfolds rather than determined in advance, and the agent has to judge when to commit to a plan and when to abandon it. A card's worth also depends on the cards and relics already held: a card that scales with Strength is weak in a deck with no source of Strength and strong in one with several, so cards cannot be valued one at a time.

    The agent builds its own action space. In combat, the actions open to the player on a turn are the cards in hand, and the hand is drawn from a deck the player assembled. Every card reward, purchase, removal and upgrade therefore decides which actions will exist in later fights: the agent chooses not only its moves but the set of moves it will later choose among. This is a sharper form of what an agent does when it builds a library of skills or tools for later use [(Wang et al., 2024)], with the difference that here the library is also a liability, since every card added is one more card that may be drawn in place of the one that was needed. Even a single turn is a small planning problem, because the order of plays matters: an attack does half as much again to an enemy made Vulnerable first, so Bash is played before the Strikes it sets up.

    Each fight tests the deck differently. A deck is not good or bad in general but against a particular fight. Groups of enemies call for damage that hits all of them; long fights against enemies that grow stronger call for cards that scale, while short ones call for damage up front; and some enemies punish a kind of play outright: Gremlin Nob gains Strength whenever a Skill is played, the Awakened One whenever a Power is played, and the Time Eater takes over the turn once a set number of cards has been played. A card bought to pass one of these checks can weaken the deck against another, and every card added dilutes the draws for all of them, so the player must decide which checks the deck has to pass, which it can afford to scrape through, and in what order the run will set them.

    Risk is amortized over the run. HP, gold, potions and the deck form one irreversible pool that carries from floor to floor. Taking an elite fight costs HP now for a relic that pays out over every later fight; resting at a campfire recovers HP at the price of an upgrade. The right choice depends on what the rest of the run will demand, so the agent must price present resources against a future it can only estimate, and how well it does so shows in how well calibrated those estimates are.

    The challenges ahead are known in kind but not in detail. Each act draws its fights from a fixed pool, and the map shows the types of room ahead, so a player who remembers what the act's elites and bosses do can build the deck to meet them; one who does not meets each as a surprise. Doing well therefore needs memory across runs as well as within one, which is the setting in which memory mechanisms for LLM agents are proposed [(Park et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023)] but seldom tested over long, stochastic episodes.

    Some of the game is fixed and some is dealt. Within a fight, each enemy shows its intended action for the coming turn, and enemies follow move patterns that can be learned, so the threat on the current turn is known exactly and a turn can be planned as a deterministic puzzle. What the player will draw next turn, which cards a reward will offer, and what an unknown room holds are random; the player knows which cards are in the draw pile but not their order. The map is visible from the start of each act, but not what will be on offer along a route. A good player therefore treats different parts of the same decision differently, solving what is fixed and pricing what is dealt, and an agent has to tell the two apart, neither gambling on a turn whose outcome it could have computed nor planning the run as though the draws were known. The models we test divide along this line: they forecast the next turn's HP far better than their chance of surviving the act (Sec.4).

    These properties are the parts of the horizon gap [(Chen et al., 2026)] that short benchmarks cannot reach, and a single run of the game, about an hour of human play, sits at the task lengths on which agent progress is now charted [(Kwa et al., 2025)]. The game also has three practical properties that make it a good testbed. It is turn-based and fully described in text, so what is tested is decision-making rather than perception or reaction time. Its outcomes mix skill with luck in a measured proportion [(Trojanowski and Andersson, 2021)], and its maps pose genuine route decisions under uncertainty [(Bazzaz and Cooper, 2025)], so a fixed set of seeds gives a paired, repeatable comparison. And it has a large, well-documented population of human players, from general game telemetry to expert streamers, against which models can be placed.

    Appendix B Harness

    Figure5 gives an overview of the components of the harness. Figure6 follows the messages exchanged between the game, the harness and the model through the four points at which the harness calls the model: the start of an act, each combat turn, the end of a floor and the end of a run (Sections3 and 3). The subsections then describe the game interface, the agent harness, notes and memory and the knowledge reskin, and Sec.B.5 lists every feature of the harness that the model can see.

    B.1 Game interface

    Our fork of CommunicationMod [(ForgottenArbiter and others, 2019)], CommunicationModPlus, adds a file-based channel that survives restarts of the game’s Java process, tracking of the three keys that unlock Act 4, and intermediate state snapshots around each enemy’s turn, from which the harness attributes damage, block and status changes to the enemy that caused them. Every run loads the same mod list: BaseMod, StSLib, CommunicationModPlus, rngFix, permNeow (a Neow blessing on every run), SuperFastMode (animation speed only), RelicStats and fast_multicast. None changes the rules a human plays by. Each run executes in an isolated game profile, and every act boss is marked as seen, so each run’s seed, and not the profile’s history, picks the act bosses.

    B.2 Agent harness

    Each call carries a cached system prompt in two parts. The first is stable across runs: task instructions and a compendium of the game’s rules, keywords, status effects, cards, relics and potions with their effects. The second is stable within a run: the memory bank (Sec.3). The first user message of a floor adds the act map, the run’s notes, a history of the floors played so far and the player’s current state (HP, gold, deck, relics, potions and keys). In combat, each turn’s message reports what each of the model’s actions did, what each enemy did, and the full state at the start of the new turn. Outside combat the message describes the current screen and its legal choices.

    The tools are: playing a card or a sequence of cards, ending the turn, using or discarding a potion, choosing an option by index or by name, choosing a map node, planning a route, taking notes, predicting the floor’s outcome, and the end-of-run memory operations. The full tool set is sent on every call, so that the cached prefix never changes, and an action illegal on the current screen is refused with an explanation. By default the model may return several actions in one response (multi-action), and the harness executes them in order, stopping at the first that fails. At the start of each act the model is asked for a route plan over the whole act map. At the end of each floor it is asked for its chance of surviving the current act and of winning the run, and may reflect and update its notes; when it ends a turn it may also predict its HP at the start of the next turn and at the end of the fight.

    Two principles shaped the harness. The model is shown what a human player sees and nothing more: the prompts describe the task on the current screen without steering towards a strategy (they never say, for instance, to check first whether an enemy can be killed this turn), and the system prompt holds only the documentation a player has in the game itself, namely its tutorial, tips and compendium. And the model is asked to do as much as possible per call, to keep cost down. Many combat actions have a deterministic effect, so the model plans the whole turn and returns every action it wants in one response, up to the first whose outcome is random. MiniStS makes one call per action and re-prompts with the new state [(Bateni and Whitehead, 2024)]. Orak’s agent may also return several actions at once, but spends three calls on each decision (reflection, planning, then the actions) and shows the model only the state its actions leave [(Park et al., 2026)]. Multi-action play asks the model to hold the intervening states in mind, which is harder. Batching also helped play in our preliminary runs. Because the model had to plan the whole turn before acting, it committed to a plan, and it did not spend reasoning deriving the same plan again after each action when that action had revealed nothing new. On the main seeds, one action per response needs 3.0 more calls per floor, costs 23% more and clears 0.07 fewer acts (Table2). So that it can still see what each action did, the harness diffs the game state between actions and returns each change as the result of the tool call that caused it, with enemies’ turns attributed enemy by enemy. A call that names a card imprecisely is resolved where the intended card is unambiguous, and otherwise answered with a “did you mean” suggestion rather than executed.

    Names, not indices.

    The model refers to what it acts on by name: a card by the name it is shown under (play_card(card_name="Bash", enemy_index=0)), and an event option, rest-site action, shop item or card on a selection screen by its label (choose_by_name(name="Rest")). Arguments are passed by name too, never by position. Only enemies, card rewards and the reward list are chosen by index, which is shown beside each entry. There are two reasons for this.

    The first is batching. A batch is written against the state at the start of the turn, but the hand changes while the batch runs: every card played moves the positions of the others, and cards are drawn, created, upgraded and moved by the plays themselves. A position in the hand goes stale after the first change, but a name still identifies the same card. A batch can therefore play a card that an earlier call in it creates, and it can answer, in the same call, a choice that a card opens (the card that Armaments upgrades, the card that Headbutt puts back), through target_card_names. This is what lets the model play a whole turn in one response without giving up any of the game’s mechanics. How Orak handles the same cases is in Sec.B.7.

    The second is reliability. In preliminary runs, weaker models sometimes reasoned their way to one option and then gave the index of another. A name states the intended option in the call itself, so it cannot pick a different option by mistake. A name that matches nothing is refused with a suggestion (Sec.B.5). On the main seeds this concern did not show up: with one action per response, the models tested chose no worse by index than by name (Table2).

    B.3 Notes and memory

    Run notes are rendered back to the model as tags. The memory ablation (Table27) varies the mechanism while holding everything else fixed. Consolidate (xml) is the default of Sec.3. Keep notes copies each run’s notes into the bank verbatim, with no consolidation call, so it keeps persistence but removes the rewriting. None discards the notes at the end of each run. In the compact arms the model instead writes a single prose summary through a one-argument compact tool, overwriting it at the end of every floor and, when consolidating, at the end of every run. Every prompt that asks the model to write something down includes the same generic guidance: distil insights rather than log events, and record what went well, what went wrong and what the model wishes it had known. It names nothing specific to the game.

    A cohort with a read-write bank is a chain. Seed k starts from the bank that seed k-1 left behind, so the seeds are played in order and a cohort’s bank is never shared with any other configuration: each bank is partitioned by model, character, the full configuration tag and the seed list.

    B.4 Knowledge reskin

    The names replaced are those of cards, relics, potions, enemies, events, powers and keywords, the character, and the map’s node labels. Names are replaced through placeholders, so that one replacement can never trigger another, and each replacement evokes the original’s effect rather than its name. The harness’s own text (the system prompt, state descriptions and tool results) is renamed; the model’s own text is not, so a real game name in a note is evidence of recognized prior knowledge rather than something to be laundered.

    The five mappings of the reskin ablation (Table29) are all generated in the same format, so that only the mapping file changes between arms. None shows the real names. Themed is the default. Random replaces every word with a pronounceable nonsense word, consistently, so that multiword names keep their shared structure. Permuted gives each entity the real name of a different entity of the same kind (cards within their colour and type), which is coherent but actively misleading. Permuted and themed applies the same permutation in the themed vocabulary. The permuted mappings keep every rule word that the themed mapping leaves unrenamed, so the arms differ only in the names. Table4 gives examples.

    B.5 Model-facing features

    This subsection lists everything the harness does that the model can see, beyond the outline in Sec.B.2. The harness never makes a strategic choice for the model. When it acts by itself, there is only one legal action, or the action has no strategic content. When it corrects a call, it either resolves the call where the intent is unambiguous or refuses it with an explanation. Quoted messages are given as the model receives them, before renaming.

    What the model is shown.

  • •

    Map. The act map is drawn with labelled nodes (Monster(5,2): floor 5, column 2). Burning elites, which carry the Emerald Key, are marked, and the act boss is named. The current floor is marked >> and the reachable next nodes *. On map screens the model may revise its route plan before choosing.

  • •

    Player overview. HP, gold, keys, the deck (identical copies merged as 3x Strike), relics with their descriptions and counters (e.g. (2/3), (USED)), and potions. It is omitted from a message when nothing in it has changed.

  • •

    Combat turn. Each enemy is shown with its index, HP, Block, intent (e.g. Attack for 6x2) and powers with their current descriptions. Dead enemies are removed and the rest renumbered. The player’s HP, Block, energy, powers, stance and orbs are shown, and the hand lists one card per line with cost, type, whether it targets and why it cannot be played. The draw, discard and exhaust piles are listed in full when they are relevant (on a new turn, after a change or a reshuffle, or when a card in hand refers to that pile) and as counts otherwise.

  • •

    Card names. Cards are referred to by name, not hand position. Copies that differ get a qualifier, e.g. [Strike (0 cost)] when an effect (e.g. Snecko Eye, Mummified Hand) has changed a cost, and so does a card whose value has grown past its base (Ritual Dagger, Genetic Algorithm).

  • •

    Effects. The result of each tool call is the change in game state that call caused, e.g. “Played Bash. Energy -2 (3→1). Enemy [0] Jaw Worm HP -8 (40→32); Vulnerable +2.” Cards drawn, created and exhausted are named.
