Between turns, the next message reports the end of the player’s turn, then one line per acting enemy, then the end of the round (powers/statuses decaying or expiring) and the start of the new turn (Block kept, start-of-turn relics, reshuffles). These are split using game-state snapshots from the mod (Sec.B.1). Where several effects land together (the end of a fight, a room, a selection screen), the harness reports the net change without naming a cause, leaving the attribution to the model, which can see its relics.

  • •

    Non-combat screens. Each screen lists its legal choices with what the model needs to choose: shop prices with (can’t afford) and the card-removal price; the HP a rest would heal; card, relic and potion rewards as one numbered list; event options with (DISABLED) marked; and the Match and Keep board. Each choice is confirmed with what it changed, e.g. “Chose to rest. HP +24 (…)”.

  • •

    History. One line per floor played so far (room type, encounter, turns taken, HP and gold change, cards added, upgraded and removed, relics gained), with the act’s route plan and the run notes.

    • Reading the model’s calls.

  • •

    Lenient matching. Card, potion, relic and option names are matched case-insensitively, with brackets, stray quotes and parentheses, and non-breaking spaces removed. A qualified name matches if its qualifiers match the card’s current values. A bare name resolves to the upgraded copy when only that copy is in hand (Bash→Bash+), but not the reverse. Numbers given as strings are converted. Under the reskin, names are mapped back to the game’s names and checked against what is on screen.

  • •

    Copies. If the copy of a card that a call names has left the hand by the time the call runs, the harness plays an identical copy that is still in hand, and refuses the call only if there is none.

  • •

    Deferred plays. A card named before it exists (one an earlier call in the batch will create or upgrade) is looked up again when its call comes up, and refused only if it is still missing then.

  • •

    Targets. An attack or potion that needs a target gets the only living enemy when there is one, and is refused otherwise. Enemy indices refer to the list the model was shown, not the game’s internal one. If a targeted enemy has died, the refusal says that the remaining enemies have been renumbered.

  • •

    Pre-targeted selections. A card that makes the player choose another card (Armaments, Headbutt, a discard) can name its target in the same call (target_card_names). The harness then makes the choice on the selection screen that opens and reports what was picked, so the batch continues without a further call to the model. Similarly, choose_by_name(name, target_name) buys a card removal, or picks Smith or Toke at a rest site, and then names the card in a single tool call.

  • •

    Aliases.choose_by_name("skip") or ("leave") means skip, and ("proceed") means proceed. A number given as a name is treated as an index. Phrases like “remove” map to the shop’s card removal. An event option can also be named by its effect text when exactly one option matches.

  • •

    Calls written as text. When a response contains no tool call, the harness reads calls written in its text: function-call notation (play_card(card_name="Strike")), JSON objects in the shapes models commonly use, a bare argument object that fits exactly one expected tool, or key: value lines when one tool is required. It reads the reasoning only when there is no visible text, and then only the final draft of the turn. It does not read a response that was cut off. A recovered call is executed like any other and counted as an error in Table23.

    • Corrections and refusals.

    A refused call costs nothing in the game. Its result says why, and usually what would be accepted:

  • •

    Did you mean. A card not in hand is refused with the cards that are, plus the closest name in hand if one is close enough (fuzzy match, similarity at least 0.6), with an example call: “Did you mean ‘Strike (1 cost)’? Example: play_card(card_name="Strike (1 cost)", enemy_index=0)”. Names that match more than one card are refused with the candidates. In preliminary runs, these suggestions stopped models from repeating the same refused call.

  • •

    Wrong tool or screen. A tool that does nothing on the current screen is refused with the tools that do: “not available on {SCREEN}. Valid tools here: […]”. The same applies to an action the game reports as unavailable (e.g. too little energy), to a disabled event option, and to an unaffordable shop item.

  • •

    Energy check.end_turn takes, as a required argument, the energy the model expects to have left. If the model ends its turn with more energy than it declared while a card in hand is still playable, the end of turn is refused: “Rejected end_turn: declared expected_energy_remaining=E, but you actually have A energy. Your turn plan didn’t match what happened…”. The model can then play more cards or end the turn again. This catches a model that has lost track of its own turn. For example, the relic Nunchaku gives an energy for every tenth Attack played; a model that does not notice the tenth Attack coming would end its turn with energy it could have spent. These miscounts are reported as tool errors (Table23).

  • •

    Actions the game would ignore. The game silently ignores some actions, which would leave the harness waiting for a state change that never comes. These are refused before they are sent: buying or picking up a potion with every potion slot full, drinking a potion the game marks as unusable here, taking a potion under Sozu, and buying a second card removal in one shop visit. The refusal names what is possible instead.

  • •

    Event fallback. If a named choice matches no option on an event, the event is shown again with both indices and labels, and choose_by_index is offered. Events whose options share a label (Memory Stone) are numbered from the start.

  • •

    Malformed arguments. A required argument left as a … placeholder, a missing argument, or a text argument under the wrong name is refused with an example of the correct call. A note given under a sibling field name is accepted, and the confirmation says so.

  • •

    No tool call. A response with no executable call gets one retry: “Your reply contained no tool call. Text describing a call, whether JSON or play_card(…) notation, is not a call. Call one or more of these tools now: …”. The model’s own reasoning is quoted back above this message. If the response was cut off at the length limit, the message says that nothing in it was executed.

  • •

    Game errors. An error from the mod is passed on as “Action failed: {error}. Choose a different action.”, with the player’s remaining energy added for an unplayable card. The harness does not retry the action itself.

  • •

    Repeated failure. After two batches in a row on the same screen with every call refused, the full screen state is sent again with the available tools.

    • Batches and interruptions.

    The model’s calls are executed one at a time, and the state is read after each. The rest of the batch is dropped, with a result for every dropped call, when:

  • •

    a call is refused (“Skipped: an earlier action in your batch was rejected… Your planned sequence is stale…”);

  • •

    cards are drawn or created mid-turn that the plan could not have foreseen (cards that fetch a named card do not count);

  • •

    an enemy’s intent changes to a different move;

  • •

    a Lightning orb hits a random enemy while more than one is alive;

  • •

    a selection screen opens that the plan did not account for;

  • •

    the fight or the floor ends.

    • Calls after end_turn are dropped as stale. Note writes always run. A batch with a single card play gets a reminder to send the whole turn in one response, unless that card draws cards or creates random ones, which the model cannot plan past. A card that makes the player choose another card does not excuse the batch, since the choice can be named in the same call. The exemption is decided from the card’s text: a card whose text says it draws, is random or has the player choose is exempt, which among Ironclad and colourless choice cards exempts Dual Wield and Discovery.

    Actions the harness takes by itself.

  • •

    Ending the turn when no card is playable and no potion usable (“No more playable options. Turn ended automatically.”).

  • •

    Single legal choices. The harness takes an event window with one option, a single reachable map node, and a selection screen where the number of eligible cards equals the number to pick. The skipped event windows are shown to the model at the start of its next call, with what they changed.

  • •

    Screens with no choice. The harness proceeds when proceeding is the only action, confirms a selection once the model has picked, opens chests (except with Cursed Key), and enters a shop it has walked into. It leaves a shop when nothing is affordable, or after 30 actions in it.

  • •

    Rewards with no trade-off. Gold, stolen gold and the Emerald Key are collected automatically, as are potions when they all fit. Each card reward is opened in the background so that its cards appear in the one reward list the model chooses from.

  • •

    Waiting for the game to deal the opening hand, finish a transform, or show a purchase before reporting it, so a reported effect is never one the game has not yet applied.

    • Guards.

    Ten consecutive failed model calls, or ten consecutive responses with no executable game action, end the run as a harness failure, and it is resumed from its autosave. Over the main runs (190 runs and 36,486 model calls) the first fired three times, each when an API account ran out of credit, and the second 16 times, all for Grok 4.6 on five of its seeds, each after ten responses that chose an option with an empty name. Transient API errors are retried with exponential backoff (five retries by default); 48 calls (0.13%) still failed after their retries. Authentication, billing and quota errors stop the whole seed queue rather than skipping the seed, because a skipped seed would change the memory every later seed in a read-write chain starts from; this happened twice. play_combo repeats a card sequence for an infinite combo, up to 1,000 times or until a pass changes nothing; it was called 149 times, and neither limit was reached. Reflection is capped at 20 turns and consolidation at 200; the longest took 13 and 47. When a conversation outgrows the model’s context window, the oldest turns of the floor are dropped (always keeping the floor’s first message and the latest turn) and a note tells the model how many were removed. This happened on 154 calls (0.4%), all from two models with 128k-token windows: Nemotron 3 Nano Omni (139 of its 708 calls, in every run) and gpt-oss-120b (15 calls, in three runs).

    B.6 What the model receives

    The excerpts below are quoted verbatim from Claude Opus 5's first run of the main cohort, so names appear as the model saw them under the themed reskin (“room” for floor, Guard for Block, Artifacts for relics).

    System prompt.

    A short preamble states the task, followed by the compendium: the game's rules and tips (42 points adapted from the game's own tutorial and loading-screen tips), its keywords and status effects, and the character's cards, the colourless, status and curse cards, and every relic and potion with its effect. On the first seed, before any memory exists, this is 30,715 characters, and with the tool definitions about 18,000 tokens. The memory bank is appended as it grows; by the tenth seed this model's system prompt had reached 227,089 characters.

    Tools.

    Seventeen tools are sent on every call (required arguments marked *): play_card(card_name*, enemy_index, target_card_names), play_combo(card_names*, enemy_index), end_turn(expected_energy_remaining*, predicted_hp_after_turn, predicted_hp_after_fight), use_potion(potion_name*, enemy_index), discard_potion(potion_name*), choose_by_index(choice_index*), choose_by_name(name*, target_name), choose_path(choice_index*), skip(), plan_route(route*, notes*), predict(act_win_probability*, run_win_probability*), save_note(key*, note*), delete_note(key*), finish_reflection(), save_memory(key*, memory*), delete_memory(key*), finish_consolidation().

    A combat turn.

    The message that opens a turn, here turn 3 of an elite fight on floor 8. The effect of each card played on the previous turn has already been returned as the result of its own tool call (e.g. “Played Trip Attack. Energy -2 (4→2). Enemy [2] Bolt Sprite HP -8 (41→33); Ward cleared.”).

    Lines longer than the page are wrapped with an indent; the text is otherwise as sent.

    End of a floor.

    After the floor's last screen the model is asked to reflect, then to forecast:

    End of the run.

    The consolidation message carries the run's result and final state, each act's full map, route plan and path taken, the history of every floor and the run notes, and ends:

    B.7 Coverage compared with Orak and Bottled AI

    Orak's own rule bot plays the map, events, shops, rest sites, chests, boss relics, Neow and potions, so its model decides combat and card rewards only. Even within a fight its model decides less than ours. Orak asks the model only when a card can be played, so every card choice that a card or potion opens mid-fight (Armaments, True Grit+, Dual Wield, Headbutt, Exhume, an Attack Potion) goes to the rule bot, which picks from a fixed card ranking rather than the fight at hand: the best-ranked card to upgrade or copy, the worst-ranked to exhaust, and, since the flag that would select the best is never set, the worst-ranked card for Headbutt and Exhume. The model is not told which card was chosen, and the rest of its planned turn is dropped. Orak's agent returns several actions at once, as ours does, but plays each card by its position in the hand as shown when the model decided, so a response cannot play a card that arrives mid-turn. Queued actions keep executing through draws and random effects, re-resolved by card identity so a shifted hand still plays the intended card, but the model sees what was drawn only once its queue is spent; Orak's paper describes the state as returned after each action, where its code returns it after the queue. Ours puts every such choice to the model, lets a card-targeting card name its target in the same call, and interrupts the queue when cards are drawn or created, orbs evoke at random or an enemy's intent changes, naming what changed [(Park et al., 2026)].

    Game coverage.

    Table5 goes through the game by feature. It refines the Model plays and Choices columns of Table2, and adds Bottled AI. Orak’s model sees no orbs, stance, potions or card piles, so a Defect under Orak plays its orb cards without seeing the orbs they make. Orak builds on spirecomm, a Python client for CommunicationMod whose last commit predates the Watcher, and so cannot play the Watcher at all; our harness adds the Watcher to spirecomm itself. Orak’s rule bot never chooses Recall at a rest site, so it never collects the Ruby Key and can never reach Act 4.

    Card coverage.

    Table6 estimates how much of the game each harness lets its player use in full. For Orak, a card counts as unsupported if playing it opens a choice (either version, so Armaments counts although Armaments+ upgrades every card without asking). Orak’s rule bot makes those choices, not the model. 33 cards open a choice when played, among them Headbutt, Warcry, Dual Wield and Exhume, and every card that has the player pick a card to discard, scry or keep, or pick one of three. Bottled AI plays only cards its combat simulator models, and treats any other card as one it can never play. Its gaps are mostly cards that open a choice or have a random effect (Armaments, Headbutt, Discovery, Infernal Blade), plus a few powers (Brutality, Combust, Rupture). Our harness passes every selection a card opens to the model, so every card is supported. The count covers playing a card, not how well a player uses it.

item.title: 程序说门开了，画面开了吗？PROWBench 用 170 个可程序构造的片段查视频模型的规则保真度 ｜ PROWBench: Do Video Models Render What the Program Specifies?
item.description:
一句话：可编程世界模型把规则执行和画面生成分开后，画面到底有没有照着程序走，缺一套能核对的评测。

要点：

  • 170 个程序化构造的片段、600 段代理视频，覆盖多样场景与交互，并记录实体状态与带时间戳的事件（含视野外事件）
  • 事件记录可回放，据此渲染同步视角与代理表示，让生成的视频能对照程序执行的可观测后果来核对
  • 评的是实体控制、长程记忆，以及两个基于 VLM 的指标：逻辑-画面一致性与可交互性；覆盖第一人称与第三人称

为什么值得看：把规则交给程序、画面交给模型，是「AI 原生引擎」最现实的一种分工；这套评测就是这种分工下最该先立起来的验收标准。

中文摘要：可编程世界模型把可执行的动力学与视觉生成分开，为下一代游戏引擎提供了有希望的基础；但生成的画面是否真的遵守显式规则与交互，一直缺少足够细的评测。现有基准多测画面质量、可控性、指令与物理遵从，很少检查对程序规定的细粒度世界事件的保真度。PROWBench 由 170 个程序化构造的片段与 600 段代理视频组成，覆盖多样场景与交互；它记录实体状态与带时间戳的事件（包括相机视野之外发生的事件）作为可回放的世界记录，再由这些记录渲染出同步视角与代理表示，于是生成的视频可以对照程序执行的可观测后果逐项核对。框架可扩展，支持构建场景、控制行为，并能用不同表示（如粗粒度 3D、包围盒）渲染各相机视角；评测覆盖第一与第三人称，部分片段提供同步多视角观测。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

原文发布：2026-10-01

本期推送：2026-10-25

ROWBench: Do Video Models Render
What the Program Specifies?

October 5, 2026

Abstract

Programmable world models separate executable dynamics from visual generation, offering a promising foundation for next-generation game engines. However, their visual adherence to explicit rules and interactions remains insufficiently evaluated. Existing benchmarks assess visual quality, controllability, and instruction or physical adherence, but rarely test fidelity to fine-grained, program-specified world events. We introduce PROWBench, comprising 170 programmatically constructed episodes and 600 proxy videos covering diverse scenes and interactions. PROWBench logs entity states and timestamped events, including those outside the camera’s field of view, as replayable world records, from which it renders synchronized views and proxy representations. This enables generated videos to be checked against the observable consequences of program execution. An extensible framework constructs scenes, controls behaviors, and can render each camera view in different representations, such as coarse 3D, and bounding boxes. The benchmark covers first- and third-person perspectives, with synchronized multi-view observations available for a subset of episodes. Grounded in these records, PROWBench evaluates entity control, long-horizon memory, and, with two VLM-based metrics, Logic-Render Alignment and Interaction Success Rate, adherence to the prescribed timeline and the visual realization of timestamped engine-recorded events.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in video world models have enabled increasingly realistic, open-ended interactive environments. However, maintaining persistent world states and enforcing user-defined rules remain challenging when entities, attributes, and interaction outcomes are represented implicitly through visual histories or latent context. Programmable World Model and Code World Model address these limitations by separating world-state evolution from visual generation [(Huang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026b)]: coding agents and executable programs maintain states and interaction rules, while video models generate observations conditioned on structured representations of the world. This separation combines explicit state control with visual generation, but correct program execution does not guarantee faithful visual realization. A generated video may appear plausible while violating a rule or failing to depict a specified interaction. This raises a central evaluation question: can video models faithfully render the scene structure, rules, and interactions of a programmable world?

Existing benchmarks evaluate video quality [(Huang et al., 2024)], controllability and dynamics [(Duan et al., 2025)], instruction following and physical adherence [(Li et al., 2025a)], and interactive control and consistency [(Ye et al., 2026; Shang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Ying et al., 2026)]. However, as summarized in Table 6.1, they rarely test fidelity to fine-grained, program-specified world events: without replayable records of entity states and timestamped events, a generated video can be judged for plausibility but not against what the program executed. None of them renders the same recorded scene in paired proxy representations, and synchronized views are rare, although both are needed to isolate the effects of representation and viewpoint while holding scene content and actions fixed.

To address these gaps, we introduce PROWBench, a benchmark for evaluating the visual realization of programmable worlds. Figure 1 provides an overview of our extensible framework and benchmark. PROWBench combines a programmatically constructed dataset with complementary metrics for logic adherence and interaction realization. The data engine is available for extension. It logs entity states and timestamped events, including those outside the camera’s field of view, as replayable world records and renders them into synchronized views and proxy representations, so that generated videos can be checked against the observable consequences of program execution.

PROWBench contains 170 dynamic scene episodes covering diverse environments and interactions. Each episode currently provides three synchronized representations (coarse 3D, semantic proxy, and colored oriented bounding boxes) from shared state, action, and interaction records, enabling controlled comparisons across representations. Some episodes additionally provide synchronized multi-view observations for cross-view comparisons. Grounded in these records, PROWBench evaluates entity control and the long-horizon memory of entities that leave and re-enter the view, and introduces two VLM-based metrics: Logic-Render Alignment assesses adherence to the prescribed timeline, while Interaction Success Rate checks whether recorded events are visually realized at the corresponding times using engine logs as ground truth. An extensible programmatic framework separates scene construction, behavior control, state recording, and rendering, allowing researchers to expand scene layouts, actions, and representations while generating aligned observations from shared state records.

We evaluate state-of-the-art models with the inputs produced by this data engine: coarse 3D, semantic-proxy, and colored-OBB renders of the recorded states, together with text prompts obtained by converting the engine’s recorded events. Our experiments assess their logic adherence and interaction realization across viewpoints and representation settings. Surprisingly, with appropriate prompts, existing general-purpose video generation models such as MiniMax-H3 [(MiniMax-AI, 2026)], without task-specific training, follow the prescribed entity trajectories and event logic well, and perform on par with camera-conditioned world models in camera following without explicit camera injection. Additional task- or domain-specific training can still improve several aspects, such as entity placement and the realization of domain-specific events. The proxy itself also matters: outputs sometimes follow the input geometry too closely and inherit the coarse shapes of low-poly proxies, while box proxies leave open which described appearance belongs to which entity, so designing a good proxy remains an open problem. Long-video generation remains challenging in terms of both camera following and entity persistence, while direct multi-view generation still yields unsatisfactory results.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    Benchmark. We introduce PROWBench, comprising 170 episodes and 600 synchronized proxy videos covering multiple perspectives, visual representations, and diverse interactions, with shared world-state and action records.

  • •

    Metrics. We evaluate entity control and long-horizon memory against the recorded world states, and propose Logic-Render Alignment and Interaction Success Rate to assess whether generated videos follow the prescribed timeline and visually realize engine-recorded interaction events.

  • •

    Extensible framework. We provide a reusable programmatic generation framework that supports extensions to scene layouts, actions, and visual representations, enabling aligned multi-view and multi-representation data generation from shared state records.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video World Models and Programmable World States

    Video world models predict future observations from visual context and actions. Genie [(Bruce et al., 2024)] learns controllable environments from unlabeled videos, while GameNGen [(Valevski et al., 2025)] enables real-time action-conditioned game generation. GameFactory [(Yu et al., 2025)], Matrix-Game [(Zhang et al., 2025)], Yume1.5 [(Mao et al., 2026a)], and LingBot-World [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)] advance generalization, interaction, and long-horizon consistency. Memory-enhanced WorldPlay [(Sun et al., 2025)], Matrix-Game 3.0 [(Wang et al., 2026)], and AlayaWorld [(Team et al., 2026)] improve persistence through spatial-context retrieval or reconstruction.

    While these models infer states from visual history and memory, programmable world models externalize state evolution. Code World Model [(Chen et al., 2026b)] uses a coding agent to maintain executable states and interaction logic, while Programmable World Model [(Huang et al., 2026a)] feeds persistent structured states to a generative renderer. Other approaches similarly separate state or dynamics from appearance [(Meng et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026b; Cai et al., 2026a)]. PROWBench evaluates whether generated observations faithfully realize these explicit states and interactions.

    2.2 Structured Representations for Visual Generation

    Structured conditions offer direct spatial control through depth, trajectories, bounding boxes, masks, and camera motion [(Esser et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024d; Luo et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025c)]. Geometry-aware methods incorporate 3D boxes, bird’s-eye-view layouts, world volumes, and structured traffic scenes [(Gao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024c; Wang et al., 2025)]. Generative rendering uses explicit geometry or renderer-derived signals: Coarse-to-Real [(Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026)] and VideoFrom3D [(Kim et al., 2025)] use coarse 3D scenes, while Diffusion Renderer [(Liang et al., 2025)], AlayaRenderer [(Huang et al., 2026b)], its real-time extension [(Lin et al., 2026a)], and LiVER [(Cai et al., 2026b)] use denser rendering cues. These approaches span sparse object controls to dense geometric representations. Comparisons across representations are often confounded by differences in models, datasets, and tasks. PROWBench derives paired proxy representations from the same recorded world-state trajectory and camera configuration, isolating representation effects on visual realization under fixed scene evolution.

    2.3 World Model Benchmarks and Evaluation

    VBench [(Huang et al., 2024)] and EvalCrafter [(Liu et al., 2024)] assess video quality, temporal consistency, motion, and semantic alignment. WorldSimBench [(Qin et al., 2025)], WorldModelBench [(Li et al., 2025a)], and WorldScore [(Duan et al., 2025)] extend evaluation to physical plausibility, controllability, and world dynamics. MIND [(Ye et al., 2026)], WorldMark [(Xu et al., 2026)], Omni-WorldBench [(Wu et al., 2026)], WorldArena [(Shang et al., 2026)], and iWorld-Bench [(Fang et al., 2026)] further target interactive behavior, memory, and long-horizon consistency.

    WBench [(Ying et al., 2026)] evaluates multi-turn navigation, subject actions, event editing, and perspective switching for instruction adherence, consistency, and physical plausibility. These benchmarks generally assess complete pipelines, coupling errors in action understanding, state prediction, memory, dynamics, and rendering.

    PROWBench isolates rendering fidelity using engine-recorded frame-level states, rules, and timestamped interactions, enabling comparisons across synchronized perspectives and proxy representations under the same trajectory. Logic-Renderer Alignment measures whether specified rules are visibly realized, while Interaction measures whether recorded events appear at the corresponding times.

    3 Benchmark

    We construct the PROWBench dataset using a programmable world generation pipeline that produces aligned conditioning inputs and evaluation records. Figure 2 outlines the pipeline, while Figure 6.2 illustrates the dataset’s content and diversity. We describe the pipeline and evaluation suite below, with detailed dataset statistics provided in Section 6.1.

    3.1 World Generation Pipeline

    We introduce a pipeline for constructing programmable worlds and producing structured conditioning inputs and evaluation annotations for generative video models. The pipeline provides three complementary capabilities: world synthesis, control compilation, and final process. Together, these capabilities produce replayable world trajectories, synchronized conditioning inputs, and structured evaluation records.

    World Synthesis. The pipeline constructs dynamic worlds from configurations specifying the environment, entity layout, participating actors, task controllers, random seeds, and execution duration. Procedural routines generate terrain, buildings, roads, interiors, and interaction objects, together with collision surfaces, collision constraints, and interaction anchors. Entities have persistent episode-level identifiers, semantic categories, component hierarchies, and task-relevant attributes. Random seeds control variations in scene layouts, motion paths, speeds, and animation phases.

    Specialized controllers coordinate articulated poses, object trajectories, and participant interactions through procedural animation and motion models. They support three broad categories of behavior. Interaction controllers organize tasks into explicit phases: for example, carrying proceeds through approaching, grasping, lifting, transporting, and releasing an object, with corresponding updates to hand targets and object ownership. Activity and locomotion controllers support animal behaviors and simplified flight and swimming dynamics. Driving controllers provide closed-loop control of vehicle motion. During execution, these controllers report action phases, participating entities, and relationship changes for recording and validation. External agents can query entities, submit supported actions or plans, advance the world by fixed ticks, and inspect execution feedback.

    Each execution produces a structured episode record containing shared scene geometry, entity definitions and hierarchies, initial conditions, and temporal records of entity transforms, articulated poses, visibility, and appearance changes. Controller events and available input traces accompany these records, with explicit temporal mappings linking world execution, saved states, and video frames. Each saved state can be reconstructed independently from the shared scene description and its corresponding dynamic record. Configurations, random seeds, and source information are retained for provenance tracking.

    Control Compilation. The pipeline compiles recorded world states and camera trajectories into synchronized visual conditioning inputs for generative video models.

    Third-person cameras follow task-dependent trajectories, while first-person cameras are derived from recorded head positions, character or vehicle orientations, and task-specific gaze information. The observing character’s display geometry is hidden in its first-person view, while its entity and articulated state remain in the shared world record. Final camera trajectories include intrinsics, camera-to-world and world-to-camera matrices, projection parameters, and clipping planes. Additional cameras can be associated with different participants to provide multiple perspectives of the same episode.

    Rendering adapters map shared world records to conditioning representations. Our current implementation provides three representations. Coarse 3D representation (Coarse 3D) uses neutral materials to preserve scene shape, object silhouettes, and articulated motion. Semantic proxy (CWM proxy) combines semantically colored environments with simplified entity proxies, retaining global trajectories, orientations, and task-relevant posture while reducing local articulation and shape detail. Colored oriented bounding boxes (Colored-OBB) represent selected entities through spatial envelopes, stable instance colors, and directional cues, with a semi-transparent white face marking the front of each entity, while retaining geometry for environmental structures and simple objects. OBB bounds are updated over time, while instance colors remain consistent across frames and views.

    Rendering adapters specify entity selection, proxy templates, transparency, occlusion, and clipping behavior. Given shared scene geometry G, recorded world state Sᵢ, camera parameters Cᵢᵛ for view v, and representation r, a conditioning frame is generated as Iᵢ^v,r=ℝᵣ(G,Sᵢ,Cᵢᵛ), where ℝᵣ is the representation-specific rendering adapter. Different views observe the same saved state, and representations within each view share camera parameters. Additional camera policies and rendering adapters can reuse recorded episodes without rerunning behavior controllers, provided the required information is available in the world records, whereas new behaviors produce new recorded executions. This separation preserves temporal alignment and enables controlled comparisons across representations and viewpoints while keeping the underlying world evolution fixed.

    Final Process. The pipeline exports three categories of outputs: scene and motion records, rendered observations, and text and interaction labels. Scene and motion records support replay and include scene geometry, entity identities and semantic categories, spatial and articulated states, joint poses, bounding volumes, and entity and camera trajectories with associated camera parameters. Rendered observations comprise synchronized proxy videos across viewpoints and representations, accompanied by metric depth interpreted with respect to its recorded geometry. Text and interaction labels describe action phases, participant relationships, and timestamped events, together with accompanying textual descriptions and contact targets and residuals.

    Validation comprises four complementary components. Task and timeline checks assess scenario-specific phases, terminal conditions or state validity, and recording coverage. They also verify task-level interaction labels against the applicable annotation policy and required participant categories. Geometric checks evaluate penetration, support, and contact consistency at saved states using canonical geometry. Replay and alignment checks assess state reconstruction, camera alignment, and consistency with the selected representation. They further establish correspondence among videos, depth, and state labels using source records, frame indices, camera information, and timestamps. Visual and media quality checks combine first-frame visibility measurements based on canonical-geometry pixel counts and view-frustum tests with documented visual inspection of first frames and selected temporal samples. These inspections assess subject visibility and observation readability, while media decoding and hash checks assess output integrity. Visibility measurements and visual reviews are interpreted within the scope of the recorded frames and geometry.

    To preserve provenance and revision history, failed attempts and their available diagnostics are retained separately from accepted episodes. For each batch-specific revision, affected outputs are backed up, changes to world records, camera trajectories, or representation policies are documented, and the corresponding media and metadata are updated together. Hash checks verify the integrity of unchanged source records where applicable. Sample metadata and source hashes link released observations to their source records, rendering configurations, and verification reports.

    3.2 Evaluation Suite

    We evaluate five complementary capabilities: controllability, visual and temporal quality, logic and state alignment, multi-view consistency, and long-horizon memory. Engine-recorded trajectories, events, and states provide references for evaluating adherence to the prescribed world evolution, while established perceptual metrics assess video quality.

    Controllability. We evaluate whether entities and the camera follow their prescribed trajectories. For entity control, we consider dynamic and interaction-relevant entities visible in the reference view, excluding terrain, effects, and scene geometry. Generated entities are localized with SAM 3 [(Carion et al., 2026)] from semantic-label prompts and matched to engine-projected references by label-compatible Hungarian matching. BBox IoU measures spatial alignment over the visible trajectory, with missed detections assigned zero IoU, while Center Error measures normalized center displacement conditional on detection. We report clip-level averages over evaluable entities; full visibility, matching, and aggregation details are provided in Appendix 7.

    Interaction Success Rate. Global similarity alone does not determine whether a prescribed interaction is successfully executed. We therefore evaluate registered engine events, each defined by its participants, temporal window, action, and expected end state. For each event, Qwen3.6-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026)] is provided with eight frames sampled around the event window, including both full-frame context and an engine-localized crop, and independently judges the prescribed action, expected end state, and participant presence. An event is considered successful only when the response is valid and both the action and end state are judged present. For a generated scene-camera sample s with event set 𝔼ₛ, we define

    ISRₛ=(1)/(|𝔼ₛ|)∑_e∈𝔼ₛ1[valid response, action=yes, end state=yes].

    		(1)

    Table entries average ISRₛ equally across samples, preventing samples with more annotated events from receiving greater weight.

    We additionally report gISRₛ, an IoU-weighted variant of ISR that jointly reflects interaction success and entity placement:

    gISRₛ=ISRₛ·IoUₛ,

    		(2)

    where IoUₛ is the clip-level BBox IoU of sample s. Table entries average gISRₛ equally across samples.

    Logic-Render Alignment. Logic-Render Alignment measures whether each segment of the action timeline in the engine-derived prompt is visibly depicted within its time window. For each annotated timeline segment, the judge receives twelve frames sampled from the corresponding temporal window, together with the expected event description and neighboring descriptions as context. The metric evaluates whether the action prescribed by the engine logic is visibly realized within the corresponding segment. For a sample s with annotated timeline segments Tₛ, we define

    LRAₛ=(1)/(|Tₛ|)∑_τ∈Tₛ1[prescribed action in segmentτis judged present],

    		(3)

    so that LRAₛ is the fraction of timeline segments whose prescribed actions are visually consistent with the engine-defined logic.

    Similarly, we report gLRAₛ, an IoU-weighted variant of LRA that jointly reflects timeline adherence and entity placement:

    gLRAₛ=LRAₛ·IoUₛ.

    		(4)

    Table entries average gLRAₛ equally across samples.

    Figure 8.4 illustrates the distinction between the two behavioral metrics. ISR evaluates whether a registered interaction is successfully completed, requiring both the prescribed action and expected end state, whereas LRA evaluates whether the generated video realizes the engine-defined event logic by depicting each prescribed action in its corresponding temporal segment.

    Memory over Long Horizons. For the 30-second evaluation, we test whether entities that leave the field of view reappear at the location and in the state prescribed by the engine. We define an absence event when an entity becomes invisible and later re-enters the view. Reappearance IoU measures spatial recovery after re-entry by comparing the reference box with label-compatible detections, with missed detections assigned zero IoU. State Persistence measures whether a returning person preserves the prescribed locomotion state, classified as walking or standing and judged from post-return frames by Qwen3.6-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026)]. Both metrics are averaged first within scenes and then across scenes with valid events.

    Additional metric definitions, implementation details, and evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix 7.

    3.3 Benchmark Tracks

    PROWBench organizes its evaluation cases into two tracks with four settings. Each setting uses its own evaluation set, and the scenes of the two main-track settings are disjoint.

    Main Track. The main track evaluates controlled generation of five-second clips in two settings that differ in the appearance reference and use disjoint scenes. When the agent already has an appearance reference, such as a concept image or a prescribed character design, it can supply it as the RGB first frame. The Verified-FF setting evaluates this case with 40 scene-camera pairs (31 third-person follow, 9 first-person; top of Table 1). Its RGB first frame is part of the benchmark: it is generated with MiniMax-H3 from the colored-OBB proxy and the scene description and checked against the recorded person count, positions, facing and layout (Appendix 6.2), and every method that accepts a first frame receives this identical image. In procedural game-world construction, the agent usually has no ready-made RGB appearance reference. The Unverified-FF setting therefore prescribes only the world state, the text, and the control signals, and asks whether models can jointly solve entity control, appearance generation, and identity binding. It contains 90 pairs (78 third-person follow, 12 first-person; bottom of Table 1), and appearance must be determined by each model from the text and the control signal. The curation of this set used MiniMax-H3 outputs, so results involving MiniMax-H3 should be read with this potential bias in mind.

    Challenge Track. The challenge track tests whether short-clip control extends to two harder settings. Control in short clips does not guarantee that a model maintains one world state over longer horizons, in which entities leave the view, re-enter later and keep their state and motion across generation windows. The long-horizon setting (Table 2) contains ten 30-second recordings, one camera each. In a multi-player game, each player observes the same world through their own camera. Even when each view is generated independently, the views must agree on where each participant is, who they are, what they look like, and the scene structure. The multi-view setting (Table 3) contains ten four-player scenes, each with four synchronized third-person follow views, one per player, generated independently.

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments address a central question: can current video generation and video world models faithfully render a prescribed dynamic world, rather than merely produce visually plausible videos? For game worlds, visual quality alone is insufficient. A successful model must follow prescribed entity trajectories, camera motion, and event timelines, while maintaining consistency over long horizons and across synchronized views. We therefore organize the evaluation into a main track of five-second clips and a challenge track of long-horizon and multi-view settings. Sections 4.3 and 4.4 report the results, and Section 4.5 compares the method classes across both tracks and draws the main takeaways. The experimental setup is detailed in Section 4.2.

    4.1 Evaluated Methods

    We evaluate 11 models, grouped into three families by the control information they receive. (a) Camera-conditioned world models. EchoWM [(Zhang et al., 2026)], SANA-WM [(Zhu et al., 2026)], LingBot-World 2.0 [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)] and AlayaWorld v1.1 [(Team et al., 2026)] receive an RGB first frame, the text prompt, and the recorded camera trajectory. They obtain explicit camera control but no entity trajectories. (b) Proxy-video-to-RGB models. These models translate an engine-rendered control representation into a realistic RGB video. Cosmos-Transfer2.5 [(Ali et al., 2025)] receives engine depth and class-level segmentation; C2R [(Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026)] receives the coarse 3D proxy and the text; CWM [(Chen et al., 2026b)] (fine-tuned from MiniMax-H3) receives the CWM proxy, depth, the RGB first frame, and the text; LynnReal-Omni [(Mao et al., 2026b)], which builds directly on MiniMax-H3 and extends it with native support for heterogeneous visual controls, including editable 3D renders and game recordings; and PWM [(Huang et al., 2026a)] receives colored-OBB proxy, the RGB first frame, and the text prompt. Because PWM is trained only on gunfight scenes, it is evaluated only on the gunfight set of Section 4. (c) Video foundation models. MiniMax-H3 [(MiniMax-AI, 2026)], Seedance 2.5 [(ByteDance Seed Team, 2026)] are used without any adaptation to our proxy representations. They take the colored-OBB proxy video as a reference video together with the text prompt, and RGB references as specified in each table.

    4.2 Experimental Setup

    All evaluation samples come from recorded game-world states and are scored against the engine state; each sample is one scene observed by one camera. Every recorded state is provided in three proxy representations, Coarse 3D, CWM proxy and Colored-OBB, together with engine depth, the camera trajectory, a scene description and the state of every object, and each method receives the control representation of its native interface. Text prompts are generated automatically from the recorded scene, entities, and action timeline. All models are evaluated in their native output formats against the same engine records; the engine renders of the proxies are scored as diagnostic references. The tracks and settings are defined in Section 3.3. Methods whose native interface requires an RGB image (the world models and CWM) receive frame 0 of the MiniMax-H3 output for the same scene and camera; this frame is not a prescribed reference, but it can transmit MiniMax-H3’s appearance assignments, and analyses of appearance identity account separately for effects inherited from it.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：可编程世界模型把规则执行和画面生成分开后，画面到底有没有照着程序走，缺一套能核对的评测。

要点：

  • 170 个程序化构造的片段、600 段代理视频，覆盖多样场景与交互，并记录实体状态与带时间戳的事件（含视野外事件）
  • 事件记录可回放，据此渲染同步视角与代理表示，让生成的视频能对照程序执行的可观测后果来核对
  • 评的是实体控制、长程记忆，以及两个基于 VLM 的指标：逻辑-画面一致性与可交互性；覆盖第一人称与第三人称

为什么值得看：把规则交给程序、画面交给模型，是「AI 原生引擎」最现实的一种分工；这套评测就是这种分工下最该先立起来的验收标准。

中文摘要：可编程世界模型把可执行的动力学与视觉生成分开，为下一代游戏引擎提供了有希望的基础；但生成的画面是否真的遵守显式规则与交互，一直缺少足够细的评测。现有基准多测画面质量、可控性、指令与物理遵从，很少检查对程序规定的细粒度世界事件的保真度。PROWBench 由 170 个程序化构造的片段与 600 段代理视频组成，覆盖多样场景与交互；它记录实体状态与带时间戳的事件（包括相机视野之外发生的事件）作为可回放的世界记录，再由这些记录渲染出同步视角与代理表示，于是生成的视频可以对照程序执行的可观测后果逐项核对。框架可扩展，支持构建场景、控制行为，并能用不同表示（如粗粒度 3D、包围盒）渲染各相机视角；评测覆盖第一与第三人称，部分片段提供同步多视角观测。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

原文发布：2026-10-01

本期推送：2026-10-25

ROWBench: Do Video Models Render
What the Program Specifies?

October 5, 2026

Abstract

Programmable world models separate executable dynamics from visual generation, offering a promising foundation for next-generation game engines. However, their visual adherence to explicit rules and interactions remains insufficiently evaluated. Existing benchmarks assess visual quality, controllability, and instruction or physical adherence, but rarely test fidelity to fine-grained, program-specified world events. We introduce PROWBench, comprising 170 programmatically constructed episodes and 600 proxy videos covering diverse scenes and interactions. PROWBench logs entity states and timestamped events, including those outside the camera’s field of view, as replayable world records, from which it renders synchronized views and proxy representations. This enables generated videos to be checked against the observable consequences of program execution. An extensible framework constructs scenes, controls behaviors, and can render each camera view in different representations, such as coarse 3D, and bounding boxes. The benchmark covers first- and third-person perspectives, with synchronized multi-view observations available for a subset of episodes. Grounded in these records, PROWBench evaluates entity control, long-horizon memory, and, with two VLM-based metrics, Logic-Render Alignment and Interaction Success Rate, adherence to the prescribed timeline and the visual realization of timestamped engine-recorded events.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in video world models have enabled increasingly realistic, open-ended interactive environments. However, maintaining persistent world states and enforcing user-defined rules remain challenging when entities, attributes, and interaction outcomes are represented implicitly through visual histories or latent context. Programmable World Model and Code World Model address these limitations by separating world-state evolution from visual generation [(Huang et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026b)]: coding agents and executable programs maintain states and interaction rules, while video models generate observations conditioned on structured representations of the world. This separation combines explicit state control with visual generation, but correct program execution does not guarantee faithful visual realization. A generated video may appear plausible while violating a rule or failing to depict a specified interaction. This raises a central evaluation question: can video models faithfully render the scene structure, rules, and interactions of a programmable world?

Existing benchmarks evaluate video quality [(Huang et al., 2024)], controllability and dynamics [(Duan et al., 2025)], instruction following and physical adherence [(Li et al., 2025a)], and interactive control and consistency [(Ye et al., 2026; Shang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Ying et al., 2026)]. However, as summarized in Table 6.1, they rarely test fidelity to fine-grained, program-specified world events: without replayable records of entity states and timestamped events, a generated video can be judged for plausibility but not against what the program executed. None of them renders the same recorded scene in paired proxy representations, and synchronized views are rare, although both are needed to isolate the effects of representation and viewpoint while holding scene content and actions fixed.

To address these gaps, we introduce PROWBench, a benchmark for evaluating the visual realization of programmable worlds. Figure 1 provides an overview of our extensible framework and benchmark. PROWBench combines a programmatically constructed dataset with complementary metrics for logic adherence and interaction realization. The data engine is available for extension. It logs entity states and timestamped events, including those outside the camera’s field of view, as replayable world records and renders them into synchronized views and proxy representations, so that generated videos can be checked against the observable consequences of program execution.

PROWBench contains 170 dynamic scene episodes covering diverse environments and interactions. Each episode currently provides three synchronized representations (coarse 3D, semantic proxy, and colored oriented bounding boxes) from shared state, action, and interaction records, enabling controlled comparisons across representations. Some episodes additionally provide synchronized multi-view observations for cross-view comparisons. Grounded in these records, PROWBench evaluates entity control and the long-horizon memory of entities that leave and re-enter the view, and introduces two VLM-based metrics: Logic-Render Alignment assesses adherence to the prescribed timeline, while Interaction Success Rate checks whether recorded events are visually realized at the corresponding times using engine logs as ground truth. An extensible programmatic framework separates scene construction, behavior control, state recording, and rendering, allowing researchers to expand scene layouts, actions, and representations while generating aligned observations from shared state records.

We evaluate state-of-the-art models with the inputs produced by this data engine: coarse 3D, semantic-proxy, and colored-OBB renders of the recorded states, together with text prompts obtained by converting the engine’s recorded events. Our experiments assess their logic adherence and interaction realization across viewpoints and representation settings. Surprisingly, with appropriate prompts, existing general-purpose video generation models such as MiniMax-H3 [(MiniMax-AI, 2026)], without task-specific training, follow the prescribed entity trajectories and event logic well, and perform on par with camera-conditioned world models in camera following without explicit camera injection. Additional task- or domain-specific training can still improve several aspects, such as entity placement and the realization of domain-specific events. The proxy itself also matters: outputs sometimes follow the input geometry too closely and inherit the coarse shapes of low-poly proxies, while box proxies leave open which described appearance belongs to which entity, so designing a good proxy remains an open problem. Long-video generation remains challenging in terms of both camera following and entity persistence, while direct multi-view generation still yields unsatisfactory results.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    Benchmark. We introduce PROWBench, comprising 170 episodes and 600 synchronized proxy videos covering multiple perspectives, visual representations, and diverse interactions, with shared world-state and action records.

  • •

    Metrics. We evaluate entity control and long-horizon memory against the recorded world states, and propose Logic-Render Alignment and Interaction Success Rate to assess whether generated videos follow the prescribed timeline and visually realize engine-recorded interaction events.

  • •

    Extensible framework. We provide a reusable programmatic generation framework that supports extensions to scene layouts, actions, and visual representations, enabling aligned multi-view and multi-representation data generation from shared state records.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video World Models and Programmable World States

    Video world models predict future observations from visual context and actions. Genie [(Bruce et al., 2024)] learns controllable environments from unlabeled videos, while GameNGen [(Valevski et al., 2025)] enables real-time action-conditioned game generation. GameFactory [(Yu et al., 2025)], Matrix-Game [(Zhang et al., 2025)], Yume1.5 [(Mao et al., 2026a)], and LingBot-World [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)] advance generalization, interaction, and long-horizon consistency. Memory-enhanced WorldPlay [(Sun et al., 2025)], Matrix-Game 3.0 [(Wang et al., 2026)], and AlayaWorld [(Team et al., 2026)] improve persistence through spatial-context retrieval or reconstruction.

    While these models infer states from visual history and memory, programmable world models externalize state evolution. Code World Model [(Chen et al., 2026b)] uses a coding agent to maintain executable states and interaction logic, while Programmable World Model [(Huang et al., 2026a)] feeds persistent structured states to a generative renderer. Other approaches similarly separate state or dynamics from appearance [(Meng et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026b; Cai et al., 2026a)]. PROWBench evaluates whether generated observations faithfully realize these explicit states and interactions.

    2.2 Structured Representations for Visual Generation

    Structured conditions offer direct spatial control through depth, trajectories, bounding boxes, masks, and camera motion [(Esser et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024d; Luo et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025c)]. Geometry-aware methods incorporate 3D boxes, bird’s-eye-view layouts, world volumes, and structured traffic scenes [(Gao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2024c; Wang et al., 2025)]. Generative rendering uses explicit geometry or renderer-derived signals: Coarse-to-Real [(Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026)] and VideoFrom3D [(Kim et al., 2025)] use coarse 3D scenes, while Diffusion Renderer [(Liang et al., 2025)], AlayaRenderer [(Huang et al., 2026b)], its real-time extension [(Lin et al., 2026a)], and LiVER [(Cai et al., 2026b)] use denser rendering cues. These approaches span sparse object controls to dense geometric representations. Comparisons across representations are often confounded by differences in models, datasets, and tasks. PROWBench derives paired proxy representations from the same recorded world-state trajectory and camera configuration, isolating representation effects on visual realization under fixed scene evolution.

    2.3 World Model Benchmarks and Evaluation

    VBench [(Huang et al., 2024)] and EvalCrafter [(Liu et al., 2024)] assess video quality, temporal consistency, motion, and semantic alignment. WorldSimBench [(Qin et al., 2025)], WorldModelBench [(Li et al., 2025a)], and WorldScore [(Duan et al., 2025)] extend evaluation to physical plausibility, controllability, and world dynamics. MIND [(Ye et al., 2026)], WorldMark [(Xu et al., 2026)], Omni-WorldBench [(Wu et al., 2026)], WorldArena [(Shang et al., 2026)], and iWorld-Bench [(Fang et al., 2026)] further target interactive behavior, memory, and long-horizon consistency.

    WBench [(Ying et al., 2026)] evaluates multi-turn navigation, subject actions, event editing, and perspective switching for instruction adherence, consistency, and physical plausibility. These benchmarks generally assess complete pipelines, coupling errors in action understanding, state prediction, memory, dynamics, and rendering.

    PROWBench isolates rendering fidelity using engine-recorded frame-level states, rules, and timestamped interactions, enabling comparisons across synchronized perspectives and proxy representations under the same trajectory. Logic-Renderer Alignment measures whether specified rules are visibly realized, while Interaction measures whether recorded events appear at the corresponding times.

    3 Benchmark

    We construct the PROWBench dataset using a programmable world generation pipeline that produces aligned conditioning inputs and evaluation records. Figure 2 outlines the pipeline, while Figure 6.2 illustrates the dataset’s content and diversity. We describe the pipeline and evaluation suite below, with detailed dataset statistics provided in Section 6.1.

    3.1 World Generation Pipeline

    We introduce a pipeline for constructing programmable worlds and producing structured conditioning inputs and evaluation annotations for generative video models. The pipeline provides three complementary capabilities: world synthesis, control compilation, and final process. Together, these capabilities produce replayable world trajectories, synchronized conditioning inputs, and structured evaluation records.

    World Synthesis. The pipeline constructs dynamic worlds from configurations specifying the environment, entity layout, participating actors, task controllers, random seeds, and execution duration. Procedural routines generate terrain, buildings, roads, interiors, and interaction objects, together with collision surfaces, collision constraints, and interaction anchors. Entities have persistent episode-level identifiers, semantic categories, component hierarchies, and task-relevant attributes. Random seeds control variations in scene layouts, motion paths, speeds, and animation phases.

    Specialized controllers coordinate articulated poses, object trajectories, and participant interactions through procedural animation and motion models. They support three broad categories of behavior. Interaction controllers organize tasks into explicit phases: for example, carrying proceeds through approaching, grasping, lifting, transporting, and releasing an object, with corresponding updates to hand targets and object ownership. Activity and locomotion controllers support animal behaviors and simplified flight and swimming dynamics. Driving controllers provide closed-loop control of vehicle motion. During execution, these controllers report action phases, participating entities, and relationship changes for recording and validation. External agents can query entities, submit supported actions or plans, advance the world by fixed ticks, and inspect execution feedback.

    Each execution produces a structured episode record containing shared scene geometry, entity definitions and hierarchies, initial conditions, and temporal records of entity transforms, articulated poses, visibility, and appearance changes. Controller events and available input traces accompany these records, with explicit temporal mappings linking world execution, saved states, and video frames. Each saved state can be reconstructed independently from the shared scene description and its corresponding dynamic record. Configurations, random seeds, and source information are retained for provenance tracking.

    Control Compilation. The pipeline compiles recorded world states and camera trajectories into synchronized visual conditioning inputs for generative video models.

    Third-person cameras follow task-dependent trajectories, while first-person cameras are derived from recorded head positions, character or vehicle orientations, and task-specific gaze information. The observing character’s display geometry is hidden in its first-person view, while its entity and articulated state remain in the shared world record. Final camera trajectories include intrinsics, camera-to-world and world-to-camera matrices, projection parameters, and clipping planes. Additional cameras can be associated with different participants to provide multiple perspectives of the same episode.

    Rendering adapters map shared world records to conditioning representations. Our current implementation provides three representations. Coarse 3D representation (Coarse 3D) uses neutral materials to preserve scene shape, object silhouettes, and articulated motion. Semantic proxy (CWM proxy) combines semantically colored environments with simplified entity proxies, retaining global trajectories, orientations, and task-relevant posture while reducing local articulation and shape detail. Colored oriented bounding boxes (Colored-OBB) represent selected entities through spatial envelopes, stable instance colors, and directional cues, with a semi-transparent white face marking the front of each entity, while retaining geometry for environmental structures and simple objects. OBB bounds are updated over time, while instance colors remain consistent across frames and views.

    Rendering adapters specify entity selection, proxy templates, transparency, occlusion, and clipping behavior. Given shared scene geometry G, recorded world state Sᵢ, camera parameters Cᵢᵛ for view v, and representation r, a conditioning frame is generated as Iᵢ^v,r=ℝᵣ(G,Sᵢ,Cᵢᵛ), where ℝᵣ is the representation-specific rendering adapter. Different views observe the same saved state, and representations within each view share camera parameters. Additional camera policies and rendering adapters can reuse recorded episodes without rerunning behavior controllers, provided the required information is available in the world records, whereas new behaviors produce new recorded executions. This separation preserves temporal alignment and enables controlled comparisons across representations and viewpoints while keeping the underlying world evolution fixed.

    Final Process. The pipeline exports three categories of outputs: scene and motion records, rendered observations, and text and interaction labels. Scene and motion records support replay and include scene geometry, entity identities and semantic categories, spatial and articulated states, joint poses, bounding volumes, and entity and camera trajectories with associated camera parameters. Rendered observations comprise synchronized proxy videos across viewpoints and representations, accompanied by metric depth interpreted with respect to its recorded geometry. Text and interaction labels describe action phases, participant relationships, and timestamped events, together with accompanying textual descriptions and contact targets and residuals.

    Validation comprises four complementary components. Task and timeline checks assess scenario-specific phases, terminal conditions or state validity, and recording coverage. They also verify task-level interaction labels against the applicable annotation policy and required participant categories. Geometric checks evaluate penetration, support, and contact consistency at saved states using canonical geometry. Replay and alignment checks assess state reconstruction, camera alignment, and consistency with the selected representation. They further establish correspondence among videos, depth, and state labels using source records, frame indices, camera information, and timestamps. Visual and media quality checks combine first-frame visibility measurements based on canonical-geometry pixel counts and view-frustum tests with documented visual inspection of first frames and selected temporal samples. These inspections assess subject visibility and observation readability, while media decoding and hash checks assess output integrity. Visibility measurements and visual reviews are interpreted within the scope of the recorded frames and geometry.

    To preserve provenance and revision history, failed attempts and their available diagnostics are retained separately from accepted episodes. For each batch-specific revision, affected outputs are backed up, changes to world records, camera trajectories, or representation policies are documented, and the corresponding media and metadata are updated together. Hash checks verify the integrity of unchanged source records where applicable. Sample metadata and source hashes link released observations to their source records, rendering configurations, and verification reports.

    3.2 Evaluation Suite

    We evaluate five complementary capabilities: controllability, visual and temporal quality, logic and state alignment, multi-view consistency, and long-horizon memory. Engine-recorded trajectories, events, and states provide references for evaluating adherence to the prescribed world evolution, while established perceptual metrics assess video quality.

    Controllability. We evaluate whether entities and the camera follow their prescribed trajectories. For entity control, we consider dynamic and interaction-relevant entities visible in the reference view, excluding terrain, effects, and scene geometry. Generated entities are localized with SAM 3 [(Carion et al., 2026)] from semantic-label prompts and matched to engine-projected references by label-compatible Hungarian matching. BBox IoU measures spatial alignment over the visible trajectory, with missed detections assigned zero IoU, while Center Error measures normalized center displacement conditional on detection. We report clip-level averages over evaluable entities; full visibility, matching, and aggregation details are provided in Appendix 7.

    Interaction Success Rate. Global similarity alone does not determine whether a prescribed interaction is successfully executed. We therefore evaluate registered engine events, each defined by its participants, temporal window, action, and expected end state. For each event, Qwen3.6-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026)] is provided with eight frames sampled around the event window, including both full-frame context and an engine-localized crop, and independently judges the prescribed action, expected end state, and participant presence. An event is considered successful only when the response is valid and both the action and end state are judged present. For a generated scene-camera sample s with event set 𝔼ₛ, we define

    ISRₛ=(1)/(|𝔼ₛ|)∑_e∈𝔼ₛ1[valid response, action=yes, end state=yes].

    		(1)

    Table entries average ISRₛ equally across samples, preventing samples with more annotated events from receiving greater weight.

    We additionally report gISRₛ, an IoU-weighted variant of ISR that jointly reflects interaction success and entity placement:

    gISRₛ=ISRₛ·IoUₛ,

    		(2)

    where IoUₛ is the clip-level BBox IoU of sample s. Table entries average gISRₛ equally across samples.

    Logic-Render Alignment. Logic-Render Alignment measures whether each segment of the action timeline in the engine-derived prompt is visibly depicted within its time window. For each annotated timeline segment, the judge receives twelve frames sampled from the corresponding temporal window, together with the expected event description and neighboring descriptions as context. The metric evaluates whether the action prescribed by the engine logic is visibly realized within the corresponding segment. For a sample s with annotated timeline segments Tₛ, we define

    LRAₛ=(1)/(|Tₛ|)∑_τ∈Tₛ1[prescribed action in segmentτis judged present],

    		(3)

    so that LRAₛ is the fraction of timeline segments whose prescribed actions are visually consistent with the engine-defined logic.

    Similarly, we report gLRAₛ, an IoU-weighted variant of LRA that jointly reflects timeline adherence and entity placement:

    gLRAₛ=LRAₛ·IoUₛ.

    		(4)

    Table entries average gLRAₛ equally across samples.

    Figure 8.4 illustrates the distinction between the two behavioral metrics. ISR evaluates whether a registered interaction is successfully completed, requiring both the prescribed action and expected end state, whereas LRA evaluates whether the generated video realizes the engine-defined event logic by depicting each prescribed action in its corresponding temporal segment.

    Memory over Long Horizons. For the 30-second evaluation, we test whether entities that leave the field of view reappear at the location and in the state prescribed by the engine. We define an absence event when an entity becomes invisible and later re-enters the view. Reappearance IoU measures spatial recovery after re-entry by comparing the reference box with label-compatible detections, with missed detections assigned zero IoU. State Persistence measures whether a returning person preserves the prescribed locomotion state, classified as walking or standing and judged from post-return frames by Qwen3.6-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026)]. Both metrics are averaged first within scenes and then across scenes with valid events.

    Additional metric definitions, implementation details, and evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix 7.

    3.3 Benchmark Tracks

    PROWBench organizes its evaluation cases into two tracks with four settings. Each setting uses its own evaluation set, and the scenes of the two main-track settings are disjoint.

    Main Track. The main track evaluates controlled generation of five-second clips in two settings that differ in the appearance reference and use disjoint scenes. When the agent already has an appearance reference, such as a concept image or a prescribed character design, it can supply it as the RGB first frame. The Verified-FF setting evaluates this case with 40 scene-camera pairs (31 third-person follow, 9 first-person; top of Table 1). Its RGB first frame is part of the benchmark: it is generated with MiniMax-H3 from the colored-OBB proxy and the scene description and checked against the recorded person count, positions, facing and layout (Appendix 6.2), and every method that accepts a first frame receives this identical image. In procedural game-world construction, the agent usually has no ready-made RGB appearance reference. The Unverified-FF setting therefore prescribes only the world state, the text, and the control signals, and asks whether models can jointly solve entity control, appearance generation, and identity binding. It contains 90 pairs (78 third-person follow, 12 first-person; bottom of Table 1), and appearance must be determined by each model from the text and the control signal. The curation of this set used MiniMax-H3 outputs, so results involving MiniMax-H3 should be read with this potential bias in mind.

    Challenge Track. The challenge track tests whether short-clip control extends to two harder settings. Control in short clips does not guarantee that a model maintains one world state over longer horizons, in which entities leave the view, re-enter later and keep their state and motion across generation windows. The long-horizon setting (Table 2) contains ten 30-second recordings, one camera each. In a multi-player game, each player observes the same world through their own camera. Even when each view is generated independently, the views must agree on where each participant is, who they are, what they look like, and the scene structure. The multi-view setting (Table 3) contains ten four-player scenes, each with four synchronized third-person follow views, one per player, generated independently.

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments address a central question: can current video generation and video world models faithfully render a prescribed dynamic world, rather than merely produce visually plausible videos? For game worlds, visual quality alone is insufficient. A successful model must follow prescribed entity trajectories, camera motion, and event timelines, while maintaining consistency over long horizons and across synchronized views. We therefore organize the evaluation into a main track of five-second clips and a challenge track of long-horizon and multi-view settings. Sections 4.3 and 4.4 report the results, and Section 4.5 compares the method classes across both tracks and draws the main takeaways. The experimental setup is detailed in Section 4.2.

    4.1 Evaluated Methods

    We evaluate 11 models, grouped into three families by the control information they receive. (a) Camera-conditioned world models. EchoWM [(Zhang et al., 2026)], SANA-WM [(Zhu et al., 2026)], LingBot-World 2.0 [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)] and AlayaWorld v1.1 [(Team et al., 2026)] receive an RGB first frame, the text prompt, and the recorded camera trajectory. They obtain explicit camera control but no entity trajectories. (b) Proxy-video-to-RGB models. These models translate an engine-rendered control representation into a realistic RGB video. Cosmos-Transfer2.5 [(Ali et al., 2025)] receives engine depth and class-level segmentation; C2R [(Gomez-Nogales et al., 2026)] receives the coarse 3D proxy and the text; CWM [(Chen et al., 2026b)] (fine-tuned from MiniMax-H3) receives the CWM proxy, depth, the RGB first frame, and the text; LynnReal-Omni [(Mao et al., 2026b)], which builds directly on MiniMax-H3 and extends it with native support for heterogeneous visual controls, including editable 3D renders and game recordings; and PWM [(Huang et al., 2026a)] receives colored-OBB proxy, the RGB first frame, and the text prompt. Because PWM is trained only on gunfight scenes, it is evaluated only on the gunfight set of Section 4. (c) Video foundation models. MiniMax-H3 [(MiniMax-AI, 2026)], Seedance 2.5 [(ByteDance Seed Team, 2026)] are used without any adaptation to our proxy representations. They take the colored-OBB proxy video as a reference video together with the text prompt, and RGB references as specified in each table.

    4.2 Experimental Setup

    All evaluation samples come from recorded game-world states and are scored against the engine state; each sample is one scene observed by one camera. Every recorded state is provided in three proxy representations, Coarse 3D, CWM proxy and Colored-OBB, together with engine depth, the camera trajectory, a scene description and the state of every object, and each method receives the control representation of its native interface. Text prompts are generated automatically from the recorded scene, entities, and action timeline. All models are evaluated in their native output formats against the same engine records; the engine renders of the proxies are scored as diagnostic references. The tracks and settings are defined in Section 3.3. Methods whose native interface requires an RGB image (the world models and CWM) receive frame 0 of the MiniMax-H3 output for the same scene and camera; this frame is not a prescribed reference, but it can transmit MiniMax-H3’s appearance assignments, and analyses of appearance identity account separately for effects inherited from it.

item.title: 规则没人告诉它、预训练也没见过：Learn2Play 用新设计的文字游戏测 agent 到底能不能从试错里学 ｜ Learn2Play Bench: How Well Do LLM Agents Learn from Experience in Unfamiliar Environments?
item.description:
一句话：现有基准的规则要么写在指令里、要么模型早就熟悉，于是「从交互中学」被混成了「用已有知识推理」。

要点：

  • 新设计一批规则新颖甚至反直觉的文字游戏，逼 agent 靠交互获取知识，而不是依赖预训练里的先验
  • 反馈可复现、评分自动，能跨重复尝试做受控比较；并变换游戏实例，检验学到的能否迁移到新情况
  • 系统比较骨干模型、自进化方法与 agent harness 的影响，发现保留完整动作-反馈记录比总结成规则更利于学习

为什么值得看：要让 agent 当关卡/规则的自适应测试员，前提是它真能从交互里学；这套基准把「学习」和「回忆」分开了。

中文摘要：从经验中学习是 LLM agent 适应陌生动态环境的关键能力，但现有基准大多要么把规则写在指令里，要么规则本身就是预训练熟悉的，于是很难把「从交互中学」与「用已有知识推理」区分开。Learn2Play Bench 由一批新设计的文字游戏组成，规则新颖甚至反直觉，agent 必须靠交互获取知识；游戏提供可复现反馈与自动评分，因此能对多次重复尝试做受控评测，并通过变换游戏实例检验能否把学到的东西用在新的情形上。作者据此系统评估了骨干模型、自进化方法与 agent harness 对学习能力的影响，并给出几条发现：保留动作与反馈的完整记录，比把经验总结成规则或策略更有利于学习；不同 harness 的学习效率差别明显；以及迁移到新实例时的表现普遍低于在同实例上重复尝试。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·AI原生（English）

原文发布：2026-10-06

本期推送：2026-10-25

Learn2Play Bench: How Well Do LLM Agents Learn from Experience in Unfamiliar Environments?

Abstract

Learning from experience is essential for LLM agents to adapt to unfamiliar and dynamic environments. Evaluating this ability is therefore important for understanding how effectively agents acquire and use new knowledge. Existing benchmarks have sought to evaluate this ability, but they primarily evaluate tasks whose rules are provided in the instructions or already familiar to pretrained models, making it difficult to distinguish learning from interactions from reasoning with existing knowledge. To address this, we introduce Learn2Play Bench, a benchmark of newly designed text-based games, whose rules are novel or counterintuitive, requiring agents to acquire knowledge through interaction rather than rely solely on pretrained knowledge. These games provide reproducible feedback and automatic scoring, enabling controlled evaluation of learning across repeated attempts. We also vary game instances to test whether agents can apply what they have learned to new situations. Therefore, we evaluate how backbone models, self-evolving methods, and agent harnesses affect agents’ learning ability, revealing three findings: (1) Experience retention: Retaining complete records of actions and feedback can support more effective learning than summarizing these experiences into rules or strategies. (2) Human–agent gap: Top-performing human players achieve higher peak scores than the evaluated agents. Humans explore more varied strategies, and repeat actions less. (3) Harness matters: With the backbone fixed, changing the harness can improve performance while reducing estimated inference cost.
