    Appendix A Training and Dataset Details

    A.1 Dataset Construction and Mixture Accounting

    All configurations allocate 85% of training tokens to gameplay trajectories and 15% to a fixed vision–language anchor. The gameplay pool combines VPT, D2E, and OpenP2P [Baker et al., 2022, Choi et al., 2025, Yue et al., 2026]. The vision–language anchor comprises LLaVA-OneVision, Zebra-CoT, GameQA, Embodied-Reasoner, and Cambrian-S data [Li et al., 2025a, Li et al., 2026, Tong et al., 2026, Zhang et al., 2026c, Yang et al., 2026]. The general vision–language data does not include game content from the 85% gameplay component. This prevents the fixed general vision–language data from providing additional exposure to these game worlds when we vary the diversity of the gameplay component. Its composition and token share remain unchanged across S1–S5. We vary data diversity by changing the balance between Minecraft and a fixed pool of other game worlds. Across S2–S5, the non-Minecraft worlds remain the same, and their relative proportions within that pool are approximately unchanged. This shifts training from Minecraft-dominated data toward a more balanced mix of 79 worlds, without progressively adding new non-Minecraft games. Holding the pool fixed helps separate the effect of world proportions from the effect of the number of worlds. Running the 120-condition grid with one training seed required approximately 45,000 H200 GPU-hours. Given this cost, we leave repeated training with different seeds and experiments that vary the number of worlds to future work.

    We normalize source-specific mouse coordinates, sample observations at 5 Hz, and construct 20-turn windows with a 10-turn stride. Each window supervises 4.0 seconds of actions and spans 3.8 seconds between its first and last observations. We use the latter interval to measure gameplay duration. Actions are converted to the unified six-substep format, and idle-dominated windows are downsampled. For the heterogeneous pool, we sample complete recordings and cap each source stream to limit dominance by long streams. S2–S4 use nested subsets of this capped pool, while S5 follows the same procedure after removing Minecraft. So the measured Minecraft shares among gameplay segments are 100%, 51.4%, 27.1%, and 2.8%, respectively. S5 removes these residual Minecraft trajectories, reducing the share to 0%.

    Fixed training-game inventory. S2–S5 draw from the same inventory of 124 non-Minecraft source streams; the mixtures change only how many segments are drawn from those streams. S2–S4 additionally contain Minecraft, whereas S5 removes both D2E and OpenP2P Minecraft streams. S1 contains only VPT Minecraft. The 124 shared streams correspond to 79 canonical non-Minecraft labels; adding Minecraft gives the 80 labels listed in Table 4. Thus, “124” refers to the fixed source-stream inventory, not to 124 title-disjoint commercial games. Two very small residual metadata labels (Roblox: Debug and Other / Unlabeled) are retained in the accounting table rather than silently reassigned.

    Mixture diversity. Because the world inventory is fixed, S1–S5 cannot be ordered by the number of worlds: S2, S3, and S4 contain the same 80 canonical labels. What changes is how gameplay experience is distributed over them. Let p_w be the share of gameplay segments from canonical world w in a mixture. We measure mixture diversity by the effective number of worlds,

    D=\exp(-∑_wp_w\logp_w),

    		(4)

    the Hill number of order one [Hill, 1973, Jost, 2006]. D equals the number of equally weighted worlds that would give the same Shannon entropy. It combines how many worlds are present with how evenly experience is spread across them, so it is 1 for a single world and 80 for 80 equally weighted worlds. Table 3 reports D together with the inverse Simpson index 1/∑_wp_w², which weights dominant worlds more heavily, and the largest single-world share. Both indices order S1–S4 identically. Only the step from S1 to S2 enlarges the world set; from S2 to S4 the set is unchanged, and diversity grows because Minecraft’s dominant share is reassigned to the heterogeneous worlds. S5 has nearly the same diversity as S4 and differs from it mainly by excluding the residual 2.8% of Minecraft, so it serves as a source-free control rather than a further diversity step. At a fixed budget, raising D also raises the hours of each heterogeneous world and lowers the Minecraft hours, because S2–S4 draw nested subsets from the same capped pool.

    We use the six game categories shown in the dataset table: AVG (adventure/survival), STG (shooting), RPG (role-playing), RAC (racing), SIM (simulation), and OTH (platform, sports, MOBA, and other games). The category assignment remain fixed across S1–S5.

    Validation sets. We use three fixed held-out sets to evaluate action loss. The Minecraft set consists of trajectories from the VPT test split. The in-corpus set is game-balanced and draws from D2E and OpenP2P recordings held out from the S4–S5 construction, together with a size-matched Minecraft subset from the VPT test split. The out-of-distribution (OOD) set contains only game titles absent from every S1–S5 mixture. All three sets use the same observation and action representation as training. Recordings and adjacent overlapping windows are kept separate across training and validation to prevent leakage.

    OOD source and construction. The OOD set is drawn from the processed Gaming500 [Markov AI, 2026] recording pool, which is not used to construct any S1–S5 training mixture. We first remove exact-title overlaps with VPT, D2E, and OpenP2P, as well as obvious aliases, games from the same retained franchise, and emulator labels that resolve to a training title. We then retain keyboard–mouse recordings only. A recording is rejected when at least 5% of its foreground events belong to a browser, desktop, launcher, or other non-game application; when at least half of its mouse events exhibit cursor recentering; or when its keyboard–mouse activity is too sparse (fewer than 60 input events per minute, fewer than three keyboard or click events per minute, or more than 60% idle windows). We additionally require at least 60% of a title’s clean recordings to satisfy the keyboard–mouse criteria. These filters remove gamepad sessions whose labels are all zero, cursor-locked sessions whose mouse deltas are uninformative, and recordings dominated by menus or unrelated applications.

    The resulting set contains 28 games and 4,480 clips. We sample exactly 160 non-idle clips per game, so every title contributes 1/28=3.57% of the set, and distribute those clips as evenly as possible over two to four independent recording sessions (92 sessions in total). The set is therefore balanced by game rather than by the amount of available source video duration. Using the rendered interaction space as the taxonomy, it comprises 21 3D games (3,360 clips; 75.0%), three 2.5D games (480 clips; 10.7%), and four 2D games (640 clips; 14.3%). We count isometric scenes rendered with 3D geometry, such as Dota 2, as 3D; 2.5D denotes side-view or planar interaction with mixed 2D/3D presentation. Under the same game-category taxonomy used for the training inventory, the OOD set contains six AVG, five STG, three RPG, four RAC, four SIM, and six OTH titles. Table 5 gives the complete composition.

    A.2 Sparse Retrospective Reasoning Annotations and Action Template

    Qwen3.5 natively places deliberation within a span before producing its final output. We preserve this structure across all CPT configurations because the same behavior frequently occurs during online gameplay evaluation. Retaining the reasoning channel keeps the training response format aligned with the reason-then-act format used at evaluation.

    Annotation procedure. For selected gameplay windows, GPT-5.6-Luna receives the recorded visual context together with the action that the player subsequently executed. It is instructed to adopt the player’s perspective and reconstruct a short retrospective explanation of the apparent observation, intent, and chosen action. The annotation describes the recorded behavior rather than proposing or relabeling an action, so the original keyboard–mouse supervision remains unchanged. We inject these rationales sparsely among ordinary gameplay turns and apply the same procedure to S1–S5, preventing reasoning density from becoming an unintended diversity variable. Table 6 reports the resulting density for each mixture. A 20-frame training sample carries 1.08–1.19 non-empty rationales on average, 74–78% of samples contain at least one, and only 5.4–6.0% of assistant turns include reasoning. Each rationale averages 64.5–65.4 tokens under the Qwen3.5 tokenizer (pooled median 65; 10th–90th percentile 56–74), or 70–78 reasoning tokens per sample. Because rationale count, coverage, and length differ only marginally across S1–S5, reasoning supervision does not act as an additional variable alongside data diversity.

    Training format.

    User:
    Assistant:
    [Sparse reasoning, when available]

    <|action_start|> ΔxΔyΔz ; k₁ ; … ; k₆ <|action_end|>

    When no retrospective annotation is attached, the chat template supplies an empty span, keeping the response grammar identical across examples. At evaluation, the model is free to generate a non-empty reasoning segment before the action packet. Figure 5 shows five consecutive turns from an S4 training window, two with rationales and three without.

    A.3 Full Accounting of the 120-Condition Factorial Grid

    Table 7 outlines the 20 primary Warmup–Stable–Decay (WSD) trunks [Hu et al., 2024]. For every evaluated checkpoint, the reported gameplay-hour budget T∈{50,100,200,400,800,1600} includes all three phases: warmup, stable training, and cosine decay. Thus, the 50-hour model has a total budget of 50 hours, including its decay stage. For each model–mixture pair, the shorter-budget models branch from earlier trunk checkpoints and complete their cosine decay when the cumulative budget reaches T. The 1,600-hour condition uses the trunk’s own final decay endpoint. This reuse produces six completed checkpoints per model–mixture pair and 120 conditions in total.

    A.4 Training Hyperparameters and Optimization Stability

    All CPT runs use bf16 AdamW [Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019] (β₁=0.9, β₂=0.95, weight decay 0.01) with gradient clipping at 1.0 and a fixed target batch budget of 2,359,296 tokens. The language-model peak learning rate is 1×10⁻⁵ at every parameter scale. The vision encoder is unfrozen and uses a separate rate of 7×10⁻⁶. The WSD schedule [Hu et al., 2024] allocates 3% of training to linear warmup, 87.3% to the stable phase, and the final 9.7% to cosine decay with a minimum learning-rate ratio of 0.1. All three phases are included in the reported training budget, as defined in Appendix A.3. Every condition uses 854×480 frames, a 20-frame gameplay context, a fixed 15% vision–language token share, and seed 3407.

    Appendix B Evaluation Details

    B.1 Benchmark Evaluation Environments

    Level 1: Source-World Benchmarks (Minecraft and ViZDoom). MCU [Zheng et al., 2025] uses 30 long-horizon Minecraft tasks spanning navigation, survival, GUI interaction, combat, and crafting. ViZDoom [Wydmuch et al., 2019] evaluates first-person control on four skill-1 DOOM maps; the scoring protocol is given in Appendix B.3. Both environments are represented in the gameplay corpus, but at opposite densities: Minecraft spans 0–100% of the gameplay budget across S1–S5, whereas footage of the classic DOOM titles on whose engine ViZDoom runs never exceeds one to two percent of any mixture; later DOOM releases in the corpus (e.g., DOOM Eternal) share the first-person shooting skill but differ in art style and rules. ViZDoom therefore probes a rare world and a frequent skill: DOOM itself is minimally exposed, but the first-person aiming and firing it tests is common to the games that dominate the heterogeneous pool, which is why the main text treats the pool, not DOOM, as its source.

    Level 2: Related-World Benchmark (OmniGameArena - OGA). Consists of 7 diverse photorealistic Unreal Engine 5 games. Scenarios cover third-person exploration, tactical combat, target shooting, and obstacle platforming, running on native UE5 execution environments.

    Level 3: Distant OOD Benchmark (GameWorld - GW). Comprises 170 tasks across 34 environments, mostly 2D and 2.5D, including classic arcade platformers, puzzle solvers (2048, Sokoban), and word-guessing games, whose visual styles, physics, and control logic depart from the training worlds.

    Action-interface adaptation. OGA natively consumes a packet similar to the <|action_start|> … <|action_end|> format described in Section 3; we set its mouse-displacement range and the number of keys per substep to match ours, and change nothing else. MCU, ViZDoom, and GameWorld do not. For each of these three benchmarks we add a thin adapter that parses the packet into the harness’s native keyboard–mouse events: the six per-substep key sets are replayed as a 6×33 ms key timeline, and the mouse displacement is mapped to the environment’s native camera or cursor control. The adapter changes only the action interface. Task definitions, observation resolution, episode length, step caps, success criteria, scoring, and every other evaluation parameter remain those of the original benchmark, and the same adapter is used for every model we evaluate in Table 2, including the frontier models, which receive the packet grammar through the same prompt and are parsed by the same code.

    B.2 Evaluation Protocol

    Episodes and averaging. Every reported score is a mean over tasks of the mean over episodes. MCU runs each of its 30 tasks 5 times and report the mean and standard deviation over 5 runs in Table 1; OGA runs each of its 7 games 10 times; ViZDoom runs each of its 4 maps 10 times; GameWorld runs each of its 170 tasks once. The same counts apply to every model and every checkpoint in the grid, and to every model in Table 2. The average score on the four benchmarks is reported in Table 2.

    Provenance of the two comparison tables. The prior-model rows of Table 1 are quoted from their source papers. Their backbones, action interfaces, training data, and harnesses are therefore not aligned with ours, and the table should be read as a reference to the published state of Minecraft agents rather than as a controlled comparison. Table 2 is different: we evaluated every model in it ourselves, under our action interface, with the adapters above, the same prompts, the same observation resolution and history, and the same episode counts. Only the model changes between rows.

    Episode budgets and termination. Each benchmark keeps its native budget. MCU allows a fixed 600 step budget in the time-paused setting and 3 minutes of game time per task in the real time setting. ViZDoom and GameWorld use a fixed step cap. OGA ends an episode when either its game-time limit or its step cap is reached, whichever comes first. On MCU, ViZDoom, and OGA an episode stops immediately when the task fails or the agent dies, and the episode is scored as it stands. On GameWorld, failure or death restarts the game, and the agent keeps playing until the step cap is reached; the score is the progress accumulated within the cap. Under real-time interaction, the difference is that the world advances while the model reasons.

    B.3 ViZDoom Scoring Protocol

    Maps and per-map score. We use four maps at doom_skill 1: battle1 and battle2 from Direct Future Prediction, and the standard defend_the_center and defend_the_line scenarios. The two families carry different native units. On the battle maps we record the frag count, following the convention of the work that introduced them. On the defend maps we record the cumulative engine reward, which awards +1 per kill and -1 on death. The battle WADs also expose a per-kill reward through ACS global 0, and we verified over 3,358 episodes that it equals the frag count on every one, so the two conventions coincide there and a paper reporting “average episode reward” on these maps reports the same quantity.

    Aggregate score. The reported ViZDoom number is the unweighted mean of the four per-map scores after each is divided by 100:

    S_ViZDoom = 1/4∑_m∈M(s̄ₘ)/(100), M={\textttbattle1,\textttbattle2,\textttdtc,\textttdtl},

    where s̄ₘ averages 10 episodes on map m.

    B.4 Serving and Deployment Configurations

    All GameScaling checkpoints are deployed in bf16 on an NVIDIA H200 cluster and evaluated through vLLM API endpoints. The context length is sized to the observation history, limit-mm-per-prompt equals the history length plus one, sampling uses temperature 1.0, and generation stops at <|action_end|>. Under time-paused interaction, every MCU, ViZDoom, OGA, and GameWorld evaluation job reserves eight H200 GPUs and serves the model through vLLM. Under real-time interaction, where inference latency enters the score, the 0.8B and 2B models use tensor-parallel size 1 on one H200 per vLLM instance, while the 9B and 27B models use tensor-parallel size 4 on four H200 GPUs per instance. Table 8 summarizes these protocol-dependent layouts.

    Time-paused interaction. Because the environment is frozen while the model reasons, decision latency does not enter the score and requests may be scheduled for throughput. Every time-paused run on MCU, ViZDoom, OGA, and GameWorld uses an eight-H200 job with vLLM serving. The environment backend remains benchmark-specific: Minecraft, ViZDoom, and Chromium execute outside the model server, while OGA uses UE5 instances on GPU. For OGA, each UE5 instance retains a dedicated GPU because packing multiple instances on one GPU starves real-time rendering during the 6×33 ms action chunk and can depress the score without producing an execution error.

    Real-time interaction. Under real-time interaction the measured latency of each decision is part of the score: the environment keeps advancing and the model keeps idle until the new one arrives. Actually, once model latency significantly exceeds 200 ms (such as 0.5s), both executing the previous action chunk and staying idle result in a severe performance degradation by more than 5×. Due to high latency, our 27B model also suffers an obvious performance drop. Each live worker therefore uses a dedicated vLLM endpoint rather than sharing a request queue. The 0.8B and 2B models are served on one H200 with TP = 1; the 9B and 27B models are served on four H200 GPUs with TP = 4. Splitting the 0.8B model across four GPUs raised its per-step latency from about 130 ms to 178–190 ms.

    Frontier models. Proprietary and hosted open-source models are evaluated through their provider APIs with the same adapter and prompt. All six models run at the default reasoning effort documented by their providers, which we do not override: medium for GPT-5.6-Sol, GPT-5.6-Luna, and Gemini-3.8-Flash; adaptive thinking at high effort for Claude-Opus-5.0; high for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision; and max for GLM-5.3-Flash, whose thinking cannot be disabled. The output cap is 2,048 tokens on MCU, ViZDoom and OGA and 4,096 on GameWorld, the same for every model and both protocols. Models are run strictly one at a time with 5 concurrent workers under time-paused interaction and 2 under real-time interaction; their real-time scores therefore include provider-side latency, which is the latency a deployed agent would experience.

    Appendix C Supplementary Experiments

    C.1 Frontier Progress by Release Date

    Progress in general models can bring larger gains than game-specific CPT. Figure 6 shows substantial improvements in gameplay across successive GPT and Qwen models under time-paused evaluation. Over the release range shown, gains in frontier-model performance can exceed those from our game-specific CPT on a fixed backbone. This difference is particularly clear on GameWorld, where CPT provides limited gains while newer frontier models improve markedly. These results suggest that general model capability is a major contributor to gameplay performance. Game-specific CPT develops useful skills, but improving the backbone itself remains an important route to stronger game agents.

    C.2 Loss Scaling Against Model Size

    Figure 7 replots the losses of Figure 3 with model size on the horizontal axis and one column per duration. Across the six budgets, larger models generally have lower Minecraft and mixed-training in-corpus losses. OOD loss behaves differently: mixed training limits its later increase in larger models, while single-game training can weaken their advantage.

    C.3 Benchmark Scaling Against Gameplay Hours

    Figure 8 replots the 100 scores of Figure 4 with gameplay hours on the horizontal axis and one column per model size, so the duration dynamics of Section 4.1 can be read directly: the monotone gains of 0.8B and 2B under every mixture, the flattening of 9B and 27B after 100–400 h, the decline of S1 at 9B and 27B on OGA and ViZDoom, and the decline of every 27B mixture on GameWorld.

    C.4 Test-Time Scaling on MCU

    The standard MCU protocol caps every rollout at 600 steps, and all MCU numbers in the paper use this cap. Figure 9 asks how much of the remaining failure is a step budget rather than a competence limit. We rerun GameScaling-0.8B-S1 and GameScaling-9B-S1 at 1,600 h, together with their untrained Qwen3.5 backbones, with the cap raised to 3,000 steps and record, for each threshold, the fraction of the 150 rollouts that have succeeded within it. Success rises roughly log-linearly with the allowed steps for both models: from about 42% and 51% at the standard 600 steps to 59.3% and 69.3% at 3,000, with no sign of a plateau. The two curves are nearly parallel, so the gain from more interaction steps is about the same for a 0.8B and a 9B model, and the size gap of about 10 points is preserved at every budget. The backbones do not scale this way. Qwen3.5-0.8B completes no task at any budget, and Qwen3.5-9B rises only from about 2% at 600 steps to 4.0% at 3,000. More steps help only a model that can already act in the world: CPT raises both the level and the test-time slope, and within the range we tested a GameScaling model given more time keeps converting it into completed tasks, independent of its size.

    C.5 Inference Latency and Output Length

    The real-time columns of Table 2 compare API-served frontier models with GameScaling models on one or four H200 GPUs, and this setup does not favor GameScaling on hardware. The providers serve models of hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters on production clusters with far more compute than the single H200 behind GameScaling-0.8B and 2B or the four behind 9B and 27B. Even so, Table 9 shows frontier models taking 4.0–23.7 s per step, against 0.13–0.69 s for GameScaling; GameScaling-0.8B and 2B decide within the 200 ms action chunk. The reason is output length: at their default reasoning efforts (Appendix B.4), counting hidden reasoning, visible content, and the action, frontier models generate 123–1,027 tokens per step, 3 to 29 times the 35–39 of GameScaling, which learns sparse reasoning by continued pre-training on gameplay trajectories annotated with sparse rationales. Frontier models are slow in real time because they are large and reason at length before every action. Even the fastest of them takes about 20 times the 200 ms action chunk per step. GameScaling acts within a second on one to four GPUs, which makes it the practical choice when both competence and latency count.

    C.6 More Experiments on Scaling Law

    This section details the fits behind Section 4.4. We first describe the fitting procedure and check which losses decrease with training at all. We then derive Eq. (3) from the Chinchilla law, compare it with a categorical-mixture model, and report hold-out predictions and bootstrap uncertainty.

    Fitting procedure. Following Chinchilla [Hoffmann et al., 2022], we minimize the Huber loss of the log residual \logL̂-\logL with δ=10⁻³, so that errors are relative and single outliers do not dominate. The optimizer is L-BFGS-B, started from 192 initializations for Eq. (3) and 324 for the two-factor law, and the best optimum is kept. E, A, B and C are optimized in log space; the remaining parameters are bounded by α,β∈[0,3], η∈[-3,3], γ∈[0,5] and ε∈[10⁻⁴,1]. N is measured in billions of parameters and T in gameplay hours. Unless a subset is stated, validation-loss laws are fitted to all 120 conditions of Figure 3, namely four sizes, five mixtures and six budgets from 50 to 1,600 h. Each 50 h validation point comes from its own annealing branch, like every other budget. The training loss is the 100-step EMA of the WSD trunk and is fitted at the five stable-phase budgets from 100 to 1,600 h, giving 100 conditions. At 50 h the trunk has just left its 3% warmup, and its loss still falls faster than any power law in T.

    Besides RMSE and R² over all conditions, we report the within-mixture R²_w, which is the share of variance explained after the five mixture means are removed. Between-mixture differences account for 79%, 88% and 84% of the total variance of the Minecraft, in-corpus and OOD losses. Any model with a mixture-dependent level therefore already reaches a high R², and R²_w measures what the N and T terms add on top of it. Two further points matter when reading the exponents. First, the objective is the Huber loss rather than R², so a parameter value that maximizes R² along a profile need not equal the estimate. Second, since ρ takes five values, we draw only two qualitative conclusions from the ρ-dependent part of Eq. (3), namely that a world with ρ=0 has a finite floor and that η>0, and we do not interpret γ or ε on their own.

    Which losses admit a scaling law. A power law in T presupposes that loss falls with hours, so before fitting we check this on the raw curves, one per model size and mixture, or 20 per loss. On the Minecraft loss, 19 of the 20 curves end lower at 1,600 h than at 50 h, and all curves without a clear decrease belong to S5, which contains no Minecraft. On the in-corpus loss, the four rising curves are exactly those of S1, which contains no pool games. A world’s loss thus decreases with hours whenever the world is in the corpus, and the exceptions are the mixtures that lack it. This is the pattern that the share ρ and the floor term of Eq. (3) have to describe.

    The OOD loss behaves differently in every cell. CPT lowers it from 0.24–0.31 for the backbone to about 0.17, but this gain is already realized at 50 h, and further hours raise the loss again. All 20 curves end 0.007–0.019 higher at 1,600 h than at 50 h, the rank correlation between hours and loss is positive in all 20 with a median of 0.91, the loss rises over 76 of the 100 doublings, and the per-curve slope ranges from +0.001 to +0.004 per doubling. The OOD loss therefore violates the premise of a data scaling law before any law is fitted. We do not model its dynamics, because a form that can follow a rising curve, such as one with an added D\logT term, would describe drift rather than scaling. Instead, we fit Eq. (3) to the OOD loss only as a negative control, to test whether a nine-parameter law manufactures a data term out of mixture differences alone. As shown below, it does not: β goes to zero, as the raw curves imply it should.

    Fitted parameters. Table 10 lists the point estimates behind the last column of Figure 3; their uncertainty is analysed at the end of this section. The reading that survives this analysis is structural: the floor term C/(ρ+ε)^γ produces the gap between mixtures with and without a world. On the Minecraft loss, going from ρ=1 to ρ=0 raises the floor term by 0.08 and removes a data term worth 0.05 at 100 h. The net increase of 0.03 matches the observed gap of 0.032 between S5 and S1. On the in-corpus loss the corresponding numbers are 0.08, 0.04 and 0.04, against an observed gap of 0.040 between S1 and S2. Within mixtures, where the floor term is constant and only N and T act, the law still explains 91% of the variance of the Minecraft loss and 96% of the in-corpus loss, compared with 8% of the OOD loss. The individual exponents are less certain. α is of order 0.2 for both validation losses but has wide intervals, β trades off against the offset E along a ridge, and on the OOD loss β sits on its lower bound.

    From Chinchilla to Eq. (3). The Chinchilla law L=E+A/N^α+B/D^β assumes that a single distribution is both trained on and evaluated, so that D counts data from the scored distribution, and that loss falls monotonically with D. Our grid trains on mixtures and scores four distributions, which breaks the first assumption, and the OOD loss breaks the second. Like the Chinchilla and D-CPT laws, Eq. (3) is an empirical description rather than a law derived from a model of learning, and we make no claim beyond the grid. Its components are nevertheless not free design choices. The share ρ is neither fitted nor tuned but fixed by how the mixtures are built (Appendix A.1). The functional form is the published D-CPT law with its domain ratio replaced by ρ. Each term is forced by an observation that a simpler form cannot accommodate. We reached Eq. (3) by relaxing the Chinchilla assumptions one at a time on the Minecraft loss, each step guided by the residuals of the previous one (Table 11). The form is then tested against a categorical model of the same size and on held-out blocks, including held-out mixtures.

  • 1.

    Total hours, D=T. On S1–S3 the fit reaches only R²=0.925. The three mixtures share every value of T, yet their losses differ by up to 0.007, which the law cannot separate. Total hours are therefore not the data variable of an evaluated world.

  • 2.

    Minecraft hours, D=rT.R² rises to 0.959, but the residuals are ordered by mixture, from +0.0016 for S1 to -0.0012 for S3. At equal Minecraft hours, the mixture with more pool hours has the lower Minecraft loss, so hours on other worlds also lower a world’s loss, at a lower rate.

  • 3.

    Two data terms. Adding a shared term in total hours, L=E+A/N^α+B/(rT)^β+C/T^γ, removes the ordering and reaches R²=0.989; the fitted γ≈0.5 means that the shared term saturates early. This form is undefined at r=0, however, whereas S4 and S5 reach finite Minecraft losses of 0.229 and 0.236, far below the backbone. A world absent from training thus has a floor rather than an infinite loss, and the share must enter the law in a form that admits ρ=0.

  • 4.

    Eq. (3). The D-CPT form [Que et al., 2024], with D replaced by T and the domain ratio by ρ, covers all five mixtures with one parameter set and reaches R²=0.982. Its RMSE is at most 0.0015 on S1–S3 and 0.003 on S4–S5, where only two mixtures anchor the floor. The shares are the measured Minecraft trajectory shares of 100, 51.4, 27.1, 2.8 and 0% from Appendix A.1, not the nominal VPT fractions.

  • 5.

    What the fitted form says.η is positive, 0.24 for Minecraft and 0.10 for the pool, so the data term does not reduce to effective hours ρT. Forcing η=-β, which gives B/(ρT)^β, lowers R² to 0.825 on the Minecraft loss and 0.945 on the in-corpus loss, and to 0.923 and 0.953 when the ρ=0 mixture is excluded. Constraining η≤0 on the ρ>0 conditions alone drives η to the bound and lowers the Minecraft R² from 0.979 to 0.934. The sign of η follows from the shape of the curves rather than from how the shares are labelled. Mixtures with small ρ are nearly flat in T while ρ=1 decays, so the amplitude of the T term must grow with ρ. At 0.8B, for example, the S5 Minecraft loss moves only from 0.239 to 0.237 over 50–1,600 h, while the S1 loss falls from 0.220 to 0.198. This is step 2 seen from inside the final law: the floor term, not the data term, carries the mixture dependence.

  • 6.

    Second evaluation world. With ρ=1-r the same form describes the in-corpus loss, while the ranking of the restricted baselines inverts. D=T fits S2–S5 well, with R²=0.991, because the four diverse mixtures have almost identical in-corpus losses. D=(1-r)T is worse, at 0.955, because Minecraft hours also lower the loss on pool games. Only Eq. (3) admits S1, where ρ=0. S1 remains the largest residual, with RMSE 0.0024 against at most 0.0007 for the other mixtures, because its in-corpus loss rises with hours, which no monotone law can reproduce.

  • 7.

    Training and OOD loss. The training loss is scored on each mixture’s own stream, so ρ is undefined and the law reduces to Chinchilla with a per-mixture offset E_S. On the OOD loss monotonicity already fails in the raw curves, so Eq. (3) is applied there only as a negative control. Replacing it with a form that fits a rising loss would no longer yield a scaling law.

    • Two alternatives were set aside. A weighted sum of two Chinchilla laws, one per validation slice with D=rT and D=(1-r)T, is easier to interpret but diverges at r=0 and r=1, so it covers only S2–S4. Treating the number of worlds as a variable cannot be tested on this grid, because S2–S5 share one fixed pool.

    The Minecraft slice of the in-corpus set. The in-corpus set contains 30 pool games and Minecraft with 160 clips each, so Minecraft makes up π=1/31=3.2% of it and ρ=1-r is an approximation. To measure its effect, we write the measured loss as Lᵢₙ=πL_mc+(1-π)Lₚₒₒₗ and remove the Minecraft slice using the measured Minecraft loss. Relative to Lᵢₙ, this shifts Lₚₒₒₗ by +0.0007 for S1 and by -0.0007 to -0.0017 for S2–S5. The shift is largest for S4 and S5, whose Minecraft loss is highest, so the slice slightly narrows the gap between S1 and the diverse mixtures. Fitting Eq. (3) with ρ=1-r to Lₚₒₒₗ gives R²=0.995 and the same per-mixture RMSEs. Combining the two laws as πL̂_mc+(1-π)L̂ₚₒₒₗ predicts Lᵢₙ with R²=0.995 and RMSE 0.0013. Replacing ρ by the validation-weighted share πr+(1-π)(1-r) fits worse, with R²=0.989, so the Minecraft slice enters additively rather than through the share.

item.title: 把失败动作写进 transcript 反而是暗示：8 个模型上，错误动作更容易被再下一遍 ｜ Feedback That Backfires in Games: Do LLM Players Repeat the Move They Just Watched Fail?
item.description:
一句话：失败记录通过动作的表面形式起作用：非法动作更容易被重复，因输了而失败的动作则不会。

要点：

  • 在推箱子、四子棋、黑白棋上用扰动弹构造固定探针，失败分两类：非法（可精确判定）与合法但输（也可判定）
  • 8 个指令微调模型（135M–1.7B）汇总，记录反而让失败动作更可能被再次输出，纠正增益 G=-1.38 nats/token
  • 效应只出现在非法动作上、且不适用于所有模型；只描述失败而不写出动作字符串，则模型的偏好得以保留

为什么值得看：agent 当测试员或 NPC 时，harness 怎么写错误反馈会直接改变行为；这条结论说明「把失败原样贴回去」是个反模式。

中文摘要：当 LLM agent 的一步走错时，harness 通常会把这一步和错误信息写进对话记录再问一次。在工具调用里，这个记录会让小模型更倾向于重复失败动作。这篇工作检验同样的现象在游戏里是否成立，选的是推箱子、四子棋与黑白棋——在这些游戏里，一步棋可以因为非法而失败，也可以合法但导致输局，两种都能精确验证。作者用扰动正确着法的方式构造固定探针项，汇总 8 个指令微调模型（135M 到 1.7B）后，记录确实让失败动作更可能被重复（纠正增益 G=-1.38 nats/token），但这种反转是通过动作的表面形式起作用的：非法动作有、因输而失败的动作没有，而且并非每个模型都有。进一步分析显示，记录之后失败动作的对数概率几乎不再依赖它此前的概率（斜率 0.18）：模型原本不会下的着法变得更可能，贪心解码开始真的输出它们；而只说清失败原因、不写出动作字符串，则能保住模型原有的偏好。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-25

Feedback That Backfires in Games:
Do LLM Players Repeat the Move They Just Watched Fail?

Abstract

When an LLM agent’s move fails, the harness writes the move and the failure message into the transcript and asks again. In tool calling, this record makes small models more likely to repeat the failed action. We test whether the same holds in games (Sokoban, Connect Four, Othello), where a move can fail by being illegal or by being legal but losing, both verified exactly. On fixed probe items built by perturbing a correct move, the record backfires: pooled over 8 instruction-tuned models (135M–1.7B) it makes the failed move more likely (corrective gain G=-1.38 nats per token), through the move’s surface form, for illegal moves but not for losing ones, and not for every model. An exploratory analysis shows what sets the sign: after the record, the failed move’s log-probability barely depends on how likely it was before (slope 0.18). Moves the model would not have played become more likely, and greedy decoding starts to produce them; moves it was about to play become less likely, but greedy decoding still repeats 38% of them. A description of the failure that omits the move string keeps the model’s preference instead. Along the OLMo 2 1B post-training ladder the inversion is present in the base model and largely removed at the DPO stage. RAGEN’s default models invert in RAGEN’s own Sokoban format before any RL. A “do not repeat” instruction does nothing, a clean retry is the worst harness, and a decoder ban stops exact repeats but not illegal play. All measurements ran in float32 on a free Colab GPU, which first reproduced the original paper’s number.

1 Introduction

When an LLM plays a game through a harness, some of its moves fail. The harness then does what agent harnesses do with a failed tool call: it writes the move into the transcript, adds the referee’s message (Illegal move: that column is already full.) and asks for another move. The message is ground truth, and a player that reads it should not try the same move again. Yet LLM players are known to get stuck repeating rejected moves; in XiangqiBench, rejected moves make up a third of all calls in failed trials of one protocol [(Chai et al., 2026)].

In earlier work we measured what such a failure record does to a small model’s next action in tool calling and program repair [(Gumaan, 2026)]. Defining the corrective gainG of the record as the drop in log-probability of re-emitting the failed action, we found it negative for every instruction-tuned model we tested: the record made the failed call more likely, mostly because the call’s surface form was now in the context. This paper asks whether that holds for game play, where the setting allows three things tool calling did not.

First, a move can fail in two ways: it can be illegal, or legal but losing, and both can be verified exactly (a one-ply check in Connect Four, an exhaustive search for Sokoban deadlocks). Second, the same move can be written in different notations, which varies the surface form while holding the decision fixed. Third, a completion format lets us probe base models, so the measurement can follow one model through the stages of post-training. We use Sokoban, Connect Four and Othello, and ask four questions: RQ1, does the failure record backfire in games, for illegal and for losing moves? RQ2, which stage of training produces it, along the public OLMo 2 1B ladder from base to Instruct [(OLMo et al., 2024)]? RQ3, how do the default models of RAGEN [(Wang et al., 2025)], the standard multi-turn RL framework for these games, behave in RAGEN’s own prompt format? RQ4, do the original paper’s remedies transfer?

Findings.

  • •

    On fixed probe items built by perturbing a correct move, as in the original, the record backfires: pooled over 8 instruction-tuned models it makes the failed move more likely, G=-1.38 nats per token (Section 5), carried by the surface form (Δ_copy=1.34) rather than the failure message (Δₛₑₘ=0.04). The effect holds for illegal moves and not for losing ones, and it is not universal: 4 of the 8 models invert clearly, and Llama-3.2-1B does the opposite.

  • •

    The sign depends on how plausible the failed move was (Section 6). After the record, the failed move’s log-probability barely depends on its value before the attempt (slope 0.18 per nat). Moves the model would not have played become more likely; greedy decoding, which never produced them, produces 22% of them after the record. Moves the model was likely to play become less likely, but greedy decoding still repeats 38% of them. This flattening comes with writing the move: a description of the failure without the move string keeps the model’s preference.

  • •

    Along the OLMo 2 ladder the inversion is already present in the base model, and the DPO stage removes most of it (Section 7).

  • •

    In RAGEN’s format, both untrained default models invert on illegal Sokoban actions, with RAGEN’s own feedback as well (Section 9).

  • •

    A “do not repeat” instruction does nothing and a clean retry is the worst harness for repetition, as in tool calling. The runtime-generated description removes most of the inversion on average but not for every model; a decoder ban removes exact repeats but not illegal play (Section 10).

    • We could not run the RL half of RQ3 or a 7B scale check; everything reported here ran in float32 on a free Colab GPU after the GPU reproduced the original paper’s headline number (Section 4). Code, items, raw per-item records and run metadata are available at https://github.com/Esmail-ibraheem/feedback-that-backfires/tree/games.

    2 Related work

    The measurement this paper extends.

    [Gumaan (2026)] define the corrective gain and find it negative for six instruction-tuned models (135M–1.7B) in simulated tool calling and MBPP program repair, with most of the damage carried by the failed call’s surface form. Replacing the call with a runtime-generated description of the failure removed most of the inversion; an explicit “do not repeat” instruction and a clean retry did not. That study left three things open, and they define this one: whether the effect appears outside tool use, in a setting where a failure can be illegal or merely bad; which stage of training produces it; and whether training on the task, rather than editing the harness, removes it.

    LLMs that repeat themselves in decisions.

    [Schmied et al. (2025)] identify greediness, frequency bias and a knowing-doing gap in LLM agents on bandits and tic-tac-toe, and show that RL fine-tuning on self-generated rationales reduces but does not remove them. Their frequency bias is a tendency to repeat the action that is most frequent in the context; they do not condition on failure feedback, and they measure behaviour, not log-probabilities. We ask the narrower counterfactual question of what a failure record does to the probability of the failed move, which their setup does not separate from frequency.

    Multi-turn RL for LLM agents.

    RAGEN and its StarPO objective [(Wang et al., 2025)] train small models on Sokoban, FrozenLake and bandits and describe an “Echo Trap”, a training-time collapse into repetitive reasoning with falling reward variance. That is a property of the training dynamics; ours is an inference-time property of the transcript. We probe RAGEN’s default models in RAGEN’s own prompt format, which is where RL on the game would start; measuring the same models after training is left open.

    Games as agent benchmarks.

    XiangqiBench [(Chai et al., 2026)] evaluates frontier LLMs as closed-loop players; in its restricted-observation protocol, rejected moves make up a third of all calls in failed trials and about a fifteenth in successful ones. It reports the symptom without isolating a cause, and we use it as motivation only, since our experiments include no chess-family game. BALROG [(Paglieri et al., 2024)], TextArena [(Guertler et al., 2025)], SmartPlay [(Wu et al., 2023)] and GTBench [(Duan et al., 2024)] score policies across many games; like the agent benchmarks the original discussed, they are built to rank models, not to expose the counterfactual observations a decomposition needs.

    Feedback in the transcript.

    ReAct [(Yao et al., 2022)], Reflexion [(Shinn et al., 2023)] and Self-Refine [(Madaan et al., 2023)] append actions, observations or critiques to a growing transcript on the premise that feedback is informative. Work on context contamination [(Yang, 2026)] finds that retries in a context that still holds the failed attempt fail more often and prescribes clearing the context; the original showed that this clean retry was the worst harness under greedy decoding.

    Copying.

    Induction heads implement prefix matching and copying [(Olsson et al., 2022)], and repetition is self-reinforcing in open-ended generation [(Xu et al., 2022)]. If the inversion is copying, it should already be present in a base model, before any instruction tuning; the post-training ladder of OLMo 2 [(OLMo et al., 2024)], whose checkpoints differ only in post-training, makes that testable.

    Negative instructions.

    Naming something raises its probability even under an instruction to avoid it [(Castricato et al., 2024; Vrabcová et al., 2025)]; the original’s “do not repeat” result is an instance, and we test whether it transfers.

    3 Measuring the gain in games

    3.1 The quantity

    We use the original paper’s definitions unchanged [(Gumaan, 2026)]. Fix a decision point: a context C that ends with a position s and a request for a move, a move a^× that fails at s, the runtime’s observation o^×, and a correct move a^✓. The corrective gain of the failure record is

    G(a^×)=\logπ(a^×|C)-\logπ(a^×|C⊕(a^×,o^×)),

    		(1)

    where \logπ(a|c) is the summed token log-probability of the move string and ⊕ appends one agent turn and one runtime turn to the transcript. G>0 is what a harness is for: after the failure is recorded the failed move is less likely. G<0 is feedback inversion. With a valence-free observation o^∅ (Move received.) the gain splits into a surface-form and a semantic term,

    Δ_copy=\logπ(a^×|C⊕(a^×,o^∅))-\logπ(a^×|C),(2)
    Δₛₑₘ=\logπ(a^×|C⊕(a^×,o^×))-\logπ(a^×|C⊕(a^×,o^∅)),(3)

    with -G=Δ_copy+Δₛₑₘ by construction. Δ_copy is what merely having written the move does; Δₛₑₘ is what saying that it failed adds. A counterfactual success observation o^✓ (Move accepted.) gives the polarity contrast Δₚₒₗ=\logπ(a^×|C⊕(a^×,o^×))-\logπ(a^×|C⊕(a^×,o^✓)). We report every quantity in nats and, because move strings differ in length across notations, per token of the move (the original’s normalisation), and we add the original’s two readouts: the probability of the failed move normalised over a fixed four-move candidate set {a^×,a^✓,d₁,d₂}, and whether greedy decoding would reproduce a^× token for token, which is read off the argmax path of the teacher-forced pass at no extra cost.

    3.2 Two kinds of failure

    Games let us ask a question tool calling could not: does it matter why the move failed?

    Illegal moves.

    The runtime rejects the move and the position is unchanged: a full or non-existent column in Connect Four; an occupied square, a placement that flips nothing, or an off-board square in Othello; an unknown action, a walk into a wall, or a push against a wall or box in Sokoban.

    Legal but losing moves.

    The move is accepted and is a mistake, and the harness lets the agent retry from the restored position. The loss is verified exactly, never judged: in Connect Four a move is losing if, after it, the opponent has an immediate winning reply (checked by trying every reply; a move that wins at once is never labelled losing); in Sokoban a push is a deadlock if the room was solvable before it and is not after it (an exact breadth-first search over player and box positions). The message says so and that the position has been restored.

    3.3 Conditions

    All conditions of an item share the system prompt, the goal, the successful prefix and the position s, byte for byte. Every post-attempt condition re-shows the same position s after its message, so conditions differ in exactly one thing, the record of the attempt (Table 8 in the appendix lists them all). The core set is the original’s: pre (no attempt; also the clean-retry context), fail (the move and its failure message), succ, neut, and abstract (a runtime-generated description of the failure, with no move string). The remedy and control set adds fail_instr (a “do not repeat” instruction in the system prompt), fail_echo (the message also quotes the move), fail_k2 (the move fails twice), fail_other (a different failing move failed; the scored move was never written) and abstract_min (a bare failure marker). In the RAGEN format a further condition, fail_native, uses RAGEN’s own feedback: its invalid-action warning, or nothing at all after a blocked move.

    Two rules from the original keep the decomposition clean. First, the primary failure message never contains the move string (Illegal move: that column is already full., not column 4 is full); otherwise fail would hold the move twice and neut once, and occurrence count would leak into Δₛₑₘ. Naming the move is the separate fail_echo manipulation. Second, the abstract description contains no move string and no digit in any notation: its counter is an ordinal word ([first attempt failed: the chosen column was already full; that move is not repeatable]), because a digit would be the move in the numeric notations.

    3.4 Which failed move to probe

    The original fixed the failing action by a perturbation operator so that every model was probed on byte-identical items; sampling each model’s own mistakes would confound model with item difficulty. We keep that as the primary design and add two other sources, recording the source of every item. (b) Perturbation items apply an operator to the correct move: an adjacent or mirrored column; an adjacent, transposed or mirrored square; the opposite or a perpendicular direction, or a compass synonym (North for Up). An item is kept only if the result fails at s, and items are balanced over failure types. (c) Random items draw the failing move uniformly from every failing move expressible at s, a control. (a) Model-proposed items are the realistic case and are model-specific by construction: a proposal pass scores every move of the game, legal and illegal, at pre, and the item is the highest-ranked failing move among that model’s top three. They are analysed as a robustness check, never pooled with the shared items in a cross-model comparison.

    3.5 Mechanism test: notation

    If the inversion is carried by the move’s surface form, the way a move is written should change its size. Each game has three notations: a short code (4, d3, U), a verbose phrase (drop a disc into column 4, place a disc on column d, row 3, move the player one square up) and a plain zero-based index (3, 19, 0). Othello indices are zero-padded so that no move string is a prefix of another, which the unterminated scoring of the original requires. The board, rules and messages are otherwise identical across notations; only Connect Four’s column labels follow the notation. For every item and model we record the move’s length in tokens and its token overlap with the legal alternatives at s (the largest multiset overlap with any legal move), and regress the per-token gain on notation, length and overlap with random effects for position and model.

    3.6 Formats, and why there are three

    A post-training ladder starts at a base model, which has no chat template. We therefore probe every checkpoint of the ladder in one completion format: the rules, a blank line, then Referee: and Player: lines, ending in Player:, with the scored continuation ␣move, exactly as the move appears once written. Chat checkpoints are also probed in their own chat template, as a robustness check and for the cross-model study. RAGEN’s default models are also probed in the RAGEN format: RAGEN’s system prompt, Turn k: and State: blocks, Reward: lines, answers in tags, and our messages in RAGEN’s warning slot. Our tests extract RAGEN’s own prompt-building functions from its source and check that the messages we build are identical, so the models are probed on exactly the prompt shape that RL on the game would train them on. All three formats are rendered from one transcript representation, so a condition is defined once and cannot drift between formats.

    3.7 Scoring and statistics

    Scoring is the original’s code, vendored unchanged: teacher-forced, in float32, with a prefix key/value cache that crops to the longest common prefix of consecutive contexts and a finite-logits check at load and on every forward pass. On SmolLM2-135M a sample of items in each of the three formats is re-scored without the cache and must agree to 10⁻³ nats. Items that share a position share a context, so every interval is a 95% cluster bootstrap over positions (10,000 resamples), and contrasts between conditions, checkpoints or harnesses are paired item by item. The bootstrap is the original’s estimator; we compute it without its per-resample loop, from the same random draws, and a test checks that both give the same intervals.

    The new code reproduces the old number.

    Before any game was scored, the original paper’s 100 tool-calling items were run through the new pipeline on SmolLM2-135M, first on the original’s laptop CPU and then on the GPU used for every result here. The CPU run returns G=-23.92 nats, against −23.92 in the original, with every stored log-probability reproduced to within 9.5×10⁻⁵ nats; the GPU run returns −23.92, within 3.5×10⁻⁴ nats of the CPU rows.

    4 Experimental setup

    4.1 Games

    We use three games and no others; none involves chance or a chess-family piece set.

    Sokoban.

    Rooms come from RAGEN’s own generator [(Wang et al., 2025)], vendored unchanged, with its SimpleSokoban parameters: 6×6, one box, text grid. Step semantics and rewards follow gym-sokoban [(Schrader, 2018)], which RAGEN wraps. The agent is shown the moves it has made so far (at most 3), so a probe context starts at the room’s first turn, as a RAGEN transcript does. Failure types: unknown action, walk into a wall, push against a wall or box (illegal), and deadlock push (losing).

    Connect Four

    (6×7). Positions are taken from seeded self-play between random and one-ply-greedy players. The context shows the position two agent turns earlier and the two most recent agent moves with the opponent’s replies. Failure types: full column and non-existent column (illegal), and losing move (legal; the opponent can win at once).

    Othello

    (8×8). Positions from seeded self-play as above, with the same two-turn window; windows that contain a pass are skipped so that turns alternate. Failure types: occupied square, placement that flips nothing, off-board square (all illegal). We do not label losing moves in Othello.

    4.2 Items

    Each game contributes one decision point per position: 100 for Sokoban, 80 for Connect Four and 80 for Othello. Perturbation items are balanced over failure types (20 per type) and 20 random-source items are added per game; Appendix E gives the counts by failure type, source and operator. A run scores a prefix of one fixed order of the positions that cycles over failure types: 40 positions per game for the RQ1 models up to 0.6B and for the remedy study, 30 for the four larger RQ1 models, 20 for each OLMo 2 checkpoint, and 60 Sokoban positions in the RAGEN format. These sample sizes were set for a laptop CPU (Appendix A). A smaller sample is a prefix of a larger one, so a model scored on fewer positions sees a subset of the same items. Every decision point is rendered in every notation, so the notation contrast is within position. All messages are fixed in a versioned file (Appendix C). A check found that the failed move is not always new to the context: in 15/80 of the Connect Four and 24/100 of the Sokoban decision points the failed move equals one of the agent’s own earlier moves (in Sokoban, the deadlock push often continues the previous direction). Tool calls in the original never had this property; we record it per item and use it as a covariate.

    4.3 Models

    Instruction-tuned models (RQ1).

    The original paper’s models for continuity, plus two: SmolLM2-135M, SmolLM2-360M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen3-0.6B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B, Qwen3-1.7B, each probed in its own chat template [(Allal et al., 2025; Qwen et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024)].

    The OLMo 2 1B post-training ladder (RQ2).

    The five public checkpoints of allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B: base, SFT, DPO, RLVR and the released Instruct model [(OLMo et al., 2024)], which follow the Tulu 3 recipe [(Lambert et al., 2024)]. All five share one tokenizer and one architecture and differ only in post-training, which is what makes the stage comparison interpretable. Every checkpoint is probed in the completion format, the four post-trained ones also in their chat template.

    The RAGEN format (RQ3).

    Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, RAGEN’s default models and members of the RQ1 set, probed on Sokoban in RAGEN’s own SimpleSokoban prompt, in no-think mode with one action per turn, the setting in which RAGEN trains them [(Wang et al., 2025)]. These are the untrained starting points of RL on the game. Training them with StarPO and probing again, which our proposal planned as the second half of RQ3, needed more GPU time than we had (Section 12).

    Every checkpoint is pinned to a Hugging Face revision (Table 7 in the appendix).

    4.4 Hardware and numerics

    All reported scoring and free play ran on one Tesla T4 in Google Colab’s free tier, in float32 with TF32 matrix multiplication disabled, under PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130 and Transformers 4.56.1, the Transformers version of the original run of record. Items were built, and the pipeline was developed and first validated, on the original paper’s laptop (Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-6820HQ CPU @ 2.70GHz, PyTorch 2.4.0+cpu). Before any game was scored, the GPU had to reproduce the original paper’s number (Section 3.7; tolerance 10⁻² nats per log-probability) and cached and uncached scoring had to agree on it in all three formats. A small CPU pilot run during development is not used for any reported number, so every result in this paper comes from one device.

    5 RQ1: does the failure record backfire in games?

    Table 1 gives the corrective gain of a failure record for each instruction-tuned model, per game and pooled over the three games, on the shared items. Pooled over the 8 models, the record raises the probability of the move that just failed: G=-1.38 \scriptsize [\textminus1.85, \textminus0.95] nats per move token, negative on 61% of the 840 (model, item) pairs. On a probability scale, the normalised probability of the failed move over the four-move candidate set rises from 0.24 before the attempt to 0.35 after it, and greedy decoding reproduces the failed move token for token on 23% of items after the failure, against 12% before it.

    As in tool calling, the increase is carried by the surface form. Writing the move into the transcript with a valence-free acknowledgement accounts for Δ_copy=+1.34 \scriptsize [+0.95, +1.76] nats per token; replacing that acknowledgement with the failure message changes the failed move’s log-probability by a further Δₛₑₘ=+0.04 \scriptsize [\textminus0.10, +0.17], an interval that includes zero (Figure 1).

    Not every model.

    The pooled number hides a spread. 4 of the 8 models invert with intervals entirely below zero (SmolLM2-135M, SmolLM2-360M, Qwen3-0.6B and SmolLM2-1.7B), and 3 more have point estimates below zero but intervals that include it (Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen3-1.7B). Llama-3.2-1B goes the other way: its gain is positive, +0.66  [+0.26, +1.05], and its copy term is negative, −0.52  [−0.95, −0.08]. For this model, seeing its own move in the transcript makes that move less likely. The pooled mean is also strongly influenced by Qwen3-0.6B, whose inversion (−5.45  [−6.08, −4.85]) is the largest we measured. In the original’s tool-calling study every model inverted; in games, 7 of the 8 point estimates are below zero.

    Illegal versus losing moves.

    Figure 2 and Table 2 separate the two kinds of failure. Illegal moves invert clearly: G=-1.61 \scriptsize [\textminus2.16, \textminus1.11] nats per token, negative on 66% of items, with a copy term of +1.52  [+1.07, +2.01]. Legal but losing moves invert much less, G=-0.39 \scriptsize [\textminus0.90, +0.06] (23 positions), an interval that includes zero. Their copy term is still positive (+0.59  [+0.10, +1.09]), but greedy decoding repeats a losing move less often after the failure (21%) than before it (26%). By game, losing moves in Connect Four give −0.84  [−1.48, −0.22] and deadlock pushes in Sokoban +0.23  [−0.26, +0.60].

    The model’s own mistakes go the other way.

    On the realistic items, where the failed move is the highest-ranked failing move among the model’s own top three, the sign flips: G=+1.34 \scriptsize [+1.18, +1.49] nats per token (759 items), negative on only 26%. These items differ between models by construction and are never pooled with the shared ones, but the difference is too large to be a detail. Section 6 shows what separates the two kinds of item: how plausible the failed move was before the attempt.

    Answer.

    H1 holds on the fixed items: a recorded illegal move makes that move more likely, through its surface form, for most but not all of the models. H2 does not hold: for legal but losing moves the pooled gain is indistinguishable from zero. On the models’ own likely mistakes the record lowers the failed move’s probability instead.

    6 What sets the sign: the record flattens the model’s preference

    This analysis was not part of our plan. We report it because it explains the opposite signs of Section 5, and because it changes what the inversion means for an agent.

    Call a failed move’s log-probability before the attempt, \logπ(a^×|C), its prior. If a failure record shifted every failed move by the same amount, the log-probability after the record would follow the prior with slope one. It does not (Figure 3, left). Over all 2079 RQ1 items, shared and model-proposed, the per-token log-probability of the failed move after the verbatim failure record has a slope of +0.18  [+0.14, +0.21] on its prior; per model the slope lies between 0.02 and 0.35. After the record, how likely the model is to repeat a move hardly depends on how much it wanted the move before. The valence-free record does nearly the same (slope +0.24  [+0.19, +0.28]), so the flattening comes with writing the move into the transcript, not with the failure message. The abstract description, which reports the same failure without the move string, keeps most of the preference (+0.75  [+0.72, +0.78]).

    Flattening has opposite consequences at the two ends of the prior (Figure 3, right).

  • •

    Moves the model would not have played (prior below 1%, 652 items) become more likely: G=-2.62 \scriptsize [\textminus3.08, \textminus2.16] nats per token. Greedy decoding never produced them before the attempt (0%); after the verbatim record it produces them on 22% of items, after the abstract description on 0%.

  • •

    Moves the model was likely to play (prior above 30%, 469 items) become less likely: G=+1.68 \scriptsize [+1.46, +1.91]. Greedy repetition falls from 91% to 38% after the verbatim record, but only to 60% after the abstract description.

    • The fixed items of the original design lean towards the first kind. A perturbed or random failing move is usually one the model would not propose: 48% of the shared items have a prior below 1% and 10% one above 30%, against 2% and 44% of the model-proposed items. That is why the fixed items invert. A failure in free play is of the second kind by construction, since the agent wrote the move because it was likely. On the model-proposed items, greedy decoding repeats the failed move on 32% of items after the verbatim record, against 66% before the attempt and 36% after the abstract description.

    Two qualifications. First, G contains the prior, so a slope below one is the same statement as G growing with the prior, and any change of context unrelated to the move would weaken the dependence on the prior to some degree. The informative comparison is therefore between records that differ in one thing: writing the move flattens the preference, describing the failure without it does not. Second, the flattening is format-dependent. In the completion format of RQ2 the slope is larger (+0.45  [+0.37, +0.55] for the OLMo 2 base model), in RAGEN’s format of RQ3 smaller (+0.09  [+0.04, +0.13]).

    7 RQ2: which training stage?

    The five OLMo 2 1B checkpoints differ only in post-training, and all are probed on the same items in one completion format (Table 3, Figure 4). Each stage is compared with the one before it item by item, so the contrasts below are paired over the same 180 (item, notation) pairs from 60 positions.

    The base model already inverts.

    Before any post-training, the failure record raises the failed move’s probability: G=-0.52 \scriptsize [\textminus0.70, \textminus0.34] nats per token, negative on 82% of items. The surface form carries it (Δ_copy=+0.49 \scriptsize [+0.31, +0.67]); the failure message adds almost nothing (Δₛₑₘ=+0.03 \scriptsize [+0.02, +0.05]). H4 holds: the inversion does not need instruction tuning, which fits a copying mechanism learned in pretraining.

    Preference tuning is where it shrinks.

    Supervised fine-tuning changes the gain little (paired change +0.10  [−0.00, +0.20]), although it already lowers the copy term (−0.21  [−0.32, −0.09]). The DPO stage is the largest step: the gain rises by +0.30  [+0.21, +0.38] nats per token, and at DPO it is -0.12 \scriptsize [\textminus0.39, +0.15], an interval that includes zero. The copy term falls by −0.51  [−0.59, −0.42] and is no longer positive (−0.23  [−0.51, +0.05]): after DPO, having written a move with a neutral acknowledgement no longer makes it more likely. The semantic term moves the other way, by +0.21  [+0.18, +0.24], to +0.35  [+0.30, +0.39]. Relative to a neutral acknowledgement, being told that the move failed now makes it more likely, which keeps the gain from turning clearly positive. RLVR (−0.03  [−0.06, −0.00]) and the final Instruct model (−0.01  [−0.03, +0.01]) change little after that. In their own chat template the post-trained checkpoints show the same step from SFT to DPO (+0.46  [+0.33, +0.59]).

    Answer.

    Within this ladder, the inversion comes from the base model, and preference tuning, not supervised fine-tuning or RL with verifiable rewards, is the stage that removes most of it. One ladder at one scale cannot say whether this is a property of DPO or of this recipe’s preference data.

    8 Mechanism test: does the notation matter?

    If the inversion is carried by the move’s surface form, the way a move is written should change its size (H3: more inversion for longer moves and for moves that share more tokens with the legal alternatives). Notation varies within position in two places: the OLMo 2 ladder, where every item is probed in all three notations, and two of the RQ1 models (SmolLM2-360M and Qwen2.5-0.5B), which we also probed in the verbose and index notations. Table 4 gives the mixed-effects regressions.

    The ladder.

    Longer moves invert more per token (-0.36 (SE 0.11, p<0.001) per standard deviation of length), in line with H3. The index notation inverts slightly more than the short one (-0.19 (SE 0.08, p=0.015)), the verbose one, if anything, less (+0.48 (SE 0.25, p=0.056)). Token overlap with a legal move goes against H3: moves that share more tokens with a legal alternative invert less (+0.86 (SE 0.17, p<0.001)).

    The chat models.

    With notation varied on two models only, neither notation contrast is distinguishable from zero (verbose -0.16 (SE 0.78, p=0.835), index -0.06 (SE 0.20, p=0.756)) and neither is length (-0.03 (SE 0.28, p=0.908)); overlap again goes against H3 (+1.12 (SE 0.36, p=0.002)).

    Controlling for the prior.

    Section 6 showed that the failed move’s prior largely sets the sign of G. Notation, length and overlap all change the prior, so we add it as a covariate (the “+ prior” columns). The prior then dominates (+0.81 (SE 0.02, p<0.001) in the ladder, +0.92 (SE 0.01, p<0.001) in the chat models; it also enters G itself), and several coefficients change sign: overlap now increases the inversion in the ladder (-0.55 (SE 0.11, p<0.001)), as H3 predicted, and the verbose notation inverts much more in the chat models (-2.12 (SE 0.34, p<0.001)).

    Answer.

    The notation changes the size of the inversion, and longer moves invert more per token, but the direction of the other effects depends on whether the prior is held fixed. Given equally plausible moves, overlap with a legal move increases the inversion, as a copying account predicts; across moves as they come, overlap goes with plausibility and the net effect is the opposite. We read H3 as supported for length and only conditionally for overlap.

    9 RQ3: the RAGEN format, before RL
